Without law or control.
example: The system is economically inefficient and politically anarchic.
etymology: From anarchy + -ic.

definition: A revolutionary anarchist doctrine that advocates the abolition of both the state and private ownership of the means of production.
etymology: From anarcho- + collectivism.

definition: A political and social system that no longer governs (especially the system that existed in France before the French Revolution).
A moderately slow tempo (a walking pace).
etymology: Borrowed from Italian andante.

definition: A dark grey volcanic rock.
etymology: From Andes + -ite.

definition: Male sex hormone that is produced in the testes and responsible for typical male sexual characteristics.
etymology: From andro- + -gen.

definition: Relating to or exhibiting both female and male sex organs but with a predominantly female appearance.
example: Nicknames like Pat, Sam, and Chris are androgynous, used by both men and women.
etymology: From Latin androgynus (“man-woman, hermaphrodite”), from Ancient Greek ἀνδρόγῠνος (andrógŭnos), from ἀνήρ (anḗr, “man”) + γῠνή (gŭnḗ, “woman”) + -ος (-os, “-ous”, adjectival suffix), equivalent to andro- + gyno- + -ous.

definition: Showing characteristics of both sexes.
etymology: From andro- + -gyny. See androgynous.

definition: Hypoxia resulting from a decreased concentration of hemoglobin.
A drug that is designed to prevent the growth of blood vessels that nourish tumors.
An operation to repair a damaged blood vessel or unblock a coronary artery.
etymology: From angio- + -plasty.

definition: Any of several vasoconstrictor substances (trade name Hypertensin) that cause narrowing of blood vessels.
etymology: From angio- + (hyper)tens(ion) + -in. Compare also the morphologic parallels of vasopressin.

definition: A compound formed from one or more other compounds in a reaction resulting in removal of water.
etymology: From an- + hydride. Compare anhydrous and -ide.

definition: Without water; especially without water of crystallization.
etymology: From an- + Ancient Greek ὕδωρ (húdōr, “water”) + -ous.

definition: Oily poisonous liquid amine obtained from nitrobenzene and used to make dyes and plastics and medicines.
Any of many dyes made from aniline.
Oily poisonous liquid amine obtained from nitrobenzene and used to make dyes and plastics and medicines.
Of or pertaining to animalism.
etymology: From animal + -istic.

definition: The construction of robots to look like animals (developed for Disneyland).
etymology: Blend of animation + electronics, from the Disney trademark "Audio-Animatronics". Compare -tronics.

definition: Of or relating to anions.
etymology: From anion + -ic.

definition: A compound characterized by an active anion.
An organic compound that is widely used as a flavoring substance.
Not invariant with respect to direction.
example: Anisotropic crystals.
etymology: From an- + isotropic.

definition: The property of being anisotropic; having a different value when measured in different directions.
example: Velvet exhibits anisotropy when rotated about its geometric normal.
etymology: From an- + isotropy.

definition: A shoe for a child or woman that has a strap around the ankle.
etymology: From ankle + -et, based on bracelet.

definition: Kill in large numbers.
example: An atom bomb can annihilate a whole city.
etymology: Borrowed from Latin annihilātus, perfect passive participle of annihilō (“to reduce to nothing”) (see -ate (verb-forming suffix)), from ad (“to”) + nihil (“nothing”) + -ō (verb-forming suffix). See also an-.

definition: Wreaking or capable of wreaking complete destruction.
example: Possessing annihilative power.

definition: Add explanatory notes to or supply with critical comments.
example: The scholar annotated the early edition of a famous novel.
etymology: From Latin annotātus, past participle of annotāre (an alternative form of adnotāre), from ad- (“to”) + notāre (“to mark, note”). By surface analysis, an- + note + -ate.

definition: Declare invalid.
example: The contract was annulled.
etymology: From Middle English annullen, from Old French anuller, from Latin annullō (“annihilate, annul”), from ad (“to”) + nūllus (“none, not any”).

definition: A toroidal shape.
Choose by or as if by divine intervention.
example: She was anointed the head of the Christian fundamentalist group.
etymology: From Middle English enointen, anointen, borrowed from Old French enoint, past participle of enoindre (“to anoint”). Doublet of inunct.

definition: Relating to or marked by a severe deficiency of oxygen in tissues or organs.
Antbirds superficially resembling shrikes.
Toothless mammal of southern Africa and Asia having a body covered with horny scales and a long snout for feeding on ants and termites.
etymology: From ant + eater, from their typical diet.

definition: Occurring or existing before birth.
example: Antenatal care.
etymology: From Latin ante (“before”) + nātālis (“natal”), from nāscor (“to be born”), equivalent to ante- + natal.

definition: In an anterior direction.
etymology: From anterior + -ly.

definition: The part of the stamen that contains pollen; usually borne on a stalk.
etymology: From French anthère, from Ancient Greek ἀνθηρός (anthērós, “flowery, blooming”), from ἄνθος (ánthos, “a flower”).

definition: Not in favor of (an action or proposal etc.).
etymology: Conversion of the prefix anti- to an adjective.

definition: Opposition to traditionalism.
Designed for defense from a surface position against air attack.
Firing at enemy aircraft.
Artillery designed to shoot upward at airplanes.
A chemical substance derivable from a mold or bacterium that can kill microorganisms and cure bacterial infections.
example: When antibiotics were first discovered they were called wonder drugs.

definition: Ludicrously odd.
example: Hamlet's assumed antic disposition.
etymology: Probably from Italian antico (“ancient”), used to describe ancient wall paintings from classical times, from Latin antiquus (“venerable”). See also Italian grottesco (“grotesque”). Doublet of antique.

definition: Used in the treatment of cancer.
example: Anticancer drug.
etymology: From anti- + cancer.

definition: In anticipation.
example: The children were all wearing anticipatory grins as the cake was served.
etymology: From anticipate + -ory.

definition: A breach of contract committed prior to the time of required performance.
Medicine that prevents or retards the clotting of blood.
etymology: From anti- + coagulant.

definition: A protagonist who lacks the characteristics that would make them a hero (or her a heroine).
etymology: From anti- + hero.

definition: A medicine used to treat allergies and hypersensitive reactions and colds; works by counteracting the effects of histamine on a receptor site.
etymology: From anti- + histamine.

definition: An expert or collector of antiquities.
etymology: From Latin antīquārius (“pertaining to antiquity, one fond of or employed in antiquities”), from antīquus (“ancient”) + -ārius; equivalent to antique + -ary.

definition: Made in or typical of earlier times and valued for its age.
example: The beautiful antique French furniture.
etymology: Borrowed from French antique (“ancient, old”), from Latin antiquus (“former, earlier, ancient, old”), from ante (“before”); see ante-. Doublet of antic.

definition: Designed for defense against armored vehicles.
example: A TOW missile is an antitank weapon capable of killing everyone in a tank from great distance.
etymology: From anti- + tank.

definition: The excretory opening at the end of the alimentary canal.
etymology: Either from Middle French anus or Latin ānus (“ring, anus”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₁eh₂nos (“ring”). First attested in 1658. See also anal, annular, annelid.

definition: (poetic, literary) quickly.
example: Construction of the new offices is proceeding apace.
etymology: From Middle English apās (“step by step, slowly; quickly, rapidly; at once, promptly”), from Old French à pas (“at a quick pace”).

definition: Any of various primates with short tails or no tail at all.
etymology: Clipping of apeshit (“ape-shit (crazy)”).

definition: Alcoholic beverage taken before a meal as an appetizer.
Any of various small plant-sucking insects.
etymology: From New Latin aphis (plural aphides), coined by Swedish botanist Carolus Linnaeus in 1758. His inspiration for the name remains unclear;

definition: Carnivorous larva of lacewing flies.
A short pithy instructive saying.
Stimulating sexual desire.
etymology: Borrowed from Ancient Greek ἀφροδισιακός (aphrodisiakós, “venereal”), from Ἀφροδίσιος (Aphrodísios, “pertaining to Aphrodite”).

definition: Great coolness and composure under strain.
example: His nonchalance and aplomb during hard times have always been his best character trait.
etymology: Unadapted borrowing from French aplomb (“plumb line”).

definition: A formal written defense of something you believe in strongly.
etymology: Borrowed from Ancient Greek ἀπολογία (apología, “speech in defense of a position”). Doublet of apology.

definition: Pertaining to or characteristic of apoplexy.
example: Apoplectic seizure.
etymology: From French apoplectique, from Late Latin apoplēcticus, from Ancient Greek ἀποπληκτικός (apoplēktikós), from ἀπόπληκτος (apóplēktos), from ἀποπλήσσω (apoplḗssō), from ἀπό (apó, “of, from”) + πλήσσω (plḗssō, “I strike”).

definition: A type of cell death in which the cell uses specialized cellular machinery to kill itself; a cell suicide mechanism that enables metazoans to control cell number and eliminate cells that threaten the animal's survival.
etymology: From Ancient Greek ἀπόπτωσις (apóptōsis, “a falling off”), from ἀπό (apó, “away from”) + πτῶσις (ptôsis, “falling”).

definition: Model of excellence or perfection of a kind; one having no equal.
example: The turn of the century saw the apotheosis of digital technology.

definition: To an appalling extent.
example: The prisoners were appallingly thin.
etymology: From appalling + -ly.

definition: Surgical removal of the vermiform appendix.
etymology: From appendix + -ectomy.

definition: Bright green aphid; feeds on and causes curling of apple leaves.
A disease of apple trees.
Fritter containing sliced apple.
Distilled from hard cider.
etymology: From apple + jack, referring to the increase in alcohol concentration due to freeze distillation.

definition: A Java application; an application program that uses the client's web browser to provide a user interface.
etymology: From app + -let, but perhaps also influenced by Apple (the term originated in AppleScript).

definition: A decorative design made of one material sewn over another.
etymology: Borrowed from French appliqué.

definition: Given out in portions.
The act of distributing by allotting or apportioning; distribution according to a plan.
example: The apportionment of seats in the House of Representatives is based on the relative population of each state.
etymology: From apportion + -ment.

definition: To a noticeable degree.
example: The weather was appreciably colder.
etymology: From appreciable + -ly.

definition: Official approval.
In an approving manner.
example: She nodded approvingly.
etymology: From approving + -ly.

definition: A domed or vaulted recess or projection on a building especially the east end of a church; usually contains the altar.
example: Meronyms: ambulatory, apse chapels.
etymology: From Latin apsis, hapsis, from Ancient Greek ἁψίς (hapsís, “arch, vault”), from ἅπτω (háptō, “to bind, join”).

definition: Acid used especially in the production of fertilizers and explosives and rocket fuels.
etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin aqua fortis (literally “strong water”).

definition: A yellow fuming corrosive mixture of nitric and hydrochloric acid that dissolves metals (including gold).
etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin aqua rēgia (literally “royal water”), so named because it is one of the few solvents capable of dissolving noble metals.

definition: Position in which the dancer has one leg raised behind and arms outstretched in a conventional pose.
etymology: Borrowed from French arabesque, from Italian arabesco, from arabo (“Arab”). By surface analysis, Arab + -esque.

definition: Air-breathing arthropods characterized by simple eyes and four pairs of legs.
etymology: From international scientific vocabulary, from French arachnide (1809, Lamarck), from New Latin, from Ancient Greek ἀράχνη (arákhnē, “spider”) with the suffix -id. By surface analysis, arachn- + -id.

definition: Any of various strong liquors distilled from the fermented sap of toddy palms or from fermented molasses.
example: They use perfume freely, paint their eyes with kohl, and are constantly polishing their teeth with twigs of green arak-wood.
etymology: From Arabic عَرَق (ʕaraq, “sweat”), a reference to the condensate in the distillation process. Doublet of ara, raki, and rakija.

definition: Relating to or resulting from arbitration.
example: The arbitral adjustment of the controversy.
etymology: From French arbitral, from Latin arbitrālis, from arbiter.

definition: Act between parties with a view to reconciling differences.
example: To arbitrate a disputed case.
etymology: From Latin arbitratus, past participle of arbitrari (“to be a witness, act as umpire”), from arbiter (“umpire”); see arbiter.

definition: Of or relating to or formed by trees.
example: An arborous roof.
etymology: From Latin arboreus (“tree-like”) + -al, mid-17th century.

definition: A framework that supports climbing plants.
etymology: From Middle English arbere, arber, an alteration of herber, erber (“pleasure garden; herb garden”) influenced by Latin arbor (“tree”).

definition: (used with regard to idealized country life) idyllically rustic.
example: A country life of arcadian contentment.
etymology: From arcade + -ian.

definition: An anthropologist who studies prehistoric people and their culture.
In an ardent manner.
etymology: From Middle English ardauntly; equivalent to ardent + -ly.

definition: A feeling of strong eagerness (usually in favor of a person or cause).
example: They were imbued with a revolutionary ardor.
etymology: From Middle English ardour, ardowr, ardure, from Anglo-Norman ardour, from Old French ardur, from Latin ardor, from ardere (“to burn”).

definition: A feeling of strong eagerness (usually in favor of a person or cause).
Of or relating to or involving an area.
example: Areal flood warning.
etymology: Borrowed from Latin āreālis; by surface analysis, area + -al. Cognate with English areolar. False cognates include English arena, adrenal, anear.

definition: Small space in a tissue or body part such as the area between veins on a leaf or an insect's wing.
etymology: Borrowed from Latin āreola (“small vacant space, garden”), diminutive of ārea. Doublet of areole.

definition: Of lustrous grey; covered with or tinged with the color of silver.
etymology: From Middle English argent, from Norman argent m (“silver”), from Latin argentum n (“white money, silver”).

definition: Arrangement of aerial photographs forming a composite picture.
Bristlelike process near the tip of the antenna of certain flies.
etymology: From New Latin arista. Doublet of arête.

definition: Money given by a buyer to a seller to bind a contract.
Weaponry used by military or naval force.
etymology: From Latin armāmentum, from armō (“to arm”).

definition: Chair with a support on each side for arms.
example: I collapsed into an armchair.
etymology: From arm + chair.

definition: The act of equipping with weapons in preparation for war.
etymology: Inherited from Middle English armyng.

definition: The hollow under the arm where it is joined to the shoulder.
example: They were up to their armpits in water.
etymology: From Middle English armpitt, arme-pitt, armput, equivalent to arm + pit. (something unpleasant): Presumably a reference to underarm body odor.

definition: A support for the arm.
etymology: From arm + rest.

definition: Weapons considered collectively.
example: The arms of England are: gules, three lions passant guardant or.
etymology: From Middle English armes, from Old French armes, from Latin arma (“weapons”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₂er-mo-, a suffixed form of *h₂er- (“to fit together”), hence ultimately cognate with etymology 2.

definition: An industry that manufacturers weapons of war.
Reach a destination; arrive by movement or progress.
example: She arrived home at 7 o'clock.
etymology: From Middle English arriven, ariven, from Old French ariver, from Early Medieval Latin adrīpāre (“to land, come ashore”), derived from Latin rīpa (“shore, river-bank”). Displaced native oncome, tocome.

definition: In an arrogant manner.
etymology: From arrogant + -ly.

definition: An aquatic plant of the genus Peltandra; North America.
etymology: Because its leaves resemble arrowheads.

definition: All the weapons and equipment that a country has.
example: He arrived with a large arsenal of cleansers and tools, and got right to work.
etymology: From Italian arsenale, from Arabic دَار الصِّنَاعَة (dār aṣ-ṣināʕa, “manufacturing shop”), from دَار (dār) + صِنَاعَة (ṣināʕa).

definition: A white powdered poisonous trioxide of arsenic; used in manufacturing glass and as a pesticide (rat poison) and weed killer.
Any of various composite shrubs or herbs of the genus Artemisia having aromatic green or greyish foliage.
etymology: From taxonomic name Artemisia, from Latin artemisia, from Ancient Greek ἀρτεμισία (artemisía), from Ἄρτεμις (Ártemis, “Artemis, the goddess”).

definition: (of water) rising to the surface under internal hydrostatic pressure.
example: An artesian well.
etymology: From French puits artésien (“artesian well”), from the former province of Artois, where the technique of artesian wells was elaborated by monks in the 12th century.

definition: A well drilled through impermeable strata into strata that receive water from a higher altitude so there is pressure to force the water to flow upward.
Of or pertaining to arthritis.
example: Her arthritic wrists bothered her most in the winter.
etymology: From Latin arthriticus (“gouty, arthritic”), from Ancient Greek.

definition: Invertebrate having jointed limbs and a segmented body with an exoskeleton made of chitin.
etymology: From New Latin Arthropoda, from Ancient Greek ἄρθρον (árthron, “joint”) + πούς (poús, “foot”), equivalent to arthro- + -pod.

definition: Any of the arthropods.
Nonfictional prose forming an independent part of a publication.
example: An article of clothing.

definition: Someone who is the first to think of or make something.
etymology: From Middle English artificer, from Middle French artificier, from Latin artificiarius.

definition: Relating to or characteristic of art or artists.
example: His artistic background.
etymology: Borrowed from French artistique, from artiste + -ique. By surface analysis, artist + -ic.

definition: Showily imitative of art or artists.
etymology: From art + -y.

definition: Erect European annual often grown as a salad crop to be harvested when young and tender.
etymology: Probably from a Southern Italian dialect word equivalent to Standard Italian rucola, whence also, since c. 1967, English rucola. Also cognate to rocket (“plant”), eruca, roquette.

definition: Starch resembling sago that is obtained from cuckoopint root.
etymology: From the botanical name Arum, from Latin arum, from Ancient Greek ἄρον (áron).

definition: Anthurium; calla lily; jack-in-the-pulpit; philodendron.
South African plant widely cultivated for its showy pure white spathe and yellow spadix.
The doctrine that through renunciation of worldly pleasures it is possible to achieve a high spiritual or intellectual state.
A vitamin found in fresh fruits (especially citrus fruits) and vegetables; prevents scurvy.
Not having or involving sex.
example: An asexual spore.

definition: Anemic looking from illness or emotion.
example: A face turned ashen.
etymology: From Middle English aschen, asshen, from Old English æsċen (“made of ashwood”), equivalent to ash (“ash tree”) + -en (“made or consisting of”). Cognate with Scots aishen (“ashen”).

definition: An artificial sweetener made from aspartic acid; used as a calorie-free sweetener.
etymology: Commercial name, from aspartic. The -ame is perhaps because aspartame is an amide. Compare aspartamine.

definition: A condition in which insufficient or no oxygen and carbon dioxide are exchanged on a ventilatory basis; caused by choking or drowning or electric shock or poison gas.
example: Asphyxia may result from choking, drowning, electric shock, or injury.
etymology: Learned borrowing from New Latin asphyxia, itself borrowed from Ancient Greek ἀσφυξία (asphuxía, “stopping of the pulse”).

definition: Inflammation of the lungs caused by inhaling or choking on vomitus; may occur during unconsciousness (anesthesia or drunkenness or seizure or cardiac arrest).
A murderer (especially one who kills a prominent political figure) who kills by a surprise attack and often is hired to do the deed.
example: His assassins were hunted down like animals.
etymology: From either French assassin or Italian assassino, from Arabic أَسَاسِيِّين (ʔasāsiyyīn, “people who are faithful to the foundation [of the faith]”) and the folkloric etymology Arabic حَشَّاشِين (ḥaššāšīn, “hashish users;

definition: Murder; especially of socially prominent persons.
example: Anwar Sadat was assassinated because many people did not like his peace politics with Israel.
etymology: From assassin + -ate, after Middle French assassiner.

definition: Murdered by surprise attack for political reasons.
example: The 20th century has seen too many assassinated leaders.

definition: Anything of material value or usefulness that is owned by a person or company.
example: His assets are much greater than his liabilities.
etymology: From Anglo-Norman asetz, from Old French assez (“enough”). Originally singular, with the meaning "enough to meet liabilities"; later reanalyzed as a plural form.

definition: With care and persistence.
example: She worked assiduously on the senior thesis.
etymology: From assiduous + -ly.

definition: Capable of taking (gas, light, or liquids) into a solution.
example: An assimilative substance.

definition: Suicide of a terminally ill person that involves an assistant who serves to make dying as painless and dignified as possible.
The county courts of England (replaced in 1971 by Crown courts).
Aphasia in which the lesion is assumed to be in the association tracts connecting the various language centers in the brain; patient's have difficulty repeating a sentence just heard.
(ophthalmology) impaired eyesight resulting usually from irregular conformation of the cornea; common in nearsighted people.
etymology: From a- (negative prefix) + stem of Ancient Greek στίγμα (stígma, “mark, point”) + -ism. Coined by English polymath William Whewell in 1846.

definition: Affect with wonder.
Affect with wonder.
example: 1637, John Milton, Comus, London: Humphrey Robinson, p. 8, These thoughts may startle well, but not astound The vertuous mind […].
etymology: From Middle English astouned, astoned, astuned, past participle of astounen, astonen, astunen (“to astonish”). More at astonish.

definition: The theory and practice of navigation through air or space.
etymology: From French astronautique (“astronautics”) + English -ics. By surface analysis, astro- (“space”) + nautics (“navigation”).

definition: Toward an asymptote.
example: It grew asymptotically.
etymology: From asymptotic + -ally.

definition: In a dispute or confrontation.
example: Sam and his parents were at loggerheads over the question of car privileges.
etymology: Uncertain; possibly from the use of a loggerhead (“metal tool consisting of a long rod with a bulbous end”) as a weapon during a fight.

definition: Dead.
Essential oil or perfume obtained from flowers.
Rejecting any belief in gods.
etymology: From atheist + -ic.

definition: A support for the genitals worn by men engaging in strenuous exercise.
A nuclear weapon in which enormous energy is released by nuclear fission (splitting the nuclei of a heavy element like uranium 235 or plutonium 239).
A scientific instrument that increases the kinetic energy of charged particles.
etymology: So called because it causes atoms to collide at high speeds.

definition: Bomb with atomic weapons.
A nuclear weapon in which enormous energy is released by nuclear fission (splitting the nuclei of a heavy element like uranium 235 or plutonium 239).
example: Nine different countries have the atomic bomb as of 2022.
etymology: Coined by British science fiction author H. G. Wells in his 1914 novel The World Set Free.

definition: A weapon of mass destruction whose explosive power derives from a nuclear reaction.
A dispenser that turns a liquid (such as perfume) into a fine mist.
etymology: From atomize + -er.

definition: An allergic reaction that becomes apparent in a sensitized person only minutes after contact.
A severe form of dermatitis characterized by atopy.
A severe form of dermatitis characterized by atopy.
(of an organ or body part) diminished in size or strength as a result of disease or injury or lack of use.
example: Partial paralysis resulted in an atrophied left arm.

definition: (military) an offensive against an enemy (using weapons).
example: The attack began at dawn.
etymology: Borrowed from French attaque, derived from the verb attaquer, from Italian attaccare (“to join, attach”) (used in attaccare battaglia (“to join battle”)), from Frankish *stakkijan (“to stick, stick to, attach”).

definition: Of or relating to attention.
etymology: From attention + -al.

definition: Paying particular notice (as to children or helpless people).
example: His attentiveness to her wishes.
etymology: From attentive + -ness.

definition: Weaken the consistency of (a chemical substance).
etymology: The verb is first attested in 1530, the adjective in 1626;

definition: Dressed or clothed especially in fine attire; often used in combination.
example: The elegantly attired gentleman.

definition: In a beautiful manner.
etymology: From attractive + -ly.

definition: An entertainer who attracts large audiences.
Cooked while covered with browned breadcrumbs (and sometimes cheese).
etymology: Unadapted borrowing from French au gratin.

definition: Hairy upright herb native to southeastern Asia but widely cultivated for its large glossy edible fruit commonly used as a vegetable.
The measurement of hearing.
etymology: From audio- + -logy.

definition: A quantity of no importance; thing (object:), singular, negative pronoun; pronoun, thing, singular; quantifier: negative existential.
example: It was all for naught.
etymology: From Middle English aught, ought, from Old English āht, āwiht, from ā (“always", "ever”) + wiht (“thing", "creature”). More at wight.

definition: Indicate, as with a sign or an omen.
example: Every circumstance augured success.
etymology: Borrowed from Latin augur, of uncertain origin; akin to augurō (“interpret omens”).

definition: Black-and-white short-necked web-footed diving bird of northern seas.
etymology: From Icelandic álka, from Old Norse alka (“auk”), from Proto-Germanic *alkǭ, from Proto-Indo-European *h₁el- (“a kind of bird”).

definition: Of the south or coming from the south.
example: Sailed the austral seas.
etymology: Borrowed from Latin australis (“southern”).

definition: A filmmaker who has a personal style and keeps creative control over his or her works.
etymology: Borrowed from French auteur (“author”).

definition: Of or by or typical of an author.
example: Authorial comments.
etymology: From author + -ial.

definition: In an authoritative and magisterial manner.
example: She spoke authoritatively.
etymology: From Middle English auctoritatively, auctoritativeli; compare Medieval Latin auctoritātīve; equivalent to authoritative + -ly.

definition: (psychiatry) an abnormal absorption with the self; marked by communication disorders and short attention span and inability to treat others as people.
example: Weaponized autism.

definition: Characteristic of or affected with autism.
example: Autistic behavior.
etymology: From autism + -istic or -tic. First attested in 1913. The modern clinical sense is first used in 1943 by Leo Kanner.

definition: An expressway in a German-speaking country.
A device for heating substances above their boiling point; used to manufacture chemicals or to sterilize surgical instruments.
etymology: Borrowed from French autoclave, formed with prefix auto- + Latin clavis (“key”).

definition: A cruel and oppressive dictator.
etymology: Borrowed from French autocrate, itself from Ancient Greek αὐτοκρατής (autokratḗs, “sovereign”), from αὐτο- (auto-, “self”) (combining form of αὐτός (autós)) + κράτος (krátos, “strength, power”) + -ης (-ēs).

definition: Offensively self-assured or given to exercising usually unwarranted power.
example: An autocratic person.
etymology: From autocrat + -ic, equivalent to auto- + -cratic.

definition: Derived from organisms of the selfsame individual.
example: Autologous blood donation.
etymology: From autology + -ous.

definition: A firearm that reloads itself and keeps firing until the trigger is released.
A firearm that reloads itself and keeps firing until the trigger is released.
A firearm that reloads itself and keeps firing until the trigger is released.
Any of the ganglia of the autonomic system whose unmyelinated fibers innervate the internal organs.
A plexus of sympathetic and parasympathetic nerve fibers.
An examination and dissection of a dead body to determine cause of death or the changes produced by disease.
example: The autopsy revealed he had died of multiple bullet wounds.
etymology: From New Latin autopsia, from Ancient Greek αὐτοψῐ́ᾱ (autopsĭ́ā, “seeing with one's own eyes”). By surface analysis, auto- + -opsy.

definition: Bulbous autumn-flowering herb with white, purple or lavender-and-white flowers; native to western and central Europe.
A building where birds are kept.
etymology: From Latin aviārium, from avis (“bird”).

definition: In an avid manner.
example: Whatever the flavor or color of your local paper, do remember that these are read avidly for local information.
etymology: From avid + -ly.

definition: 100 avos equal 1 pataca in Macao.
etymology: Borrowed from Portuguese avo.

definition: Having or showing a feeling of mixed reverence and respect and wonder and dread.
example: In grim despair and awestruck wonder.
etymology: From awe + struck.

definition: A pointed tool for marking surfaces or for punching small holes.
etymology: From Middle English aul, alle, al, from Old English æl, from Proto-West Germanic *al, from Proto-Germanic *alaz, from Proto-Indo-European *h₁ólos.

definition: Shaped like an awl.
A weapon with a hammer on one side and an axe on the other.
With respect to an axis.
example: The jet was directed axially toward the cathode.
etymology: From axial + -ly.

definition: Of or relating to the axil.
The part of the main artery of the arm that lies in the armpit and is continuous with the subclavian artery above and the brachial artery below.
The hollow under the arm where it is joined to the shoulder.
Any of the lymph glands of the armpit; fights infections in the neck and chest and arm regions.
A continuation of the basilic vein and brachial vein that becomes the subclavian vein.
Of or relating to or resembling an axon.
etymology: From axon + -al.

definition: (in India) a native nursemaid who looks after children.
etymology: From various Indian languages (e.g. Hindi आया (āyā, “dry nurse, nanny”)), from Portuguese aia (“nurse, governess”), from Latin avia (“grandmother”).

definition: Used as a Hindi courtesy title; equivalent to English ‘Mr’.
etymology: Borrowed from Hindi बाबू (bābū), from Proto-New Indo-Aryan *बाब्ब (bābba), imitative of baby talk.

definition: A person who looks after babies (usually in the person's own home) while the babies' parents are working.
A person engaged to care for children when the parents are not home.
example: My neighbor is sometimes a babysitter for other mothers’ children.
etymology: From baby + sitter.

definition: A card game played in casinos in which two or more punters gamble against the banker; the player wins who holds 2 or 3 cards that total closest to nine.
etymology: First attested in the 19th century.

definition: Backfire from a recoilless weapon.
Any of the seats occupied by backbenchers in the House of Commons.
example: His spacious quarters indicate his transition from backbench upstart to established member of the governing team.
etymology: From back + bench.

definition: The offensive football players who line up behind the linemen.
example: Maryland's football team practiced for the third straight day yesterday without its starting backfield.
etymology: From back + field.

definition: The backward escape of gases and unburned gunpowder after a gun is fired.
etymology: From back + fire.

definition: A board game for two players; pieces move according to throws of the dice.
etymology: Probably from back + Middle English gamen, from Old English gamen (“amusement, game”).

definition: The board on which backgammon is played.
The execution of low priority programs while higher priority programs are not using the processing system.
etymology: background + processing

definition: (of racket strokes) made across the body with back of hand facing direction of stroke.
etymology: From back + hand + -ed.

definition: An excavator whose shovel bucket is attached to a hinged boom and is drawn backward to move earth.
etymology: From back + hoe.

definition: Lacking a back.
example: A stool is a backless and armless seat.
etymology: From back + -less.

definition: Lack of normal development of intellectual capacities.
etymology: From backward + -ness.

definition: The branch of medical science that studies bacteria in relation to disease.
etymology: From bacterio- + -logy.

definition: The principal bad character in a film or work of fiction.
example: In a western, the baddie typically wears a black hat.
etymology: From bad + -ie.

definition: Large naked-muzzled skunk with white back and tail; of southwestern North America and Mexico.
The act of harassing someone.
That which is below standard or expectations as of ethics or decency.
etymology: From Middle English baddenes, badnes, badnesse; equivalent to bad + -ness.

definition: (Yiddish) glazed yeast-raised doughnut-shaped roll with hard crust.
etymology: Compare obsolete English bee, Old English bēag, Old Frisian bāg, Old Saxon bōg, Middle Low German bōg, Old Norse baugr. Also compare Austrian German Beugel and dialectal Beigel. See also beag.

definition: Cases used to carry belongings when traveling.
example: Please put your baggage in the trunk.
etymology: From Middle English bagage, from Old French bagage, baguage, from bague (“bundle, sack”), of Germanic/North Germanic origin, probably from the same ultimate source as Old Norse baggi (“pack, bundle”). Compare also bag.

definition: A workman employed to pack things into containers.
etymology: Inherited from Middle English bagger, baggere, baggare, equivalent to bag + -er (agent noun suffix).

definition: A tubular wind instrument; the player blows air into a bag and squeezes it out through the drone.
An officer of the court who is employed to execute writs and processes and make arrests etc.
etymology: From Middle English baillif, baylyf, from Anglo-Norman and Old French bailif (plural bailis), probably from Vulgar Latin *bāiulivus (“castellan”), from Latin bāiulus (“porter; steward”), whence also bail.

definition: Harass with persistent criticism or carping.
example: To bait a bear with dogs.
etymology: From Middle English bayte, bait, beite, from Old Norse beita (“food, bait”), from Proto-Germanic *baitō (“that which is bitten, bait”), from Proto-Indo-European *bʰeyd- (“to cleave, split, separate”).

definition: Dried out by heat or excessive exposure to sunlight.
example: Land lying baked in the heat.

definition: Rich Middle Eastern cake made of thin layers of flaky pastry filled with nuts and honey.
etymology: Borrowed from Turkish baklava, from Ottoman Turkish باقلوا (baklava) (see for more); possibly from Middle Mongol ᠪᠠᠭᠯᠠᠭ᠎ᠠ (baɣlaɣ-a, “bundle, package”).

definition: An acrobat who balances themself in difficult positions.
etymology: From balance + -er.

definition: (football) the player who is carrying (and trying to advance) the ball on an offensive play.
Strong lightweight wood of the balsa tree used especially for floats.
etymology: Borrowed from Spanish balsa, from Paleo-Hispanic, probably Basque [Term?] or Iberian [Term?]. Not related to balsam.

definition: A light raft made of balsa.
Strong lightweight wood of the balsa tree used especially for floats.
A railing at the side of a staircase or balcony to prevent people from falling.
A young child who is just beginning to walk.
etymology: Borrowed from Italian bambino.

definition: A trite or obvious remark.
etymology: From French banalité, from banal, equivalent to banal + -ity.

definition: A ship designed to transport bananas.
Large and brightly colored handkerchief; often used as a neckerchief.
Web-footed Australian stilt with reddish-brown pectoral markings.
An armed thief who is (usually) a member of a band.
The leader of a dance band.

definition: Something causing misery or death.
example: The bane of my life.
etymology: * Old Saxon bano (“death; murder”), beni (“mortal injury; wound”)

definition: Strike violently.
example: The fireworks banged away all through the night.
etymology: In the sense of abrupt left turn, from Boston left and associated risk of a crash.

definition: A financier who owns or is an executive in a bank.
example: May 20 1815, John Quincy Adams, letter to a merchant I think the 584 Bankers may be put down 36,540 tons, navigated by 4,627 men and boys.

definition: A piece of paper money (especially one issued by a central bank).

definition: Eating an elaborate meal (often accompanied by entertainment).
(Irish folklore) a female spirit who wails to warn of impending death.
Weighs 115-126 pounds.

A mass attack of troops without concern for casualties; originated by Japanese who accompanied it with yells of ‘banzai’.
etymology: From banzai + charge. "Banzai" from Japanese 天皇陛下万歳 (Tennō Heika banzai, “long live His Imperial Majesty”), a common battle cry used by Japanese soldiers.

definition: Go from one pub to the next and get progressively more drunk.
A member of an uncivilized people.
The quality of being shockingly cruel and inhumane.
Meat that has been barbecued or grilled in a highly seasoned sauce.
etymology: From mid-17th century. Borrowed from Spanish barbacoa, from Taíno barbakoa (“framework of sticks”), the raised wooden structure the natives used to either sleep on or cure meat. Originally “meal of roasted meat or fish”.

definition: Cooked over an outdoor grill.
Chicken wings cooked in barbecue sauce.
Having the breasts uncovered or featuring such nudity.

definition: Enema in which a contrast medium (usually barium sulfate) is injected into the rectum and X-rays are taken to search for lesions.
A white insoluble radiopaque powder used as a pigment.
A female bartender.

definition: Marked by spirited enjoyment.
etymology: From barm (“foam rising upon beer or other malt liquors when fermenting, and used as leaven”) + -y (suffix meaning ‘having the quality of’ forming adjectives).

definition: Large owl of eastern North America having its breast and abdomen streaked with brown.
A tube through which a bullet travels when a gun is fired.

definition: Put in or stored in a barrel.

definition: Of or relating to or containing basalt.

definition: (baseball) a play executed by a baseball team.
(classical mythology) a serpent (or lizard or dragon) able to kill with its breath or glance.

A play executed by a basketball team.
A clef that puts the F below middle C on the fourth line of a staff.
Viol that is the bass member of the viol family with approximately the range of the cello.

definition: An oboe pitched an octave below the ordinary oboe.
A basket (usually hooded) used as a baby's bed.

definition: An adult male singer with the lowest voice.

definition: Cover with liquid before cooking.

etymology: Late Middle English, from Old French bastir (“build, construct, sew up (a garment)”).

Diminished or moderated.

An arrangement of sights that makes possible the rapid aiming of a firearm at short ranges.
A broadax used as a weapon.
Someone who fights (or is fighting).

definition: Informal or slang terms for mentally irregular.
etymology: From bat + -y. In sense “insane”, attested 1903, from expression have bats in one's belfry, from tendency of bats to fly around erratically. Compare also batshit (“insane”) and squirrelly (“jumpy, eccentric”).

definition: A mock scepter carried by a court jester.
etymology: From Middle English bable, babel, babull, babulle, from Old French babel, baubel (“trinket, child's toy”), most likely a reduplication of bel, ultimately from Latin bellus (“pretty”).

definition: (computer science) a data transmission rate (bits/second) for modems.

definition: A portable rocket launcher used by infantrymen as an antitank weapon.

A bridgehead on the enemy's shoreline seized by an amphibious operation.

Small and round and shiny like a shiny bead or button.

definition: Having eyes that gleam with malice.
Having or resembling a beak.
Aromatic annual Old World herb cultivated for its finely divided and often curly leaves for use especially in soups and salads.
Fish of sandy areas of western Pacific and Indian oceans having an angular snout for burrowing into sand.
Any of several whales inhabiting all oceans and having beaklike jaws with vestigial teeth in the upper jaw.
Blackish aphid that infests e.g. beans and sugar beets.
A small cloth bag filled with dried beans; thrown in games.

definition: Someone who works in a beauty parlor.

definition: Someone suffering from enuresis; someone who urinates while asleep in bed.
Be sexually active with more than one partner.
example: During his university days he would bed-hop whenever he got the chance.

definition: A room used primarily for sleeping.
etymology: From Middle English bedchambre, bedchaumbre, equivalent to bed + chamber.

definition: Space by the side of a bed (especially the bed of a sick or dying person).
example: The doctor stood at her bedside.
etymology: From Middle English bedsyde, bedde syde (also as beddes side, beddes syde), equivalent to bed + -side. Compare German Bettseite (“bedside”).

definition: Decorative cover for a bed.
etymology: From bed + spread.

definition: Eurasian marten having a brown coat with pale breast and throat.
Wood of any of various beech trees; used for flooring and containers and plywood and tool handles.
etymology: From beech + wood.

definition: Tallow obtained from a bovine animal.
A photograph of a muscular man in minimal attire.
etymology: From beef + cake. In sense 1, by analogy with cheesecake (“an image of a sexy young woman”).

definition: The most direct route.
example: He made a beeline for the bathroom.
etymology: From bee + line, due to the belief that a bee returns to its hive in a straight course, originally an Americanism.

definition: Stupefied by alcoholic drink.
example: The wino's poor befuddled mind.

definition: Call upon in supplication; entreat.
example: I beg you to stop!
etymology: Inherited from Middle English beggen, of uncertain origin. Possibly from Old English *becgian, *bedcian, syncopated forms of bedecian (“to beg”), itself of obscure origin.

definition: Make (offspring) by reproduction.
example: The King intends to beget a child within the next five years.
etymology: From Middle English begeten [influenced by Old Norse geta ("to get, to guess")], from Old English beġietan (“to get”), from Proto-Germanic *bigetaną (“to find, seize”), equivalent to be- + get.

definition: Of or relating to behaviorism.

definition: Execution by cutting off the victim's head.
example: A large crowd gathered to see the beheading.

definition: Turn a rope round an object or person in order to secure it or them.

A person who rings church bells (as for summoning the congregation).

definition: Western North American frog with a taillike copulatory organ.
Fast-growing herbaceous evergreen tree of South America having a broad trunk with high water content and dark green oval leaves.

Creative writing valued for esthetic content.
etymology: Borrowed from French belles-lettres (“fine writings”), a parallel construction with the beaux arts (“fine arts”). Littré considered the belles-lettres to embrace grammar, rhetoric, and poetry.

definition: Having or showing a ready disposition to fight.

definition: A man employed as an errand boy and luggage carrier around hotels.
etymology: From Middle English belleman, equivalent to bell + man.

definition: Someone who assumes leadership of a movement or activity.
example: Mortgage delinquencies often act as a bellwether for a forthcoming recession.
etymology: From Middle English belwether, belleweder, equivalent to bell + wether (“castrated ram”).

definition: Ammunition (usually of small caliber) loaded in flexible linked strips for use in a machine gun.
Refuse to talk or stop talking; fall silent.
Ammunition (usually of small caliber) loaded in flexible linked strips for use in a machine gun.
Regret strongly.
example: He bemoaned the drought but went on watering his lawn.
etymology: From Middle English bemenen, bimenen, from Old English bemǣnan (“to bemoan, bewail, lament”); equivalent to be- (“about, concerning”) + moan. Alteration of vowel from Middle to Modern English due to analogy with moan.

definition: Used of the back and knees; stooped.
example: On bended knee.

definition: A tool for bending.
example: He used pliers as a bender.

definition: The act of praying for divine protection.
example: To pronounce / give / say the benediction.

definition: An endowed church office giving income to its holder.
etymology: From Old French benefice, from Latin beneficium.

definition: A relatively permanent inclination to react in a particular way.

Leave or give by will after one's death.

definition: Censure severely or angrily.

etymology: From be- + rate (“to scold, upbraid”).

definition: A person who has suffered the death of someone they loved.
example: The bereaved do not always need to be taken care of.

Small tree with pear-shaped fruit whose oil is used in perfumery; Italy.
A narrow ledge or shelf typically at the top or bottom of a slope.

Very drunk.

definition: Resembling a beast; showing lack of human sensibility.

Seed of betel palm; chewed with leaves of the betel pepper and lime as a digestive stimulant and narcotic in southeastern Asia.
One who reveals confidential information to the police or other authority.

definition: A mutual promise to marry.

definition: Production of a chemical compound by a living organism.

Any weapon usable in biological warfare.

definition: A branch of biology that studies biological phenomena and observations by means of statistical analysis.

definition: Having two feet.
example: Bipedal locomotion.

definition: Old fashioned airplane; has two wings one above the other.
etymology: From bi- + plane.

definition: A gun dog trained to locate or retrieve birds.
etymology: Compound of bird + dog.

definition: A cage in which a bird can be kept.
etymology: From bird + cage.

definition: A catcher's mask with a strong wire face.
A shelter for birds.
etymology: From bird + house.

definition: A passage in the uterus and vagina through which a fetus passes during vaginal birth.
A blemish on the skin that is formed before birth.
example: Facial birthmark.

definition: The ratio of live births in an area to the population of that area; expressed per 1000 population per year.

definition: An Indian dish made with highly seasoned rice and meat or fish or vegetables.

definition: Sexually attracted to both sexes.
example: Midrash and Zohar present Adam as hermaphroditic or bisexual.
etymology: From bi- + -sexual, via the French bisexuel (bi-, sexuel). Attested since 1792 as a synonym in botany for "hermaphroditic" ("having male and female parts").

definition: A person who is sexually attracted to both sexes.
Showing characteristics of both sexes.
etymology: From bisexual + -ity.

definition: A thick cream soup made from shellfish.

definition: An image represented as a two dimensional array of brightness values for pixels.

Poisonous perennial Old World vine having violet flowers and oval coral-red berries; widespread weed in North America.
Resembling or containing bitumen.

definition: Rich in tarry hydrocarbons; burns readily with a smoky yellow flame.
Temporary living quarters specially built by the army for soldiers.

definition: Divulge confidential information or secrets.

definition: Divulge confidential information or secrets.
Common European twining vine with tuberous roots and cordate leaves and red berries.

Herb of the Mediterranean region having pungent seeds used like those of caraway.
A crappie that is black.

definition: Make or become black.

Any of several human or animal diseases characterized by dark urine resulting from rapid breakdown of red blood cells.

definition: Severe and often fatal malaria characterized by kidney damage resulting in dark urine.
A disorder of the urinary bladder.
The sphincter muscle of the urinary bladder; made up of a thickened muscular layer of bladder around the urethral opening.
Pompous or pretentious talk or writing.

definition: Anemic looking from illness or emotion.

definition: Covered with (or as if with) a blanket.
A die that produces a flat piece of material by cutting the desired shape in one operation.
example: Generally a blanking die may only cut the outside contour of a part, often used for parts with no internal features.

etymology: From blaze (“to reflect or send forth a bright light; (figurative) to be conspicuous; etc.”, verb) + -er (suffix forming agent nouns).

definition: Garden plant having deep-pink drooping heart-shaped flowers.

Very drunk.

definition: A disease of the central nervous system affecting especially horses and cattle; characterized by an unsteady swaying gait and frequent falling.

definition: A light that flashes on and off; used as a signal or to send messages.

definition: Lacking or showing a lack of due concern.

definition: Become bloated or swollen or puff up.

definition: Blocking entrance to and exit from seaports and harbors.

definition: A football player whose responsibility is to block players attempting to stop an offensive play.

definition: A feud in which members of the opposing parties murder each other.

definition: Formerly used as a treatment to reduce excess blood (one of the four humors of medieval medicine).

definition: Covered with blood.

definition: A burner that mixes air and gas to produce a very hot flame.

definition: An instrumental version of the blues (especially for piano).

A chemical compound with chemical formula BN, consisting of equal numbers of boron and nitrogen atoms.
