definition: The tendency for a visual object to be perceived as having the same brightness under widely different conditions of illumination.
Having a grey or brown streak or a pattern or a patchy coloring; used especially of the patterned fur of cats.
etymology: Back-formation from brindled, a variant of brinded (“streaked, spotted”), apparently reanalyzed as brindle + -ed. Attested from the late seventeenth century.

definition: Quality of being active or spirited or alive and vigorous.
etymology: From Italian brio (“finesse, talent”), from Spanish brío, ultimately from Proto-Celtic *brīgos.

definition: A cut of meat from the breast or lower chest especially of beef.
etymology: From Middle English brusket, probably from Old Danish bryske (“cartilage, gristle”), from Old Norse brjósk, from Proto-Germanic *briuskiz (compare German Brausche (“knot on the head”)).

definition: Having or covered with protective barbs or quills or spines or thorns or setae etc.
example: A horse with a short bristly mane.
etymology: From Middle English bristled, ibrustled, iburstled, equivalent to bristle + -ed.

definition: (used in the plural) informal term for breeches.
Of a cask or barrel.
example: The cask was set abroach.

definition: (of hats) having a broad brim.
Having relatively broad rather than needlelike or scalelike leaves.
An advertisement (usually printed on a page or in a leaflet) intended for wide distribution.
etymology: From broad + sheet.

definition: A sword with a broad blade and (usually) two cutting edges; used to cut rather than stab.
etymology: From broad + sword.

definition: Plant grown for its pungent edible leafy shoots.
Plant grown for its pungent edible leafy shoots.
etymology: Ultimately from Italian broccoli di rapa (“sprouts or stalks of the turnip”).

definition: A thick and heavy shoe.
etymology: Borrowed from Irish bróg (“boot, shoe”), from Old Irish bróc (“shoe, greave, legging, hose, breeches”), likely from Old Norse brók (“breeches”), from Proto-Germanic *brōks (“breeches”).

definition: Cook under a broiler.
example: Broil fish.

definition: Cooked by radiant heat (as over a grill).
Full of sorrow.
etymology: From broken + hearted.

definition: Non-sexual but intense relationship between two men.
etymology: Blend of bro + romance.

definition: A nonmetallic heavy volatile corrosive dark brown liquid element belonging to the halogens; found in sea water.
Tall tufted grass of southeastern United States.
The handle of a broom.
etymology: From broom + stick.

definition: A building where prostitutes are available.
A woman who runs a house of prostitution.
Light carriage; pulled by a single horse.
etymology: Named after British statesman Lord Brougham (1778–1868), who either invented or popularized the vehicle.

definition: Of a color similar to that of wood or earth.
etymology: * Sanskrit बभ्रु (babhrú, “reddish-brown”)

definition: A copper-brown type of goldstone.
Of northwestern Canada and Alaska.
A large and strong and heavyset man.
example: A thick-skinned bruiser ready to give as good as he got.
etymology: From bruise + -er.

definition: Marked by dark or relatively dark pigmentation of hair or skin or eyes.
example: A brunette beauty.
etymology: From French brunet. Compare also Middle English brunet, burnet (“brown”), from Old French brunet, which is the same word.

definition: Marked by rude or peremptory shortness.
example: Try to cultivate a less brusque manner.
etymology: The adjective is borrowed from French brusque, from Italian brusco (“abrupt, sudden, brusque; brisk; eager; sour, tart; unripe; grim-looking”); further etymology unknown. The verb is derived from the adjective.

definition: A vine of the genus Bryonia having large leaves and small flowers and yielding acrid juice with emetic and purgative properties.
etymology: From Middle English brionie, from Latin bryōnia (“bryony”), from Ancient Greek βρυωνία (bruōnía, “bryony”), from βρύω (brúō).

definition: Of or relating to or toward the cheek.
example: The buccal aspect of the gum.
etymology: From Latin bucca (“the cheek”) + -al. By surface analysis, bucc- + -al.

definition: A branch of the maxillary artery that supplies blood to the buccinator muscle and the cheek.
The cavity between the jaws and the cheeks.
etymology: From buccal (“of or pertaining to the cheek or mouth”) + cavity (“hollow area”).

definition: Someone who robs at sea or plunders the land from the sea without having a commission from any sovereign nation.
etymology: From French boucanier, from boucaner (“to smoke or broil meat and fish, to hunt wild beasts for their skins”), from boucan (“(Tupi-style) grill”), from Old Tupi moka'ẽ, mboka'ẽ (“wooden grill”).

definition: Local names for a cowboy (‘vaquero’ is used especially in southwestern and central Texas and ‘buckaroo’ is used especially in California).
example: Many cowboy poets have a buckaroo look and feel about them.
etymology: Modified from Spanish vaquero (“cowboy”), with the spelling influenced by buck (“(noun) male antelope, deer, etc.; adventurous or high-spirited young man;

definition: A list of things you plan to do before you die.
example: A winter bucket list.
etymology: From bucket + list. Sense 1 (“list of tasks arising during a meeting”) may allude to a notional bucket in which tasks to be dealt with later are placed.

definition: Work very hard, like a slave.
example: If he would buckle down and do his homework, he could be an excellent student.
etymology: From buckle + down.

definition: Armor carried on the arm to intercept blows.
etymology: From Middle English bukler, bokler, bokeler, bokeleer, from Old French bocler, boucler, bucler, (French bouclier) from Vulgar Latin *bucculārius (“bossed”), from Latin buccula (“boss”). Merged with buckle + -er.

definition: Any of various ferns of the genera Dryopteris or Polystichum or Lastreopsis having somewhat shield-shaped coverings on the sori.
etymology: From the shape of the indusia (membranes) that cover the fern's sori (spores).

definition: Plant of southeastern Europe having yellow flowers like those of mustard and pods with open valves resembling bucklers.
Small lead shot for shotgun shells.
etymology: From buck + shot.

definition: Horse of a light yellowish dun color with dark mane and tail.
etymology: From Middle English bukskyn; equivalent to buck + skin.

definition: A member of the genus Fagopyrum; annual Asian plant with clusters of small pinkish white flowers and small edible triangular seeds which are used whole or ground into flour.
(used with regard to idealized country life) idyllically rustic.
example: A pleasant bucolic scene.
etymology: PIE word *gʷṓws Borrowed from Latin būcolicus, from Ancient Greek βουκολικός (boukolikós, “rustic, pastoral; meter used by pastoral poets”, literally “pertaining to cowherds”).

definition: Small Australian parakeet usually light green with black and yellow markings in the wild but bred in many colors.
example: She keeps a ton of budgies in her home.
etymology: From a clipping of budgerigar + -ie.

definition: Large shaggy-haired brown bison of North American plains.
etymology: Borrowed from Portuguese or Spanish búfalo (“buffalo”), from Late Latin būfalus, from Latin būbalus, from Ancient Greek βούβαλος (boúbalos, “antelope, wild ox”). Doublet of bubale and buffle.

definition: Small blackish stout-bodied biting fly having aquatic larvae; sucks the blood of birds as well as humans and other mammals.
Pounded or hit repeatedly by storms or adversities.
etymology: From buffet + -ed.

definition: A wheel that is covered with soft material.
A rude or vulgar fool.
etymology: From Middle French bouffon, from Italian buffone (“jester”), from buffare (“to puff out the cheeks”), of onomatopoeic origin. Compare Middle High German buffen ("to puff";

definition: Someone who plays a bugle.
etymology: From bugle + -er.

definition: A disorder of eating in which the person alternates between strong craving for food and aversion to food; characterized by excessive eating followed by periods of fasting or self-induced vomiting.
etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin būlīmia, from Ancient Greek βουλῑμῐ́ᾱ (boulīmĭ́ā, “ravenous hunger”), from βοῦς (boûs, “ox”) + λῑμός (līmós, “hunger, famine”) + -ῐ́ᾱ (-ĭ́ā, “-ia”), and Latin nervōsa (“nervous”).

definition: Flatten with or as if with a bulldozer.
example: He's certainly very chirpy for a man whose house has just been bulldozed down.
etymology: From earlier bulldose (noun, literally “bull-dose, a dose fit for a bull”), equivalent to bull + dose.

definition: A projectile that is fired from a gun.
etymology: From Middle English bullet (“an official tag or badge of registration or identification”), from Old French bullete, diminutive of boule (“ball”). Later influenced by Middle French boulette and French boulet.

definition: Identification of the gun that fired a bullet from an analysis of the unique marks that every gun makes on the bullet it fires and on the shell ejected from it.
The activity at a bullfight.
etymology: From bull + fighting.

definition: Largest North American frog; highly aquatic with a deep-pitched voice.
etymology: From bull + frog.

definition: A portable loudspeaker with built-in microphone and amplifier.
Kill intentionally and with premeditation.
A sudden happening that brings good fortune (as a sudden opportunity to make money).
etymology: Costermonger jargon bunts, perhaps from bonus.

definition: Make a mess of, destroy or ruin.
etymology: The origin of the verb is uncertain; it is either: * onomatopoeic in origin (compare bumble (“to act in an inept, clumsy or inexpert manner; to make mistakes”), fumble (“to grope awkwardly in trying to find something;

definition: Spoiled through incompetence or clumsiness.
example: A bungled job.
etymology: From bungle + -ed.

definition: Showing lack of skill or aptitude.
example: A bungling workman.
etymology: From the verb bungle.

definition: A gas burner used in laboratories; has an air valve to regulate the mixture of gas and air.
A gas burner used in laboratories; has an air valve to regulate the mixture of gas and air.
Any of several plants of the genus Bidens having yellow flowers and prickly fruits that cling to fur and clothing.
Nonelective government officials.
example: At that time the administration replaced the system of patronage in the civil service with a bureaucracy.
etymology: From bureau + -cracy, from French bureaucratie, coined by Jean Claude Marie Vincent de Gournay from bureau (“office”) + -cratie (“rule of”).

definition: A sandwich consisting of a fried cake of minced beef served on a bun, often with other ingredients.
example: She was planning to have a burger for dinner.
etymology: Clipping of hamburger, rebracketing it as ham + burger. First use appears c. 1937. Sense 5 is likely a back-formation from Burgerland.

definition: The ritual placing of a corpse in a grave.
example: His whole family was present at his burial.
etymology: From Middle English biriel, a backformation from biriels, which was re-interpreted as a plural, itself from from Old English byrġels, from byrġan (“to bury”) + -els.

definition: Cloth used to cover a corpse in preparation for burial.
Murder without leaving a trace on the body.
etymology: Eponymous, from William Burke.

definition: The wood cut from a tree burl or outgrowth; often used decoratively in veneer.
Dark brown pigment obtained by heating umber.
A fully automatic pistol; a small submachine gun.
A reflex that expels gas noisily from the stomach through the mouth.
Small donkey used as a pack animal.
Long-eared deer of western North America with two-pronged antlers.
Having or covered with protective barbs or quills or spines or thorns or setae etc.
etymology: From Middle English burry, bury, equivalent to bur + -y.

definition: A low woody perennial plant usually having several major stems.
example: Bushes to support pea vines.
etymology: From the sign of a bush usually employed to indicate such places.

definition: A player on a minor-league baseball team.
An African shrike.
A male dweller in the Australian bush country.
etymology: From bush + -man.

definition: An executive in a business corporation.
People who transact business (especially business executives).
Exhibiting methodical and systematic characteristics that would be useful in business.
etymology: From business + -like.

definition: People who transact business (especially business executives).
Ruin completely.
example: He busted my radio!
etymology: From Middle English busten, a variant of bursten, bresten (“to burst”). Compare Low German basten, a variant of barsten (“to burst”). Cognate with burst and bost.

definition: Either of the two large fleshy masses of muscular tissue that form the human rump.
etymology: Inherited from Middle English buttok, probably from Old English buttuc (“end; end piece”; also, “short piece of land”). Attested with its current anatomical meaning since 1300.

definition: Held up by braces or buttresses.
example: Only the buttressed outer walls still stood.

definition: Synthetic rubber made by polymerizing isobutylene.
(of a woman's body) having a large bosom and pleasing curves.
Be killed or die.
example: He claims that he'll pay me back, but I don't buy it.
etymology: * In the die sense, apparently attested since the 1820s, thus earlier than the variant buy the farm, which may be an extension of it. * In the have it sense, an elliptical allusion to believing a sales pitch.

definition: A New World vulture that is common in South America and Central America and the southern United States.
etymology: From Middle English bosart, from Anglo-Norman buisart, from Old French busart, busard, a derivative ( + -ard) of Old French buison, buson (French buse), possibly from Latin būteō (“hawk”).

definition: Tree with shaggy unpleasant-smelling toxic bark and yielding strong durable wood; bark and seeds used as a purgative and vermifuge and narcotic.
Small two-wheeled horse-drawn carriage; with two seats and a folding hood.
etymology: Borrowed from French cabriolet.

definition: An indication of approved or superior status.
example: I remember when this diner was a quiet hangout, but lately it seems to be losing its cachet.
etymology: Borrowed from French cachet, first appearing in Scottish English, from 1630.

definition: Talk or utter in a cackling manner.
example: The women cackled when they saw the movie star step out of the limousine.
etymology: From Middle English caclen, cakelen, perhaps from Old English *caclian, *cacolian, from Proto-West Germanic *kakulōn, *kakilōn (“to cackle, gaggle, yelp, snarl”), perhaps of imitative origin.

definition: The dead body of a human being.
example: The cadaver was intended for dissection.
etymology: From Middle English cadaver, from Latin cadāver.

definition: Ore of cadmium; a rare yellowish mineral consisting of cadmium sulphide in crystalline form.
Strong espresso coffee with a topping of frothed steamed milk.
Showing self-interest and shrewdness in dealing with others.
example: A cagey lawyer.
etymology: Initially US colloquial, of unknown origin. A connection with the behavior of caged prisoners (wary and closed-lipped) and caged animals (wary) has been speculated. If so, by surface analysis, cage + -y.

definition: A strutting dance based on a march; was performed in minstrel shows; originated as a competition among Black dancers to win a cake.
etymology: From cake + walk. Originally an African-American form of dance and music that developed after the Civil War, later popularised by minstrel shows.

definition: Dark brown highly poisonous seed of the calabar-bean vine; source of physostigmine and used in native witchcraft.
Round gourd of the calabash tree.
etymology: From French calebasse, from Spanish calabaza (“gourd;

definition: A pipe for smoking; has a curved stem and a large bowl made from a calabash gourd.
Tropical American evergreen that produces large round gourds.
(of events) having extremely unfortunate or dire consequences; bringing ruin.
example: A calamitous defeat.

definition: A process that impregnates something with calcium (or calcium salts).
etymology: From calcify + -ation.

definition: The practice of calisthenic exercises.
example: Calisthenics is recommended for general good health.
etymology: From Ancient Greek κάλλος (kállos, “beauty”) + σθένος (sthénos, “strength”) + English -ics.

definition: A female prostitute who can be hired by telephone.
South African plant widely cultivated for its showy pure white spathe and yellow spadix.
South African plant widely cultivated for its showy pure white spathe and yellow spadix.
A musical instrument consisting of a series of steam whistles played from a keyboard.
etymology: From Ancient Greek Καλλιόπη (Kalliópē, “Calliope, the muse of poetry”), from καλός (kalós, “beautiful”) + ὄψ (óps, “voice”).

definition: Devoid of passion or feeling; hardheartedness.
example: Fred was known for his callousness; local panhandlers had long since learned not to try their sob stories on him.
etymology: From callous + -ness.

definition: Young and inexperienced.
example: Those three young men are particularly callow youths.
etymology: From Middle English calwe (“(adjective) bald; (noun) bald person”), from Old English calu, caluw (“without hair, bald, callow”), from Proto-West Germanic *kalu, from Proto-Germanic *kalwaz (“bald;

definition: Giving birth to a calf.
(botany) the whorl of sepals of a flower collectively forming the outer floral envelope or layer of the perianth enclosing and supporting the developing bud; usually green.
etymology: From Latin calyx, from Ancient Greek κάλυξ (kálux, “case of a bud, husk”). Doublet of chalice and kelch.

definition: The cuplike or ringlike or tubular structure of a flower which bears the sepals and stamens and calyx (as in Rosaceae).
A darkened enclosure in which images of outside objects are projected through a small aperture or lens onto a facing surface.
etymology: From New Latin camera obscūra (literally “dark chamber”); compare camera.

definition: A prostitute who provides service to military personnel.
Someone living temporarily in a tent or lodge for recreation.
example: There were thousands of campers at the music festival.
etymology: From camp (verb) + -er.

definition: A resin obtained from the camphor tree; used in making celluloid and liniment.
A small sphere of camphor or naphthalene used to keep moths away from stored clothing.
Annual of southern United States and Mexico having bristly leaves and pale yellow flowers.
A cerate made of camphor and wax and spermaceti and castor oil.
Oil distilled from camphor resin.
A solution of alcohol and camphor that can be used as a steam inhalant to bring relief in respiratory illness; it can also be applied topically on the skin.
Large evergreen tree of warm regions whose aromatic wood yields camphor.
Providing sophisticated amusement by virtue of having artificially (and vulgarly) mannered or banal or sentimental qualities.
example: Campy Hollywood musicals of the 1940's.
etymology: From camp (“an affected or exaggerated style”) + -y.

definition: An engine shaft with cams attached to it.
etymology: From cam + shaft.

definition: Airtight sealed metal container for food or drink or paint etc.
example: I keep a can of fuel for emergencies.
etymology: From Middle English canne, from Old English canne (“glass, container, cup, jar”), from Proto-Germanic *kannǭ (“can, tankard, mug, cup”).

definition: A deliberately misleading fabrication.
etymology: Borrowed from French canard (“duck, hoax”).

definition: Any of several drugs that control or kill neoplastic cells; used in chemotherapy to kill cancer cells; all have unpleasant side effects that may include nausea and vomiting and hair loss and suppression of bone marrow function.
Relating to or affected with cancer.
example: A cancerous growth.
etymology: From Middle English cancerous, from Latin cancerōsus, from cancer (“crab; tumor, cancer”) + -ōsus (adjective-forming suffix). By surface analysis, cancer + -ous.

definition: Branched candlestick; ornamental; has several lights.
The campaign of a candidate to be elected.
etymology: From French candidature, equivalent to candidate + -ure.

definition: The quality of being honest and straightforward in attitude and speech.
A viral disease of young dogs characterized by high fever and respiratory inflammation.
Work made of interlaced slender branches (especially willow branches).
A metallic cylinder packed with shot and used as ammunition in a firearm.
etymology: From Middle English canustyr (“basket”), a borrowing from Latin canistrum. Doublet of canaster and knaster. * (metal receptacle): Through influence of unrelated can.

definition: A metallic cylinder packed with shot and used as ammunition in a firearm.
A fungal disease of woody plants that causes localized damage to the bark.
example: The canker of destitution and violence.
etymology: From Middle English canker, cancre, from Old English cancer (“cancer; crab”), akin to Dutch kanker, Old High German chanchar. Ultimately from Latin cancer (“a cancer”).

definition: North American evergreen fern having pinnate leaves and dense clusters of lance-shaped fronds.
An ulceration (especially of the lips or lining of the mouth).
Any plant of the genus Canna having large sheathing leaves and clusters of large showy flowers.
etymology: Borrowed from translingual Canna, from Latin canna (“reed”), from Ancient Greek κᾰ́ννᾰ (kắnnă, “reed”), from Akkadian 𒂵𒉡𒌑𒌝 (qanûm).

definition: Plants grown for their large bright yellow to red flowers.
Any plant of the genus Cannabis; a coarse bushy annual with palmate leaves and clusters of small green flowers; yields tough fibers and narcotic drugs.
A resin obtained from the hemp plant; thought to be the active narcotic agent in marijuana.
A hunt for animals that have been raised on game ranches until they are mature enough to be killed for trophy collections.
Characteristic of cannibals or exhibiting cannibalism.
example: Cannibalistic behavior.
etymology: From cannibal + -istic.

definition: A large artillery gun that is usually on wheels.
A small flexible tube inserted into a body cavity for draining off fluid or introducing medication.
etymology: The plural form cannulae is borrowed from Late Latin cannulae.

definition: Vegetable oil made from rapeseed; it is high in monounsaturated fatty acids.
etymology: From Canola.

definition: Vegetable oil made from rapeseed; it is high in monounsaturated fatty acids.
In a canonical manner.
example: The deacon was canonically inducted.
etymology: From canonical + -ly.

definition: Stock phrases that have become nonsense through endless repetition.
example: He had the look of a prince, but the cant of a fishmonger.
etymology: From Latin cantō, probably via Old Northern French canter (“sing, tell”). Doublet of chant.

definition: Stubbornly obstructive and unwilling to cooperate.
etymology: Perhaps derived from earlier contenkerous, from contentious + rancorous.

definition: A musical composition for voices and orchestra based on a religious text.
etymology: From Italian cantata. Doublet of chanty.

definition: Of or relating to a canton.
etymology: From canton + -al.

definition: Temporary living quarters specially built by the army for soldiers.
etymology: From French cantonnement.

definition: Putting a condemned person to death.
etymology: From the original meaning of capital (“relating to the head”); originally referring to executions by beheading or decapitating.

definition: Writing in capital letters.
example: English and French have different rules for the capitalisation of the names of the days of the week.
etymology: From capitalise + -ation.

definition: Indian macaque with a bonnet-like tuft of hair.
Colorless pungent crystalline compound derived from capsicum; source of the hotness of hot peppers of the genus Capsicum such as chili and cayenne and jalapeno.
etymology: Arbitrary alteration of earlier capsicine, capsicin (“material extracted from cayenne pepper”), presumably to prevent confusion, from German Capsicin, from New Latin capsicum + German -in.

definition: Any of various tropical plants of the genus Capsicum bearing peppers.
etymology: Borrowed from New Latin capsicum, from Ancient Greek καψικός (kapsikós, “like a box”), from Latin capsa (“box”).

definition: Overturn accidentally.
example: Don't rock the boat or it will capsize!
etymology: Attested since 1788. Origin unknown. Possibly related to Spanish chapuzar (“to sink by the head”).

definition: A hooded cloak for women.
etymology: First use appears c. 1589, from French capuchin, from earlier capucin, from Italian cappuccino, ultimately from Late Latin cappa (“cape, hood”).

definition: A Eurasian plant with small white flowers yielding caraway seed.
etymology: From Middle English caraway, carewey, carwey, from Medieval Latin carui, from Arabic كَرَاوِيَا (karāwiyā), via Aramaic from Ancient Greek καρώ (karṓ), κάρον (káron, “caraway”).

definition: Aromatic seeds of the caraway plant; used widely as seasoning.
A diet of foods high in starch that increases carbohydrate reserves in muscles.
example: Carbo loading is used by endurance athletes just before competing.

definition: A fullerene molecule having a cylindrical or toroidal shape.
Relating to or consisting of or yielding carbon.
etymology: From carbon + -aceous.

definition: Sauce for pasta; contains eggs and bacon or ham and grated cheese.
etymology: From the Italian carbonara, shortening of alla carbonara (literally “in the manner of charcoal burners”, or “in the manner of the Carbonari”), ultimately from carbone (“coal”).

definition: Saturation with carbon dioxide (as soda water).
example: Soda pop is basically sugar water with a little bit of flavoring and added carbonation.
etymology: From carbonate + -ion.

definition: A fully automatic system for high volume carbonation of products, which consists of a carbonator, CO2 infusion tube, and finished product holding tank with transfer pump.
Relating to or consisting of or yielding carbon.
etymology: From carbon + -ic.

definition: A weak acid known only in solution; formed when carbon dioxide combines with water.
The dead body of an animal especially one slaughtered and dressed for food.
etymology: Dated from the late 13th Century C.E.; from Anglo-Norman carcois, possibly related to Old French charcois. Cognate with French carcasse. But cf.

definition: Absence of systole; failure of the ventricles of the heart to contract (usually caused by ventricular fibrillation) with consequent absence of the heart beat leading to oxygen lack and eventually to death.
(mathematics) the number of elements in a set or group (considered as a property of that grouping).
example: The empty set has a cardinality of zero.
etymology: Derived from Latin cardinālitās. By surface analysis, cardinal + -ity.

definition: Of or pertaining to or affecting both the heart and the lungs and their functions.
example: Cardiopulmonary resuscitation.
etymology: From cardio- + pulmonary.

definition: Absence of systole; failure of the ventricles of the heart to contract (usually caused by ventricular fibrillation) with consequent absence of the heart beat leading to oxygen lack and eventually to death.
Affectionate play (or foreplay without contact with the genital organs).
Arctic deer with large antlers in both sexes; called ‘reindeer’ in Eurasia and ‘caribou’ in North America.
etymology: Borrowed from Canadian French caribou, from Mi'kmaq qalipu (“caribou”; compare qalipi, “to shovel snow”), from Proto-Algonquian *maka·lipowa (“caribou”, literally “it shovels snow”).

definition: Soft decayed area in a tooth; progressive decay can lead to the death of a tooth.
Set of bells hung in a bell tower.
etymology: Borrowed from French carillon.

definition: Playing a set of bells that are (usually) hung in a tower.
Any of various keel-shaped structures or ridges such as that on the breastbone of a bird or that formed by the fused petals of a pea blossom.
etymology: Borrowed from Latin carīna (“keel”). Doublet of careen and carene.

definition: A shrub of the genus Carissa having fragrant white flowers and plumlike red to purple-black fruits.
Edible scarlet plumlike fruit of a South African plant.
The violent theft of an occupied car.
etymology: Blend of car + hijacking.

definition: The savage and excessive killing of many people.
example: There was carnage after the school play ended with 96 deaths.

definition: Any lascivious contact by an adult with the sexual organs of a child (especially not involving sexual intercourse).
Sexual activity between individuals, especially the insertion of a man's penis into a woman's vagina until orgasm and ejaculation occur.
example: To have carnal knowledge of someone.

definition: Garage for one or two cars consisting of a flat roof supported on poles.
example: Franklin decided to improve his carport by walling in the sides and turning it into a garage.
etymology: From car + port, coined by American architect Frank Lloyd Wright in 1936 and modeled on the French porte cochère (literally “coach entrance”).

definition: A junction where one street or road crosses another.
The act of accomplishing some aim or executing some order.
Of or relating to cartilage.
example: Cartilaginous fish such as the angler fish have a skeletal structure made up of cartilage.
etymology: Borrowed from Latin cartilāginōsus (“full of cartilage, very gristly”), from cartilāgō (“cartilage, gristle”) + -ōsus (“-ous, -ose”); compare French cartilagineux.

definition: Fishes in which the skeleton may be calcified but not ossified.
A duct with cartilaginous walls.
The work of taking something away in a cart or truck and disposing of it.
etymology: From cart + -ing.

definition: A person who makes maps.
etymology: From cartography + -er.

definition: Of or relating to the making of maps or charts.
etymology: From cartography + -ic.

definition: A metal frame or container holding cartridges; can be inserted into an automatic gun.
A mechanism in a firearm that ejects the empty shell case after firing.
A mechanism in a firearm that pulls an empty shell case out of the chamber and passes it to the ejector.

definition: Obscene terms for penis.

Sexual activity between individuals, especially the insertion of a man's penis into a woman's vagina until orgasm and ejaculation occur.

definition: Bowl-shaped strainer; used to wash or drain foods.

Disparagement of a plan or hope or expectation.

definition: Soviet communism.

definition: Subscribing to the socialistic doctrine of ownership by the people collectively.

definition: A revolutionary anarchist doctrine that advocates the abolition of both the state and private ownership of the means of production.
The organization of a nation or economy on the basis of collectivism.

definition: Characterized by or having authority vested equally among colleagues.

definition: A cone-shaped chuck used for holding cylindrical pieces in a lathe.

definition: The part of the large intestine between the cecum and the rectum; it extracts moisture from food residues before they are excreted.

definition: Exploitation by a stronger country of weaker one; the use of the weaker country's resources to strengthen and enrich the stronger country.

definition: A believer in colonialism.

definition: Of or relating to the colon.

Visual examination of the colon (with a colonoscope) from the cecum to the rectum; requires sedation.

definition: The tendency for a color to look the same under widely different viewing conditions.

definition: Any of various tall perennial herbs constituting the genus Frasera; widely distributed in warm dry upland areas of California, Oregon, and Washington.
etymology: The spelling was probably influenced by Columbo (an old spelling of Colombo), under the assumption that the plant came from there.

definition: Having the form of a column.

definition: An epithelial cell that is shaped like a column; some have cilia.
A small band of jazz musicians.
example: The jazz combo played nightly at the little restaurant.

definition: Cause to burn or combust.

etymology: From Middle English combust (“burnt”), from Middle French combust, from Latin combustus, the perfect passive participle of Latin combūrere (“to burn up, to burn away”, transitive), whence also English combure.

definition: Move toward, travel toward something or somebody or approach something or somebody.

definition: The temperature range (between 28 and 30 degrees Centigrade) at which the naked human body is able to maintain a heat balance without shivering or sweating.
example: The demanding interview panel took him well out of his comfort zone.

definition: A source language consisting of procedural operators that invoke functions to be executed.
(computer science) the processing time required by a device prior to the execution of a command.
The act of commercializing something; involving something in commerce.
example: My father considered the commercialization of Christmas to be a sacrilege.

definition: Transactions (sales and purchases) having the objective of supplying commodities (goods and services).

definition: A municipal government that combines legislative and executive authority in the members of a commission.

Marine limpet.
Annual Old World plant with clusters of pink or white flowers; naturalized in United States.
Omnivorous opossum of the eastern United States; noted for feigning death when in danger; esteemed as food in some areas; considered same species as the crab-eating opossum of South America.
Deciduous semi-evergreen shrub used for hedges.

A form of socialism that abolishes private ownership.

definition: The travel of a commuter.

etymology: Borrowed from Italian concerto grosso.

definition: (anatomy) a structure that resembles a shell in shape.

definition: Willing to entrust personal matters.

Compatibility between persons.

The quality of agreeing; being suitable and appropriate.

definition: Relating to or resembling a cone.

The legal right in a prison for the inmate and spouse to have sexual intercourse.

definition: The quality of being enduring and free from change or variation.

definition: In a manner dependent on context.

definition: A device or control that is very useful for a particular job.

definition: Occupied with or fond of the pleasures of good company.

A public official who investigates by inquest any death not due to natural causes.

Control of a state or organization by large interest groups.

definition: Of or relating to corporatism.

definition: The dead body of a human being.
