etymology: From Japanese コスプレイヤー (kosupureiyā). Equivalent to cos- + player or cosplay + -er.

definition: Someone who designs or supplies costumes (as for a play or masquerade).
etymology: From costume + -er (occupational suffix) or + -er (Variety “-er”).

definition: Sudden and unexpected death of an apparently healthy infant during sleep.
An exclusive circle of people with a common purpose.
example: The new junior employee joined our merry after-hours coterie.

definition: Large American feline resembling a lion.
example: A cougar approached Warren at the Palomino Club and asked for a dance.
etymology: From French couguar, from Portuguese cuguardo, a deformation of Brazilian Portuguese suçuarana (earlier çuçuarana), from Old Tupi sûasuarana.

definition: A woman who is a council member.
etymology: From council + -woman.

definition: Going counter to the facts (usually as a hypothesis).
etymology: From counter- + factual.

definition: An action taken to offset another action.
etymology: From counter- + measure.

definition: Someone who designs clothing.
European annual with pale rose-colored flowers; cultivated flower or self-sown grainfield weed; introduced in North America; sometimes classified as a soapwort.
Tall coarse plant having thick stems and cluster of white to purple flowers.
Fecal matter of a cow.
A bell hung around the neck of cow so that the cow can be easily located.
example: This song would sound better with the addition of a cowbell.
etymology: From cow + bell.

definition: A hired hand who tends cattle and performs other duties on horseback.
etymology: From Middle English couherde, from Old English cūhierde, equivalent to cow + herd (“herder”). Doublet of Coward (the surname). Cognate with German Kuhhirte (“cowherd”). Compare shepherd, goatherd, swineherd, etc.

definition: Protective covering consisting of a metal part that covers the engine.
example: The mechanic removed the cowling in order to repair the plane's engine.
etymology: From cow + -ling.

definition: Domesticated bovine animals as a group regardless of sex or age.
example: Wait till the cows come home.

definition: Annoyed and irritable.
etymology: From crab + -y.

definition: A quarrelsome grouch.
Become fractured; break or crack on the surface only.
example: The glass cracked when it was heated.
etymology: Compare typologically English crevice (<< Latin crepō), Bulgarian пукнатина (puknatina) (akin to пу́кам (púkam)), Russian тре́щина (tréščina) (akin to треск (tresk)), щель (ščelʹ) (akin to щёлкать (ščólkatʹ)).

definition: Someone addicted to crack cocaine.
A purified and potent form of cocaine that is smoked rather than snorted; highly addictive.
etymology: So named due to the crackling sound of the pieces when it is smoked.

definition: A thin crisp wafer made of flour and water with or without leavening and shortening; unsweetened or semisweet.
example: A lobster and crab shell cracker.
etymology: From Middle English craker (“a boaster”), equivalent to crack (“to break, snap, utter, make a sound”) + -er. From crack (verb), the sound made when one is broken.

definition: A creator of great skill in the manual arts.
example: The jewelry was made by internationally famous craftsmen.
etymology: From craft + -er.

definition: Housing for a crankshaft.
etymology: From crank + case.

definition: A long narrow depression in a surface.
etymology: Borrowed from Hindustani किरानी (kirānī) / کِرانِی (kirānī).

definition: Small sunfishes of the genus Pomoxis of central United States rivers.
etymology: Borrowed from French crapet (“sunfish”).

definition: Expressions used when two dice are thrown and both come up showing one spot.
etymology: From Louisiana Creole craps, a corruption of English crabs.

definition: A rugged box (usually made of wood); used for shipping.
Neckwear worn in a slipknot with long ends overlapping vertically in front.
etymology: From French cravate, an appellative use of Cravate (“Croat”), from Dutch Krawaat, from German Krawatte, from Serbo-Croatian Hr̀vāt/Хр̀ва̄т (“Croat”).

definition: A pouch in many birds and some lower animals that resembles a stomach for storage and preliminary maceration of food.
Tiny lobster-like crustaceans usually boiled briefly.
etymology: 1620s, folk etymology (compare crawl) from Middle English crevis, from Old French crevice (“crab”) (French écrevisse), influenced by fish. Compare crayfish.

definition: In an insane manner.
example: He behaves crazily when he is off his medication.
etymology: From crazy + -ly.

definition: Worn and broken down by hard use.
example: A creaky shack.
etymology: From creak + -y.

definition: Make creamy by beating.
example: Cream the butter.

definition: Of the color of cream.
example: Creamy translucent pebbles.
etymology: From Middle English cremy, equivalent to cream + -y. Piecewise doublet of cremey.

definition: A manual or electric machine, used for creasing paper documents, hard covers and other types of coverstock.
A living organism characterized by voluntary movement.
example: Insects and other creatures.
etymology: Inherited from Middle English creature (“a created thing”), borrowed via Old French creature, from Late Latin creātūra, from creō. By surface analysis, create + -ure. Displaced native Old English ġesċeaft.

definition: Trustworthiness with money as based on a person's credit history; a general qualification for borrowing.
etymology: From creditworthy + -ness.

definition: Tendency to believe readily.
example: A tall story that strains credulity.
etymology: Inherited from Middle English credulite (“faith, belief”), borrowed from Middle French credulité (French crédulité), from Latin crēdulitās. Corresponding to credulous + -ity (compare credulosity).

definition: Disposed to believe on little evidence.
example: The gimmick would convince none but the most credulous.
etymology: Originated in 1576, borrowed from Latin crēdulus (“that easily believes a thing, credulous”), from crēdō (“I believe”).

definition: A wicker basket used by anglers to hold fish.
etymology: Inherited from Northern Middle English crele, possibly from an Old French root *creille, variant of greille (compare French grille), from Latin crāticula.

definition: Someone unpleasantly strange or eccentric.
example: Christmas creep.
etymology: From Middle English crepen, from Old English crēopan (“to creep, crawl”), from Proto-West Germanic *kreupan, from Proto-Germanic *kreupaną (“to twist, creep”), from Proto-Indo-European *grewbʰ- (“to turn, wind”).

definition: Any plant (as ivy or periwinkle) that grows by creeping.
example: Throwing it in creeper and then getting out to work alongside is strictly forbidden because it is too dangerous if anything goes wrong.
etymology: From Middle English crepere, from Old English crēopere, equivalent to creep + -er. Slang usage derived from phrase give the creeps or creep out (distinct from merely one who creeps).

definition: Creeping shrub of eastern North America having white bell-shaped flowers followed by spicy red berrylike fruit and shiny aromatic leaves that yield wintergreen oil.
The incineration of a dead body.
example: Cremation removes a significant amount of "closure" from the process of death.
etymology: Borrowed from Latin cremātiō, cremātiōnis; equivalent to cremate + -ion.

definition: A furnace where a corpse can be burned and reduced to ashes.
A mortuary where corpses are cremated.
Custard sauce flavored with vanilla or a liqueur.
A colorless or yellowish oily liquid obtained by distillation of wood tar; used as an antiseptic.
Desert shrub of southwestern United States and New Mexico having persistent resinous aromatic foliage and small yellow flowers.
etymology: Named for its smell, which resembles that of creosote, circa 1835 to 1845.

definition: Tropical shrub having glossy foliage and fragrant nocturnal flowers with crimped or wavy corollas; northern India to Thailand.
Any of various plants of the family Cruciferae with edible leaves that have a pungent taste.
Of a moderate yellow-green color that is greener and deeper than moss green and yellower and darker than pea green.
Any of various plants of the family Cruciferae with edible leaves that have a pungent taste.
Distinguished from the horned screamer by a feathery crest on the back of the head.
A person of subnormal intelligence.
etymology: From French crétin (“cretin, idiot”), likely from crestin, an Alpine dialectal form of chrétien, from Latin christiānus in the lost sense of “anyone in Christendom”, often with a sense of “poor fellow”.

definition: A deep fissure.
etymology: From French crevasse. Doublet of crevice.

definition: Sudden and unexpected death of an apparently healthy infant during sleep.
A person who weeps.
etymology: From Middle English criour, cryour, crier, from Old French crieor (Modern French crieur), derived from the verb crier. By surface analysis, cry + -er.

definition: Forbidden or tabu sexual intercourse between individuals.
Extramarital sex that willfully and maliciously interferes with marriage relations.
(law) recklessly acting without reasonable caution and putting another person at risk of injury or death (or failing to do something with the same consequences).
A specialist in criminology.
etymology: From criminology + -ist.

definition: Make wrinkles or creases on a smooth surface; make a pressed, folded or wrinkled line in; ‘crisp’ is archaic.
example: He crinkled the wrapper and threw it out.

definition: North American herb with pungent scaly or toothed roots.
North American herb with pungent scaly or toothed roots.

Psychotherapy that focuses on acute critical situations (depressive episodes or attempted suicides or drug overdoses) with the aim of restoring the person to the level of functioning before the crisis.
Cross in a pattern, often random.
etymology: From Middle English crist-crosse, crists-crosse (“Christ's cross”). By surface analysis, an apophonic reduplication of cross.

definition: Marked with crossing lines.
Pass from physical life and lose all bodily attributes and functions necessary to sustain life.
example: He'd seen my face, so I had to croak him.

definition: Needlework done by interlocking looped stitches with a hooked needle.
A black colloidal substance consisting wholly or principally of amorphous carbon and used to make pigments and ink.
example: Old crocks’ home.
etymology: From Middle English crok, crokke (“earthenware jar, pot, or other container; cauldron;

definition: Any of numerous low-growing plants of the genus Crocus having slender grasslike leaves and white or yellow or purple flowers; native chiefly to the Mediterranean region but widely cultivated.
example: A crocus bag.
etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin crocus, from Ancient Greek κρόκος (krókos, “crocus”), from an ancient Semitic language.

definition: Utter a hoarse sound, like a raven.
etymology: Imitative. Compare quonk.

definition: A singer of popular ballads.
example: My mom likes to listen to old crooners like Frank Sinatra and Tommy Dorsey.
etymology: From croon + -er.

definition: Singing in a soft low tone.
example: Her crooning soon put the child to sleep.
etymology: Inherited from Middle English cronyng.

definition: The practice of adopting the clothes or the manner or the sexual role of the opposite sex.
Dress in the clothes of the other sex.
etymology: From cross- + dress.

definition: Someone who adopts the dress or manner or sexual role of the opposite sex.
Fertilize by transferring pollen.
etymology: From cross- + pollinate.

definition: Of or relating to or characteristic of cross-pollination.
Two crossed bones (or a representation of two crossed bones) used as a symbol danger or death.
etymology: From cross + bones.

definition: The interchange of sections between pairing homologous chromosomes during the prophase of meiosis.
example: Lay one pole over the other and tie them together at the crossover.
etymology: Deverbal from cross over.

definition: A junction where one street or road crosses another.
etymology: From cross + road.

definition: The presence of an unwanted signal via an accidental coupling.
example: I couldn't hear the opening address because of all the crosstalk around me.
etymology: From cross- + talk. Usage in reference to the Chinese comedic performance is probably a loose calque from Chinese 相聲／相声 (xiàngsheng).

definition: Going or extending across a town or city.
example: The crosstown bus.
etymology: From cross- + town.

definition: Grown in many varieties for their brightly colored foliage; widely cultivated as a houseplant.
etymology: From New Latin crotōn, from Ancient Greek κροτών (krotṓn, “tick”), from the size and shape of the seed.

definition: Viscid acrid brownish-yellow oil from the seeds of Croton tiglium having a violent cathartic action.
Black birds having a raucous call.
etymology: The verb is a back-formation from crowbar.

definition: The part of a tooth above the gum that is covered with enamel.
etymology: Inherited from Middle English coroune, from Anglo-Norman corone, from Latin corōna (“crown, wreath”), from Ancient Greek κορώνη (korṓnē). Doublet of corona, korona, koruna, krona, króna, and krone.

definition: The act of executing by a method widespread in the ancient world; the victim's hands and feet are bound or nailed to a cross.
example: Rome used crucifixions as a deterrent, and standard for the 'vilest' crimes, such as slave rebellion.
etymology: From Middle English crucifixioun, from Late Latin noun of process crucifīxiō, from perfect passive participle crucifīxus (“fixed to a cross”), from crux (“cross”) + fīgō.

definition: Kill by nailing onto a cross.
example: Jesus Christ was crucified.
etymology: From Middle English crucifien, from Old French crucefier, from Late Latin crucificō, from Latin crucifigō.

definition: Fall apart.
example: He crumpled the note and threw it away.
etymology: From Middle English crumplen, cromplen, frequentative of Middle English crumpen (“to curl up, crump”), from Old English crump (“bent, crooked”). Equivalent to crump + -le.

definition: A disputant who advocates reform.
example: The crusaders of the Middle Ages.
etymology: From crusade + -er.

definition: Of or relating to or characteristic of the crust of the earth or moon.
etymology: From crust + -al.

definition: Movement resulting from or causing deformation of the earth's crust.
A rigid layer of the Earth's crust that is believed to drift slowly.
A person who lacks confidence, is irresolute and wishy-washy.
etymology: From cry + baby.

definition: Having become fixed and definite in form.
example: Distinguish between crystallized and uncrystallized opinion.

definition: Cause to take on a definite and clear shape.
example: He tried to crystallize his thoughts.
etymology: From crystal + -ize. The double l reflects the classical stem found in its etyma, Latin crystallus and Ancient Greek κρύσταλλος (krústallos), rather than the simplified spelling of the English base noun.

definition: An awkward and inexperienced youth.
example: Ew, I didn't know he also drew cub...
etymology: From earlier cubbe. Origin unknown. According to Pokorny, from Proto-Germanic *kubb-, from Proto-Indo-European *gup- (“round object, knoll”), from *gew- (“to bend, curve, convex, arch, vault”).

definition: An artistic movement in France beginning in 1907 that featured surfaces of geometrical planes.
etymology: From French cubisme. One story is that, in 1908, as a new canvas by Braque was being carried past, someone said, “Encore des cubes! assez de cubisme!”. The quotations below ascribe the coinage to Matisse.

definition: Relating to or characteristic of cubism.
example: Cubist art.
etymology: From cube + -ist.

definition: Food of a ruminant regurgitated to be chewed again.
etymology: From Middle English code, cudde, coude, quede, quide, from Old English cudu, cwidu, from Proto-West Germanic *kwidu, from Proto-Germanic *kweduz (“resin”). Doublet of quid (“material for chewing”).

definition: Affectionate play (or foreplay without contact with the genital organs).
A club that is used as a weapon.
example: The guard hefted his cudgel menacingly and looked at the inmates.

definition: The ball that the billiard player or pool player strikes with their cue.
(law) recklessly acting without reasonable caution and putting another person at risk of injury or death (or failing to do something with the same consequences).
example: One who causes another's death by culpable negligence is guilty of second-degree manslaughter.

definition: European biennial having a long fusiform root that has been made palatable through cultivation.
Someone concerned with the science or art or business of cultivating the soil.
example: As the crop gets bigger, the shank spacing on the cultivator will need to be adjusted accordingly.
etymology: From cultivate + -or, partly after French cultivateur.

definition: In a cumulative manner.
example: Mind has become self-reproducing through man's capacity to transmit experience and its products cumulatively.
etymology: From cumulative + -ly.

definition: Oral stimulation of the vulva or clitoris.
etymology: From Latin cunnilingus (literally “cuntlicker”). The meaning shift, not yet complete in the early twentieth century, perhaps derives from figurative uses where the name for a person stands for the name of a practice.

definition: In an attractive manner.
example: How cunningly the olive-green dress with its underskirt of rose-brocade fitted her perfect figure.
etymology: From cunning + -ly.

definition: A symbol for love in the form of a cherubic naked boy with wings and a bow and arrow.
Flavored with sour orange peel.
The side of a sidewalk that is bordered by a curb.
example: Policemen stood at intervals along the curbside.
etymology: From curb + -side.

definition: The process of forming semisolid lumps in a liquid.
Something unusual — perhaps worthy of collecting.
etymology: Clipping of curiosity, 1851. Compare cabinet of curiosities and French objet de curiosité.

definition: Large migratory shorebirds of the sandpiper family; closely related to woodcocks but having a down-curved bill.
Climber of southern United States having bluish-purple flowers.
Having curly leaves.
A craftsman who curries leather for use.
etymology: From Old French corier, from Latin coriarius (“tanner, currier”).

definition: Profane or obscene expression usually of surprise or anger.
Profane or obscene expression usually of surprise or anger.
Hanging cloth used as a blind (especially for a window).
example: He drew the curtains at 11:00pm before falling asleep.
etymology: Inherited from Middle English curtine, from Old French cortine, from Late Latin cōrtīna (“curtain”), a calque from Ancient Greek.

definition: (of a woman's body) having a large bosom and pleasing curves.
example: Hollywood seems full of curvaceous blondes.
etymology: From curv(e) + -aceous. Originally American English. First attested in the 1930s.

definition: Characterized by or following a curved line.
example: Curvilinear tracery.
etymology: From curve + -i- + linear, compare curve, linear.

definition: The relation between variables when the regression equation is nonlinear (quadratic or higher order).
Artifact consisting of soft or resilient material used to fill or give shape or protect or add comfort.
Stubbornly persistent in wrongdoing.
Make to specifications.
example: I had this desk custom-made for me.

definition: A reduction in quantity or rate.
etymology: Deverbal from cut back.

definition: The dead skin at the base of a fingernail or toenail.
etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin cutīcula (“cuticle, skin”). Doublet of cuticula.

definition: A low stool; formerly in Scotland, a seat in a church where an offender was publicly rebuked.
A steep-walled semicircular basin in a mountain; may contain a lake.
etymology: Unadapted borrowing from Welsh cwm (“valley”). Doublet of combe.

definition: A United States unit of weight equivalent to 100 pounds.
Predominantly photosynthetic prokaryotic organisms containing a blue pigment in addition to chlorophyll; occur singly or in colonies in diverse habitats; important as phytoplankton.
Of or relating to or characteristic of the atmosphere around a low pressure center.
example: Cyclonic cloud pattern.
etymology: From cyclone + -ic.

definition: A vacuum cleaner in which the dust is separated in a detachable cylindrical collection vessel or bin.
example: Cyclonic cleaners do not use filtration bags.

definition: A vacuum cleaner in which the dust is separated in a detachable cylindrical collection vessel or bin.
example: Cyclonic cleaners do not use filtration bags.

definition: An accelerator that imparts energies of several million electron-volts to rapidly moving particles.
etymology: From cyclo- + -tron.

definition: Tufted sedge of temperate regions; nearly cosmopolitan.
Resembling the ancient orgiastic worship of Aphrodite on Cyprus.
Of or relating to a normal cyst (as the gallbladder or urinary bladder).
etymology: From Middle French cystique, from Ancient Greek κύστις (kústis).

definition: A microscopic network of actin filaments and microtubules in the cytoplasm of many living cells that gives the cell shape and coherence.
etymology: From cyto- + skeleton.

definition: The aqueous part of the cytoplasm within which various particles and organelles are suspended.
etymology: From cyto- + sol.

definition: The degree to which something is toxic to living cells.
Pressing a marijuana concentrate to a hot surface in order to vaporize it and inhale the concentrate.
Panel forming the lower part of an interior wall when it is finished differently from the rest of the wall.
etymology: From Italian dado, first attested in 1664.

definition: A plane for making a dado groove.
A cocktail made with rum and lime or lemon juice.
etymology: First use appears c. 1920. From Cuban Spanish daiquiri, named after a beach on the south coast of Cuba, from Taíno.

definition: A farm where dairy products are produced.
example: Go and fetch the butter from the dairy.
etymology: Inherited from Middle English deyerie (“dairy, dairy farm”), from Anglo-Norman deyerie (“dairy”), from deye (“dairymaid”) + -erie (“-ery”); by surface analysis, dey (“dairymaid”) + -ry. Cognate with Scots dery, dyrie.

definition: A table linen made from linen with a damask pattern.
example: True damasks are pure silk.
etymology: From Middle English damaske, from Medieval Latin damascus, named after the city Damascus, where the fabric was originally made.

definition: Large hardy very fragrant pink rose; cultivated in Asia Minor as source of attar of roses; parent of many hybrids.
Long cultivated herb having flowers whose scent is more pronounced in the evening; naturalized throughout Europe to Siberia and into North America.
A slight wetness.
example: The dampness in the writing paper caused the ink to spread and smudge.
etymology: From damp + -ness.

definition: A condition in which white scales of dead skin are shed by the scalp.
example: Dandruff is on my collar again.
etymology: The word is first attested in 1545; the first element is obscure, but compare dander. The second element derives from a Northumbrian or East Anglian Middle English hurf (“scab”), from Old Norse hrufa.

definition: Of high quality especially of marijuana.
example: The dank cave was chilly and spooky.
etymology: From Middle English danke (“wet, damp;

definition: Having spots or patches of color.
Grey with a mottled pattern of darker grey markings.
Grey with a mottled pattern of darker grey markings.
The flesh of the legs of fowl used as food.
A camera filming from the dashboard of a car.
etymology: Blend of dash(board) + cam(era).

definition: Rape in which the rapist is known to the victim (as when they are on a date together).
The category of nouns serving as the indirect object of a verb.
etymology: From Latin datīvus (“appropriate for giving”), itself from datus (the past participle of dō (“to give”)) + -īvus (“-ive”).

definition: A covalent bond in which both electrons are provided by one of the atoms.
The category of nouns serving as the indirect object of a verb.
A female human offspring.
example: Her daughter cared for her in her old age.
etymology: From Middle English doghter, doughter, from Old English dohtor (“daughter”), from Proto-West Germanic *dohter, from Proto-Germanic *duhtēr, from Proto-Indo-European *dʰugh₂tḗr.

definition: Caused to show discomposure.
example: I was daunted by the prospect of interviewing such a heavyweight politician.

definition: A woman deacon.
etymology: Inherited from Middle English dekenesse; equivalent to deacon + -ess.

definition: A natural object consisting of a dead animal or person.
A building (or room) where dead bodies are kept before burial or cremation.
A dead season is a period during the year in which very few people want to buy a particular product or service.
example: My friend's coffeehouse suffered a dead season after Starbucks was opened nearby.

definition: At a complete standstill because of opposition of two unrelenting forces or factions.
example: The two factions are deadlocked over fringe benefits.

definition: Causing or capable of causing death.
example: A deadly enemy.
etymology: The adverb is from Middle English dedliche, from Old English dēadlīċe (adverb), from the adjective.

definition: A branch or a part of a tree that is dead.
etymology: From dead + wood.

definition: A special loved one.
etymology: From dear + -ie.

definition: The event of dying or departure from life.
example: Her death came as a terrible shock.
etymology: From Middle English deth, deeth, from Old English dēaþ, from Proto-West Germanic *dauþu, from Proto-Germanic *dauþuz, from Proto-Indo-European *dʰówtus. More at die.

definition: A bell rung to announce a death.
A concentration camp where prisoners are likely to die or be killed.
An instrument of execution by electrocution; resembles an ordinary seat for one person.
Instrument of execution consisting of a sealed chamber into which poison gas is introduced; used to kill people or animals.
The cellblock in a prison where those condemned to death await execution.
(psychoanalysis) an unconscious urge to die.
An omen of death or destruction.
A cast taken from the face of a dead person.
Putting a condemned person to death.
etymology: From death + penalty.

definition: The cellblock in a prison where those condemned to death await execution.
A clandestine military or paramilitary team who murder political dissidents or petty criminals (usually with the government's tacit approval).
A warrant to execute the death sentence.
(psychoanalysis) an unconscious urge to die.
etymology: From death + wish. Calque of German Todeswunsch.

definition: A list of persons killed in a war or other disaster.
The last few hours before death.
etymology: From Middle English dethbed, from Old English dēaþbedd (“deathbed; grave”), equivalent to death + bed. Cognate with Swedish dödsbädd (“deathbed”).

definition: Having the physical appearance of death.
example: A deathly pallor.
etymology: From Middle English dethlich, from Old English dēaþlīċ, equivalent to death + -ly.

definition: Mixed with impurities.
example: For quotations using this term, see Citations:debased.

definition: Someone who engages in debate.
example: William is a great debater.
etymology: From debate + -er.

definition: Unrestrained by convention or morality.
example: Congreve draws a debauched aristocratic society.

definition: Having a sophisticated charm.
example: A debonair gentleman.
etymology: Via Middle English debonaire from Old French de bon aire (“of good stock; noble”).

definition: Put someone through a debriefing and make them report.
example: The released hostages were debriefed.
etymology: From de- + brief.

definition: Cut the head of.
Execution by cutting off the victim's head.
example: If the headsman's axe was sharp and his aim was true, decapitation was a quick and relatively painless form of death.
etymology: From French décapitation.

definition: Dead.
example: He is deceased.
etymology: From decease + -ed, from Middle English deceas via Old French [Term?], from Latin dēcessus (“departure”), equivalent to dēced-, variation of dēcēdō, dēcēdere (“to go away”).

definition: Someone who is no longer alive.
etymology: From Latin decedens, present active participle of decedere (“to depart, die”).

definition: Someone who leads you to believe something that is not true.
etymology: Inherited from Middle English deceyvour, from Anglo-Norman decevour; by surface analysis, deceive + -er. Displaced native Old English swica.

definition: Lose velocity; move more slowly.
example: The car decelerated.
etymology: Late 19th c., from de- + (ac)celerate. Compare deaccelerate.

definition: The spread of power away from the center to local branches or governments.
etymology: From French décentralisation, decentralise + -ation or de- + centralisation.

definition: Kill one in every ten, as of mutineers in Roman armies.
example: Um, some sort of power overload. I'm afraid it decimated your breakfast.
etymology: The verb is first attested in 1591, the noun in 1641; borrowed from Latin decimātus, perfect passive participle of decimō (“to kill one tenth;

definition: Destroying or killing a large part of the population.
etymology: Borrowed from Latin decimātiō, a punishment where every 10th man in a unit would be stoned to death by the men who were spared. Used by the Romans to keep order in their military. Compare septimation and vicesimation.

definition: Relating to the use of or having the nature of a declaration.
etymology: From declare + -atory.

definition: A sentence (in the indicative mood) that makes a declaration.
Reduction or removal by the government of restrictions on a classified document or weapon.
etymology: From de- + classification.

definition: The inflection of nouns and pronouns and adjectives in Indo-European languages.
example: A page full of declensions.
etymology: From late Middle English declinson, from Middle French declinaison (Modern French: déclinaison), from Latin dēclīnātiō. Doublet of declination.

definition: A condition inferior to an earlier condition; a gradual falling off from a better state; decline.
example: Declination of the head.
etymology: From Middle English declinacioun, borrowed from Middle French declination, from Latin declinatio. Doublet of declension.

definition: Restore to its uncompressed form.
example: Decompress data.
etymology: From de- + compress.

definition: A decree issued on a first petition for divorce; becomes absolute at some later date.
etymology: See decree + Latin nisi (“unless”).

definition: Make legal.
etymology: Back-formation from decriminalization, equivalent to de- + criminalize.

definition: A deed made and executed by only one party.
example: I changed my name by deed poll.

definition: Mar or spoil the appearance of.
example: Scars defaced her cheeks.
etymology: From Middle English defacen, from Old French defacier, desfacier (“to mutilate, destroy, disfigure”), from des- (“away from”) (see dis-) + Late Latin facia.

definition: Someone who is resigned to defeat without offering positive suggestions.
etymology: From defeat + -ist, after French défaitiste.

definition: Have a bowel movement.
etymology: Borrowed from Latin dēfaecātus, the perfect passive participle of dēfaecō, see -ate (verb-forming suffix) and -ate (adjective-forming suffix). See also faeces; cognate with French déféquer.

definition: The elimination of fecal waste through the anus.
etymology: 17th century, borrowed from Late Latin dēfaecātiō.

definition: Normal response to the presence of feces in the rectum.
The weaponry available for the defense of a region.
The weaponry available for the defense of a region.
Excessive sensitivity to criticism.
example: His defensiveness was manifested in hurt silence.
etymology: From defensive + -ness.

definition: Showing deference.
etymology: From deference (or its Latin type *dēferentia) + -al; compare essence, essential; prudence, prudential, etc. Coined by Scottish novelist, poet and playwright Walter Scott.

definition: Act of putting off to a future time.
etymology: From defer + -ment.

definition: Intentionally contemptuous behavior or attitude.
etymology: From Middle English defiaunce, from Old French desfiance, from desfier. By surface analysis, defy + -ance.

definition: Capable of being defined, limited, or explained.
example: Definable terms.
etymology: From define + -able.

definition: The host in which the sexual reproduction of a parasite takes place.
example: Cats are the definitive host of Toxoplasma gondii.

definition: Associated with or tending to cause decreases in consumer prices or increases in the purchasing power of money.
example: Deflationary measures.
etymology: From deflation + -ary.

definition: An episode of deflation in which prices and wages decrease at an increasing rate and currency gains in value.
Bear the expenses of.
etymology: From Middle French desfrayer, French défrayer, from dé- + Old French fraier (“to spend”).

definition: The act of deactivating or making ineffective (as a bomb).
A degree on the centigrade scale of temperature.
The act of degrading people with respect to their best qualities.
example: Science has been blamed for the dehumanization of modern life.
etymology: From de- + humanization or dehumanize + -ation or de- + human + -ization.

definition: An appliance to extract moisture from the air and make the environment more comfortable.
example: In summer, we need to run the dehumidifier in the basement.
etymology: From dehumidify + -er.

definition: Preserve by removing all water and liquids from.
example: Carry dehydrated food on your camping trip.
etymology: From de- + hydrate.

definition: Do something that one considers to be below one's dignity.
example: He didn’t even deign to give us a nod of the head; he thought us that far beneath him.
etymology: From Middle English deinen, deynen (“to consider (something) suitable to one’s dignity or worth, condescend; to appear worthy; to condescend to grant (something), permit, vouchsafe; to regard (someone) as worthy;

definition: A type of firearms operating system which requires the bolt to overcome some initial resistance while not fully locked.
Ready-to-eat food products.
etymology: First attested 1864. From German Delikatessen, plural of Delikatesse (“delicacy, fine food”), at the time also spelled Delicatesse(n), from French délicatesse, from délicat (“fine”), from Latin delicatus (“alluring”).

definition: Ready-to-eat food products.
Extreme appetizingness.
etymology: From delicious + -ness.

definition: A line that indicates a boundary.
etymology: From French délimitation.

definition: Having the limits or boundaries established.
example: A delimited frontier through the disputed region.

definition: Guilty of a misdeed.
example: Delinquent minors.
etymology: Borrowed from Middle French délinquant, ultimately from Latin delinquens, present participle of delinquo.

definition: Suitable for or ready for delivery.
example: The packages were not deliverable because the roads had flooded out.
etymology: From deliver + -able.

definition: A person who rescues you from harm or danger.
etymology: From deliver + -er.

definition: Be false to; be dishonest with.
etymology: From Middle English deluden, borrowed from Latin dēlūdō (“mock, deceive”), from de + lūdō (“to make sport of, to mock”). See ludicrous.

definition: A light brown raw cane sugar from Guyana.
Dark rum from Guyana.
Light brown cane sugar; originally from Guyana.
A mark against a person for misconduct or failure; usually given in school or armed forces.
example: Ten demerits and he loses his privileges.
etymology: From Middle English demerit, demerite, from Old French desmerite (modern French démérite) and its etymon Latin dēmeritum. By surface analysis, de- + merit.

definition: Extensive landed property (especially in the country) retained by the owner for their own use.
A person with great powers and abilities.
etymology: From demi- + god. Calque of Latin semideus (“half-god”), which is probably a coining by the Roman poet Ovid for less important gods such as dryads.

definition: A zone from which military forces or operations or installations are prohibited.
example: Tensions exist on both sides of the demilitarized zone separating North Korea and South Korea.

definition: Act of changing from a war basis to a peace basis including disbanding or discharging troops.
example: Demobilization of factories.
etymology: From de- + mobilization or demobilize + -ation.

definition: The action of making something democratic.
etymology: From democratise + -ation or democrat + -isation.

definition: Assign to a lower position; reduce in rank.
example: She was demoted because she always speaks up.
etymology: From de- (“down”) + promote (“advance in rank/status (ending abstracted)”).

definition: Changed in nature or natural quality.
example: Denatured alcohol.
etymology: From denature + -ed.

definition: Ethyl alcohol that is unfit for drinking but is still useful for other purposes.
(used of statements) harmful and often untrue; tending to discredit or malign.
The outcome of a complex sequence of events.
Soft decayed area in a tooth; progressive decay can lead to the death of a tooth.
The branch of dentistry dealing with the prevention or correction of irregularities of the teeth.
The branch of dentistry dealing with the prevention or correction of irregularities of the teeth.
Having toothlike projections in the margin.
etymology: Borrowed from Latin dentātus, from dēns (“tooth”, oblique stem in dēnt-) + -ātus, see -ate (adjective-forming suffix).

definition: A leaf having a toothed margin.
Of metal e.g.
example: Dented fenders.

definition: The eruption through the gums of baby teeth.
etymology: From Latin dentītiō (“teething, dentition”).

definition: A denture adhesive is a product used to secure dentures in the oral cavity.
example: Denture adhesive comes in form of paste, powder or adhesive pads.

definition: Bad; unfortunate.
example: My finances were in a deplorable state.
etymology: The adjective is borrowed from French déplorable (“lamentable, regrettable”), or from its etymon Late Latin dēplōrābilis + English -able (suffix meaning ‘relevant to, suitable to’).

definition: Express strong condemnation of.
example: We deplore the government's treatment of political prisoners.
etymology: From Middle French déplorer, from Old French deplorer, from Latin dēplōrāre (“to lament over, bewail”), from dē- + plōrāre (“to wail, weep aloud”); origin uncertain.

definition: Having lost inhabitants as by war or disease.
example: The 15th century plagues left vast areas of Europe depopulated.

definition: The condition of having reduced numbers of inhabitants (or no inhabitants at all).
etymology: Inherited from Middle English depopulacion (also spelled depopulacyoun, depopolacion), borrowed from Latin dēpopulātiō. By surface analysis, depopulate + -ion.

definition: A facility where things can be deposited for storage or safekeeping.
etymology: Borrowed from Late Latin dēpositārius.

definition: Tending to diminish or disparage.
example: Managed a deprecating smile at the compliment.

definition: A prayer to avert or remove some evil or disaster.
etymology: From Middle French deprecation (French: déprécation), from Latin dēprecātiōnem, from dēprecātiō (“deprecation, invocation”), from dēprecor (“to avert, warn off; to deprecate”).

definition: Belittle.
example: The teacher should not deprecate his student's efforts.
etymology: Inherited from Middle English depreciaten, borrowed from Late Latin dēpretiātus / dēpreciātus, perfect passive participle of dēpretiō / dēpreciō (see -ate (verb-forming suffix)), from dē- + pretium (“price”) + -ō.

definition: Tending to decrease or cause a decrease in value.
example: A depreciating currency.

definition: In a depressing manner or to a depressing degree.
etymology: From depressing + -ly.

definition: A group of representatives or delegates.
example: The general sent a deputation to the enemy to propose a truce.
etymology: From Middle French députation, from Late Latin deputatio.

definition: Worn and broken down by hard use.
example: There was a derelict ship on the island.
etymology: The adjective and verb are a learned borrowing from Latin dērelictus (“(completely) abandoned, deserted, forsaken; discarded”), the perfect passive participle of dērelinquō (“to abandon, desert, forsake;

definition: Treat or speak of with contempt.
example: He derided his student's attempt to solve the biggest problem in mathematics.
etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin dērīdēre, the present active infinitive of dērīdeō (“to laugh at, make fun of, mock, deride”), from dē- (prefix denoting putting down or subjecting to indignity) + rīdeō (“to laugh;

definition: Contemptuous laughter.
etymology: From Old French derision, from Latin dērīsiōnem, accusative of dērīsiō, from dērīdēre ("to mock, to laugh at, to deride").

definition: Abusing vocally; expressing contempt or ridicule.
example: Derisive laughter.
etymology: From the participle stem of Latin dērīdeō (“to deride”) + -ive.

definition: In a disrespectful and mocking manner.
example: ‘Sorry,’ she repeated derisively.
etymology: From derisive + -ly.

definition: The deep vascular inner layer of the skin.
etymology: From New Latin dermis, from Ancient Greek δέρμα (dérma, “skin, hide”), from δέρω (dérō, “to skin, to flay”).

definition: An ascetic Muslim monk; a member of an order noted for devotional exercises involving bodily movements.
etymology: From Ottoman Turkish درویش (derviş), from Persian درویش (darvêš, “poor;

definition: Going or coming down.
Violate the sacred character of a place or language.
example: Desecrate a cemetery.
etymology: From de- + stem of consecrate.

definition: Treated with disrespect and contempt.
example: Many desecrated shrines and cemeteries.

definition: The process of reducing sensitivity.
example: She laments on society's gradual desensitisation to the horrors of xenophobia.
etymology: From de- + sensitization.

definition: The gradual transformation of habitable land into desert; is usually caused by climate change or by destructive use of the land.
example: The dust storms in Korea are the result of rapid desertification in China.
etymology: From desert + -ification (“process of becoming”).

definition: Thoroughly dried out.
example: Old boxes of desiccated Cuban cigars.

definition: A bold outlaw (especially on the American frontier).
etymology: From obsolete Spanish desperado, past participle of desperar, archaic form of desesperar (“to despair”), from Latin disperare (“to despair, to lose hope”), from prefix dis- + sperare (“to hope”). Doublet of desperate.

definition: Treated with dislike or contempt.
example: The dictator's cruelty made him the most despised person in the region.

definition: A feeling of scornful hatred.
Dominance through threat of punishment and violence.
etymology: From French despotisme; equivalent to despot + -ism.

definition: A state without friends or money or prospects.
etymology: From Old French destitution, from Latin dēstitūtiō (“abandoning”), from dēstituō.

definition: Do away with, cause the destruction or undoing of.
example: The fire destroyed the house.
etymology: From Middle English destroyen, from Old French destruire, Vulgar Latin *destrugō, from Classical Latin dēstruō, from dē- (“un-, de-”) + struō (“to build”).

definition: Developed or executed with care and in minute detail.
example: A detailed plan.

definition: Precisely determined or limited or defined; especially fixed by rule or by a specific and constant cause.
example: A determinate distance.
etymology: From Middle English determinate, determynat, determinat, from Latin dēterminātus, perfect passive participle of dēterminō (“to limit, set bounds”), see -ate (adjective-forming suffix) for more.

definition: Offensive to the mind.
example: Detestable person.
etymology: From Middle French détestable. By surface analysis, detest + -able.

definition: Treated with dislike or contempt.
Remove a monarch from the throne.
example: If the King does not abdicate, he will have to be dethroned.
etymology: From de- + throne.

definition: A state or condition markedly different from the norm.
example: Socrates was sentenced to death for his deviance.

definition: Halved hard-cooked egg with the yolk mashed with mayonnaise and seasonings and returned to the white.
etymology: From associating hot or spicy food with the Devil; see devil (verb); compare deviled ham, deviled crab, devilled sausages.

definition: As a devil; in an evil manner.
etymology: From devilish + -ly.

definition: The process of declining from a higher to a lower level of effective power or vitality or essential quality.
example: It is quite disheartening to witness the devolution of our nation's political discourse over the past several years.
etymology: Borrowed from Middle French dévolution, from Medieval Latin devolutio, devolutionis, from Latin devolvo.

definition: In a devout and pious manner.
example: She was devoutly Catholic.
etymology: From devout + -ly.

definition: A corticosteroid drug (trade names Decadron or Dexamethasone Intensol or Dexone or Hexadrol or Oradexon) used to treat allergies or inflammation.
example: Many dexamethasones act as anti-inflammatory agents.
etymology: From dex- + -a- + -methasone (“prednisone or prednisolone derivative”).

definition: Skillful in physical movements; especially of the hands.
example: Dexterous of hand and inventive of mind.
etymology: From Latin dexter (“right, ready”) + -ous. Displaced native Old English handcræftiġ.

definition: An isomer of glucose that is found in honey and sweet fruits.
Acidosis with an accumulation of ketone bodies; occurs primarily in diabetes mellitus.
Retinopathy involving damage to the small blood vessels in the retina; results from chronically high blood glucose levels in people with poorly controlled diabetes.
An ornamental jeweled headdress signifying sovereignty.
etymology: From Middle English diademe, dyademe, from Old French diademe, from Latin diadēma, from Ancient Greek διάδημα (diádēma, “band, especially worn around a tiara”), from διαδέω (diadéō, “bind around”).

definition: The usage or vocabulary that is characteristic of a specific group of people.
example: The immigrants spoke an odd dialect of English.

definition: A rationale for dialectical materialism based on change through the conflict of opposing forces.
etymology: See the etymology of the corresponding lemma form.

definition: Adornment consisting of a small piece of shiny material used to decorate clothing.
etymology: Borrowed from French diamanté (“adorned with diamonds”). From past participle of diamanter (“adorn with diamonds”), from diamant (“diamond”), from oblique stem of Ancient Greek ἀδάμᾱς (adámās, “hard metal, diamond”).

definition: Large deadly rattlesnake with diamond-shaped markings.
etymology: From diamond + back.

definition: Garment consisting of a folded cloth drawn up between the legs and fastened at the waist; worn by infants to catch excrement.
Dermatitis of the thighs and buttocks of infants; supposedly caused by ammonia in the urine in the child's diapers.
Dermatitis of the thighs and buttocks of infants; supposedly caused by ammonia in the urine in the child's diapers.
Of or relating to a diastole or happening during a diastole.
etymology: From diastole + -ic.

definition: The blood pressure (as measured by a sphygmomanometer) after the contraction of the heart while the chambers of the heart refill with blood.
Plant with a wooden hand tool.
example: Dibble Spring bulbs.
etymology: Possibly dib (“to dab lightly”) + -le (frequentative suffix indicating repetition or continuousness); however, the word dibble is attested earlier than dib.

definition: Divided or dividing into two sharply distinguished parts or classifications.
etymology: From Late Latin dichotomos, from Ancient Greek διχότομος (dikhótomos, “cut in half”). By surface analysis, dichotomy + -ous.

definition: An authoritative declaration.
etymology: From Latin dictum (“proverb, maxim”), from dictus (“having been said”), perfect passive participle of dico (“to say”). Compare Spanish dicho (“saying”). Doublet of dict.

definition: Deprive of by deceit.
A small worthless amount.
etymology: Short for diddly-squat.

definition: A small worthless amount.
A small worthless amount.
etymology: The Random House Historical Dictionary of American Slang suggests that this term is a variation of doodly-squat from 1934, a phrase that likely traces its earliest usage to Israel before entering American English.

definition: Suffer from a disease that kills shoots.
Suffer from a disease that kills shoots.
Formed by forcing molten metal into a die.
example: A die-cast seal.
etymology: From die + cast: From using a mold (die) to create a molding (cast).

definition: Of or relating to the diet.
etymology: From Latin diaeteticus, from Ancient Greek διαιτητικός (diaitētikós).

definition: The scientific study of food preparation and intake.
etymology: See dietetic + -ics.

definition: A specialist in the study of diet and nutrition.
Possessing a differential coefficient or derivative.
etymology: From differentiate + -able.

definition: Spreading by diffusion.
A transparent filter that reduces the light (or some wavelengths of the light) passing through it.
Tubular passage of mucous membrane and muscle extending about 8.3 meters from mouth to anus; functions in digestion and elimination.
Tubular passage of mucous membrane and muscle extending about 8.3 meters from mouth to anus; functions in digestion and elimination.
A laborer who digs.
etymology: From Middle English dyggar, equivalent to dig + -er. In the sense of "Australian soldier", attributed to the considerable time that soldiers spent digging trenches during World War I.

definition: The act of digging something up out of the ground (especially a corpse) where it has been buried.
A powerful cardiac stimulant obtained from foxglove.
etymology: Modern Latin, from Latin digitālis (“of the fingers”) (named in reference to the German common name for the plant, Fingerhut (“thimble”)). Doublet of digital.

definition: Put into digital form, as for use in a computer.
example: He bought a device to digitize the data.
etymology: From digit + -ize.

definition: Device for converting analogue signals into digital signals.
etymology: From digitize + -er.

definition: Confer dignity or honor upon.
example: He was dignified with a title.
etymology: From Old French dignifier, from Late Latin dignificare, from dignus (“worthy”) + ficare (in comp.), facere (“to make”). See deign and fact.

definition: An important or influential (and often overbearing) person.
etymology: Borrowed from French dignitaire.

definition: Digitalis preparation (trade name Lanoxin) used to treat congestive heart failure or cardiac arrhythmia; helps the heart beat more forcefully.
etymology: First attested in c. 1930, contracted from digitoxin, from taxonomic name Digitalis lanata + toxin.

definition: A message that departs from the main subject.
example: The lectures included lengthy digressions on topics ranging from the professor's dog to the meaning of life.

definition: (slang) offensive term for a lesbian who is noticeably masculine.
etymology: From Northern Middle English dik and dike (“ditch”), from Old Norse díki (“ditch”). Influenced by Middle Dutch dijc (“ditch; dam”) and Middle Low German dīk (“dam”). See also ditch.

definition: Become wider.
example: His pupils were dilated.
etymology: First attested in 1393, in Middle English; inherited from Middle English dilaten, from Old French dilater, from Latin dīlātō (“to spread out”), from dī- + lātus (“wide”) + -ō (verb-forming suffix). Doublet of dilatate.

definition: A vibrating device that substitutes for an erect penis to provide vaginal stimulation.
etymology: Unclear; possibly an alteration of English diddle. Compare the use as an expressive nonsense syllable in often sexual songs and the spelling dil doul, found in e.g.

definition: Showing frivolous or superficial interest; amateurish.
example: His dilettantish efforts at painting.
etymology: From Italian dilettante, present participle of dilettare (“to delight”), from Latin dēlectāre (“to delight”).

definition: Postpone doing what one should be doing.
etymology: Reduplication of dally.

definition: The spatial property of having dimensions.
example: All matter has dimensionality.
etymology: From dimension + -ality.

definition: The simplest ketone; a highly flammable liquid widely used as an organic solvent and as material for making plastics.
Change toward something smaller or lower.
example: The new emission standards have produced a measurable diminution in air pollution.
etymology: From Middle English diminucioun, from Anglo-Norman diminuciun, Old French diminucion, from Latin dīminūtiō.

definition: (chemistry) the property of certain substances that enables them to exist in two distinct crystalline forms.
etymology: From di- + -morphism.

definition: Informal terms for money.
etymology: Borrowed from Spanish dinero (“money”). Doublet of denar, denarius, denier, dinar, diner, and dinheiro.

definition: The customary or habitual hour for the evening meal.
etymology: From dinner + time.

definition: A picture (or series of pictures) representing a continuous scene.
etymology: Borrowed from French diorama.

definition: Any of several toxic or carcinogenic hydrocarbons that occur as impurities in herbicides.
etymology: PIE word *dwóh₁ From di- (prefix meaning ‘double; two’) + ox(ygen) + -in (suffix indicating a neutral chemical compound), a reference to the fact that the compound has two oxygen atoms.

definition: Of a cell or organism having two sets of chromosomes or twice the haploid number.
example: Diploid somatic cells.
etymology: From diplo- + -oid. By surface analysis, di- + -ploid.

definition: A graduated rod dipped into a container to indicate the fluid level.
example: I haven't checked the oil level of my car's motor since I lost the dipstick three months ago.
etymology: From dip + stick.

definition: A transmission mechanism in which the infectious agent is transferred directly into the body via touching or biting or kissing or sexual intercourse or by droplets entering the eye or nose or mouth.
Trueness of course toward a goal.
example: Rivaling a hawk in directness of aim.
etymology: From direct + -ness.

definition: The position of a director of a business concern.
example: The corporate bylaws require a quorum of outside directors, so as to balance the directorship.
etymology: From director + -ship.

definition: A song or hymn of mourning composed or performed as a memorial to a dead person.
etymology: From Middle English dirige, from Latin dirige (“steer, direct”), from the beginning of the first antiphon in matins for the dead, Dirige, Domine, deus meus, in conspectu tuo viam meam. Doublet of dirige.

definition: A person who is deemed to be despicable or contemptible.
Thoughts about sex or sexual encounters.
example: I have dirty thoughts about young college girls.

definition: An offensive conducted by secret police or the military of a regime against revolutionary and terrorist insurgents and marked by the use of kidnapping and torture and murder with civilians often being the victims.
example: Thousands of people disappeared and were killed during Argentina's dirty war in the late 1970s.
etymology: Calque of Spanish guerra sucia.

definition: An offensive or indecent word or phrase.
example: The child was made to sit in the corner as punishment for saying a dirty word.

definition: Having lewd thoughts.
Any orchid of the genus Disa; beautiful orchids with dark green leaves and usually hooded flowers; much prized as emblematic flowers in their native regions.
Involving or creating circumstances detrimental to success or effectiveness.
example: A disadvantageous outcome.
etymology: From disadvantage + -ous.

definition: The feeling of being alienated from other people.
example: Public disaffection.
etymology: From disaffect + -ion.

definition: Clarification that follows from the removal of ambiguity.
example: The lexical disambiguation relies on looking ahead to identify possible senses.
etymology: From dis- + ambiguation.

definition: In a disappointing manner.
example: The discoverer of argon, Sir William Ramsay, looked disappointingly ordinary.
etymology: From disappointing + -ly.

definition: Remove offensive capability from.
example: To disarm a man's wrath.
etymology: From Middle English desarmen (“to divest of arms”), from Anglo-Norman desarmer.

definition: Part; cease or break association with.
example: She disassociated herself from the organization when she found out the identity of the president.
etymology: From dis- + associate.

definition: In a disastrous manner.
example: The real value of the trust capital may be disastrously less than when the trust began.
etymology: From disastrous + -ly.

definition: Denying or questioning the tenets of especially a religion.
Perceptible by the senses or intellect.
example: Things happen in the earth and sky with no discernible cause.
etymology: From Middle French discernable, equivalent to discern + -able.

definition: Someone who demands exact conformity to rules and forms.
example: He is the chief disciplinarian in the school.
etymology: From discipline + -arian or disciplinary + -an.

definition: Renounce a legal claim or title to.
etymology: From Middle English disclaimen, from Anglo-Norman disclaimer, from Old French desclamer (French déclamer), des- + clamer.

definition: Showing or experiencing dissatisfaction or restless longing.
example: Saw many discontent faces in the room.
etymology: From dis- + contented.

definition: Expressing extreme contempt.
example: He was disdainful of those he thought of as the little people. He openly sneered at them. They mocked him behind his back.
etymology: From disdain + -ful.

definition: Freeing from false belief or illusions.
example: Disenchantment with the religion led to a sharp fall in church attendance.
etymology: From dis- + enchantment. In the social sciences sense a calque of German Entzauberung, as used by sociologist Max Weber.

definition: Deprive of voting rights.
etymology: From dis- + enfranchise.

definition: The act of withdrawing certification or terminating a franchise.
etymology: From disenfranchise + -ment.

definition: Release from entanglement of difficulty.
example: I had to disentangle him from his own shoelaces.
etymology: From dis- + entangle.

definition: An appearance that has been spoiled or is misshapen.
example: There were distinguishing disfigurements on the suspect's back.
etymology: From disfigure + -ment.

definition: Highly offensive; arousing aversion or disgust.
example: A disgusting smell.
etymology: By surface analysis, disgust + -ing.

definition: A lack of harmony.
etymology: From dis- + harmony.

definition: In a corrupt and deceitful manner.
example: He acted dishonestly when he gave the contract to his best friend.
etymology: From Middle English dishonestly (“disgracefully”); equivalent to dishonest + -ly.

definition: A discharge from the armed forces for a grave offense (as sabotage or espionage or cowardice or murder).
Lacking honor or integrity; deserving dishonor.
example: Dishonorable in thought and deed.

definition: The act of washing dishes.
etymology: From Middle English dihsse-wehssinge, dischwaschyng, equivalent to dish + washing.

definition: A low-sudsing detergent designed for use in dishwashers.
A low-sudsing detergent designed for use in dishwashers.
A machine for washing dishes.
Freeing from false belief or illusions.
etymology: From dis- + illusion: literally, the removal or undoing of illusion.

definition: A negative motivational influence.
etymology: From dis- + incentive.

definition: Unwilling because of mild dislike or disapproval.
example: Disinclined to say anything to anybody.
etymology: From dis- + inclined.

definition: Deprived of your rightful heritage.
Part; cease or break association with.
example: To disjoint limbs; to disjoint bones; to disjoint poultry by carving.
etymology: From Middle English disjoynen, from Old French desjoindre (“disjoin”), from Latin disiungō, from dis- + iungō (“join”).

definition: Separate the limbs from the body.
example: The tiger dismembered the tourist.
etymology: From Middle English, from Old French desmembrer, from des- (“de-”) + membre (“limb”) + -er (“verbal suffix”).

definition: Lacking order or methodical arrangement or function.
example: A disorganized enterprise.

definition: A condition in which an orderly system has been disrupted.
