etymology: From fore- + play.

definition: Indicate, as with a sign or an omen.
etymology: The verb is derived from fore- (prefix meaning ‘before with respect to time, earlier’) + shadow (“to shade, cloud, or darken”, verb).

definition: Foreshadow or presage.
etymology: First use appears before 1400, from Middle English foretellen, equivalent to fore- + tell.

definition: Planning or plotting in advance of acting.
example: With a little forethought we'd have planned for this contingency and not been stuck here now.
etymology: From Middle English forethouht, forethoght, from Old English *foreþōht (“forethought”); equivalent to fore- + thought. See also forethink.

definition: At any future time; in the future.
etymology: Compound of for + evermore, modeled after forever (for + ever).

definition: Easily excused or forgiven.
etymology: From forgive + -able. Partially displaced non-native Middle English pardonable (“capable of being pardoned, forgivable”) from Old French pardonable (“forgivable”).

definition: The act of renouncing; sacrificing or giving up or surrendering (a possession or right or title or privilege etc.).
Concerned with or characterized by rigorous adherence to recognized forms (especially in religion or art).
example: Highly formalized plays like ‘Waiting for Godot’.

definition: Make formal or official.
example: We formalized the appointment and gave him a title.
etymology: From formal + -ize.

definition: Having no definite form or distinct shape.
example: An aggregate of formless particles.
etymology: From form + -less.

definition: Of or relating to or of the nature of a formula.
etymology: From Middle French formulaire. By surface analysis, formula + -ary.

definition: Voluntary sexual intercourse between persons not married to each other.
etymology: From Middle English fornicacioun, from Old French fornicacion, from Latin fornicātiō, from fornix (“brothel”).

definition: The act of forsaking.
The ordinal number of forty in counting order.
etymology: From earlier fourteth, from Middle English fourtithe, fourtiþe; equivalent to forty + -eth. For the modern form, see the etymological notes at twentieth.

definition: A miner who took part in the California gold rush in 1849.
Ditch dug as a fortification and usually filled with water.
etymology: From Middle English fosse, from Old French fosse, from Latin fossa (“ditch, trench”).

definition: Bearing or containing fossils.
example: Fossiliferous strata.
etymology: From fossil + -i- + -ferous.

definition: Set in a rigidly conventional pattern of behavior, habits, or beliefs.
example: Obsolete fossilized ways.

definition: Using foul or obscene language.
example: Noisy foul-mouthed women all shouting at once.

definition: Offensively malodorous.
Using foul or obscene language.
example: Noisy foul-mouthed women all shouting at once.

definition: A child who has been abandoned and whose parents are unknown.
example: Foundling hospital.
etymology: From Middle English foundlyng, fondeyng, variants of Middle English fyndling, fyndlyng. By surface analysis, found + -ling.

definition: A hospital where foundlings (infant children of unknown parents) are taken in and cared for.
A specific size and style of type within a type family.
example: He is a real fount of knowledge!
etymology: Clipping of fountain, on the pattern of the pair mount, mountain.

definition: An abundant source.
etymology: From fountain + head.

definition: Of a chemical compound having a ring with four members.
An artillery gun that throws a shot weighing four pounds.
A playing card or domino or die whose upward face shows four pips.
Four times as great or many.
example: A fourfold increase in the dosage.
etymology: From Middle English fourfold, fourefold, from Old English fēowerfeald. Equivalent to four + -fold. Cognate with Dutch viervoud, Gothic 𐍆𐌹𐌳𐌿𐍂𐍆𐌰𐌻𐌸𐍃 (fidurfalþs).

definition: Noisy quarrel.
etymology: From French fracas, derived from fracasser, from Italian fracassare, from fra- + cassare, equivalent to Latin infra + quassare.

definition: A process that uses heat to separate a substance into its components.
example: Methane is separated from other hydrocarbons in a gas fractionation plant.
etymology: By surface analysis, fraction + -ation, or, by surface analysis, fractionate + -ion.

definition: Stubbornly resistant to authority or control.
example: A fractious animal that would not submit to the harness.
etymology: From fraction (“discord”) (now obsolete) + -ous.

definition: Sweet-scented sumac of eastern America having ternate leaves and yellowish-green flowers in spikes resembling catkins followed by red hairy fruits.
Characterized by directness in manner or speech; without subtlety or evasion.
example: Tell me what you think — and you may just as well be frank.
etymology: From Middle English frank, from Old French franc (“free”), in turn from the name of an early Germanic confederation, the Franks, from Proto-West Germanic *frankō (“javelin, spear”). Doublet of Frank, franc, and farang.

definition: Position of a fetus in which the buttocks are present at the maternal pelvic outlet.
An aromatic gum resin obtained from various Arabian or East African trees; formerly valued for worship and for embalming and fumigation.
etymology: From Old French franc encens (“noble incense”).

definition: Tall spreading three-needled pine of southeastern United States having reddish-brown fissured bark and a full bushy upper head.
An illegal enterprise (such as extortion or fraud or drug peddling or prostitution) carried on for profit.
A person or animal that is markedly unusual or deformed.
example: The two-headed calf was a freak.
etymology: For the meaning development compare Russian заско́к (zaskók) akin to ско́к (skók), скака́ть (skakátʹ).

definition: Unpredictably.
example: The weather has been freakishly variable.
etymology: From freakish + -ly.

definition: Become freckled.
example: I freckle easily.
etymology: The noun is derived from Late Middle English fracle, frekel, frekle (“freckle; pimple; fleck of colour in a stone”), a variant of frakne, freken (“freckle;

definition: Relating to or covered with or resembling freckles.
example: A smile grew across Jim's freckled face.
etymology: Inherited from Middle English frekled; equivalent to freckle + -ed.

definition: Sexual intercourse between individuals who are not married to one another.
A morpheme that can occur alone.
example: Book is a free morpheme, but the -s on books is not, because -s carries no meaning until joined to a free morpheme.

definition: Any state prohibiting slavery prior to the American Civil War.
etymology: From free + state, probably a calque of German Freistaat.

definition: Use (purified cocaine) by burning it and inhaling the fumes.
Where slavery was prohibited.
example: A free-soil state.

definition: A male person who has been freed from slavery.
etymology: From freed + man.

definition: A male person who is not a serf or a slave.
etymology: From Old English frēomann, equivalent to free + -man and paralleled by similar constructions in other Germanic languages. Doublet of preman.

definition: Free of restraints or rules.
example: Freewheeling foolishness.
etymology: From freewheel + -ing.

definition: Reject with contempt.
Pertaining to or worked or produced by friction.
example: Frictional electricity.
etymology: From friction + -al.

definition: Lacking all friction.
example: A perpetual motion machine would have to be frictionless.
etymology: From friction + -less.

definition: Excluded from a society.
example: Friendless homebody.
etymology: From Middle English frendles, from Old English frēondlēas. By surface analysis, friend + -less.

definition: Fire that injures or kills an ally.
To treat as a friend although the other party has romantic feelings.
Be lazy or idle.
Used as intensifiers.
example: It all went frightfully quickly.
etymology: From frightful + -ly.

definition: Sexually unresponsive.
example: A frigid woman.
etymology: Borrowed from Latin frīgidus (“cold”), from frīgeō (“to be cold”), from frīgus (“cold, coldness”), from Proto-Indo-European *sríHgos.

definition: (paleontology) a bony plate that curves upward behind the skull of many ceratopsian dinosaurs.
etymology: Of uncertain origin.

definition: Small quantity of fried batter containing fruit or meat or vegetables.
etymology: Inherited from Middle English fryture, from Middle French friture, from Old French friture, from Vulgar Latin *frīctūra, from Latin frīgō (“to fry”); compare fry.

definition: Spend frivolously and unwisely.
example: Fritter away one's inheritance.

definition: The trait of being frivolous; not serious or sensible.
etymology: Borrowed from French frivolité.

definition: The condition of being formed into small tight curls.
example: Her hair was in a frizz.
etymology: From Middle English fryse, from the verb. See above.

definition: Any of the convolutions of the outer surface of the frontal lobe of the cerebrum.
Surgical interruption of nerve tracts to and from the frontal lobe of the brain; often results in marked cognitive and personality changes.
An ornamental facade.
etymology: From Middle French frontispice, from Italian frontespizio or Medieval Latin frontispicium, from Latin frōns (“forehead”, oblique stem in front-) + -spic- (“to watch”, combining form of speciō) + -ium.

definition: Producing or covered with lathery sweat or saliva from exhaustion or disease.
example: The rabid animal's frothing mouth.

definition: Dessert of stewed or baked fruit.
A whimsically eccentric person.
etymology: Compound of fruit + cake. First attested in c. 1687. Sense 2, predated by nutty as a fruitcake, was first attested in c. 1952.

definition: Tasting or smelling richly of or as of fruit.
example: That moist and fruity dish is simply delectable.
etymology: From fruit + -y.

definition: Primly out of date.
example: Nothing so frumpish as last year's gambling game.
etymology: Either from frump or from Middle English frumple + -y.

definition: (football) the running back who plays the fullback position on the offensive team.
etymology: From full + back.

definition: (of wood) darkened or colored by exposure to ammonia fumes.
Oak given a weathered appearance by exposure to fumes of ammonia; used for cabinetwork.
The application of a gas or smoke to something for the purpose of disinfecting it.
etymology: From Middle English fumygacioun, from Old French fumigation, from Late Latin fumigatio, fumigationem, from Latin fumigo.

definition: A call that passes control to a subroutine; after the subroutine is executed control returns to the next instruction in main program.
A worker who holds or is invested with an office.
etymology: From French fonctionnaire; by surface analysis, function + -ary.

definition: Of or relating to or characteristic of Protestant fundamentalism or its adherents.
etymology: From fundamental + -ist, after a book series called “The Fundamentals: A Testimony to the Truth“ (1910).

definition: Raise money for a cause or project.
example: We are fundraising for AIDS research.
etymology: From fund + raise, probably a back-formation from fundraising.

definition: A ceremony at which a dead person is buried or cremated.
example: Hundreds of people attended his funeral.

definition: Wood heaped for burning a dead body as a funeral rite.
Any agent that destroys or prevents the growth of fungi.
etymology: From fungi- + -cide.

definition: Minute blackish gregarious flies destructive to mushrooms and seedlings.
Offensively malodorous.
example: The kitchen smelled really funky.
etymology: From funk + -y.

definition: A sequence of drawings telling a story in a newspaper or comic book.
Arousing or provoking laughter.
example: Funny stories that made everybody laugh.
etymology: From fun + -y.

definition: The dressed hairy coat of a mammal.
example: During the colonial period, Britain used Canada as a major source of furs.
etymology: The verb is from Middle English furren, from Anglo-Norman furrer, forrer, fourrer (“to line, stuff, fill”), from the noun.

definition: An interest followed with exaggerated zeal.
etymology: Borrowed from Italian furore, from Latin furor. Doublet of furor.

definition: Covered with a dense coat of fine silky hairs.
example: Furred animals.

definition: Having long narrow shallow depressions (as grooves or wrinkles) in the surface.
example: Furrowed fields.

definition: Marked by quiet and caution and secrecy; taking pains to avoid being observed.
example: A furtive manner.
etymology: From Middle English *furtyve (implied in furtyvely (adverb)), from Middle French furtif, furtive (“furtive, stealthy”) (modern French furtif), from Latin fūrtīvus (“clandestine, furtive, secret; concealed, hidden;

definition: Wilt caused by fungi of the genus Fusarium.
Of something having a dusky brownish grey color.
etymology: From Latin fusc(us) (“dark, dusky”) + -ous.

definition: A nuclear weapon that releases atomic energy by union of light (hydrogen) nuclei at high temperatures to form helium.
An artistic movement in Italy around 1910 that tried to express the energy and values of the machine age.
etymology: From future + -ism.

definition: The time yet to come.
etymology: From future (adjective) + -ity.

definition: Any igniter that is used to initiate the burning of a propellant.
An instrument which sets the fuze time on projectiles with mechanical time fuzes.
An anticonvulsant (trade name Neurontin) used to control some types of seizures in the treatment of epilepsy; also used to manage neuralgia caused by shingles.
etymology: From GABA + pent(yl) + -in.

definition: Street names for marijuana.
etymology: From Middle English gage, from later Old French or early Middle French gager (verb), (also guagier in Old French) gage (noun), ultimately from Frankish *waddi, from Proto-Germanic *wadją (whence English wed).

definition: Yielding a fair profit.
example: How can we find gainful employment with dignity for the uneducated?
etymology: From gain (“against, contrary”) + -ful.

definition: A simple sugar found in lactose.
etymology: From Ancient Greek γάλακτος (gálaktos, “milk”) + -ose (“sugar”). Piecewise doublet of lactose.

definition: Fragile mosquito-like flies that produce galls on plants.
In a gallant manner.
example: He gallantly offered to take her home.
etymology: From gallant + -ly.

definition: A slave condemned to row in a galley.
An instrument of execution consisting of a wooden frame from which a condemned person is executed by hanging.
Elastic straps that hold trousers up.
Pertaining to or producing electric current by chemical action.
example: A galvanic cell.
etymology: From French galvanique, named after Italian physiologist Luigi Aloisio Galvani (1737–1798) + -ique.

definition: Battery consisting of a number of voltaic cells arranged in series or parallel.
An electric cell that generates an electromotive force by an irreversible conversion of chemical to electrical energy; cannot be recharged.
etymology: Named after Italian physicist Luigi Galvani, who made early experiments in electricity.

definition: Battery consisting of voltaic cells arranged in series; the earliest electric battery devised by Volta.
To stimulate to action.
example: Galvanized into action.
etymology: Learned borrowing from French galvaniser. By surface analysis, galvano- + -ize. Named after Italian physiologist Luigi Aloisio Galvani (1737–1798).

definition: Affected by emotion as if by electricity; thrilling.
example: The new leader had a galvanic effect on morale.

definition: Viol that is the bass member of the viol family with approximately the range of the cello.
example: Start a prediction on it. We want gamba!
etymology: From viola da gamba, ultimately from Italian gamba (“leg”). Doublet of gam, gamb, jamb, and jambe.

definition: A license authorizing the bearer to kill a certain type of animal during a specified period of time.
A person employed to take care of game and wildlife.
etymology: From game + keeper.

definition: Making something more engaging by incorporating ideas and mechanics from games.
A laborer in a railroad maintenance gang.
etymology: Uncertain; see Wikipedia for various speculative etymologies.

definition: Rape (someone) successively with several attackers.
example: The prisoner was gang-raped.

definition: Someone employed to collect and dispose of refuse.
Cress cultivated for salads and garnishes.
A trowel used by gardeners.
Someone who takes care of a garden.
example: "Ponder the fact that God has made you a gardener, to root out vice and to plant virtue." — St. Catherine of Siena.
etymology: From Middle English gardener, either calqued or loaned from Anglo-Norman and Old Northern French gardinier.

definition: Any of various shrubs and small trees of the genus Gardenia having large fragrant white or yellow flowers.
A medicated solution used for gargling and rinsing the mouth.
etymology: From French gargouiller (“to gargle”), from Old French gargouille, gargole (“gutter, throat”). Compare gargoyle and Spanish garganta.

definition: A spout that terminates in a grotesquely carved figure of a person or animal.
etymology: From Old French gargouille, from Latin. Doublet of gargle. The Académie Française suggests the first attestation as gargoule in 1294.

definition: Instrument of execution consisting of a sealed chamber into which poison gas is introduced; used to kill people or animals.
(pathology) a deadly form of gangrene usually caused by clostridium bacteria that produce toxins that cause tissue death; can be used as a bioweapon.
A gun that fires gas shells.
The process of changing into gas.
example: Coal gas is produced by the gasification of coal.
etymology: From gas + -ification.

definition: Resembling gas.
example: Beans are a gassy food.
etymology: From gas + -y. Doublet of chaotic.

definition: Inflammation of the lining of the stomach; nausea and loss of appetite and discomfort after eating.
etymology: From international scientific vocabulary, reflecting New Latin combining forms: gastr- + -itis, from Ancient Greek γαστήρ (gastḗr).

definition: Inflammation of the stomach and intestines; can be caused by Salmonella enteritidis.
etymology: From gastro- + enteritis.

definition: Tubular passage of mucous membrane and muscle extending about 8.3 meters from mouth to anus; functions in digestion and elimination.
Of or relating to gastronomy.
example: Gastronomic adventures.
etymology: From French gastronomique.

definition: A cowboy of the South American Pampas.
etymology: Borrowed from Spanish gaucho, of uncertain origin.

definition: An awkward stupid person.
etymology: From a variant of gowk, from Middle English gowke, goke, from Old Norse gaukr (“cuckoo”), from Proto-Germanic *gaukaz (“cuckoo”). Cognate with Danish gøg, Swedish gök, German Gauch, Old English ġēac.

definition: Bright and pleasant; promoting a feeling of cheer.
example: A gay sunny room.
etymology: From Pitman kay, which it is derived from graphically, and the sound it represents. The traditional name gee was considered inappropriate, as the Pitman letter never has the sound of that name.

definition: The movement aimed at liberating homosexuals from legal or social or economic oppression.
A homosexual man.
A female homosexual.
A sexual attraction to (or sexual relations with) persons of the same sex.
etymology: From Middle English gaynesse, equivalent to gay + -ness.

definition: A small roofed building affording shade and rest.
etymology: Possibly from gaze + Latin future indicative conjugation-ending -bō, as in vidēbō (“I will see”), comparable perhaps to lavabo from Latin lavābō (“I will wash”);

definition: Small swift graceful antelope of Africa and Asia having lustrous eyes.
etymology: Unadapted borrowing from Middle French gazelle, from Old French gazel, from Arabic غَزَال (ḡazāl).

definition: A journalist who writes for a gazette.
etymology: The noun is borrowed from French gazettier (archaic), gazetier (“journalist, newspaperman”) + English -eer (suffix forming agent nouns denoting people associated with or engaged in a specified activities).

definition: A very large indefinite number (usually hyperbole).
A man who is (usually) old and/or eccentric.
example: Hi, geezer, you alright?
etymology: From guiser. Compare also German Low German Kieser (“an obstinate person; brute; savage”).

definition: A colorless water-soluble glutinous protein obtained from animal tissues such as bone and skin.
A French policeman.
etymology: Borrowed from French gendarme, a back-formation from gendarmes, from gens d'armes (“people of arms, armed people”), from gens + d' + armes.

definition: French police force; a group of gendarmes or gendarmes collectively.

A grammatical category in inflected languages governing the agreement between nouns and pronouns and adjectives; in some languages it is quite arbitrary but in Indo-European languages it is usually based on sex or animateness.
etymology: From Middle English gendre, borrowed from Old French gendre, borrowed from Latin genere (“type, kind”). Doublet of genre and genus. The verb developed after the noun. Displaced native Old English hād (“sex, gender”).

definition: An expert in genealogy.
etymology: From genealogy + -ist.

definition: An idea or conclusion having general application.
example: He spoke in broad generalities.

definition: The officer who holds the supreme command.
etymology: Borrowed from Italian generalissimo, superlative of generale.

definition: Agile Old World viverrine having a spotted coat and long ringed tail.
etymology: From Middle English genet, ionet, from Anglo-Norman genette, Middle French genette, jenette et al., of uncertain origin.

definition: Of or relating to the external sex organs.
example: Genital herpes.
etymology: From Middle English genital, from Latin genitalis (“of or belonging to generation”), from genitus, past participle of gignō (“to beget, generate”); see genus.

definition: An infection caused by herpes simplex virus type 2 (HSV-2) that is usually transmitted by sexual contact; marked by recurrent attacks of painful eruptions on the skin and mucous membranes of the genital area.
External sex organ.
(psychoanalysis) the fifth sexual and social stage in a person's development occurring during adolescence; interest focuses on sexual activity.
(psychoanalysis) the fifth sexual and social stage in a person's development occurring during adolescence; interest focuses on sexual activity.
Blunt or penetrating trauma or rape (vaginal or anal).
A small benign wart on or around the genitals and anus.
External sex organ.
etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin (membra) genitālia, substantive use of neuter plural of genitālis (“pertaining to generation or birth”). First attested in 1651.

definition: External sex organ.
Systematic killing of a racial or cultural group.
etymology: Coined by Polish Jewish lawyer Raphael Lemkin in 1943 or 1944 in reference to the Armenian Genocide (then known by other names;

definition: A man of refinement.
example: Please escort this gentleman to the gentlemen's room.
etymology: From Middle English gentilman, morphologically gentle + man, partial calque of Old French gentilhome.

definition: Having the earth as the center.
example: A geocentric coordinate system.
etymology: From geo- + -centric.

definition: A belief that Earth is the center of the universe and does not move.
The chemistry of the earth's crust.
etymology: From geo- + chemistry.

definition: Of or relating to or determined by geodesy.
etymology: From French géodésique. By surface analysis, geodesy + -ic.

definition: A lightweight dome constructed of interlocking polygons; invented by R. Buckminster Fuller.
(mathematics) the shortest line between two points on a mathematically defined surface (as a straight line on a plane or an arc of a great circle on a sphere).
With respect to geology.
example: Geologically speaking, this area is extremely interesting.
etymology: From geological + -ly.

definition: A chemical compound which has the same molecular formula as another but differs in geometric configuration.
With respect to geometry.
example: This shape is geometrically interesting.
etymology: From geometric + -ally.

definition: The branch of geology that studies the characteristics and configuration and evolution of rocks and land forms.
etymology: From geo- + morphology.

definition: Of or having a geosynchronous orbit such that the position in such an orbit is fixed with respect to the earth.
example: A geostationary satellite.
etymology: From geo- + stationary.

definition: A geosynchronous orbit that is fixed with respect to a position on the Earth.
Small Old World burrowing desert rodent with long soft pale fur and hind legs adapted for leaping.
etymology: From French gerbille, from Latin gerbo, from Arabic جَرْبُوع (jarbūʕ) or يَرْبُوع (yarbūʕ, “jerboa”). Doublet of jerboa.

definition: The branch of medical science that deals with diseases and problems specific to old people.
etymology: From Ancient Greek γῆρας (gêras, “old age”) (see γέρων (gérōn)) + ἰατρός (iatrós, “physician”); coined in English in 1909 by Ignatz L. Nascher in the New York Medical Journal on the model of pediatrics;

definition: The use of harmful bacteria as a weapon.
Relevant and appropriate.
example: He asks questions that are germane and central to the issue.
etymology: A variant form of german (“having the same parents; related”), adapted in this sense in allusions to its use in Shakespeare's Hamlet (see quotations at germaine).

definition: A brittle grey crystalline element that is a semiconducting metalloid (resembling silicon) used in transistors; occurs in germanite and argyrodite.
Containing seeds of later development.
example: My upbringing was the germinal idea behind the opera.
etymology: From oblique stem of Latin germen, germinis (“seed”) + -al.

definition: A layer of cells on the inside of the blastula.
A layer of cells on the inside of the blastula.
Stairway in India leading down to a landing on the water.
etymology: Borrowed from Hindi घाट (ghāṭ, “flight of steps leading to a river; mountain pass”), from Sanskrit घट्ट (ghaṭṭa, “a landing-place, steps on the side of a river leading to the waters”), from Dravidian.

definition: Formerly the restricted quarter of many European cities in which Jews were required to live.
example: The Warsaw ghetto.
etymology: Borrowed from the name of the Venetian Ghetto, whose etymology and original source language is uncertain. Compare Italian ghetto.

definition: A religious dance of Native Americans looking for communication with the dead.
A writer who gives the credit of authorship to someone else.
example: Smith was listed as the author of his autobiography, but a ghostwriter did most of the work.
etymology: From ghost + writer.

definition: Someone who takes bodies from graves and sells them for anatomical dissection.
etymology: Borrowed from French goule, from Persian غول (ġul) from Arabic غُول (ḡūl).

definition: Suggesting the horror of death and decay.
etymology: From ghoul + -ish.

definition: Large shaggy-haired toothless anteater with long tongue and powerful claws; of South America.
A large schnauzer.
Larva of a saturniid moth; spins a large amount of strong silk in constructing its cocoon.
A man who has sex with and is supported by a woman.
etymology: First attested in English in 1922.

definition: A formal association of people with similar interests.
etymology: From Middle English gilden, gulden, from Old English gyldan (“to gild, to cover with a thin layer of gold”), from Proto-West Germanic *gulþijan, from Proto-Germanic *gulþijaną, from Proto-Germanic *gulþą (“gold”).

definition: An appliance that allows an object (such as a ship's compass) to remain horizontal even as its support tips.
etymology: Alteration of gemel, from Old French gemel, jumel (“twin”) (French jumeau), from Latin gemellus.

definition: Disability of walking due to crippling of the legs or feet.
etymology: Attested since about 1660, perhaps from Dutch gimp or French guimpe, and likely from Old French guimpre, a variant of guipure, a kind of trimming.

definition: A form of rummy in which a player can go out if the cards remaining in their hand total less than 10 points.
A clothing fabric in a plaid weave.
etymology: From Malay genggang (“ajar; apart”), or a corruption of French Guingamp, the name of a town in Brittany, France, where this cloth may have been made.

definition: Of or relating to the gums.
etymology: Borrowed from New Latin gingīvālis.

definition: Inflammation of the gums.
etymology: From gingiva + -itis.

definition: Deciduous dioecious Chinese tree having fan-shaped leaves and fleshy yellow seeds; exists almost exclusively in cultivation especially as an ornamental street tree.
etymology: From Japanese 銀杏 (ginkyō), from Chinese 銀杏／银杏 (yínxìng, “silver apricot”).

definition: Constituting the order Ginkgoales; includes the genus Ginkgo and extinct forms.
Befitting or characteristic of a young girl.
example: Girlish charm.
etymology: From girl + -ish.

definition: Thick-walled muscular pouch below the crop in many birds and reptiles for grinding food.
etymology: From Middle English gyser, geser, from Old French gesier, giser et al. (French gésier), from Latin gigēria.

definition: (used especially of fruits) preserved by coating with or allowing to absorb sugar.
Of or relating to or resembling gladiators or their combat.
example: Gladiatorial combats.
etymology: From Latin gladiātōrius + -al. By surface analysis, gladiator + -ial.

definition: Experiencing joy and pleasure.
etymology: From glad + -ness.

definition: Alluring beauty or charm (often with sex-appeal).
Alluring beauty or charm (often with sex-appeal).
etymology: Borrowed from Scots glamour (“magic”), alteration of Middle English gramere (“grammar”), from Old French gramaire. Doublet of glamoury, gramarye, grammar, and grimoire.

definition: Camping glamorously, i.e., with expensive equipment.
etymology: Blend of glamorous + camping. Of UK origin, first appears c. 2005 in The Guardian, adopted in the U.S. by 2007.

definition: A small rounded structure; especially that at the end of the penis or clitoris.
etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin glāns (“acorn”).

definition: The conical mass of erectile tissue that forms the head of the penis.
etymology: From New Latin glāns pēnis (“glans of the penis”), pēnis being a genitive.

definition: In a glaring manner.
example: It was glaringly obvious.
etymology: From glaring + -ly.

definition: A building with glass walls and roof; for the cultivation and exhibition of plants under controlled conditions.
etymology: From Middle English glasehows, glashous, glashows; equivalent to glass + house.

definition: Someone who cuts flat glass to size.
etymology: From Middle English glazier, glasier, glasyer, glasiere, variants (due to influence from words in -yer) of Middle English glaser, equivalent to glass + -er.

definition: Full of high-spirited delight.
etymology: From glee + -ful.

definition: Of or relating to neuroglia.
etymology: From glia + -al.

definition: A cell of the neuroglia.
Artfully persuasive in speech.
A slight suggestion or vague understanding.
A fast-growing malignant brain tumor composed of spongioblasts; nearly always fatal.
etymology: From glio- + blastoma.

definition: A tumor of the brain consisting of neuroglia.
etymology: From glia + -oma.

definition: The quality of shining with a bright reflected light.
etymology: From Middle English glisnen, glistnen, from Old English glisnian, itself from Proto-West Germanic *glisnōn, while ultimately deriving from Proto-Germanic *glisnōną.

definition: A compact mass.
example: He put a glob of paint into the cup and went on painting.
etymology: Possibly a blend of blob + gob, or a clipping of globule. An element of sound symbolism is clearly involved: compare such phonetically and semantically similar words as glop, gop, lob, blob, lump, clump and clod.

definition: Tropical American herb having rose to red or purple flowers that can be dried without losing color.
A hormone secreted by the pancreas; stimulates increases in blood sugar levels in the blood (thus opposing the action of insulin).
etymology: From gluco- + Ancient Greek ἄγων (ágōn), present participle of ἄγω (ágō, “push forward, put in motion; stir up; excite, urge”).

definition: A steroid hormone that is produced by the adrenal cortex of animals; affects functioning of gonads and has anti-inflammatory activity.
etymology: From gluco- + corticoid.

definition: An amino derivative of glucose that is a component of many polysaccharides.
etymology: From glucose + -amine.

definition: Having the sticky properties of an adhesive.
etymology: From Latin glūtinōsus. By surface analysis, gluten + -ous.

definition: A person who is devoted to eating and drinking to excess.
example: Such a glutton would eat until his belly hurts.
etymology: From Middle English glotoun, from Old French gloton, gluton, from Latin gluttō, gluttōnis (“glutton”).

definition: A metabolic process that breaks down carbohydrates and sugars through a series of reactions to either pyruvic acid or lactic acid and releases energy for the body in the form of ATP.
etymology: From glyco- + -lysis.

definition: Used of old persons or old trees; covered with knobs or knots.
example: Gnarled and knotted hands.
etymology: First attested Shakespeare 1603: : Thy sharpe and sulpherous bolt Splits the vn-wedgable [unwedgable] and gnarled Oke [oak]. : Measure for Measure, Act II, scene ii, line 116 Variant of knurled, from knurl.

definition: Any of various small biting flies: midges; biting midges; black flies; sand flies.
etymology: From Middle English gnat, from Old English gnætt (“gnat; midge;

definition: A laminated metamorphic rock similar to granite.
etymology: From German Gneis, from Middle High German gneist (“spark”), from Old High German gneisto (“spark”). More at gnast.

definition: A legendary creature resembling a tiny old man; lives in the depths of the earth and guards buried treasure.
example: The gnomes of Zurich.
etymology: From French gnome (“gnome”), from New Latin gnomus, used by Paracelsus as a synonym for pygmaeus (“pygmy”).

definition: Intuitive knowledge of spiritual truths; said to have been possessed by ancient Gnostics.
etymology: Derived from Ancient Greek γνῶσῐς (gnôsĭs, “knowledge”).

definition: Compelled forcibly by an outside agency.
example: Mobs goaded by blind hatred.

definition: A verbalization that encourages you to attempt something.
One of a pair of posts (usually joined by a crossbar) that are set up as a goal at each end of a playing field.
etymology: From goal + post.

definition: A large number or amount.
Located in a dismal or remote area; desolate.
example: A godforsaken wilderness crossroads.
etymology: From god + forsaken.

definition: Not revering god.
etymology: From god + -less. Compare Saterland Frisian godloos (“godless”), West Frisian goddeleas (“godless; wicked”), Dutch goddeloos (“godless;

definition: Look with amazement; look stupidly.
etymology: From 14th century Middle English gogelen (“to roll (eyes), to look sideways”). Earlier source is unknown. The noun is attested from the 17th century. Compare Irish gog (“a nod, a slight motion”).

definition: An electronic device that receives television signals and displays them on a screen.
etymology: From goggle (“to stare at”) + box.

definition: Of Atlantic coastal waters; commonly used for bait.
etymology: Named for its prominent eyes. From adj. google ('bulging').

definition: With eyes or mouth open in surprise.
A miner who digs or pans for gold in a gold field.
etymology: Literal sense is from c. the 1830s; the figurative sense (a woman who seeks money in a relationship) is from 1915.

definition: An elderly person.
Any of several callas of the genus Zantedeschia having yellow spathes.
Chinese clematis with serrate leaves and large yellow flowers.
Bright yellow songbird with black wings.
Giving top executives lucrative benefits that must be paid by the acquirer if they are discharged after a takeover.
Small slender woolly annual with very narrow opposite leaves and branches bearing solitary golden-yellow flower heads; southwestern Oregon to Baja California and Arizona; often cultivated.
American finch whose male has yellow body plumage in summer.
etymology: From Middle English goldfinch, goldfynch, goldefynch, from Old English goldfinċ, equivalent to gold + finch.

definition: Early-flowering perennial of southern and southeastern Europe with flower heads resembling those of goldenrod.
Aventurine spangled densely with fine gold-colored particles.
Destroyed or killed.
example: We are gone geese.
etymology: From Middle English gon, igon, gan, ȝegan, from Old English gān, ġegān, from Proto-Germanic *gānaz (“gone”), past participle of *gāną (“to go”).

definition: A person in desperate straits; someone doomed.
example: I'm a goner if this plan doesn't work.
etymology: From gone + -er. First attestations around 1850.

definition: A common venereal disease caused by the bacterium Neisseria gonorrhoeae; symptoms are painful urination and pain around the urethra.
Pod of the peanut vine containing usually 2 nuts or seeds; ‘groundnut’ and ‘monkey nut’ are British terms.
Pod of the peanut vine containing usually 2 nuts or seeds; ‘groundnut’ and ‘monkey nut’ are British terms.
etymology: From goober + pea.

definition: Large in amount or extent or degree.
example: A goodly amount.
etymology: From Middle English goodly, goodlich, gōdlich, from Old English gōdlīċ (“good, goodly”), from Proto-West Germanic *gōdalīk, from Proto-Germanic *gōdalīkaz (“good, goodly”); equivalent to good + -ly.

definition: Soft and sticky.
example: Gooey liquid covered the floor.
etymology: The adjective is derived from goo + -ey (a variant of -y (suffix forming adjectives with the sense ‘having the quality of’)). The noun is derived from the adjective.

definition: An awkward stupid person.
example: The Buddhist term 権化 is read as gonge, using the kanji's goon readings.
etymology: * Etymology 1, noun sense 5 ("guard") was influenced by both etymology 1, noun sense 1 and etymology 1, noun sense 3, though not by The Goon Show reference, which arose about 10 years after WWII.

definition: Any thick, viscous matter.
etymology: 1930s, perhaps a variant of goo; compare gloop and glob.

definition: Spiny Eurasian shrub having greenish purple-tinged flowers and ovoid yellow-green or red-purple berries.
example: Robert and Susan were so in love with each other that nobody could go near them without feeling like a gooseberry.
etymology: From goose + berry. It is possible that the first element was originally something related to the gros- of French groseille and/or the kruis- of Dutch kruisbes but has been altered by folk etymology.

definition: Any of a variety of strong alcoholic drinks made of gooseberries.
In an impressively beautiful manner.
example: The Princess was gorgeously dressed.
etymology: From gorgeous + -ly.

definition: Very spiny and dense evergreen shrub with fragrant golden-yellow flowers; common throughout western Europe.
etymology: From Middle English gorst, gors, from Old English gors, gorst, from Proto-West Germanic *gorst, from Proto-Germanic *gurstaz or Proto-West Germanic *gerstu (“barley”).

definition: Folk music consisting of a genre of a cappella music originating with Black slaves in the United States and featuring call and response; influential on the development of other genres of popular music (especially soul).
Characterized by unusual lightness and delicacy.
example: Gossamer shading through his playing.

definition: Prone to friendly informal communication.
etymology: From gossip + -y.

definition: An opaque watercolor prepared with gum.
etymology: Unadapted borrowing from French gouache, from Italian guazzo. Doublet of guazzo.

definition: Characterized by beauty of movement, style, form, or execution.
example: She is a graceful dancer.
etymology: From Middle English graceful. By surface analysis, grace + -ful.

definition: Relative position in a graded series.
example: Subtle gradations in color.
etymology: Borrowed from French gradation. By surface analysis, grade + -ation.

definition: The intoxicating agent in fermented and distilled liquors; used pure or denatured as a solvent or in medicines and colognes and cleaning solutions and rocket fuel; proposed as a renewable clean-burning additive to gasoline.
Pasture grass of plains of South America and western North America.
example: Traditionally Cucurbita maxima and Cucurbita moschata have been placed into two groups - pumpkins and grammas respectively.
etymology: Pronunciation spelling of grandma.

definition: Pasture grass of plains of South America and western North America.

A grammatical category in inflected languages governing the agreement between nouns and pronouns and adjectives; in some languages it is quite arbitrary but in Indo-European languages it is usually based on sex or animateness.
The father of your father or mother.
example: Hey gramps, get off the road!
etymology: From gramp + -s (hypocoristic suffix).

definition: The father of your father or mother.
etymology: From grand- + daddy.

definition: In a grand manner.
example: The mansion seemed grandly large by today's standards.
etymology: From grand + -ly.

definition: A recipient of a grant.
etymology: From Middle English grauntees pl, from Old French granté, participle of granter, equivalent to grant + -ee.

definition: The quality of being composed of relatively large particles.
etymology: From granular + -ity.

definition: A tiny grain.
etymology: Borrowed from French granule or directly from Late Latin grānulum, diminutive of Latin grānum (“grain”); for more, see grain. By surface analysis, grain + -ule.

definition: Small Australian parakeet usually light green with black and yellow markings in the wild but bred in many colors.
Make happy or satisfied.
example: Gratify the critics.
etymology: From French gratifier, from Latin grātificō (“to do a favor to, oblige, please, gratify”), from grātus (“kind, pleasing”) + faciō (“to make”).

definition: In an uncalled-for manner.
example: He insulted us gratuitously.
etymology: From gratuitous + -ly.

definition: A person who earns a living by digging graves.
etymology: From grave + digger.

definition: A tool used by an engraver.
etymology: From Middle English gravere, graver, gravoure, from Old English græfere, grafere (“graver; engraver; sculptor”), equivalent to grave (“to engrave”) + -er.

definition: Old World lemming.
Large shaggy-haired toothless anteater with long tongue and powerful claws; of South America.
Large flightless auk of rocky islands off northern Atlantic coasts; extinct.
etymology: Probably from an early Scandinavian word (compare Old (West) Norse álka, Norwegian alke (“razorbill”)).

definition: In a greedy manner.
example: The two dogs greedily devoured the meat.
etymology: From Middle English gredyly, gredily, from Old English grǣdiglīce, grǣdelīce; equivalent to greedy + -ly.

definition: Street names for marijuana.
etymology: Named after the stage play The Green Goddess (1921) because of its green color.

definition: A person who greets.
example: The newcomers were met by smiling greeters.
etymology: From Middle English greter, gretter, equivalent to greet + -er.

definition: Old World lemming.
In a grievous manner.
example: The resolute but unbroken Germany, grievously wounded but far from destruction, was able to lay the firm foundations for military revival.
etymology: From Middle English grevously; equivalent to grievous + -ly.

definition: Winged monster with the head of an eagle and the body of a lion.
etymology: See griffin.

definition: Large vulture of southern Europe and northern Africa having pale plumage with black wings.
A person who swindles you by means of deception or fraud.
etymology: From grift + -er; or probably an alteration of grafter (“a corrupt person, one who accepts bribes”), which is essentially a doublet of the same word. Originally circus slang (carny;

definition: A manual of black magic (for invoking spirits and demons).
etymology: Borrowed from French grimoire, a variant of grammaire, from Old French gramaire (“grammar; grimoire; conjurer, magician”), from Latin grammatica (“grammar;

definition: A revolving stone shaped like a disk; used to grind or sharpen or polish edge tools.
etymology: From Middle English grind-ston, grindistan, (also as grindel-ston), equivalent to grind + stone. Cognate with Scots grindstane.

definition: Acute abdominal pain (especially in infants).
Tough elastic tissue; mostly converted to bone in adults.
etymology: From Middle English gristel, grystyl, from Old English gristel (“gristle, cartilage”), Proto-West Germanic *gristl, of obscure origin; possibly from a pre-Germanic substrate language.

definition: Stunned or confused and slow to react (as from blows or drunkenness or exhaustion).
The crease at the junction of the inner part of the thigh with the trunk together with the adjacent region and often including the external genitals.
example: He pulled a muscle in his groin.
etymology: From earlier grine, from Middle English grinde, grynde, from Old English grynde (“abyss”) (perhaps also "depression, hollow"), probably related to Proto-Germanic *grunduz; see ground.

definition: The cutting of spiral grooves on the inside of the barrel of a firearm.
The total valuation of the estate's assets at the time of the person's death.
In a grotesque manner.
example: Behind the house lay two nude figures grotesquely bald, with deliberate knife-slashes marking their bodies.
etymology: From grotesque + -ly.

definition: A bad-tempered person.
example: I don't feel like hanging around with that grouch.
etymology: From Middle English grouchen, variant of grucchen (“to complain, mumble, murmur”). See grutch.

definition: Small pygmy rattlesnake.
(baseball) a hit that travels along the ground.
etymology: From Middle English grounder, grownder, equivalent to ground + -er.

definition: A North American vine with fragrant blossoms and edible tubers; important food crop of Native Americans.
etymology: From ground + nut. Compare Icelandic jarðhneta, German Erdnuss (both cognate with earthnut) and Hungarian földimogyoró.

definition: An oil from peanuts; used in cooking and making soap.
A North American vine with fragrant blossoms and edible tubers; important food crop of Native Americans.
Decision making by a group (especially in a manner that discourages creativity or individual responsibility).
etymology: Coined by William H. Whyte in 1952, from group + think, modelled on earlier doublethink from Orwell's Nineteen Eighty-Four.

definition: Show submission or fear.
example: She refused to grovel in front of the bully, standing her ground.
etymology: From Middle English *grovelen, from Old Norse grufla, grœfla (“to grovel”), from Proto-Germanic *grubilōną (“to dig, delve into”), from Proto-Indo-European *gʰrebʰ‑ (“to dig, scrape, scrabble, scratch”);

definition: A speaker whose voice sounds like a growl.
etymology: From growl + -er. Sense "jug" is 19th century American slang, of uncertain origin.

definition: Of especially an attitude.
example: Gave grudging consent.

definition: A thin porridge (usually oatmeal or cornmeal).
etymology: From Middle English gruel, gruwel, greuel, growel (“meal or flour made from beans, lentils, etc.”), from Old French gruel (“coarse meal;

definition: A bad-tempered person.
etymology: Uncertain. Possibly altered from grum, see there for more.

definition: Thickly covered with ingrained dirt or soot.
example: A grungy kitchen.
etymology: Probably a blend of grunt + dingy, influenced by grimy.

definition: A purine base found in DNA and RNA; pairs with cytosine.
etymology: From guano + -ine. Guanine was named by the German chemist Julius Bodo Unger in 1846 who isolated it from guano.

definition: The excrement of sea birds; used as fertilizer.
etymology: Borrowed from Spanish guano, from Quechua wanu.

definition: Drought-tolerant herb grown for forage and for its seed which yield a gum used as a thickening agent or sizing material.
A gum from seeds of the guar plant; used to thicken foods and as sizing for paper and cloth.
etymology: From guar (“type of legume”) + gum.

definition: A railing placed alongside a stairway or road for safety.
etymology: From guard + rail.

definition: Unacceptable behavior (especially ludicrously false statements).
etymology: Onomatopoeic. Compare Norwegian gufs (“puff of wind”), guffa (“to blow softly”).

definition: The passage between the pharynx and the stomach.
etymology: From Middle English golet, borrowed from Old French goulet, from Latin gula.

definition: A spasmodic reflex of the throat made as if in swallowing.
etymology: From gulp + -ing.

definition: Sound practical judgment.
etymology: Borrowed from Scots gumption (“common sense, shrewdness; drive, initiative”);

definition: A weapon that discharges a missile at high velocity (especially from a metal tube or barrel).
etymology: From Middle English gunne, gonne, possibly from Gunnhild, a female given name formerly used as a nickname for engines of war (compare Nordic Gunn, a female name meaning “battle”).

definition: A tube through which a bullet travels when a gun is fired.
etymology: From gun + barrel.

definition: A framework on which a gun is mounted for firing.
A case for storing a gun.
Chamber that is the part of a gun that receives the charge.
An emplacement for a gun.
A self-contained weapons platform housing guns and capable of rotation.
The open circular discharging end of a gun.
A ballistic pendulum consisting of a suspended gun; the velocity of a projectile in the bore of a gun can be measured by the recoil when the gun is discharged.
Lever that activates the firing mechanism of a gun.
A self-contained weapons platform housing guns and capable of rotation.
A sight used for aiming a gun.
A small shallow-draft boat carrying mounted guns; used by costal patrols.
etymology: From gun + boat.

definition: Diplomacy in which the nations threaten to use force in order to obtain their objectives.
A fight involving shooting small arms with the intent to kill or frighten.
etymology: From gun + fight.

definition: The act of shooting a gun.
example: The gunfire endangered innocent bystanders.
etymology: From gun + fire.

definition: Any thick, viscous matter.
example: I washed all the gunk off the light fixture, and found that it was white, not brown.
etymology: Apparently from Gunk, trademark name for a liquid soap; perhaps taken as a blend of grime + funk.

definition: A male professional killer who uses a gun.
etymology: From gun + -man.

definition: A type of bronze used for parts subject to wear or corrosion (especially corrosion by sea water).
etymology: From gun + metal.

definition: Coarse jute fabric.
etymology: From Hindi and Marathi गनी (ganī) or गोन (gon), from Sanskrit गोणी (goṇī), ultimately of Dravidian origin. Doublet of gunia.

definition: A bag made of burlap.
A fight involving shooting small arms with the intent to kill or frighten.
example: In the aftermath of the Iraq War, the streets of Baghdad were sometimes filled with gunplay.
etymology: From gun + play.

definition: The gun muzzle's direction.
etymology: From gun + point.

definition: The act of shooting a gun.
example: They heard gunshot all around them.
etymology: From gun + shot.

definition: A professional killer who uses a gun.
etymology: From gun + slinger.

definition: Someone who makes or repairs guns.
etymology: From gun + smith.

definition: Small freshwater fish of South America and the West Indies; often kept in aquariums.
A Hindu or Buddhist religious leader and spiritual teacher.
etymology: Borrowed from Hindi गुरु (guru) / Punjabi ਗੁਰੂ (gurū), from Sanskrit गुरु (guru, “venerable, respectable”), originally "heavy" and in this sense cognate to English grieve and, more distantly, brute. Doublet of grave.

definition: The part of the alimentary canal between the stomach and the anus.
example: You've developed quite a beer gut since I last met you.
etymology: From Middle English gut, gutte, gotte, from Old English gutt (usually in plural guttas (“guts, entrails”)), from Proto-Germanic *gut-, from Proto-Indo-European *ǵʰewd- (“to pour”).

definition: A consonant articulated in the back of the mouth or throat.
The drinking of large mouthfuls rapidly.
A specialist in gynecology.
etymology: From gynaecology + -ist.

definition: The branch of medicine that deals with the diseases and hygiene of women.
etymology: From gynaeco- + -logy.

definition: Of or relating to or practicing gynecology.
example: Gynecological examination.
etymology: From gynecology + -ic.

definition: Of or relating to or practicing gynecology.
example: Gynecological examination.
etymology: From gynecology + -ical.

definition: A laborer who moves from place to place as demanded by employment.
etymology: See Gypsy. Compare bohemian, from Bohemia.

definition: Repeated spontaneous abortion (often for no known reason).
One who works hard at boring tasks.
example: Luckily for us J company picked us up in their hack — two snowmobiles with a big inflatable raft strapped between them.
etymology: The computer senses date back to at least 1955 when it initially referred to creative problem solving.

definition: A carriage for hire.
Repeated too often; overfamiliar through overuse.
example: Hackneyed phrases.
etymology: From hackney + -ed. Most likely from the fact that hackney carriages have been used so much, that they are extremely commonplace now.

definition: A hemoprotein composed of globin and heme that gives red blood cells their characteristic color; function primarily to transport oxygen from the lungs to the body tissues.
etymology: From haemo- + globin.

definition: An ugly evil-looking old woman.
etymology: From Middle English hagge, hegge (“demon, old woman”), shortening of Old English hægtesse, hægtes (“harpy, witch”), from Proto-West Germanic *hagatussjā.

definition: A storm during which hail falls.
etymology: From hail + storm.

definition: A gun trigger that responds with little pressure.
etymology: compound hair + trigger

definition: A brush used to groom a person's hair.
etymology: From hair + brush.

definition: European vetch much cultivated as forage and cover crops.
The lean flesh of a fish similar to cod.
etymology: From Middle English *hake, from Old English hæca, haca (“hook, bolt, door-fastening, bar”), from Proto-West Germanic *hakō, from Proto-Germanic *hakô (“hook”), from Proto-Indo-European *keg-, *keng- (“peg, hook”).

definition: (of animals) having only one purebred parent.
etymology: From half- + bred.

definition: Disparaging terms for small people.
etymology: From half- + pint.

definition: Having exposed wood framing with spaces filled with masonry, as in Tudor architecture.
etymology: From half- (prefix meaning ‘half, partial; not complete’) + timbered.

definition: (football) the running back who plays the offensive halfback position.
etymology: From half + back, in reference to position on the field of play; compare fullback. In the sense of someone who moves to Florida and then to a more temperate climate, from moving "half way back"

definition: Render holy by means of religious rites.
etymology: Inherited from Middle English halowen, from halow (interjection), from Old English ēalā (“O!, alas!, oh!, lo!”, interjection), probably conflated with Old French halloer.

definition: Perceive what is not there; have illusions.
etymology: First attested in 1604; borrowed from Latin hallūcinātus, alternative form of ālūcinātus, perfect active participle of ālūcinor (“to dream”); see -ate (verb-forming suffix).

definition: Characterized by or characteristic of hallucination.
example: The bizarre hallucinatory dreams of fever.
etymology: From hallucinate + -ory.

definition: A sandwich made with a filling of sliced ham.
A weapon with a hammer on one side and an axe on the other.
A weapon with a hammer on one side and an axe on the other.
Poor acting by a ham actor.
A firearm that is held and fired with one hand.
etymology: From hand + gun.

definition: The total or partial absence of a person's bodily or mental functions, including the absence of a part of a person's body.
example: Handicapped person.

definition: A loom powered by hand.
etymology: From hand + loom.

definition: In a subordinate position.
example: Theology should be the handmaiden of ethics.
etymology: From Middle English hande mayden, handmaiden, hand mayden, hand-mayden, handmayden, hondemaiden, hond maydyn, hoondmaydyn. By surface analysis, hand + maiden.

definition: An announcement distributed to members of the press in order to supplement or replace an oral presentation.
etymology: Deverbal from hand out.

definition: A railing at the side of a staircase or balcony to prevent people from falling.
etymology: From hand + rail.

definition: Easy to reach.
example: Found a handy spot for the can opener.
etymology: From hand + -y (diminutive suffix).

definition: A male executioner who hangs the condemned person.
etymology: Inherited from Middle English hangman, hongman, hangeman, equivalent to hang + -man.

definition: A square piece of cloth used for wiping the eyes or nose or as a costume accessory.
A square piece of cloth used for wiping the eyes or nose or as a costume accessory.
Of a cell or organism having a single set of chromosomes.
example: Examples of haploid cells are prokaryotes and the gametes of eukaryotes.
etymology: From haplo- + -oid, Ancient Greek roots meaning, together, literally “simplex” or “onefoldlike”, from ᾰ̔πλόος (hăplóos, “single, simple”, literally “onefold”) and -ειδής (-eidḗs, “-like”).

definition: An event that might have been arranged although it was really accidental.
example: By happenstance.
etymology: Blend of happening + circumstance. Attested from 1855 in US publications.

definition: Of or relating to or proceeding from the sense of touch.
example: Haptic data.
etymology: From Ancient Greek ἁπτικός (haptikós, “able to come in contact with”), from ἅπτω (háptō, “to touch”) + -ικός (-ikós, suffix forming adjectives from nouns).

definition: A sensation localized on the skin.
Ritual suicide by self-disembowelment on a sword; practiced by samurai in the traditional Japanese society.
example: Regarded logically, therefore, Japan’s decision to go to war made no sense. It was hara-kiri.
etymology: Borrowed from Japanese 腹切り (harakiri), ultimately from 腹 (hara, “belly”) + 切る (kiru, “to cut”).

definition: Not easy; requiring great physical or mental effort to accomplish or comprehend or endure.
example: Why is it so hard for you to keep a secret?
etymology: From Middle English hard, from Old English heard, from Proto-West Germanic *hard(ī), from Proto-Germanic *harduz, from Proto-Indo-European *kort-ús, from *kret- (“strong, powerful”).

definition: A narcotic that is considered relatively strong and likely to cause addiction.
Someone who works as hard as a slave.
A car that resembles a convertible but has a fixed rigid top.
etymology: From hard + top.

definition: In a harmless manner.

definition: Hybrids of Petunia axillaris and Petunia integrifolia: a complex group of petunias having single or double flowers in colors from white to purple.
Any of various deciduous or evergreen shrubs of the genus Hydrangea.
etymology: Borrowed from taxonomic name Hydrangea, from Ancient Greek ὕδωρ (húdōr, “water”) + ἀγγεῖον (angeîon, “vessel, capsule”). Named by Carl Linnaeus after the shape of its fruits.

definition: Sometimes included in the family Saxifragaceae.
In a hydraulic manner.
example: The block is then tested hydraulically to its full design test pressure on each stream separately.
etymology: From hydraulic + -ally.

definition: A colorless fuming corrosive liquid; a powerful reducing agent; used chiefly in rocket fuels.
etymology: Borrowed from German Hydrazin, coined by Emile Fischer in 1875 as a derivative from Diazin, an obsolete name for diimide, of which hydrazine is a hydrogenated analog. By surface analysis, hydr- + azo (“nitrogen”) + -ine.

definition: Of or relating to hydrodynamics.
etymology: From hydro- + dynamic.

definition: A colloidal gel in which water is the dispersion medium.
etymology: From hydro- + gel.

definition: A nuclear weapon that releases atomic energy by union of light (hydrogen) nuclei at high temperatures to form helium.
A chemical process that adds hydrogen atoms to an unsaturated oil.
example: Food producers use hydrogenation to keep fat from becoming rancid.
etymology: From hydrogen + -ation.

definition: Of or relating to aquiculture.
example: Hydroponic lettuce.
etymology: Back-formation from hydroponics. By surface analysis, hydro- (“water”) + Ancient Greek πόνος (pónos, “work, labour”) + -ic.

definition: A technique of growing plants (without soil) in water containing dissolved nutrients.
etymology: From hydro- (“water”) + -ponics, which is from geoponics.

definition: The internal and external use of water in the treatment of disease.
etymology: From hydro- + therapy.

definition: A fold of tissue that partly covers the entrance to the vagina of a virgin.
etymology: From Middle French hymen, from Late Latin hymēn, from Ancient Greek ὑμήν (humḗn, “skin; membrane”).

definition: A songbook containing a collection of hymns.
etymology: From Middle English hymnale, from Medieval Latin hymnāle, noun use of neuter of hymnālis.

definition: Of or relating to the hyoid bone.
example: This stick has a hyoid shape.
etymology: Borrowing from French hyoïde, from New Latin hȳoīdēs, from Ancient Greek ῡ̔οειδής (hūoeidḗs, “shaped like the letter "υ"”), from ὖ (û, “the Greek letter upsilon”) + -ο- (-o-) + -ειδής (-eidḗs, “-like, -oid”).

definition: A U-shaped bone at the base of the tongue that supports the tongue muscles.
A large chamber in which the oxygen pressure is above normal for the atmosphere; used in treating breathing disorders or carbon monoxide poisoning.
Abnormally high blood sugar usually associated with diabetes.
etymology: From hyper- + glycemia or hyper- + glyc + -emia.

definition: A link from a hypertext file to another location or file; typically activated by clicking on a highlighted word or icon at a particular location on the screen.
example: Click the hyperlink to go to the next page.
etymology: From hyper- + link, or a blend of hypertext + link.

definition: Abnormal increase in number of cells.
etymology: From hyper- + -plasia.

definition: Having an allergy or peculiar or excessive susceptibility (especially to a specific factor).
example: Hypersensitive to pollen.
etymology: From hyper- + sensitive. Doublet of supersensitive.

definition: Having abnormally high blood pressure.
etymology: From hyper- + tensive or hypertension + -ive.

definition: Abnormally high body temperature; sometimes induced (as in treating some forms of cancer).
etymology: From New Latin, from Ancient Greek ὑπέρ (hupér, “over”) + θέρμη (thérmē, “heat”) + -ία (-ía). By surface analysis, hyper- + -therm + -ia.

definition: An overactive thyroid gland; pathologically excessive production of thyroid hormones or the condition resulting from excessive production of thyroid hormones.
etymology: From hyper- + thyroid + -ism.

definition: The use of hypnosis in psychotherapy.
etymology: From hypno- + therapy.

definition: Having your attention fixated as though by a spell.
The act of inducing hypnosis.
etymology: From hypnotise + -ism.

definition: Suffering from hypochondria.
Relating to or located below the epidermis.
example: Hypodermic needle.
etymology: From hypoderm + -ic.

definition: A hollow needle.
A piston syringe that is fitted with a hypodermic needle for giving injections.
Of or relating to the hypothalamus.
Hypoxia resulting from defective oxygenation of the blood in the lungs.
The lagging of an effect behind its cause; especially the phenomenon in which the magnetic induction of a ferromagnetic material lags behind the changing magnetic field.
etymology: Coined by Sir James Alfred Ewing from Ancient Greek ὑστέρησις (hustérēsis, “shortcoming”), from ὑστερέω (husteréō, “I am late, fall short”), from ὕστερος (hústeros, “later”).

definition: Of or consisting of iambs.
example: Iambic pentameter.
etymology: From Middle French iambique, from Late Latin ïambicus, from Ancient Greek ἰαμβικός (iambikós), from ἴαμβος (íambos) + -ικός (-ikós).

definition: Wild goat of mountain areas of Eurasia and northern Africa having large recurved horns.
etymology: From Latin ībex (“chamois”), possibly from Iberian or Aquitanian; akin to Old Spanish bezerro (“bull”) (modern becerro (“yearling”)).

definition: White goods in which food can be stored at low temperatures.
example: I moved here from the icebox of the upper Midwest.
etymology: From ice + box.

definition: Ice cream molded to look like a cake.
A male professional killer.
etymology: From ice + -man.

definition: Ice resembling a pendent spear, formed by the freezing of dripping water.
etymology: From Middle English isykle, isikel, from Old English *īsġicel, from Proto-West Germanic *īsajikil, *īsajekul, equivalent to ice + ickle.

definition: Old World annual widely naturalized in warm regions having white flowers and fleshy foliage covered with hairs that resemble ice.
Characterized by attack on established beliefs or institutions.
etymology: From iconoclast + -ic.

definition: Exalted to an ideal perfection or excellence.
An advocate of some ideology.
etymology: Borrowed from French idéologue. By surface analysis, ideo- + -logue. First attested in the 19th century.

definition: Of or relating to or conforming to idiom.
example: Idiomatic English.
etymology: From Ancient Greek ἰδιωματικός (idiōmatikós, “related to an idiom”), from ἰδίωμα (idíōma, “idiom”).

definition: An expression whose meanings cannot be inferred from the meanings of the words that make it up.
Having no employment.
etymology: From Middle English ydelnesse, from Old English īdelnes, from Proto-West Germanic *īdlanassī, equivalent to idle + -ness.

definition: Person who does no work.
etymology: From idle + -er.

definition: Love unquestioningly and uncritically or to excess; venerate as an idol.
example: Many teenagers idolized the Beatles.
etymology: From idol + -ize.

definition: An episode of such pastoral or romantic charm as to qualify as the subject of a poetic idyll.
etymology: From Latin īdyllium, from Ancient Greek εἰδύλλιον (eidúllion), from diminutive of εἶδος (eîdos, “form, shape”).

definition: (used of conduct or character) deserving or bringing disgrace or shame.
example: An ignominious retreat.
etymology: From Late Middle English ignominious (“disgraceful, shameful”), from Middle French ignominieux (modern French ignominieux), or from its etymon Latin ignōminiōsus (“disgraced;

definition: An ignorant person.
etymology: After the ignorant lawyer Ignoramus, the titular character in the 1615 play Ignoramus by the English playwright George Ruggle;

definition: A visual representation (of an object or scene or person or abstraction) produced on a surface.
Of or relating to the ilium.
etymology: From French iliaque, from Late Latin īliacus, Latin īlium.

definition: One of the large arteries supplying blood to the pelvis and legs.
One of three veins draining the pelvic area.
Offensively malodorous.
etymology: From ill + scented.

definition: Prohibited by law or by official or accepted rules.
example: An illegal chess move.
etymology: Borrowed from French illégal, from Medieval Latin illegalis, from Latin legalis, by surface analysis, il- + legal. In senses relating to immigration, via clipping of illegal alien or illegal immigrant.

definition: Narrow-minded about cherished opinions.
etymology: From Middle French illibéral, from Latin illiberalis, equivalent to il- + liberal.

definition: Contrary to accepted morality (especially sexual morality) or convention.
example: An illicit association with his secretary.
etymology: Borrowed from French illicite, from Latin illicitus, from in- (“not”) + licitus (“allowed, permitted”), from licet (“it is allowed”). By surface analysis, il- + licit.

definition: A person with unusual powers of foresight.
etymology: From illusion + -ist.

definition: Based on or having the nature of an illusion.
example: Illusive hopes of finding a better job.
etymology: Borrowed from Medieval Latin illūsīvus.

definition: With imagination.
example: The room was decorated very imaginatively.
etymology: From Middle English ymaginatyfliche; equivalent to imaginative + -ly.

definition: (psychoanalysis) an idealized image of someone (usually a parent) formed in childhood.
etymology: From Latin imāgō. Doublet of image. Compare typologically a Russian term for coordinate larva: личи́нка (ličínka) (akin to лик (lik)).

definition: Being or thrown out of equilibrium.
etymology: From im- + balanced.

definition: Having a mental age of three to seven years.
example: Hospitals for the imbecile and insane.
etymology: Borrowed from Middle French imbécile, from Latin imbēcillus (“weak, feeble”), literally “without a staff”.

definition: Take in, also metaphorically.
example: To imbibe knowledge.
etymology: From Middle English imbiben, from Latin imbibō, from im- + bibō (“to drink”) (whence also beverage), from Proto-Italic *pibō, from Proto-Indo-European *peh₃-, whence also potable, potion.

definition: Spread or diffuse through.
example: The shirt was imbued with his scent.
etymology: From Latin imbuō (“wet, moisten”). Compare imbibe.

definition: In an immaculate manner.
example: Gone was the casually dressed Canadian she had thought a backwoodsman — this man was immaculately tailored.
etymology: From immaculate + -ly.

definition: Of a mental act performed entirely within the mind.
example: A cognition is an immanent act of mind.
etymology: Entered English around 1530, via French, from Late Latin immanēns, present participle of Latin immanēre, from im- (“in”) + manēre (“to dwell, remain, stay”). Cognate with remain and manor.

definition: Unusual largeness in size or extent or number.
etymology: From Middle French immensité, equivalent to immense + -ity.

definition: In an imminent manner.
etymology: From imminent + -ly.

definition: Remaining in place.
example: Immobility is a big problem for many people who can't afford a car.
etymology: From Middle French immobilité, equivalent to immobile + -ity.

definition: Fixation (as by a plaster cast) of a body part in order to promote proper healing.
example: Immobilization of the injured knee was necessary.
etymology: From French immobilisation or im- + mobilization or immobilize + -ation.

definition: Hold as reserve or withdraw from circulation; of capital.
example: It is best to immobilize the injury until a doctor can examine it.
etymology: From French immobiliser, equivalent to immobile + -ize.

definition: Having or showing an exaggerated opinion of your importance, ability, etc.
example: Brash immodest boasting.
etymology: From im- + modest.

definition: Killing or offering as a sacrifice.
etymology: From Middle English immolacion, from Middle French immolation, from Old French, from Latin immolatio.

definition: The act of making immune (especially by inoculation).
etymology: From French immunisation. Equivalent to immunise + -ation or immune + -isation.

definition: Having been rendered unsusceptible to a disease.
Unable to develop a normal immune response usually because of malnutrition or immunodeficiency or immunosuppressive therapy.
etymology: From immuno- + compromised.

definition: Of or relating to a substance that lowers the body's normal immune response and induces immunosuppression.
etymology: From immuno- + suppressive.

definition: A drug that lowers the body's normal immune response.
In an impartial manner.
example: He smiled at them both impartially.
etymology: From impartial + -ly.

definition: Having or revealing little emotion or sensibility; not easily aroused or excited.
example: Her impassive remoteness.
etymology: From im- (prefix meaning ‘not’) + passive (“which is, or is capable of being, acted on; (obsolete) which suffers, or may suffer, pain, death, etc.”, adjective).

definition: Urge or force (a person) to an action; constrain or motivate.
example: The wind impelled the kayaks toward the shore.
etymology: From Middle English impellen, borrowed from Latin impellō.

definition: Urged or forced to action through moral pressure.
example: Felt impelled to take a stand against the issue.

definition: The blade of a rotor (as in the compressor of a jet engine).
example: Screw impeller.
etymology: From impel + er.

definition: Impossible or difficult to perceive by the mind or senses.
example: An imperceptible drop in temperature.
etymology: Inherited from Middle English imperceptible, from Middle French imperceptible and its etymon Medieval Latin imperceptibilis. By surface analysis, im- + perceptible.

definition: In an imperfect or faulty way.
example: The lobe was imperfectly developed.
etymology: From imperfect + -ly or im- + perfectly.

definition: Of or relating to imperialism.
example: Imperialistic wars.
etymology: From imperialist + -ic or imperial + -istic.

definition: Pose a threat to; present a danger to.
etymology: From im- + peril.

definition: The property of not existing for indefinitely long durations.
etymology: From Middle French impermanence, equivalent to im- + permanence.

definition: Preventing especially liquids to pass or diffuse through.
example: Impermeable stone.
etymology: Apparently from im- + permeable. Compare French imperméable, from Latin impermeābilis, from im- + permeābilis (“permeable”).

definition: Not permitted.
example: Impermissible behavior.
etymology: From im- + permissible.

definition: An impudent statement.
etymology: Borrowed from Middle French impertinence, from impertinent (“impertinent”); by surface analysis, im- + pertinent.

definition: Impinge or infringe upon.
example: This impinges on my rights as an individual.
etymology: Borrowed from Latin impingō (“dash against, impinge”). Compare impact, derived from the perfect passive participle of impingō.

definition: Hit against; come into sudden contact with.
Influencing strongly.
example: They resented the impingement of American values on European culture.
etymology: From impinge + -ment.

definition: The act of accomplishing some aim or executing some order.
example: The agency was created for the implementation of the policy.
etymology: From implement + -ation.

definition: Take temporary possession of as a security, by legal authority.
example: The customs agents impounded the illegal shipment.
etymology: From im- + pound.

definition: Fill, as with a certain quality.
example: I was impregnated at a clinic but don't know who the sperm donor is.
etymology: The adjective is first attested in 1540, the verb in 1605; borrowed from Medieval Latin impraegnātus, perfect passive participle of Latin impraegnō, see -ate (verb-forming suffix) and -ate (adjective-forming suffix).

definition: Material with which something is impregnated.
example: The impregnation, whatever it was, had turned the rock blue.
etymology: From Middle English impregnacioun, from Old French impregnacion, in turn from Late Latin impregnatio.

definition: Of or relating to or based on an impression rather than on facts or reasoning.
example: A surprisingly impressionistic review bearing marks of hasty composition.
etymology: From impressionist + -ic, or from impression + -istic.

definition: Formal and explicit approval.
example: The Cheats · A Comedy · Written in the Year, M.DC.LXII. Imprimatur, Roger L'estrange. Nov. 5. 1663. By John Wilson.
etymology: From Latin imprimātur (“let it be printed”), third person singular present subjunctive passive form of imprimere (“to imprint”).

definition: A learning process in early life whereby species specific patterns of behavior are established.
Not easy to believe.
etymology: From improbable + -ly.

definition: Not prudent or wise.
example: Very imprudent of her mother to encourage her in such silly romantic ideas.
etymology: From Middle French imprudent, from Latin imprūdens (“not foreseeing, ignorant”), prefix im- (“not”) + prūdens (“foreseeing, skilled, judicious”).

definition: An impudent statement.
etymology: From Middle French impudence, from Latin impudentia.

definition: Marked by casual disrespect.
example: The student was kept in for impudent behavior.
etymology: From Middle English impudent, originally meaning immodest, shameless, from Latin impudēns (“shameless”), ultimately from in- + pudere (“to feel shame”).

definition: A statement attributing something dishonest (especially a criminal offense).
example: He denied the imputation.
etymology: From Middle French imputation, from Latin imputatio.

definition: At the point of death.
etymology: Borrowed from Latin in extrēmīs.

definition: Without or deprived of the use of speech or words.
example: Inarticulate beasts.
etymology: From Latin inarticulatus and from in- + articulate. See -ate (adjective-forming suffix).

definition: Lack of attention.
etymology: From French inattention.

definition: Showing a lack of attention or care.
example: Inattentive students.
etymology: From in- + attentive.

definition: Not auspicious; boding ill.
etymology: From in- + auspicious.

definition: False or fake; not what it appears to be.
etymology: From in- + authentic. Piecewise doublet of unauthentic.

definition: Located within the hull or nearest the midline of a vessel or aircraft.
example: The inboard flaps on the wing.

definition: Present at birth but not necessarily hereditary; acquired during fetal development.
example: Inborn talent.

definition: An automatic instinctive unlearned reaction to a stimulus.
Produced by inbreeding.
etymology: From the past participle of inbreed, equivalent to in- + bred.

definition: Existing as an essential constituent or characteristic.
etymology: From in- + built.

definition: Not able to be computed or enumerated.
example: The loss the National Library suffered from the fire is incalculable.
etymology: From in- + calculable.

definition: Make unable to perform a certain action.
example: The police officer was incapacitated by a blow to the head.
etymology: Mid-17th century, from incapacity + -ate (verb-forming suffix). Compare French incapaciter.

definition: That cripples or disables or incapacitates.
An option granted to corporate executives if the company achieves certain financial goals.
Sexual intercourse between persons too closely related to marry (as between a parent and a child).
example: Genetic problems caused by incest are thought to have plagued many royal families in the Middle Ages.
etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin incestus. Displaced Old English mǣġhǣmed (literally “relative-sex”). Doublet of inchaste.

definition: Resembling incest as by excessive intimacy.
example: If you engaged in an incestuous relationship with a family member, that would make you an inbreeder.
etymology: From incest + -ous.

definition: Become reduced to ashes.
example: The paper incinerated quickly.
etymology: From Latin incinerātus, perfect participle of incinerō (“to burn into ashes”), from cinis (“ashes”).

definition: Lack of cohesion or clarity or organization.
In an incoherent manner.
example: He talked incoherently when he drank too much.
etymology: From incoherent + -ly or in- + coherently.

definition: Not to a full degree or extent.
example: Words incompletely understood.
etymology: From incomplete + -ly.

definition: Without showing consistency.
example: He acted inconsistently when he bought these stocks.
