etymology: From inconsistent + -ly.

definition: Sad beyond comforting; incapable of being consoled.
example: Inconsolable when her son died.
etymology: Middle French inconsolable, from Latin inconsolabilis; by surface analysis, in- + consolable, or, by surface analysis, in- + console + -able.

definition: Involuntary urination or defecation.
example: Verbal incontinence.
etymology: From Middle English incontinence, from Old French incontinence or its etymon Latin incontinentia. Doublet of incontinency.

definition: Not having control over urination and defecation.
example: An incontinent river of pure water.
etymology: From Middle English incontinent, from Old French incontinent, from Latin incontinens, from in + continens.

definition: Impossible to deny or disprove.
example: Incontrovertible proof of the defendant's innocence.
etymology: From in- + controvertible.

definition: Incapable of being morally corrupted.
example: Incorruptible judges are the backbone of the society.
etymology: Borrowed from Middle French incorruptible, from Latin incorruptibilis. By surface analysis, in- + corruptible.

definition: An accusation that you are responsible for some lapse or misdeed.
example: His incrimination was based on my testimony.
etymology: Borrowed from Medieval Latin incriminatus ( + -ion), from incrimino, from Latin crimino. Equivalent to incriminate + -ion.

definition: Grow under conditions that promote development.
etymology: First attested in 1641;

definition: A male demon believed to lie on sleeping persons and to have sexual intercourse with sleeping women.
example: It increaseth fearful dreams, incubus, night-walking, crying out, and much unquietness […] .
etymology: From Late Latin incubus, from Latin incubō (“nightmare, one who lies down on the sleeper”), from incubō (“to lie upon, to hatch”, from in- (“on”) + cubō (“to lie down”)).

definition: Teach and impress by frequent repetitions or admonitions.
example: Inculcate values into the young generation.

definition: The term during which some position is held.
etymology: From incumbent + -cy.

definition: Vulgar and offensive nakedness in a public place.
In an indelible manner.
example: This tradition has left its mark indelibly upon the social, political, educational and industrial fabric of this country.
etymology: From indelible + -ly.

definition: A sum of money paid in compensation for loss or injury.
Set in from the margin.
example: Indent the paragraphs of a letter.
etymology: Partly from Middle English indenten (“to dent in”), equivalent to in- + dent (see dent);

definition: An agency of the United States government that is created by an act of Congress and is independent of the executive departments.
A system of economic regulation: wages and interest are tied to the cost-of-living index in order to reduce the effects of inflation.
etymology: From French indexation.

definition: Liable to be accused, or cause for such liability.
example: An indictable offense.
etymology: From indict + -able.

definition: Fire delivered on a target that is not itself used as the point of aim for the weapons.
Lacking discretion; injudicious.
example: Her behavior was indiscreet at the very best.
etymology: From in- + discreet.

definition: Somewhat ill or prone to illness.
example: Feeling a bit indisposed today.
etymology: From in- + disposed.

definition: In a dim indistinct manner.
etymology: From indistinct + -ly or in- + distinctly.

definition: A rare soft silvery metallic element; occurs in small quantities in sphalerite.
etymology: Coined as a New Latin term from German Indigo (“indigo”), based on the color of its spectral lines.

definition: Teach doctrines to; teach uncritically.
example: The Moonies indoctrinate their disciples.
etymology: From in- + doctrine + -ate (verb-forming suffix). Compare French endoctriner.

definition: A white or yellowish crystalline heterocyclic compound extracted from coal tar and used in perfumery, medicine, and as a flavouring agent.
example: Indole is widely distributed in the natural environment and can be produced by a variety of bacteria.
etymology: From ind(igo) + Latin ole(um) (“oil”); see -ole.

definition: Disinclined to work or exertion.
example: An indolent hanger-on.
etymology: From French indolent or directly from Late Latin indolēns, from in- (“not”) + dolēns (“hurting”), from doleo (“to hurt”). The later sense of “living easily, slothful” perhaps developed in French.

definition: Place ceremoniously or formally in an office or position.
example: There was a ceremony to induct the president of the Academy.
etymology: Originated 1350–1400 from Middle English induct, borrowed from Latin inductus, perfect passive participle of indūcō, equivalent to induce + -tus (past participle suffix).

definition: An electrical phenomenon whereby an electromotive force (EMF) is generated in a closed circuit by a change in the flow of current.
example: The power cable itself has enough inductance to disrupt the digital signal of the video output cable, due to poor shielding.
etymology: From induct + -ance.

definition: A measure of the property of an electric circuit by which an electromotive force is induced in it.
A person inducted into an organization or social group.
example: Ty Cobb and Babe Ruth were 1936 inductees in the National Baseball Hall of Fame.
etymology: From induct + -ee.

definition: An electrical device (typically a conducting coil) that introduces inductance into a circuit.
etymology: Borrowed from Medieval Latin inductor, from Latin induco.

definition: A canal that is operated by one or more industries.
By industrial means.
example: Industrially produced.
etymology: From industrial + -ly.

definition: Lacking the power to be effective.
etymology: From ineffective + -ness.

definition: Not elastic.
example: Economists speak of an inelastic price structure.
etymology: From in- + elastic.

definition: A situation in which any change in the price of a given good does not equal a corresponding change in its supply.
Not equitable or fair.
example: The inequitable division of wealth.
etymology: From French inéquitable. Morphologically in- + equitable.

definition: In a cheap manner.
etymology: From inexpensive + -ly.

definition: The quality of never making an error.
Sudden and unexpected death of an apparently healthy infant during sleep.
The death rate during the first year of life.
A person who murders an infant.
etymology: From French infanticide, from Latin īnfanticīdium. By surface analysis, infant + -i- + -cide.

definition: A man who fights on foot with small arms.
etymology: From infantry + man.

definition: Not capable of being carried out or put into practice.
etymology: From in- + feasible. Cognate to French infaisable.

definition: An acute but benign form of viral hepatitis caused by an RNA virus that does not persist in the blood serum and is usually transmitted by ingesting food or drink that is contaminated with fecal matter.
Able to cause disease.
example: Infective agents.
etymology: From infect + -ive.

definition: An agent capable of producing infection.
The act of imposing something (as a tax or an embargo).
etymology: From Latin īnflīctiōnem (“imposition”), from Latin īnflīctus, from in- + flīctus, past participle of īnflīgō (“to knock or strike against”), from in- + flīgō (“strike”) (whence in-). By surface analysis, inflict + -ion.

definition: Make furious.
etymology: First attested in 1667; borrowed from Medieval Latin infuriātus (“enraged”), perfect passive participle of infuriō (“to enrage”) (see -ate (verb-forming suffix)), from Latin furia (“rage, fury, frenzy”);

definition: In an ingenious manner.
etymology: From ingenious + -ly.

definition: (used of conduct or character) deserving or bringing disgrace or shame.
example: Inglorious defeat.
etymology: From Latin inglōriōsus. By surface analysis, in- + glorious.

definition: Metal that is cast in the shape of a block for convenient handling.
etymology: From Middle English ingot (“mould for casting metal”), of uncertain origin.

definition: Iron of high purity.
A lack of gratitude.
example: Blondie: Tut, tut. Such ingratitude after all the times I saved your life.
etymology: From in- + gratitude, from Old French ingratitude, from Late Latin ingrātitūdō. By surface analysis, in- + Latin grat(us) + -itude.

definition: Growing abnormally into the flesh.
example: An ingrown toenail.
etymology: From in- + grown.

definition: A hair that does not emerge from the follicle but remains embedded in the skin (usually causing inflammation).
Obtain from someone after their death.
example: I inherited a castle from my French grandparents.
etymology: From Middle English enheriten, from Old French enheriter, from Late Latin inhereditare (“make heir”). Displaced native Old English ierfan.

definition: Assign an initial value to a computer program.
etymology: From initial + -ize.

definition: Someone injured or killed in an accident.
In an innate manner.
example: The child is said to be innately disposed to learn language.
etymology: From innate + -ly.

definition: Introduce an idea or attitude into the mind of.
example: My teachers inoculated me with their beliefs.
etymology: First attested in c. 1440;

definition: Not working or taking effect.
example: An inoperative law.
etymology: From in- + operative.

definition: Not opportune.
example: Arrived at a most inopportune hour.
etymology: From Latin inopportūnus. By surface analysis, in- + opportune.

definition: An optically inactive alcohol that is a component of the vitamin B complex.
etymology: From its former name inosite + -ol (“an alcohol”), from Ancient Greek ἰνός (inós, genitive singular of ἴς (ís, “sinew, tendon”)) + -ite.

definition: An inquiry into the cause of an unexpected death.
etymology: From Middle English enquest, from Old French enqueste (Modern French enquête), from Vulgar Latin inquirere, or from Medieval Latin inquesta < in + Latin quaesita.

definition: A hospital for mentally incompetent or unbalanced person.
A chemical used to kill insects.
A chemical used to kill insects.
etymology: From French insecticide, as insect + -icide.

definition: The quality of having little or no significance.
etymology: From in- + significance.

definition: In an insistent manner.
etymology: From insistent + -ly.

definition: An insect or other arthropod between molts.
etymology: From Latin instar (“form, likeness”), which is of obscure origin.

definition: Enter drop by drop.
example: Instill medication into my eye.

definition: Officially placed in or committed to a specialized institution.
example: Had hopes of rehabilitating the institutionalized juvenile delinquents.

definition: By an institution.
example: Institutionally controlled.
etymology: From institutional + -ly.

definition: Lacking material form or substance; unreal.
example: As insubstantial as a dream.
etymology: Probably from Middle French insubstantiel, from Latin insubstantiālis, from in- + substantiālis. By surface analysis, in- + substantial.

definition: Expressing extreme contempt.
example: He received an insulting letter.

definition: The process of taking food into the body through the mouth (as by eating).
example: The intake of air.
etymology: From English dialectal (Northern England/Scotland), deverbal of take in, equivalent to in- + take. More at in-, take.

definition: In an integral manner.
etymology: From integral + -ly.

definition: The quality of language that is comprehensible.
etymology: From intelligible + -ity.

definition: Expressive of intentions.
(genetics) the act of mixing different species or varieties of animals or plants and thus to produce hybrids.
An ecclesiastical censure by the Roman Catholic Church withdrawing certain sacraments and Christian burial from a person or all persons in a particular district.
etymology: From Middle English entrediten, from Old French entredire (“forbid”), from Latin interdīcō (“prohibit, forbid”), from inter- (“between”) + dīcō (“say”), from Proto-Indo-European *deyḱ-.

definition: Relating to or situated at an interface.
example: An interfacial layer.
etymology: From interface + -ial.

definition: Surface tension at the surface separating two non-miscible liquids.
Intrusive in a meddling or offensive manner.
example: An interfering old woman.

definition: To insert between other elements.
example: She interjected clever remarks.
etymology: From Latin interiectus, perfect passive participle of intericiō (“place between”).

definition: Any of several lymphokines that promote macrophages and killer T cells and B cells and other components of the immune system.
etymology: From inter- + leuko- + -in; *inter-: from Latin inter- (“between, amid”), a form of prepositional inter (“between”).

definition: A performer in the middle of a minstrel line who engages the others in talk.
etymology: Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin interlocūtor, from the agent noun counterpart (via the suffix -tor) of Latin interloquor (“speak between, issue an interlocutory decree”), from inter- + loquor (“speak”).

definition: Someone who intrudes on the privacy or property of another without permission.
example: They disliked the interloper, and forced him to leave.
etymology: From inter- + loper (“runner, rover”), as in landloper (“vagrant”) (from lope (“to leap, to jump”) (originally dialectal)).

definition: The ritual placing of a corpse in a grave.
etymology: From Middle English enterement, interment, from Old French enterrement. By surface analysis, inter + -ment.

definition: Learning (of values or attitudes etc.) that is incorporated within yourself.
etymology: From internal + -ization.

definition: The doctrine that nations should cooperate because their common interests are more important than their differences.
etymology: From international + -ism.

definition: (of conflict) within a group or organization.
example: An internecine feud among proxy holders.
etymology: Borrowed from Latin internecīnus (“deadly”), from internecium (“a massacre, bloodbath; an eradication”) + -īnus.

definition: A specialist in internal medicine.
etymology: From German Internist, corresponding to intern (“internal”) + -ist.

definition: Able to exchange and use information.
etymology: From interoperate + -able; alternatively inter- + operable.

definition: That provides interpretation.
A form of modern dance in which the dancer's movements depict an emotion or tell a story.
A form of modern dance in which the dancer's movements depict an emotion or tell a story.
(computer science) a program that translates and executes source language statements one line at a time.
Relating to verbs in the so-called interrogative mood.
example: Not all questions have an interrogative construction.
etymology: From Late Latin interrogātīvus, equivalent to interrogate + -ive.

definition: Some linguists consider interrogative sentences to constitute a mood.
A pronoun used in a question.
example: In English and many other languages (e.g. French, Russian and Czech), the sets of relative and interrogative pronouns are nearly identical.

definition: A sentence of inquiry that asks for a reply.
example: He had trouble phrasing his interrogations.

definition: One having both male and female sexual characteristics and organs; at birth an unambiguous assignment of male or female cannot be made.
etymology: Borrowed from German Intersexe. By surface analysis, inter- + sex. (This etymology is missing or incomplete. Please add to it, or discuss it at the Etymology scriptorium.

definition: Of or relating to the littoral area above the low-tide mark.
etymology: From inter- + tidal.

definition: Spin, wind, or twist together.
example: Intertwine the ribbons.
etymology: From inter- + twine.

definition: The part of the alimentary canal between the stomach and the anus.
etymology: From Latin intestīnum, neuter of intestīnus (“internal”), as Etymology 2, below.

definition: Causing intoxication.
example: An intoxicating drink.

definition: Within a muscle.
example: An intramuscular injection.
etymology: From Late Latin intramuscularis, from prefix intra-, "within", + musculum, "muscle".

definition: The trait of being intransigent; stubbornly refusing to compromise.
example: The intransigence of both sides frustrated the negotiators.
etymology: From French intransigeance, noun form of intransigeant, borrowed from Spanish intransigente at the end of the nineteenth century. Morphologically, from in- + transiger + -ant, literally "uncompromising".

definition: Impervious to pleas, persuasion, requests, reason.
example: An intransigent conservative opposed to every liberal tendency.
etymology: Borrowed from French intransigeant, from Spanish intransigente, from Latin in- (“un-, not”) + trānsigēns, present participle of trānsigō (“to come to an understanding”), from trāns (“across”) + agō (“to do”).

definition: Designating a verb that does not require or cannot take a direct object.
example: The word "drink" is a transitive verb in "they drink wine", but an intransitive one in "they drink often.".
etymology: From in- + transitive.

definition: A verb (or verb construction) that does not take an object.
example: In the English language, ‘sleep’ is an intransitive verb.

definition: An artificial lens that is implanted into the eye of someone to replace a damaged natural lens or someone who has had a cataract removed.
Pressure exerted by the fluids inside the eyeball; regulated by resistance to the outward flow of aqueous humor.
example: Glaucoma can result from increased intraocular pressure.

definition: Relating to or existing within the boundaries of a state.
example: Intrastate as well as interstate commerce.
etymology: From intra- + state.

definition: Within the womb.
etymology: From intra- + uterine.

definition: Contraceptive device consisting of a piece of bent plastic or metal that is inserted through the vagina into the uterus.
Marked by elaborately complex detail.
example: The intricacy of a knot.
etymology: From intric(ate) + -acy.

definition: The condition of being folded inward or sheathed.
etymology: From New Latin intrōversio, from intrōvertere (“to turn within”), from Classical Latin intro (“within”) and vertere (“to turn”). Equivalent to introvert + -sion or intro- + -version.

definition: Know or grasp by intuition or feeling.
etymology: A back-formation from intuition and intuitive; compare Latin intuitus (“observed; considered”), perfect participle of intueor (“to look at, upon or towards; to observe, regard;

definition: The rising of a body of water and its overflowing onto normally dry land.
example: Plains fertilized by annual inundations.
etymology: From Old French inundacion (“flood”) (French inondation), from Latin inundatio (“flood”), form of inundō (“to flood, overflow”) (English inundate). By surface analysis, inundat(e) + -ion.

definition: The quality of being resistant to variation.
etymology: From in- + variance.

definition: Abusive or venomous language used to express blame or censure or bitter deep-seated ill will.
example: Politics can raise invective to a low art.
etymology: From Middle French invective, from Medieval Latin invectiva (“abusive speech”), from Latin invectīvus, from invectus, perfect passive participle of invehō (“bring in”), from in- + vehō (“carry”).

definition: The inverse function of the cosine; the angle that has a cosine equal to a given number.
The ceremony of installing a new monarch.
etymology: From Middle French investiture, from Medieval Latin investītūra, from investīre (“to clothe”).

definition: Habitual.
example: An inveterate disease.
etymology: The adjective is first attested in 1528, the verb in 1574;

definition: Heighten or intensify.
example: The cold water invigorated him.
etymology: First attested in 1646; borrowed from New Latin invigōrātus, perfect passive participle of invigōrō, see -ate (verb-forming suffix) and -ate (adjective-forming suffix). By surface analysis, in- + vigor + -ate.

definition: With restored energy.
The property being difficult or impossible to defeat.
etymology: From Middle French invincibilité, from Latin invincibilitas.

definition: Incapable of being transgressed or dishonored.
example: The person of the king is inviolable.
etymology: From Middle French inviolable, from Latin inviolābilis (“untouchable”), from violō (“violate”). Equivalent to in- + violable. Piecewise doublet of unviolable.

definition: Without being seen.
example: These organisms enter the body invisibly.
etymology: From invisible + -ly. Piecewise doublet of unvisibly.

definition: The outer region of the Earth's atmosphere; contains a high concentration of free electrons.
etymology: From iono- + -sphere.

definition: By the fact itself.
example: Ipso facto, her innocence was established.
etymology: Borrowed from Latin ipsō factō (“by the fact itself”).

definition: Quickly aroused to anger.
etymology: From Middle English, from Old French irascible, from Late Latin īrāscibilis, from Latin īrāscī (“to be angry, enraged”) + -bilis. See also -ible.

definition: Irritate or vex.
example: It irks me doing all this work and have someone wreck it.
etymology: Inherited from Middle English irken (“to tire, grow weary”), from Old Norse yrkja (“to work”), from Proto-Germanic *wurkijaną (“to work”), from Proto-Indo-European *werǵ- (“to work”).

definition: So lacking in interest as to cause mental weariness.
example: What an irksome task the writing of long letters is.
etymology: From Middle English irkesome, irksum, equivalent to irk + -some, or perhaps continuing (in altered form) from Old English weorcsum (“painful, hurtful”).

definition: A heavy ductile magnetic metallic element; is silver-white in pure form but readily rusts; used in construction and tools and armament; plays a role in the transport of oxygen by the blood.
example: Today we studied about metals — including iron — at school.

definition: An instrument of torture that is used to heat or crush the foot and leg.
An instrument of execution for execution by strangulation.
An instrument of torture that is used to heat or crush the foot and leg.
Instrument of torture consisting of a hollow iron frame shaped like the human body and lined with spikes to impale the victim.
A man of great strength or bravery.
etymology: From Ironside.

definition: Handsome East Indian evergreen tree often planted as an ornamental for its fragrant white flowers that yield a perfume; source of very heavy hardwood used for railroad ties.
etymology: From iron + wood, because of its toughness.

definition: Handsome East Indian evergreen tree often planted as an ornamental for its fragrant white flowers that yield a perfume; source of very heavy hardwood used for railroad ties.
The workplace where iron is smelted or where iron goods are made.
Insusceptible of reform.
example: Irredeemable sinners.
etymology: From ir- + redeemable.

definition: Having no bearing on or connection with the subject at issue.
example: An irrelevant comment.
etymology: From ir- + relevant.

definition: Hostile or indifferent to religion.
etymology: From Latin irreligiōsus. By surface analysis, ir- + religious.

definition: In an irretrievable manner.
example: It is irretrievably lost.
etymology: From irretrievable + -ly.

definition: An irreverent mental attitude.
etymology: From Middle English irreverence, from Latin irreverentia, from irreverēns (“irreverent”) + -ia (suffix forming abstract nouns). By surface analysis, ir- + reverence.

definition: A compound that exists in forms having different arrangements of atoms but the same molecular weight.
etymology: From iso- + -mer.

definition: Having similar appearance but genetically different.
(biology) similarity or identity of form or shape or structure.
Alcohol used as antifreeze or a solvent.
Of a process or change taking place at constant temperature.
etymology: From iso- + thermal or isotherm + -al.

definition: Nervous and unable to relax.
example: An itchy rash.
etymology: From Middle English *yicchy, *ȝicchi, from Old English ġiċċiġ (“itchy”), equivalent to itch + -y. Cognate with Scots yeukie (“itchy”), West Frisian jokkerich (“itchy”), Dutch jeukachtig and jeukerig (“itchy”).

definition: Specify individually.
example: To itemize the cost of a railroad.
etymology: From item + -ize.

definition: (computer science) a single execution of a set of instructions that are to be repeated.
example: The solution took hundreds of iterations.
etymology: From Latin iterātiō, from iterō. Morphologically iterate + -ion.

definition: (used informally) little or tiny.
Evergreen liana widely cultivated for its variegated foliage.
The 26th letter of the Roman alphabet.
example: He doesn't know A from izzard.
etymology: From Middle English izod, ezod, ezed, probably from Middle French et zede (literally “and zed”), as spoken when reciting the alphabet.

definition: Rapid and indistinct speech.
etymology: From Middle English jaberen, javeren, chaveren (“to chatter, babble”), dissimilated forms of jablen, chavelen (“to jabber”), from Middle English chavel ("jaw"; > modern English jowl).

definition: A sharp hand gesture (resembling a blow).
A small worthless amount.
example: You don't know jack.
etymology: Inherited from Middle English jakke, from Anglo-Norman jacke, Middle French jaque, jacque, from jacques (“peasant”), from the proper name Jacques. Compare jacquerie.

definition: A hammer driven by compressed air.
etymology: From jack + hammer.

definition: Slang for masturbation.
Large hare of western North America.
etymology: Blend of jackass + rabbit.

definition: A semiprecious gemstone that takes a high polish; is usually green but sometimes whitish; consists of jadeite or nephrite.
etymology: Borrowed from French le jade, rebracketing of earlier l'éjade (“jade”), from Spanish piedra de ijada (“flank stone”), via Vulgar Latin *iliata from Latin ilia (“flank”). (Jade was thought to cure pains in the side.)

definition: A sharp projection on an edge or surface.
example: He clutched a jag of the rock.
etymology: The noun is from late Middle English jagge, from Old English giagga, giacga.

definition: Upright consisting of a vertical side member of a door or window frame.
etymology: From Middle English jambe, jaumbe, from Old French jambe (“leg”), from Late Latin gamba (“hock, shank, leg, thigh”), from Ancient Greek καμπή (kampḗ, “turning post, bend or flexure”).

definition: Spicy Creole dish of rice and ham, sausage, chicken, or shellfish with tomatoes, peppers, onions, and celery.
etymology: Borrowed from Louisiana Creole jambalaya.

definition: (usually plural) loose-fitting nightclothes worn for sleeping or lounging; have a jacket top and trousers.
A metallic sound.
example: The jangle of spurs.
etymology: From Middle English janglen (“to talk excessively, chatter; to talk idly, gossip; to nag; to complain, grumble; to argue, debate; to discuss, talk; to talk indistinctly, jabber; to make a noise or outcry;

definition: Like the discordant ringing of nonmusical metallic objects striking together.
example: Cowboys with jangling spurs.

definition: Greenhouse shrub with glossy green leaves and showy fragrant rose-like flowers; cultivated in many varieties.
etymology: From New Latin japō̆nica, the species name.

definition: Abusing vocally; expressing contempt or ridicule.
example: A jeering crowd.

definition: Pose a threat to; present a danger to.
etymology: From jeopardy + -ise.

definition: A dull stupid fatuous person.
example: When I yell "OK," give the mooring line a good jerk!
etymology: Denominal verb of jerky, itself borrowed from Spanish charqui, from Quechua ch'arki.

definition: Terms of abuse for a masturbator.
Propelled violently in a usually narrow stream.
Covered with beads or jewels or sequins.
A headdress adorned with jewels.
Covered with beads or jewels or sequins.
10 jiao equal 1 yuan in China.
etymology: Borrowed from Mandarin 角 (jiǎo). Doublet of kak.

definition: Be compatible, similar or consistent; coincide in their characteristics.
example: That explanation doesn’t jibe with the facts.
etymology: Uncertain; possibly from Old French giber (“to engage in horseplay; to play roughly in sport”). Compare English jib (“usually of a horse: to stop and refuse to go forward”), Old Norse geipa (“to talk nonsense”).

definition: Having a series of high-pitched ringing sounds like many small bells.
example: Jingling sleigh bells.

definition: Noisy and mischievous merrymaking.
(usually used colloquially) causing or accompanied by misfortune.
Small rapid variations in a waveform resulting from fluctuations in the voltage supply or mechanical vibrations or other sources.
example: That creepy movie gave me the jitters.
etymology: Possibly alteration of chitter (“to tremble, shiver”), from Middle English chittern (“to twitter, chatter”). Ultimately onomatopoeic; compare didder and teeter as well as German zittern.

definition: A style of jazz played by big bands popular in the 1930s; flowing rhythms but less complex than later styles of jazz.
example: Don’t give me that jive. I know where you were last night.
etymology: Unknown. Slang attested in African-American and rural American culture. Frequently used to imply lying, verbal deception or trickery. Has a possible historical antecedent in gyve (“shackle”).

definition: Someone who buys large quantities of goods and resells to merchants rather than to the ultimate customers.
example: An act to restrain the number and ill practice of brokers and stock jobbers: 8 & 9 Wm. 3, ch. 32 (1697) [legislation of English parliament].
etymology: From job + -er.

definition: A person trained to compete in sports.
example: Compiler jock.
etymology: From Jock, a Scottish hypocoristic form of John (compare Jack).

definition: (used in the plural) flared trousers ending at the calves; worn with riding boots.
A resolution passed by both houses of Congress which becomes legally binding when signed by the Chief Executive (or passed over the Chief Executive's veto).
Beam used to support floors or roofs.
etymology: From Old French giste, feminine of gist, the past participle of gesir (“to lie down”).

definition: Bumped or shaken jerkily.
example: The jolted passengers.

definition: The act of jostling (forcing your way by pushing).
A male skilled worker who practices some trade or handicraft.
example: Everyone must follow safety guidelines whether you're an apprentice, journeyman, or even master electrician.
etymology: From Middle English jorneman; from journe (from Old French jornee (“a day's work, a journey”)) and mon; equivalent to journey + -man.

definition: A combat between two mounted knights tilting against each other with blunted lances.
example: Medieval joust.
etymology: From Middle English, borrowed from Old French jouster (modern French jouter), from Vulgar Latin *juxtō, *iuxtō, *iuxtāre, from Latin iūxta (“close to”). English since the early 14th century.

definition: Not experiencing or inspiring joy.
example: A joyless man.
etymology: From joy + -less.

definition: In a joyous and gleeful manner.
etymology: From Middle English joyously, equivalent to joyous + -ly.

definition: A sale of property by the sheriff under authority of a court's writ of execution in order satisfy an unpaid obligation.
Torture that is sanctioned by the state and executed by duly accredited officials.
example: The English renounced judicial torture in 1640.

definition: As ordered by a court.
etymology: From judicial + -ly.

definition: In a judicious manner.
example: Let's use these intelligence tests judiciously.
etymology: From judicious + -ly.

definition: A massive inexorable force that seems to crush everything in its way.
A vegetable cut into thin strips.
Start (a car engine whose battery is dead) by connecting it to another car's battery.
example: Giving a really good speech at the convention could jump-start her political career.

definition: Start (a car engine whose battery is dead) by connecting it to another car's battery.
A semiconductor that consists of a p-n junction.
Severe form of malaria occurring in tropical regions.
Dessert made of sweetened milk coagulated with rennet.
etymology: From Middle English jonket (“basket made of rushes”), from Medieval Latin iuncta, possibly from Latin iuncus (“rush, reed”) and therefore a possible doublet of jonquil.

definition: Of or relating to the law or jurisprudence.
example: Juridical days.
etymology: From juridic + -al or alternatively borrowed from Latin iuridicalis.

definition: The principle that a person's nationality at birth is determined by the place of birth.
etymology: From Latin iūs (“law”) + solī (“of soil”).

definition: Small semi-evergreen tree of South Africa having dense clusters of clear scarlet flowers and red seeds.
South African cycad; the farinaceous pith of the fruit used as food.
Widely distributed wildcat of Africa and Asia Minor.
Important for human and animal food; growth habit and stem form similar to Indian corn but having sawtooth-edged leaves.
etymology: This name for sorghum is probably connected with both the distinction of Muslim versus non-Muslim and the distinction of sub-Saharan Black race versus other race;

definition: Important for human and animal food; growth habit and stem form similar to Indian corn but having sawtooth-edged leaves.
A stately dance of the Shinto religion that now forms a part of Japanese village festivals.
etymology: From Japanese 神楽 (kagura, literally “god music”). See more at the Japanese entry.

definition: Continually shifting or rapidly changing.
etymology: From kaleidoscope + -ic.

definition: A fighter plane used for suicide missions by Japanese pilots in World War II.
etymology: Borrowed from Japanese 神風(かみかぜ) (kamikaze, “divine wind”), from 神(かみ) (kami, “divine”) + 風(かぜ) (kaze, “wind”); which originally referred to the typhoon that destroyed the Mongol navy attacking Japan in 1281.

definition: A fine usually white clay formed by the weathering of aluminous minerals (as feldspar); used in ceramics and as an absorbent and as a filler (e.g., in paper).
An alcoholic drink made from the aromatic roots of the kava shrub.
etymology: From Tongan kava, in turn from Proto-Polynesian *kawa.

definition: A blow that renders the opponent unconscious.
etymology: Respelling of the initial letters KO.

definition: A toy wind instrument that has a membrane that makes a sound when you hum into the mouthpiece.
etymology: Probably onomatopoeic.

definition: Eurasian bulbous plant.
A game in which numbered balls are drawn at random and players cover the corresponding numbers on their cards.
etymology: From French quine, with reference to a set of five winning lottery numbers.

definition: An adulterous man; a man who has an ongoing extramarital sexual relationship with a woman.
etymology: From kept + man.

definition: An adulterous woman; a woman who has an ongoing extramarital sexual relationship with a man.
etymology: From kept + woman.

definition: Someone who drives slowly along the curb seeking sex from prostitutes or other women.
A disorderly outburst or tumult.
etymology: Probably from Scots curfuffle, equivalent to ker- + fuffle, or related to Irish cíor thuathail (“confusion, bewilderment”). Similar to modern Welsh cythrwfl (“uproar, trouble, agitation”)

definition: Small North American falcon.
etymology: From Middle English castrel (“staniel, bird of prey”), from Middle French cresserelle, crecerelle (“bird of prey”), usually assumed to be from crecelle (“rattle, wooden reel”) (modern crécelle), of obscure origin.

definition: A sailing vessel with two masts; the mizzen is forward of the rudderpost.
example: 'Squire Ketch rejoices as much to hear of a new Vox, as an old Sexton does to hear of a new Delight.
etymology: From Jack Ketch, a hangman of the 17th century.

definition: A ketone that is an intermediate product of the breakdown of fats in the body; any of three compounds (acetoacetic acid, acetone, and/or beta-hydroxybutyric acid) found in excess in blood and urine of persons with metabolic disorders.
An abnormal increase of ketone bodies in the blood as in diabetes mellitus.
etymology: From keto- + -osis.

definition: A neckline that forms a hole bellow the collarbones.
Lacking or not requiring a key.
example: A keyless lock operated by a series of pushbuttons.
etymology: From key + -less.

definition: The stroke of a key; one depression of a key on a keyboard.
example: The number of keystrokes was used as a measure of work.
etymology: From key + stroke.

definition: Of a yellowish brown color.
etymology: Borrowed from Hindustani خاکی (xākī) / ख़ाकी (xākī), from Classical Persian خَاکِی (xākī, “dusty, earthy, earth-colored”).

definition: Coarsely ground grain in the form of pellets (as for pet food).
etymology: Unknown; the verb is first attested in 1790 in William Marshall’s dictionary of agricultural provincialisms, of Shropshire dialect, perhaps variant of chip or derived from kibble (“an iron bucket”).

definition: A young person of either sex.
example: They're just kids.
etymology: Of uncertain origin. Possibly from Middle English *kidde, from Old English *cydde (“pouch, belly”), from Proto-West Germanic *kuddijā, derived from or related to Proto-Germanic *kuddô (“bag, sack, pod, shell, husk”).

definition: The illegal use of children in pornographic pictures or films.
Informal term for a young child.
etymology: From kid + -y.

definition: The illegal use of children in pornographic pictures or films.
Either of two bean-shaped excretory organs that filter wastes (especially urea) from the blood and excrete them and water in urine.
example: Urine passes out of the kidney through ureters to the bladder.
etymology: From Middle English kideney, kydeney, alteration of earlier kidenere (“kidney”) after ey (“egg”), of obscure origin and formation.

definition: An Australian boomerang; one side flat and the other convex.
Cause to die; put to death, usually intentionally or knowingly.
example: This man killed several people when he tried to rob a bank.
etymology: From Middle English killen, kyllen, cüllen (“to strike, beat, cut”), of obscure origin. Cognate with Scots kele, keil (“to kill”).

definition: Kill en masse; kill on a large scale; kill many.
etymology: From kill + off.

definition: Strain oneself more than is healthy.
Someone who causes the death of a person or animal.
example: There’s a killer on the loose.
etymology: From Middle English killer, kyller. By surface analysis, kill + -er.

definition: T cell with CD8 receptor that recognizes antigens on the surface of a virus-infected cell and binds to the infected cell and kill it.
An event that causes someone to die.
example: He made a killing on the stock market.
etymology: From Middle English kyllyng; equivalent to kill + -ing.

definition: In working order.
example: Out of kilter.
etymology: A variant of dialectal kelter (“good condition, order”), of unknown origin;

definition: The basic unit of money in Papua New Guinea.
etymology: From Tolai kina (“oyster or clamshell”).

definition: Set afire.
example: A kindled fire.

definition: The branch of mechanics concerned with motion without reference to force or mass.
etymology: French cinématique, from Ancient Greek κίνημα (kínēma, “motion”) + -ics.

definition: The branch of physiology that studies the mechanics and anatomy in relation to human movement.
etymology: From kinesi- + -ology.

definition: Having the rank of or resembling or befitting a king.
example: Symbolizing kingly power.
etymology: From Middle English kyngly, from Old English *cyninglīċ (“kingly, royal”), equivalent to king + -ly. Cognate with Dutch koninklijk (“kingly, royal”), German königlich (“kingly”), Swedish kunglig (“kingly”).

definition: An important person who can bring leaders to power through the exercise of political influence.
example: The Earl of Warwick was the first kingmaker.

definition: (used of sexual behavior) showing or appealing to bizarre or deviant tastes.
etymology: From kink + -y. Compare Spanish canquiñi (“nappy”).

definition: Salted and smoked herring.
etymology: From Old English cypera (“male salmon”), perhaps related to Old English coper (“reddish-brown metal”) (see copper), on resemblance of color.

definition: From fermented juice of black morello cherries.
etymology: Borrowed from French kirsch, from German Kirschwasser (“cherry water”). Doublet of cerise and cherry.

definition: (Islam) the will of Allah.
etymology: From Ottoman Turkish قسمت (kısmet, “fate, destiny”) (Turkish kısmet), from Arabic قِسْمَة (qisma, “division, lot, destiny”).

definition: Affectionate play (or foreplay without contact with the genital organs).
etymology: From Middle English kissynge, cussinde, from Old English cyssende, from Proto-West Germanic *kussijandī, from Proto-Germanic *kussijandz, equivalent to kiss + -ing.

definition: Small kitchen.
Hardware utensils for use in a kitchen.
example: The new chef reorganized the space where we keep the pots, pans, and other kitchenware.
etymology: From kitchen + -ware.

definition: Your friends and acquaintances.
example: All his kith and kin.
etymology: From Middle English kitthe (“kinsmen, relations”), from Old English cȳþþ, cȳþþu (“kinship, kinsfolk, relations”), from Proto-Germanic *kunþiþō (“knowledge, acquaintance”), from Proto-Indo-European *ǵneh₃- (“to know”).

definition: A bag carried by a strap on your back or shoulder.
etymology: From Low German knapzak or Dutch knapzak (older form cnapsack), from Middle Dutch cnappen (“to bite with teeth”), ultimately from knappen (“to eat, crack”), of imitative origin, + sack. German Knappsack is from Dutch.

definition: A big wooden board used for kneading dough.
example: When it comes to making pizza dough, a good wooden kneading board makes a big difference.

definition: Ring as in announcing death.
etymology: From Middle English knyllen, from Old English cnyllan (“to strike; knock; clap”), from Proto-West Germanic *knuʀlijan, from Proto-Germanic *knuzlijaną (“to beat; push;

definition: Characteristic of the time of chivalry and knighthood in the Middle Ages.
example: The knightly years.
etymology: From Middle English knyghtly, knightlich; equivalent to knight + -ly (adjectival suffix). Cognate with Old English cnihtlīċ (“boyish”), Dutch knechtelijk (“servile”), German knechtlich (“menial”).

definition: A circular rounded projection or protuberance.
Get rid of (someone who may be a threat) by killing.
etymology: In the verb sense of stopping work, said to be from the practice aboard slave galleys to have a man beat time for the rowers by knocking on a block or drum; when he stopped, the rowers could rest.

definition: A form of rummy in which a player can go out if the cards remaining in their hand total less than 10 points.
Having the knees abnormally close together and the ankles wide apart.
(Yiddish) a big shot who knows it and acts that way; a boastful immoderate person.
etymology: From knock + -er.

definition: An unauthorized copy or imitation.
example: It's not a name-brand bag; it's just a cheap knockoff.
etymology: Deverbal from knock off.

definition: Work very hard, like a slave.
example: You should knuckle down and do your homework!
etymology: 1864 in American English, from the game of marbles.

definition: (used in the plural) a small metal weapon; worn over the knuckles on the back of the hand.
(used in the plural) a small metal weapon; worn over the knuckles on the back of the hand.
Japanese stringed instrument that resembles a zither; has a rectangular wooden sounding board and usually 13 silk strings that are plucked with the fingers.
etymology: From Japanese 箏 (koto).

definition: A musician who plays the koto.
The basic unit of money in Norway.
etymology: From Danish krone (“crown”) and Norwegian krone. Doublet of corona, crown, korona, koruna, krona, and króna.

definition: Of or relating to the lips of the mouth.
example: Labial stops.
etymology: Borrowing from Medieval Latin labiālis (“of or pertaining to the lips”), from labium (“a lip”) + -ālis (“-al”, adjectival suffix). By surface analysis, labi(um) + -al.

definition: An artery that is a branch of the facial artery that supplies the lips of the mouth.
A consonant whose articulation involves movement of the lips.
Organ pipe whose tone is produced by air passing across the sharp edge of a fissure or lip.
A stop consonant that is produced with the lips.
Veins draining the lips of the vulva.
In a laborious manner.
example: Their lives were spent in committee making decisions for others to execute on the basis of data laboriously gathered for them.
etymology: From laborious + -ly.

definition: Relating to or affecting or originating in the inner ear.
example: Labyrinthine deafness.
etymology: From labyrinth + -ine from Ancient Greek λᾰβύρῐνθος (lăbúrĭnthos, “a maze”).

definition: An artery that is a branch of the basilar artery that supplies the labyrinth.
A sensory system located in structures of the inner ear that registers the orientation of the head.
Veins that drain the inner ear.
Irregularly slashed and jagged as if torn.
example: Lacerate leaves.

definition: Lacking brilliance or vitality.
example: A dull lackluster life.
etymology: From lack + lustre.

definition: A Gram-positive rod-shaped bacterium that produces lactic acid (especially in milk).
etymology: From the genus name. lacto- + bacillus

definition: A blank gap or missing part.
example: Long lacunae in this inscription make interpretation difficult.
etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin lacūna (“a ditch, pit; a hollow, cavity; a gap, defect”). Doublet of lacune and lagoon.

definition: A male child (a familiar term of address to a boy).
etymology: From lad + -ie.

definition: Goods carried by a large vehicle.
etymology: Gerund of lade (verb). Cognate with Dutch lading (“cargo, charge”), German Ladung (“cargo, charge”), Polish ładunek (“cargo, charge”), Swedish laddning (“charge”). Doublet of loading.

definition: Befitting a woman of good breeding.
example: Ladylike manners.
etymology: From lady + -like.

definition: Pathetically lacking in force or effectiveness.
example: A lame argument.
etymology: From Middle English lame, from Old English lama (“lame”), from Proto-West Germanic *lam, from Proto-Germanic *lamaz (“lame”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₃lemH- (“to tire; to break”).

definition: Disability of walking due to crippling of the legs or feet.
example: His lameness may have prevented him from walking but it didn't stop him from running for public office.
etymology: From lame + -ness.

definition: Bad; unfortunate.
example: A lamentable decision.
etymology: From Middle English lamentable, from Middle French lamentable, from Latin lāmentābilis (“full of sorrow, mournful; deplorable”), from lāmentor (“lament”), from lāmenta (“wailing, weeping”).

definition: A cry of sorrow and grief.
example: Their pitiful laments could be heard throughout the ward.
etymology: Recorded since 1375, from Middle English lamentacioun, from Middle French lamentation and its etymon Latin lāmentātiō (“wailing, moaning, weeping”), from the deponent verb lāmentor, from lāmentum (“wail;

definition: (folklore) a corpse that rises at night to drink the blood of the living.
etymology: From Latin lamia, from Ancient Greek Λάμια (Lámia).

definition: A thin plate or layer (especially of bone or mineral).
etymology: Borrowed from Latin lāmina (“a thin piece of metal, wood, marble; a plate, leaf, layer”). Doublet of lame.

definition: A layered structure.
etymology: From laminate + -ion.

definition: A composition that imitates or misrepresents somebody's style, usually in a humorous way.
etymology: From French lampon (“satire, mockery, ridicule”), built on French lampons (“let us drink — a popular refrain for scurrilous songs”), from lamper (“to quaff, to swig”).

definition: A cartoonist who draws parodies or satirical renditions of cultural or social or political situations.
A metal post supporting an outdoor lamp (such as a streetlight).
etymology: From lamp + post.

definition: Primitive eellike freshwater or anadromous cyclostome having round sucking mouth with a rasping tongue.
A protective ornamental covering for a lamp, used to screen a light bulb from direct view.
etymology: From lamp + shade. The verb sense comes from the idea of making something more conspicuous by hanging a lampshade on it.

definition: A veranda or roofed patio often furnished and used as a living room.
etymology: Borrowed from Hawaiian lānai.

definition: A long pointed rod used as a tool or weapon.
etymology: From Middle English launce, from Old French lance, from Latin lancea.

definition: (of a leaf shape) shaped like a lance head; narrow and tapering to a pointed apex.
etymology: From Latin lanceolātus.

definition: A leaf shaped like a lance head; tapering to a point at each end.
Of southwestern Europe; cultivated in Florida.
Someone who arranges features of the landscape or garden attractively.
etymology: From landscape + -er.

definition: Past times remembered with nostalgia.
A cord with an attached hook that is used to fire certain types of cannon.
A dog small and tame enough to be held in the lap.
An azure blue semiprecious stone.
Beginning with the cecum and ending with the rectum; includes the cecum and the colon and the rectum; extracts moisture from food residues which are later excreted as feces.
Plant having variegated foliage and used for window boxes.
Of stocks of companies with a market capitalization of five billion dollars or more.
Having relatively large leaves.
A large black bass; the angle of the jaw falls behind the eye.
etymology: From large + mouth.

definition: Flesh of largemouth bass.
A gift or money given (as for service or out of benevolence); usually given ostentatiously.
etymology: From Middle English larges, largess, largesse [and other forms], from Anglo-Norman largece, largesce, Middle French largece, largesce, largesse, and Old French largesce (“breadth, width; request for a monetary gift;

definition: A long noosed rope used to catch animals.
etymology: From Spanish la reata (“the lasso”).

definition: North American songbirds having a yellow breast.
etymology: Uncertain, either * from a northern English dialectal term lake /laik (“to play”) (around 1300, from Old Norse leika (“to play (as opposed to work)”)), with an intrusive -r- as is common in southern British dialects;

definition: Of or relating to or situated in the larynx.
example: Laryngeal infection.
etymology: Derived from New Latin laryngeus + -al, from larynx (“larynx”) + -eus (adjectival suffix). By surface analysis, laryng- + -al or -ial.

definition: Either of two arteries that supply blood to the larynx.
One of two veins draining the larynx.
Inflammation of the mucous membrane of the larynx; characterized by hoarseness or loss of voice and coughing.
etymology: Attested since 1822 C.E. Learned borrowing from New Latin laryngitis, from larynx + -itis. By surface analysis, laryng- + -itis.

definition: Driven by lust; preoccupied with or exhibiting lustful desires.
etymology: From Latin lascīviōsus, from lascīvia (“sportiveness, lustfulness”).

definition: A large number or amount.
The point of death or exhaustion or completion.
example: The last gasp of the cold war.

definition: The last walk of a condemned person to the execution place.
example: The problem getting to all these remote customers is still the last mile, no matter how far they live from the switch.

definition: A Catholic sacrament; a priest anoints a dying person with oil and prays for salvation.
Aromatic Turkish tobacco.
etymology: From Latakia (“the Syrian port from where the tobacco is shipped, and near where it is produced”), from Arabic اللَاذِقِيَّة (al-lāḏiqiyya).

definition: (psychoanalysis) the fourth period (from about age 5 or 6 until puberty) during which sexual interests are supposed to be sublimated into other activities.
(psychoanalysis) the fourth period (from about age 5 or 6 until puberty) during which sexual interests are supposed to be sublimated into other activities.
(psychoanalysis) the fourth period (from about age 5 or 6 until puberty) during which sexual interests are supposed to be sublimated into other activities.
Quality of coming late or later in time.
example: His chronic lateness will cost him a promotion if not his job.
etymology: From late + -ness.

definition: The basic unit of money in Latvia.
etymology: See the etymology of the corresponding lemma form.

definition: Narcotic consisting of an alcohol solution of opium or any preparation in which opium is the main ingredient.
etymology: From New Latin, from lādanum (“a gum resin”), from Ancient Greek λᾱ́δανον (lā́danon). Originally the same word as ladanum, labdanum, compare French laudanum, Italian laudano, ladano.

definition: So as to arouse or deserve laughter.
example: Her income was laughably small, but she managed to live well.
etymology: From laughable + -ly.

definition: A victim of ridicule or pranks.
etymology: From laughing + stock.

definition: Small aromatic evergreen shrub of California having paniculate leaves and whitish berries; in some classifications included in genus Rhus.
The act of making or enacting laws.
etymology: From law + making.

definition: A male officer of the law.
etymology: From Middle English laweman, laȝaman (as a man's name, Laȝamon, Layamon), from Old English lahmann, borrowed from Old Norse lǫgmaðr. In present use as a law-enforcement officer, law + -man.

definition: Stimulating evacuation of feces.
etymology: From Middle French laxatif, from Latin laxātīvus (literally “relaxing, loosening”).

definition: Someone who is not a clergyman or a professional person.
example: The book was written for professionals, but an intelligent layperson could understand most of it.
etymology: A lay (“non-clergy, nonclergy”) + person, along the lines of layman.

definition: An azure blue semiprecious stone.
The smallest multiple that is exactly divisible by every member of a set of numbers.
Darkened with overcast.
example: The sky was leaden and thick.
etymology: From Middle English leden, leaden, from Old English lēaden (“leaden, of lead”). Cognate with West Frisian leaden (“leaden”), Dutch loden (“leaden”). By surface analysis, lead + -en.

definition: Having leaves or leaves as specified; often used in combination.
example: A fully leafed tree.
etymology: See the etymology of the corresponding lemma form.

definition: An accidental hole that allows something (fluid or light etc.) to enter or escape.
example: One of the tires developed a leak.
etymology: From Middle English leken (“to let water in or out”), from Old English *lecan (“to leak”), Middle Dutch leken (“to leak, drip”) or Old Norse leka (“to leak, drip”);

definition: Faithful and true.
example: Leal to the core of her intrepid Scottish heart.
etymology: Inherited from Middle English leel, lel, borrowed from Anglo-Norman leal and Old French leial, from Latin lēgālis. Doublet of loyal and legal.

definition: Smallest American sandpiper.
Having leathery leaves.
A substance used to produce fermentation in dough or a liquid.
etymology: From Middle English levayn, borrowed from Old French levain, from Vulgar Latin *levāmen, a noun based on Latin levō (“raise”).

definition: A leavening agent (also known as raising agent or leaven agent) is a substance added to dough or batter to make it lighter and softer.
example: I know I can use chemical leaveners, but I think that using yeast as a leavening agent is more healthy.

definition: Made light by aerating, as with yeast or baking powder; often used as a combining form.
example: Leavened bread.

definition: Someone who leaves.
example: This year's school leavers have excellent grades.
etymology: From leave + -er.

definition: Man with strong sexual desires.
etymology: Back-formation from lecher.

definition: Have a strong sexual desire for.
Given to excessive indulgence in sexual activity.
example: A lecherous gleam in his eye.

definition: Desk or stand with a slanted top used to hold a text at the proper height for a lecturer.
A facial expression of contempt or scorn; the upper lip curls.
etymology: Exact development uncertain, but apparently from a verb *leer (“to make a face, look sideways”), from leer (“cheek, face, profile”) (see below).

definition: Showing sly or knowing malice in a glance.
example: She had run in fear of … his evil leering eye.

definition: (of handwriting) having the letters slanting backward.
Established by or founded upon law or official or accepted rules.
example: Legal profession.
etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin lēgālis (“legal”), from lēx (“law”). Doublet of loyal and leal.

definition: A personal representative with legal standing (as by power of attorney or the executor of a will).
Make legal.
example: Marijuana should be legalized.
etymology: From legal + -ise. Piecewise doublet of loyalise.

definition: (music) without breaks between notes; smooth and connected.
example: A legato passage.
etymology: Borrowed from Italian legato, past participle of legare (“to tie up, tie together, to bind”), learned borrowing from Latin ligō (“tie, bind”). Doublet of ligate.

definition: (of plants) having tall spindly stems.
example: Fred preferred leggy blondes.
etymology: From leg + -y.

definition: Distinctness that makes perception easy.
The motile aerobic rod-shaped Gram-negative bacterium that thrives in central heating and air conditioning systems and can cause Legionnaires' disease.
etymology: From legion + translingual -ella, from Latin legio.

definition: Not having legs.
example: A legless man in a wheelchair.
etymology: From Middle English legles, equivalent to leg + -less.

definition: Degenerate wormlike burrowing lizard of California closely related to alligator lizards.
The basic unit of money in Albania.
etymology: From Germanic roots meaning "play". In the biology sense, it comes specifically from Swedish lek (“child's play”), by means of Swedish leka (“to play”).

definition: Any of various short-tailed furry-footed rodents of circumpolar distribution.
etymology: From Danish and Norwegian lemming, from Old Norse lómundr, læmingi, læmingr (“lemming”), perhaps from Sami luomek.

definition: Sweet-scented sumac of eastern America having ternate leaves and yellowish-green flowers in spikes resembling catkins followed by red hairy fruits.
An aromatic oil that smells like lemon and is widely used in Asian cooking and in perfumes and medicines.
etymology: From lemon + grass.

definition: An aromatic oil that smells like lemon and is widely used in Asian cooking and in perfumes and medicines.
Tasting sour like a lemon.
example: The walls were painted a lemony yellow colour.
etymology: From lemon + -y.

definition: A transparent optical device used to converge or diverge transmitted light and to form images.
Convex on both sides; shaped like a lentil.
example: Lenticular photography.
etymology: Inherited from Middle English lenticular, lenticuler, borrowed from Medieval Latin lenticulāris (“lentil-shaped”), from Latin lenticula, from lēns + -cula, ultimately from Latin lēns (“lentil”).

definition: A basal ganglion shaped like a lens and including the outer reddish putamen and the inner pale yellow pallidum.
Of or relating to or characterized by homosexual relations between woman.
example: Lesbian fans of the show were rooting for Jane and Amanda to get together.
etymology: From Latin Lesbiana, from Ancient Greek Λέσβος (Lésbos) + Latin adjective suffix -iana; by reference to Sappho of Lesbos (whence also sapphist, sapphic), known for her sentimental poems about women.

definition: Female homosexuality.
etymology: From lesbian + -ism.

definition: Small toothless anteater with prehensile tail and four-clawed forelimbs; of tropical South America and Central America.
The common wintergreen having many-flowered racemes of pink-tinged white flowers; Europe and North America.
Someone who grants a lease.
etymology: From Middle English lessour, from Anglo-Norman lessour.

definition: Fire as from a gun.
example: The soldiers let drive their bullets.

definition: Fire as from a gun.
example: The soldiers let drive their bullets.

definition: Of an instrument of certain death.
example: Lethal weapon.
etymology: Abbreviation of “lauric acid ethereal salt”, so called because it occurs in the ethereal salt of lauric acid.

definition: An agent capable of causing death.
The size dose that will cause death.
example: A lethal dose 50 will cause the death of 50% of a sample of test animals.

definition: Any gene that has an effect that causes the death of the organism at any stage of life.
An encephalitis that was epidemic between 1915 and 1926; symptoms include paralysis of the extrinsic eye muscle and extreme muscular weakness.
Printing from a plate with raised characters.
etymology: From letter + press.

definition: The basic unit of money in Moldova.
etymology: Borrowed from Romanian leu (“lion”), from Latin leō (“lion”). Doublet of Leo, lev, lion, and Lyon.

definition: A white crystalline amino acid occurring in proteins that is essential for nutrition; obtained by the hydrolysis of most dietary proteins.
etymology: Derived from Ancient Greek λευκός (leukós, “white”) + -ine, equivalent to leuco- + -ine.

definition: Blood cells that engulf and digest bacteria and fungi; an important part of the body's defense system.
etymology: From leuko- + -cyte.

definition: All of the words in a language; all word forms having meaning or grammatical function.
example: In this broadsheet newspaper, the reporter uses a complicated and formal lexis which I find hard to understand.
etymology: Learned borrowing from Ancient Greek λέξις (léxis, “speech, word”).

definition: A usually secretive or illicit sexual relationship.
example: As a community liaison, I work to make sure the general public knows about our organization's work.
etymology: Borrowed from French liaison (“binding”), from Latin ligātiō (stem ligātiōn-; whence the English doublet ligation), derived from ligō (“to bind”), from Proto-Indo-European *leyǵ- (“to bind”).

definition: (used of statements) harmful and often untrue; tending to discredit or malign.
example: The accusation was libelous, full of falsehoods, spite and malice.
etymology: From libel + -ous.

definition: (psychoanalysis) a Freudian term for sexual urge or desire.
The position of librarian.
etymology: From librarian + -ship.

definition: Given official approval to act.
example: Licensed pharmacist.

definition: Beat thoroughly and conclusively in a competition or fight.
example: We licked the other team on Sunday!
etymology: From Middle English likken, from Old English liccian, from Proto-West Germanic *likkōn, from Proto-Germanic *likkōną (“to lick”), from Proto-Indo-European *leyǵʰ- (“to lick”). Sense evolution towards violence unclear;

definition: Have sexual intercourse with.
A sentence of imprisonment until death.
A British peer whose title lapses at death.
Rescue equipment consisting of a buoyant belt or jacket to keep a person from drowning.
The period during which something is functional (as between birth and death).
A prisoner serving a term of life imprisonment.
etymology: From life + -er.

definition: The period during which something is functional (as between birth and death).
example: Some clams have lifespans far longer than those of human beings.
etymology: From life + span.

definition: The period during which something is functional (as between birth and death).
example: A project that will take many human lifetimes to complete.
etymology: From Middle English lyftyme, equivalent to life + time. Cognate with Icelandic líftími (“lifetime”).

definition: An amateur boxer who weighs no more than 106 pounds.
Armed with light weapons.
Weak and likely to lose consciousness.
example: Felt light in the head.

definition: Armed with light weapons.
A linear unit (1/40 inch) used to measure diameter of buttons.
etymology: From French ligne. Doublet of linea.

definition: A complex polymer; the chief constituent of wood other than carbohydrates; binds to cellulose fibers to harden and strengthen cell walls of plants.
etymology: From Latin lignum (“wood”) + -in.

definition: Intermediate between peat and bituminous coal.
etymology: From French lignite, from Latin lignum (“firewood”) + -ite.

definition: Being two more than fifty.
The act of comparing similarities.
Characterized by a buoyant rhythm.
example: An easy lilting stride.

definition: Restricted to whites only.
example: A lily-white movement which would expel Negroes from the organization.
etymology: From Middle English liliwhite, lilye-white, lilye-whyt, equivalent to lily + white.

definition: (used of e.g. personality traits) readily adaptable.
example: A limber imagination.
etymology: Unknown; possibly related to limb or limp + -er, as seen in clever, slipper (“slippery”), waker (“alert”), etc.

definition: Western North American pine with long needles and very flexible limbs and dark-grey furrowed bark.
Attach the limber.
example: Limber a cannon.

definition: Of or relating to or forming a limbus.
etymology: From French limbique, from Latin limbus (“edge, border”).

definition: A system of functionally related neural structures in the brain that are involved in emotional behavior.
A system of functionally related neural structures in the brain that are involved in emotional behavior.
Mollusk with a low conical shell.
example: He stuck to me like a limpet all day!

definition: A central cohesive source of support and stability.
example: He is the linchpin of this firm.

definition: In a straight unbroken line of descent from parent to child.
example: Lineal ancestors.
etymology: From Old French lineal, from Latin līneālis, from līnea (“a line”) + -ālis (adjective-forming suffix). By surface analysis, line + -al. Doublet of linear.

definition: Remain present although waning or gradually dying.
example: Her perfume lingered on.

definition: A common language used by speakers of different languages.
etymology: Borrowed from Italian lingua franca (literally “Frankish language”).

definition: Simple proteins that bind to nucleosomes (histones H1/H5).
A liquid polyunsaturated fatty acid abundant in plant fats and oils; a fatty acid essential for nutrition; used to make soap.
The seed of flax used as a source of oil.
example: The ancients regarded linseed as a source of medical benefits.
etymology: From Middle English linseed, lynseed, lynsede, from Old English līnsǣd (“seed of flax”), from līn (“flax”) (from Proto-Germanic *līną (“flax”)) + sǣd (“seed”). By surface analysis, lin + seed.

definition: A drying oil extracted from flax seed and used in making such things as oil paints.
Horizontal beam used as a finishing piece over a door or window.
etymology: From Middle English lyntel, from Old French lintel, from Vulgar Latin *līntellus, for *līmitellus, diminutive noun from līmes. Equivalent to limit + -el.

definition: An expression of agreement that is not supported by real conviction.
example: The candidate gave lip service to fixing the problems, but it is doubtful that he will do much.
etymology: First use appears c. 1590, in A Treatise against Witchcraft by Henry Holland. Compare earlier lip-labour.

definition: Combining audio and video recording in such a way that the sound is perfectly synchronized with the action that produced it; especially synchronizing the movements of a speaker's lips with the sound of their speech.
An enzyme secreted in the digestive tract that catalyzes the breakdown of fats into individual fatty acids that can be absorbed into the bloodstream.
etymology: Borrowed from French lipase. By surface analysis, lipo- + -ase

definition: The conversion of a solid or a gas into a liquid.
etymology: From Middle English liquefaction, from Middle French liquefaction (modern French liquéfaction), from Medieval Latin liquefactiō.

definition: Strong highly flavored sweet liquor usually drunk after a meal.
etymology: Unadapted borrowing from French liqueur. Doublet of liquor.

definition: Get rid of (someone who may be a threat) by killing.
example: The mafia liquidated the informer.
etymology: Verb sense 1.2.3 (“to kill; to abolish”) is a semantic loan from Russian ликвиди́ровать (likvidírovatʹ);

definition: A criminal who commits homicide (who performs the unlawful premeditated killing of another human being).
etymology: From liquidate + -or.

definition: Deep-rooted coarse-textured plant native to the Mediterranean region having blue flowers and pinnately compound leaves; widely cultivated in Europe for its long thick sweet roots.
etymology: From licorice by association with liquor.

definition: The literary intelligentsia.
etymology: From Latin līterātī, plural of līterātus (“lettered, literate”).

definition: Gracefully thin and bending and moving with ease.
example: Lithe weather.
etymology: From Middle English lithe, from Old English līþe (“gentle, mild”), from Proto-West Germanic *linþ(ī), from Proto-Germanic *linþaz, from Proto-Indo-European *lentos.

definition: Having a lithe body.
Of or produced by or involved in lithography.
example: Lithographic reproduction.
etymology: From lithograph + -ic.

definition: The solid part of the earth consisting of the crust and outer mantle.
etymology: From litho- + -sphere.

definition: Eminent beyond or above comparison.

definition: Come into being; become reality.

definition: Informal terms for the mouth.

definition: The jaw in vertebrates that is fused to the cranium.

definition: To a maximal degree.

definition: Containing meal or made of meal.

A motley assortment of things.

definition: In a memorable manner.

etymology: Borrowed from Middle French mental, a learned borrowing from Late Latin mentālis, from Latin mēns (“mind”) + -ālis (adjectival suffix).

definition: A specialist in microbiology.
