definition: A kind of dance step in which the dancer seems to be sliding on the spot.
example: Michael Jackson perfected the moonwalk in the 1980s.
etymology: From Moon + walk. * (backslide): Coined by Michael Jackson in 1983, when popularizing the backslide and renaming it.

definition: Move around slowly and aimlessly.
etymology: Late Middle English (as a noun meaning "simpleton, fool"), probably related to mop (“young of an animal, moppet”).

definition: Move around slowly and aimlessly.
Narrowly and conventionally moral.
example: She was glad to escape her judgmental and moralistic parents.
etymology: From moral + -istic.

definition: Indulgence in moral pronouncements; the exposition (often superficially) of a particular moral code.
example: His constant moralizing drove me mad.

definition: A soft wet area of low-lying land that sinks underfoot.
etymology: From Dutch moeras (“marsh, swamp”), an alteration (with influence from Dutch moer (“moor”)) of a direct descendant of Middle Dutch marasch (“marsh”).

definition: Harshly ironic or sinister.
example: Fun ranging from slapstick clowning … to savage mordant wit.
etymology: From French mordant, from Latin mordeō. Doublet of mordent.

definition: A South African unit of measure equal to about 2 acres.
etymology: From Dutch morgen and German Morgen, both literally "morning", probably originally indicated the amount of land that can be ploughed by a team of oxen in a morning. Doublet of morn and morrow.

definition: A building (or room) where dead bodies are kept before burial or cremation.
etymology: Borrowed from French morgue. The second sense developed from the first, via "a prison examination room", probably with reference to the haughty attitude of the jailers.

definition: Showing a brooding ill humor.
example: A morose and unsociable manner.
etymology: From French morose, from Latin mōrōsus (“particular, scrupulous, fastidious, self-willed, wayward, capricious, fretful, peevish”), from mōs (“way, custom, habit, self-will”). See moral.

definition: Minimal meaningful language unit; it cannot be divided into smaller meaningful units.
etymology: From French morphème. Ultimately from Ancient Greek μορφή (morphḗ, “shape, form”). By surface analysis, morph + -eme.

definition: An alkaloid narcotic drug extracted from opium; a powerful, habit-forming narcotic used to relieve pain.
etymology: Borrowed from French morphine or German Morphin, from Ancient Greek Μορφεύς (Morpheús, “the god and personification of dreams”).

definition: Subject to death.
example: Mortal beings.
etymology: From Middle English mortal, mortel, from Old French mortal, mortel, and their source Latin mortālis, from mors (“death”). In this sense, displaced native deadly, from Old English dēadlīċ.

definition: An enemy who wants to kill you.
An actuarial table indicating life expectancy and probability of death as a function or age and sex and occupation etc.
In such a manner that death ensues (also in reference to hatred, jealousy, fear, etc.).
example: A being of whom the forest Indians are said to be mortally afraid, with a hoof shaped like the heel of a bottle.
etymology: From Middle English mortally, equivalent to mortal + -ly.

definition: A muzzle-loading high-angle gun with a short barrel that fires shells at high elevations for a short range.
etymology: From Middle English morter, from Old French mortier, from Latin mortārium. Doublet of mortarium.

definition: Strong feelings of embarrassment.
etymology: From Middle English mortificacioun, mortification, from Middle French mortification and its etymon Latin mortificātiō. By surface analysis, mortify + -ication.

definition: Suffering from tissue death.
Causing to feel shame or chagrin or vexation.
example: It was mortifying to know he had heard every word.

definition: Of or relating to or characteristic of death.
etymology: From Middle English mortuary, from Anglo-Norman mortuarie (“gift to a parish priest from a deceased parishioner”), from Medieval Latin mortuārium (“receptacle for the dead;

definition: Low tufted perennial phlox with needlelike evergreen leaves and pink or white flowers; native to United States and widely cultivated as a ground cover.
As naked as at birth.
etymology: Meaning "as naked as when born (from one's mother)". Compare typologically Russian в чём мать родила́ (v čom matʹ rodilá).

definition: Having no living or known mother.
etymology: From Middle English moderles, from Old English mōdorlēas, from Proto-Germanic *mōdērlausaz, equivalent to mother + -less.

definition: (of spores or microorganisms) capable of movement.
etymology: From Latin mōtus, perfect passive participle of moveō (“to move”, whence English move), + -ile.

definition: Riding a motorcycle.
example: Motorcycling is a dangerous sport.

definition: Covered with or smelling of mold.
etymology: From mould + -y.

definition: Periodic shedding of the cuticle in arthropods or the outer skin in reptiles.
example: Some birds change colour during their winter moult.
etymology: From Middle English mouten, from Old English *mutian (attested in bemutian, “to exchange for”), from Latin mūtō (“to (re)move, change, vary, mutate, exchange, abandon”). Doublet of mute and mutate.

definition: (baseball) the slight elevation on which the pitcher stands.
example: The pitcher was waiting at the mound.

definition: Climber of northeastern North America having waxy purplish-blue flowers.
Low tufted perennial phlox with needlelike evergreen leaves and pink or white flowers; native to United States and widely cultivated as a ground cover.
Common nonpoisonous shrub of eastern North America with compound leaves and green paniculate flowers followed by red berries.
Mat-forming perennial found in cold springs of the eastern United States.
A person who is feeling grief (as grieving over someone who has died).
etymology: From Middle English mourner, mornere, equivalent to mourn + -er.

definition: A ring worn as a memorial to a dead person.
A trap for catching mice.
etymology: From Middle English mouse-trappe, mous trappe, mouse trape, equivalent to mouse + trap. Cognate with Dutch muizetrap, muizentrap (“mousetrap”), German Low German Muustrappe, Muustrapp (“mousetrap”).

definition: A part that goes over or into the mouth of a person.
example: The mouthpiece of a respirator.
etymology: From mouth + piece.

definition: Move in an uncontrolled manner.
Kill a large number of people indiscriminately.
Remove muck, clear away muck, as in a mine.
example: Mucking stalls.

definition: (of soil) soft and watery.
example: Wet mucky lowland.
etymology: From muck + -y.

definition: Water soaked soil; soft wet earth.
example: The campaign issues got lost in all the mud from both parties.
etymology: From Dutch mud, from West Germanic, from Latin modius. Doublet of modius and muid.

definition: A racehorse that runs well on a muddy racetrack.
etymology: From mud + -er.

definition: (of color) discolored by impurities; not bright and clear; ‘dirty’ is often used in combination.
example: The muddied grey of the sea.

definition: A landslide of mud.
etymology: From mud + slide.

definition: A warm tubular covering for the hands.
etymology: Probably from Dutch mof (“muff, mitten”).

definition: A sweet quick bread baked in a cup-shaped pan.
example: I love you, muffin!
etymology: From earlier moofin, probably a diminutive of Low German Muffe ("small cake"; Muffen (plural)), from Middle Low German muffe (“small pastry”).

definition: Suppress in order to conceal or hide.
example: Muffle one's anger.

definition: A robber who takes property by threatening or performing violence on the person who is robbed (usually on the street).
etymology: From mug + -er.

definition: A real-life version of the game of Quidditch from the Harry Potter series.
A Muslim engaged in what they consider to be a jihad.
Sweet cider heated with spices and citrus fruit.
Consisting of many cells.
example: Multicellular organisms.
etymology: From multi- + cellular.

definition: Having sections or patches colored differently and usually brightly.
etymology: Borrowed from Latin multicolor, equivalent to multi- + color; see below.

definition: The doctrine that several different cultures (rather than one national culture) can coexist peacefully and equitably in a single country.
etymology: From multicultural + -ism.

definition: Involving several ethnic groups.
etymology: From multi- + ethnic.

definition: (mathematics) one of a pair of numbers whose product is 1: the reciprocal of 2/3 is 3/2; the multiplicative inverse of 7 is 1/7.
A pill or tablet containing several vitamins.
etymology: From multi- + vitamin.

definition: A pill or tablet containing several vitamins.
A large bite.
example: He tried to talk between munches on the sandwich.
etymology: From Middle English monchen, a variant of mocchen, mucchen ("to munch (food); chew audibly"; > Modern English dialectal mouch), probably imitative in origin (compare English crunch; German mampfen).

definition: Found in the ordinary course of events.
etymology: From Middle English mondeyne, from Old French mondain, from Late Latin mundānus, from Latin mundus (“world”). Compare Danish mondæn.

definition: Seed of the mung bean plant; used for food.
etymology: From Hindi मूँग (mūṅg), from Sanskrit मुद्ग (mudga).

definition: Seed of the mung bean plant; used for food.
etymology: From Sanskrit मुद्ग (mudga, “mung bean”), via Hindi.

definition: By municipality.
example: Municipally funded.
etymology: From municipal + -ly.

definition: Weapons considered collectively.
etymology: From Latin mūnitiō (“a defence, fortification”) via French munition, from mūnīre (“fortify, defend (with a wall)”) + -tiō, from moenia (“city walls, defensive walls, or walls in general”). Equivalent to munite + -ion.

definition: An industry that manufacturers weapons of war.
An elementary particle with a negative charge and a half-life of 2 microsecond; decays to electron and neutrino and antineutrino.
etymology: Contraction of the earlier term mu-meson; the particle has now been recategorised as a lepton. Coined by Italian physicist Enrico Fermi in 1951 in his book Elementary Particles.

definition: Kill intentionally and with premeditation.
example: The mafia boss ordered his enemies murdered.

definition: An indictment charging someone with murder.
Conviction for murder.
An indictment charging someone with murder.
A narrative about a murder and how the murderer is discovered.
Someone suspected of committing murder.
Killed unlawfully.
example: The murdered woman.

definition: A criminal who commits homicide (who performs the unlawful premeditated killing of another human being).
etymology: From Middle English murderere; equivalent to murder + -er.

definition: Characteristic of or capable of or having a tendency toward killing another human being.
example: Murderous thugs.
etymology: From murder + -ous (suffix forming adjectives from nouns denoting possession or presence of a quality).

definition: Acute infection caused by rickettsia and transmitted by the bite of an infected flea; characterized by fever and chills and muscle aches and a rash.
A drug that reduces muscle contractility by blocking the transmission of nerve impulses or by decreasing the excitability of the motor end plate or by other actions.
A colorless or pale brown mica with potassium.
etymology: In 1850 from Muscovy glass + -ite, from the province Muscovy in Russia. Named by James Dwight Dana.

definition: Large crested wild duck of Central America and South America; widely domesticated.
A soiree assembled for the purpose of listening to music.
The property of sounding like music.
etymology: From musical + -ity.

definition: Tape-recorded musical and natural sounds, often electronically distorted, arranged in planned combinations, sequences, and rhythmic patterns to create an artistic work.
Bushy herb of tropical Asia grown for its yellow or pink to scarlet blooms that resemble the hibiscus.
A muzzle-loading shoulder gun with a long barrel; formerly used by infantrymen.
example: Soldier, soldier, won't you marry me, with your musket, fife and drum.

definition: A foot soldier armed with a musket.
etymology: From Middle French mousquetaire in the late 16th century. By surface analysis, musket + -eer. Doublet of mousquetaire.

definition: The brown fur of a muskrat.
etymology: Perhaps so called for its musky odour and because it resembles a rat, or perhaps called by an Algonquian name like the Abenaki moskwas, with the spelling altered under the influence of the English words musk and rat.

definition: The brown fur of a muskrat.
Resembling the smell of musk.
etymology: From musk + -y.

definition: Smelling of musk.
Capable of or tending to change in form or quality or nature.
example: A mutable substance.
etymology: From Middle English mutable, from Old French mutable, from Latin mutabilis (“liable to change”). By surface analysis, muta- + -able.

definition: An event capable of causing a mutation.
etymology: From muta- + genesis.

definition: Damage or injure severely.
example: The madman mutilates art work.
etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin mutilātus, the perfect passive participle of mutilō (“to mutilate”) (see -ate (verb-forming suffix) and -ate (adjective-forming suffix)), itself from mutilus (“maimed”).

definition: Disposed to or in a state of mutiny.
example: The men became mutinous and insubordinate.

definition: An inferior dog or one of mixed breed.
etymology: Clipping of muttonhead.

definition: Tallow from the body of a mature sheep.
A measure of the induction between two circuits; the ratio of the electromotive force in a circuit to the corresponding change of current in a neighboring circuit; usually measured in henries.
The open circular discharging end of a gun.
An obsolete firearm that was loaded through the muzzle.
The velocity of a projectile as it leaves the muzzle of a gun.
(of firearms) taking the projectile or cartridge through the muzzle.
The vegetative part of a fungus consisting of a mass of branching threadlike hyphae.
etymology: From New Latin mycelium; synchronically, myc- + -el- + -ium, where the infix -el- is of unknown origin, perhaps introduced from a rebracketing of epithelium.

definition: Rod-shaped bacteria some saprophytic or causing diseases.
etymology: From myco- + bacterium.

definition: A layer of myelin encasing (and insulating) the axons of medullated nerve fibers.
The commonest protein in muscle; a globulin that combines with actin to form actomyosin.
etymology: From myo- (“relating to muscle”), and Ancient Greek μυός (muós), genitive of μῦς (mûs, “muscle”) + -in.

definition: A story about a crime (usually murder) presented as a novel or play or movie.
Of an obscure nature.
example: Rituals totally mystifying to visitors from other lands.

definition: Bother persistently with trivial complaints.
example: She nags her husband all day long.
etymology: From Middle English nagg, nage, nagge (“horse, small riding horse, pony”), cognate with Dutch negge, neg (“horse”), German Nickel (“small horse”). Perhaps related to English neigh.

definition: Attach something somewhere by means of nails.
example: Nail the board onto the wall.
etymology: From Middle English nail, nayl, Old English næġl, from Proto-West Germanic *nagl, from Proto-Germanic *naglaz, from Proto-Indo-European *h₃nogʰ- (“nail”).

definition: A form of torture in which the fingernails or toenails are removed.
A form of torture in which the fingernails or toenails are removed.
Lack of sophistication or worldliness.
A potent narcotic antagonist (trade name Narcan) especially effective with morphine.
etymology: From nal- (“opioid receptor antagonist/agonist”) + (hydr)ox(y) + -one.

definition: Offensive term for a homosexual man.
etymology: From nancy. As a verb, cf. prance, dance, and mince.

definition: A woman who is the custodian of children.
example: The nanny was keeping a close watch on her little charges.
etymology: From nan (“grandmother; nursemaid”) + -y. The root is from nana (“grandma; nanny”), which is from nanna (“grandmother”), which is possibly derived from Proto-Celtic *nana (“grandmother”).

definition: A metric unit of length equal to one billionth of a meter.
etymology: From nano- + meter.

definition: One billionth (10^-9) of a second; one thousandth of a microsecond.
example: I just know that the nanosecond I take my eyes off my phone, somebody's going to steal it.
etymology: From nano- + second.

definition: A fullerene molecule having a cylindrical or toroidal shape.
etymology: From nano- + tube.

definition: (of fabrics) having soft nap produced by brushing.
example: Napped fabrics.

definition: (of hair) in small tight curls.
etymology: A diminutive in -y. The base is probably napkin but possibly French nappe directly (note that napkin is already a diminutive).

definition: A lawman concerned with narcotics violations.
etymology: Clipping of narcotics (control) officer.

definition: Of or relating to or designating narcotics.
example: Narcotic addicts.
etymology: From Middle French narcotique or German narkotisch and directly from Medieval Latin narcōticus, from Ancient Greek ναρκωτῐκός (narkōtĭkós).

definition: An antagonist used to counteract the effects of narcotics (especially to counteract the depression of respiration).
A lawman concerned with narcotics violations.
One of several turbinate bones in the nasal cavity.
Offensive or even (of persons) malicious.
example: In a nasty mood.
etymology: From Middle English nasty, nasti, naxty, naxte (“unclean, filthy”), whence also Early Modern English nasky (“nasty”), of obscure origin.

definition: A form of socialism featuring racism and expansionism and obedience to a strong leader.
Put under state control or ownership.
example: Mitterand nationalized the banks.
etymology: From French nationaliser. By surface analysis, national + -ize.

definition: Advocating the perpetuation of native societies.
example: The old nativist prejudice against the foreign businessman.
etymology: From native + -ist.

definition: A natural process resulting in the evolution of organisms best adapted to the environment.
etymology: Coined by British biologist Charles Darwin in 1859 in his work On the Origin of Species.

definition: Planted so as to give an effect of wild growth.
example: Drifts of naturalized daffodils.

definition: A person who practices nudity for reasons of health or religion.
etymology: From nature + -ist.

definition: Suggestive of sexual impropriety.
example: A naughty wink.
etymology: From late Middle English noughti, naughty (“evil, immoral, wicked”), from nought (“evil, immoral”) + -ī̆ (suffix forming adjectives). Analysable as naught + -y.

definition: Feeling nausea; feeling about to vomit.
Naval weaponry consisting of a large gun carried on a warship.
Naval weaponry consisting of a missile carried on a warship.
Weaponry for warships.
Literally, the contemplation of one's navel, which is an idiom usually meaning complacent self-absorption.
etymology: Calque of Ancient Greek ὀμφαλοσκοπία (omphaloskopía). By surface analysis, navel + gazing.

definition: Derogatory term for a person who is fanatically dedicated to, or seeks to control, some activity, practice, etc.
example: The most prominent and well-known nazi was Adolf Hitler.

definition: Ill-mannered and coarse and contemptible in behavior or appearance.
A very large wine bottle holding the equivalent of 20 normal bottles of wine; used especially for display.
A lover who necks.
etymology: From neck + -er, from the verb.

definition: The molding at the top of a column.
example: For Lent, he gave up necking and cigarettes.

definition: A tract of land used for burials.
The localized death of living cells (as from infection or the interruption of blood supply).
example: Usually gangrene will follow necrosis unless the dead tissue is resected.
etymology: From Ancient Greek νέκρωσις (nékrōsis), equivalent to necro- + -osis.

definition: Lace worked with a needle in a buttonhole stitch on a paper pattern.
etymology: From needle + point.

definition: Embroidery consisting of allover embroidered canvas resembling tapestry.
Large semi-evergreen tree of the East Indies; trunk exudes a tenacious gum; bitter bark used as a tonic; seeds yield an aromatic oil; sometimes placed in genus Melia.
etymology: Borrowed from Hindi नीम (nīm) / Urdu نِیم (nīm), from Sanskrit निम्ब (nimba).

definition: Residue after oil is pressed from neem seeds.
Seed of neem trees; source of pesticides and fertilizer and medicinal products.
Large semi-evergreen tree of the East Indies; trunk exudes a tenacious gum; bitter bark used as a tonic; seeds yield an aromatic oil; sometimes placed in genus Melia.
Characterized by or displaying negation or denial or opposition or resistance; having no positive features.
example: A negative outlook on life.
etymology: From Middle English negative, negatif, from Old French negatif, from Latin negātīvus (“that denies, negative”), from negāre (“to deny”); see negate.

definition: An elementary particle with a negative charge and a half-life of 2 microsecond; decays to electron and neutrino and antineutrino.
Not showing due care or attention.
example: Neglectful parents.
etymology: From neglect + -ful.

definition: In a negligent manner.
example: He did his work negligently.
etymology: From negligent + -ly.

definition: Wine and hot water with sugar and lemon juice and nutmeg.
etymology: Named after Colonel Francis Negus (1670–1732), its creator.

definition: The characteristic sounds made by a horse.
etymology: Inherited from Middle English neyen, from Old English hnǣġan, from Proto-West Germanic *hnaijan, from Proto-Germanic *hnajjaną (“to neigh”).

definition: Exhibiting the qualities expected in a friendly neighbor.
example: He's very neighborly: he always collects my mail when I'm away on vacation.
etymology: From neighbor + -ly.

definition: Something causing misery or death.
example: Batman is in constant conflict with his nemesis, The Joker.
etymology: From the Greek goddess of retribution Nemesis (Ancient Greek Νέμεσις (Némesis)).

definition: A conservative who subscribes to neoconservatism.
etymology: From neo- + conservative.

definition: A yellow trivalent metallic element of the rare earth group; occurs in monazite and bastnasite in association with cerium and lanthanum and praseodymium.
etymology: From neo- + (di)dymium.

definition: Death of a liveborn infant within the first 28 days of life.
The death rate during the first 28 days of life.
A plant that is found in an area where it had not been recorded previously.
etymology: Borrowed from Latin neophytus, from Ancient Greek νεόφυτος (neóphutos, “newly planted”), from νέος (néos, “new”) + φυτόν (phutón, “plant, child”). By surface analysis, neo- + -phyte.

definition: An abnormal new mass of tissue that serves no purpose.
etymology: From neo- + plasm, after German Neoplasma.

definition: Of or related to or having the properties of a neoplasm.
example: Neoplastic cells.
etymology: From neo- + plastic.

definition: A cell that is part of tumor.
The branch of medicine concerned with the kidney - its development and anatomy and physiology and disorders.
etymology: From nephro- + -logy.

definition: A disease affecting the kidneys.
etymology: From nephro- + -pathy.

definition: Being in a tense state.
etymology: From nerve + -y.

definition: A structure in which animals lay eggs or give birth to their young.
example: Mouse nests, wasp nests, skink nests.
etymology: From Middle English nesten, nisten, from Old English nistan, nistian, from Proto-West Germanic *nistijan (“to nest, build a nest”).

definition: Young bird not yet fledged.
etymology: From Middle English nestling, equivalent to nest + -ling.

definition: (religion) the world of the dead.
example: In some religions, one's soul departs to a netherworld, instead of the heavens.
etymology: From nether- (“beneath, lower”) + world.

definition: Remaining after all deductions.
example: Nett price; nett weight.

definition: Acute spasmodic pain along the course of one or more nerves.
etymology: From New Latin neuralgia, from Ancient Greek νεῦρον (neûron, “nerve”) + ἄλγος (álgos, “pain”). By surface analysis, neur- + -algia.

definition: Malignant tumor containing embryonic nerve cells; usually metastasizes quickly.
etymology: From neuro- + blastoma.

definition: Of or relating to the nervous and endocrine systems (especially as they function together).
example: A neuroendocrine cancer.
etymology: From neuro- + endocrine.

definition: The development of nerve tissues.
etymology: From neuro- + -genesis.

definition: Of or relating to neuropsychiatry.
etymology: From neuro- + psychiatric.

definition: Of or concerned with neuropsychology.
example: A neuropsychological examination.
etymology: From neuro- + psychological or neuropsychology + -ical.

definition: The branch of psychology that is concerned with the physiological bases of psychological processes.
etymology: From neuro- + psychology.

definition: Any toxin that affects neural tissues.
etymology: From neuro- + toxin.

definition: Neither male nor female (of grammatical gender).
example: ‘it’ is the third-person singular neuter pronoun.
etymology: Inherited from Middle English neutre, from Latin neuter, from ne (“not”) + uter (“either”), a semantic loan from Koine Greek οὐδέτερος (oudéteros); compare English either, English whether, and neither.

definition: Having testicles or ovaries removed.
The sterilization of an animal.
example: They took him to the vet for neutering.

definition: Get rid of (someone who may be a threat) by killing.
example: The double agent was neutralized.
etymology: From French neutraliser (first attested in 1642). By surface analysis, neutral + -ise.

definition: Made neutral in some respect; deprived of distinctive characteristics.
Action intended to keep a country politically neutral or exclude it from a possible war.
example: The neutralization of Belgium.
etymology: Borrowed from French neutralisation. By surface analysis, neutral + -ization or neutralize + -ation.

definition: Fire that is delivered in order to render the target ineffective or unusable.
The chief phagocytic leukocyte; stains with either basic or acid dyes.
etymology: From German Neutrophil, from neutro- (“neutro-”) + -phil (“-phile”), equivalent to neutro- + -phil.

definition: At no time hereafter.
example: Quoth the raven, nevermore!
etymology: From Middle English nevermore, from the Old English phrase nǣfre mā. Equivalent to never + -more.

definition: A term popularised by Pope John Paul II with reference to efforts to reawaken the faith in traditionally Christian parts of the world, particularly Europe.
example: The New Evangelization calls each of us to deepen our faith, believe in the Gospel message and go forth to proclaim the Gospel.

definition: (of a new kind or fashion) gratuitously new.
example: She buys all these new-fangled machines and never uses them.

definition: A male person who investigates and reports or edits news stories.
etymology: From news + -man.

definition: A male journalist employed to provide news stories for newspapers or broadcast media.
etymology: From newspaper + -man. Compare paperboy.

definition: A courteous manner that respects accepted social usage.
etymology: From nice + -ness.

definition: Any plant of the genus Nigella.
etymology: Borrowed from translingual Nigella, from Late Latin nigella. Doublet of nielle.

definition: (ethnic slur) extremely offensive name for a Black person.
etymology: Alteration of earlier neger, from Middle French nègre (“a black person”), from Spanish negro. Ultimately from Latin niger (“black”), thus a doublet of negro and noir.

definition: (informal) small and of little importance.
example: A dispute over niggling details.

definition: An alcoholic drink taken at bedtime; often alcoholic.
example: Winston wore a nightcap to stave off the cold.
etymology: From night + cap.

definition: Someone who rejects all theories of morality or religious belief.
etymology: From Latin nihil (“nothing”) + -ist.

definition: The delusion that things (or everything, including the self) do not exist; a sense that everything is unreal.
Of a chemical compound having a ring with nine members.
The cardinal number that is the sum of eight and one.
etymology: (1): From nine + -er.

definition: A member of the ninja who were trained in martial arts and hired for espionage or sabotage or assassinations; a person skilled in ninjutsu.
example: He used to work in the Japanese agency as a ninja.
etymology: Borrowed from Japanese 忍者 (ninja), of uncertain derivation but with an underlying sense of secret or hidden person.

definition: A soft grey ductile metallic element used in alloys; occurs in niobite; formerly called columbium.
etymology: From Niobe + -ium, because of the element's affinity with tantalum, named after Niobe's father Tantalus.

definition: A young person of either sex.
etymology: From nip + -er.

definition: A sharp biting taste.
example: A nippy cheese.
etymology: From nip + -y.

definition: Not final or absolute.
example: The decree is nisi and not absolute.

definition: Any of a class of organic compounds containing the cyano radical -CN.
etymology: Clipping of benzonitrile, which contains the −C≡N group. Benzonitrile was discovered and named by Hermann Fehling in 1844.

definition: Any of the nitrobacteria that oxidize ammonia into nitrites.
The circulation of nitrogen; nitrates from the soil are absorbed by plants which are eaten by animals that die and decay returning the nitrogen back to the soil.
The assimilation of atmospheric nitrogen by soil bacteria and its release for plant use on the death of the bacteria.
A heavy yellow poisonous oily explosive liquid obtained by nitrating glycerol; used in making explosives and medically as a vasodilator (trade names Nitrospan and Nitrostat).
etymology: From nitro- + glycerin.

definition: Informal term for an upper-class or wealthy person.
example: He aimed a dreadful chopper at Baily’s nob.
etymology: Pronunciation spelling of knob. Nobleman sense from white-nob (“white-head”) (18th century), referring to the powdered wigs used by those having or affecting upper middle-class status.

definition: In a noble manner.
example: She has behaved nobly.
etymology: From Middle English nobeliche, nobely, nobilliche, nobilly, nobliche, noblike, nobly, noblye, equivalent to noble + -ly.

definition: Make small marks into the surface of.
etymology: From Middle English nokke, attested since the 14th century, probably from a Scandinavian/North Germanic language (compare Swedish nock (“notch”), but compare Dutch nok, from Middle Dutch nocke (“tip, point”).

definition: Ejaculation during sleep (usually during a dream).
A small node.
etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin nōdulus (“small knot”, from nōdus (“knot”) + -ulus (“-ule”)). By surface analysis, node + -ule. Doublet of nodulus.

definition: With much noise or loud and unpleasant sound.
example: He blew his nose noisily.
etymology: From noisy + -ly.

definition: An entry in the court record to the effect that the plaintiff or prosecutor will not proceed.
Acute ulceration of the mucous membranes of the mouth or genitals; often seen in undernourished children.
etymology: Borrowed from New Latin noma from Latin nomē from Ancient Greek νομή (nomḗ, “spreading (of sores)”) from νέμω (némō, “feed, devour, spread (of sores)”).

definition: A reply that has no relevance to what preceded it.
example: Having a costumed superhero abduct the vicar was an utter non sequitur in the novel.
etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin nōn sequitur (literally “it does not follow”).

definition: The property of not being connected with or engaged in commercial enterprises.
example: Despite its proud non-commercialism, the campus-based small press may have a rampant best seller in its most recent publication.

definition: The prevention of something increasing or spreading (especially the prevention of an increase in the number of countries possessing nuclear weapons).
Where slavery was prohibited.
A word with a special meaning used for a special occasion.
etymology: From for the nonce and word. Coined by James Murray, the influential first editor of the Oxford English Dictionary.

definition: The failure to obey.
etymology: From non- + compliance.

definition: Not conforming to established customs or doctrines especially in religion.
example: The lot will become more nonconforming with respect to that particular development standard.
etymology: From non- + conforming.

definition: Not conforming to some norm or socially approved pattern of behavior or thought.
example: Their rabidly nonconformist deportment has made them legendary.
etymology: From non- + conformist.

definition: Not of prime or central importance.
example: Nonessential to the integral meanings of poetry.
etymology: From non- + essential.

definition: Without fat or fat solids.
example: Nonfat or fat-free milk.
etymology: From non- + fat.

definition: Relating to a technique that does not involve puncturing the skin or entering a body cavity.
etymology: From non- + invasive.

definition: The prevention of something increasing or spreading (especially the prevention of an increase in the number of countries possessing nuclear weapons).
example: They protested that the nonproliferation treaty was just a plot to maintain the hegemony of those who already had nuclear weapons.
etymology: From non- + proliferation.

definition: Not invested with or related to prominent position or status etc.
etymology: From non- + public.

definition: Not caused by a specific agent; used also of staining in making microscope slides.
example: Nonspecific enteritis.
etymology: From non- + specific.

definition: Not conforming to the language usage of a prestige group within a community.
example: A nonstandard dialect is one used by uneducated speakers or socially disfavored groups.
etymology: From non- + standard.

definition: (of surfaces especially of cooking utensils) permitting easy removal of adherent food particles.
example: A frying pan with a nonstick surface.
etymology: From non- + stick.

definition: Not producing or resulting from poison.
etymology: From non- + toxic.

definition: A sheltered and secluded place.
example: There was a small broom for sweeping ash kept in the nook between the fireplace bricks and the wall.
etymology: From Middle English noke, nok (“nook, corner, angle”), of uncertain origin.

definition: Used by males to address an older female.
etymology: Borrowed from Korean 누나 (nuna, “older sister of a man”).

definition: An achondroplastic dwarf whose small size is the result of a genetic defect; body parts and mental and sexual development are normal.
The imposition of standards or regulations.
etymology: From normal + -isation or normalise + -ation.

definition: Become normal or return to its normal state.
example: Let us hope that relations with this country will normalize soon.
etymology: From normal + -ise.

definition: Coming from the northeast.
example: Northeasterly winds.

definition: A kind of New World oriole.
Found in Atlantic coastal waters of North America from South Carolina to Maine; esteemed as a panfish.
A butcherbird of northern North America.
Coming from the northwest.
example: Northwesterly winds.
etymology: From north + westerly. See also northwestern.

definition: Street names for cocaine.
Street names for heroin.
A sudden sharp drop or rapid decline.
example: The stock took a nosedive.
etymology: From nose + dive.

definition: Offensively curious or inquisitive.
etymology: From nose + -y.

definition: Hypothetical remedy for all ills or diseases; once sought by the alchemists.
etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin nostrum (“ours”), nominative neuter of noster (“our, ours”).

definition: Offensively curious or inquisitive.
example: He flipped through my letters in his nosy way.
etymology: From nose + -y (adjectival suffix), or from nose + -y (diminutive suffix).

definition: A Latin phrase (or its abbreviation) used to indicate that special attention should be paid to something.
etymology: Unadapted borrowing from Classical Latin notā bene (“note well”).

definition: An announcement containing information about an event.
example: You didn't give me enough notice.
etymology: Borrowed from Middle French notice, from the Latin nōtitia. Doublet of notitia.

definition: Characteristic of someone who has risen economically or socially but lacks the social skills appropriate for this new position.
(weapons) deriving destructive energy from the release of atomic energy.
example: Nuclear war.
etymology: From Latin nū̆cleus, a contraction of the adjective nuculeus, masculine of feminine nuculea (“pertaining to a small nut”) from nucula + adjectival suffix -eus, -ea, -eum.

definition: The nations possessing nuclear weapons.
The military doctrine that an enemy will be deterred from using nuclear weapons as long as they can be destroyed as a consequence.
example: When two nations both resort to nuclear deterrence the consequence could be mutual destruction.

definition: A weapon of mass destruction whose explosive power derives from a nuclear reaction.
A painting of a naked human figure.
example: Michelangelo's David is a well-known standing male nude; Michelangelo also created several other nudes.
etymology: Entered English 1493 as a legal term, meaning "unsupported, not formally attested," from Middle English nud, from Latin nūdus (“naked, bare”).

definition: Erotic dancing with little or no clothing.
A painting of a naked human figure.
A naked person.
A statue of a naked human figure.
A statue of a naked human figure.
A solid lump of a precious metal (especially gold) as found in the earth.
example: A gold nugget.
etymology: Uncertain, first attested in reference to animals & people in Scotland and in reference to ore chunks in Australia.

definition: (law) a broad legal concept including anything that disturbs the reasonable use of your property or endangers life and health or is offensive.
example: The neighbor's dog barking throughout the night is a right nuisance - I'm going to complain.
etymology: From Middle English noysaunce, from Anglo-Norman nusaunce, nussance and Old French nuisance, from nuisir (“to harm”), from Latin nocēre. Doublet of nocence and nocency.

definition: The dividend of a fraction.
etymology: Learned borrowing from Late Latin numerātor.

definition: The study of the supposed occult influence of numbers on human affairs.
etymology: From numero- + -logy.

definition: Used by males to address an older female.
(Roman Catholic Church) a diplomatic representative of the Pope having ambassadorial status.
etymology: From Spanish nuncio, from Latin nūntius (“envoy”).

definition: (of an infant) breast-fed.
A vessel fitted with a flexible teat and filled with milk or formula; used as a substitute for breast feeding infants and very young children.
Usually large hard-shelled seed.
etymology: From Middle English note, nute, from Old English hnutu, from Proto-West Germanic *hnut, from Proto-Germanic *hnuts (“nut”), from a root *knu- possibly shared with Proto-Celtic *knūs and Latin nux (“nut”).

definition: A widely distributed perennial sedge having small edible nutlike tubers.
Someone deranged and possibly dangerous.
etymology: From nut + case. Compare headcase, mental case etc.

definition: Geranium with round fragrant leaves and small white flowers.
Of or providing nourishment.
etymology: From Middle French nutritif, from Late Latin nūtritīvus, from the participle stem of Latin nūtriō (“to suckle”).

definition: A person who is regarded as eccentric or mad.
etymology: From Middle English nutter, notere, equivalent to nut + -er.

definition: Having the flavor of nuts.
example: A nutty sherry.
etymology: From nut + -y.

definition: Move or arrange oneself in a comfortable and cozy position.
example: The horse nuzzled its foal’s head gently to wake him up.
etymology: The verb is derived from Middle English noselen (“to bend down”); further etymology uncertain, possibly: * a back-formation from noseling, noselyng (“on the back, supine;

definition: A thermoplastic polyamide; a family of strong resilient synthetic fibers.
example: I tore a hole in my nylons while walking home through the woods.
etymology: Coined by the company DuPont in 1938. According to the company, the name was formed from the random generic syllable nyl- + the common fiber suffix -on (as in rayon and Dacron), said to be ultimately from cotton.

definition: Women's stockings made from a sheer material (nylon or rayon or silk).
(used of women) affected with excessive sexual desire.
example: Nymphomaniacal.
etymology: From nymphomania + -ac. By surface analysis, nympho- + -maniac.

definition: Profane or obscene expression usually of surprise or anger.
example: Take an oath.
etymology: From Middle English ooth, oth, ath, from Old English āþ (“oath”), from Proto-West Germanic *aiþ (“oath”), from Proto-Germanic *aiþaz (“oath”).

definition: In an obedient manner.
example: Obediently she slipped off her right shoe and stocking.
etymology: From obedient + -ly.

definition: Make obscure or unclear.
example: The squid's ink obfuscated its presence.
etymology: The adjective is first attested in 1487, in Middle English, the verb in 1536;

definition: A notice of someone's death; usually includes a short biography.
etymology: From Anglo-Norman obit, Middle French obit, and their source, Latin obitus (“going down; death”), from obīre (“to go down, to die”).

definition: A notice of someone's death; usually includes a short biography.
etymology: PIE word *h₁epi Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin obituārius (“obituary”) + English -ary (suffix denoting something relating to another thing or used in a place).

definition: The machine-language output of a compiler that is ready for execution on a particular computer.
Make external or objective, or give reality to.
example: The entire notion of cheerleading is just a sexist attempt to try to objectify the female body.
etymology: From object + -ify.

definition: Destruction by annihilating something.
etymology: From obliterate + -ion.

definition: In an obnoxious manner.
example: We sat behind an obnoxiously loud couple in the cinema.
etymology: From obnoxious + -ly.

definition: Designed to incite to indecency or lust.
example: The dance often becomes flagrantly obscene.
etymology: From Middle French obscene (modern French obscène (“indecent, obscene”)), and from its etymon Latin obscēnus, obscaenus (“inauspicious; ominous; disgusting, filthy; offensive, repulsive; indecent, lewd, obscene”).

definition: To an obscene degree.
example: This man is obscenely rich.
etymology: From obscene + -ly.

definition: The trait of behaving in an obscene manner.
example: Bestiality was outlawed as an obscenity in the strongly conservative community.
etymology: From obscene + -ity, from Latin obscenitas.

definition: Sticking out; protruding.
example: The office manager is an unpleasantly obtrusive individual.
etymology: PIE word *h₁epi From Latin obtrūsus + English -ive (suffix meaning ‘of the nature of’, forming adjectives).

definition: South American wood sorrel cultivated for its edible tubers.
etymology: Borrowed from Spanish oca, from Quechua uqa.

definition: Egg-shaped terracotta wind instrument with a mouthpiece and finger holes.
etymology: Borrowed from Italian ocarina (literally “little goose”), due to the musical instrument's resemblance to the animal.

definition: Any of the convolutions of the outer surface of the occipital lobe of the cerebrum.
A believer in occultism; someone versed in the occult arts.
etymology: From occult + -ist.

definition: Among the largest bony fish; pelagic fish having an oval compressed body with high dorsal and anal fins and caudal fin reduced to a rudder-like lobe; worldwide in warm waters.
Land bordering an ocean.
etymology: From ocean + front.

definition: Fish whose flesh is dried and flaked for Japanese cookery; may be same species as skipjack tuna.
A scientist who studies physical and biological aspects of the seas.
Nocturnal wildcat of Central America and South America having a dark-spotted buff-brown coat.
etymology: From French ocelot, a word formed by Buffon from Classical Nahuatl ōcēlōtl (“jaguar”).

definition: Plant of southeastern United States having solitary white funnel-shaped flowers flushed with pink and large glossy green leaves that turn bronze-red in fall.
The size of a book whose pages are made by folding a sheet of paper three times to form eight leaves.
etymology: From Latin octavo. Doublet of octave, oitava, and ochava.

definition: Having no odor.
example: Odorless gas.
etymology: From odor + -less.

definition: The passage between the pharynx and the stomach.
etymology: From Ancient Greek οἰσοφάγος (oisophágos), from οἴσω (oísō), future form of φέρω (phérō, “to carry”) + ἔφαγον (éphagon, “to eat”).

definition: A general term for female steroid sex hormones that are secreted by the ovary and responsible for typical female sexual characteristics.
In an unpleasantly offensive manner.
example: He smelled offensively unwashed.
etymology: From offensive + -ly.

definition: People elected or appointed to administer a government.
etymology: From official + -dom.

definition: Someone who works on an oil rig.
A worker who oils engines or machinery.
etymology: From Middle English oyler, equivalent to oil + -er.

definition: The short low gruff noise of the kind made by hogs.
example: The protesters replied to the police officers' demands with a chorus of oinks.
etymology: Imitative of the sound.

definition: A woman who is old.
example: Stop being such an old woman and get on with it.

definition: (economics) a market in which control over the supply of a commodity is in the hands of a small number of producers and each one can influence prices and affect competitors.
etymology: PIE word *h₃ligos From oligo- (prefix meaning ‘few; several’) + -poly (suffix meaning ‘pertaining to the number of sellers in a market’), by analogy with monopoly.

definition: A mineral consisting of magnesium iron silicate; a source of magnesium.
etymology: From olive + -in, later remodelled after -ine.

definition: The 15th letter of the Greek alphabet.
example: ... They include Mira itself (omicron Ceti) which can be seen shortly before dawn.
etymology: From Latin omicron, from Koine Greek ὂ μῑκρόν (ò mīkrón, “little o”), named in contrast with omega (“big o”). The uncommon form omicra is similarly borrowed from Latin and Greek.

definition: Feeding on both plants and animals.
etymology: From omni- + -vorous.

definition: A gene that disposes normal cells to change into cancerous tumor cells.
etymology: From onco- + gene.

definition: One part in a billion equal parts.
The property of having one dimension.
Having one hump.
example: A one-humped camel.

definition: A domino or die whose upward face shows one pip.
Someone who looks on.
example: I wasn’t involved in the fight; I was only an onlooker.
etymology: From on- (prefix meaning ‘at; on, upon’) + looker (“one that looks”), from the verb look on. Compare Old English onlōciend (“one who looks on or watches”), which did not survive into Middle English;

definition: A female gametocyte that develops into an ovum after two meiotic divisions.
etymology: From oo- + -cyte.

definition: A large number or amount.
Chinese tea leaves that have been partially fermented before being dried.
etymology: 1850s. From either Mandarin 烏龍 /乌龙 (wūlóng) due to hypercorrection, or directly from Hokkien 烏龍 /乌龙 (o͘-liông), from 烏 /乌 (o͘, “black”) + 龍 /龙 (liông, “dragon”).

definition: Attractiveness to the opposite sex.
example: Use a mild cleanser, but pick something with enough oomph to do the job.
etymology: Onomatopoeic.

definition: Start firing a weapon.
A marriage in which each partner is free to enter into extraneous sexual relationships without guilt or jealousy from the other.
etymology: From open + marriage.

definition: (computer science) software that controls the execution of computer programs and may provide various services.
etymology: From operating + system. First use appears c. the 1950s.

definition: Financial transactions at a brokerage; having to do with the execution of trades and keeping customer records.
example: They get the job done, but operations is the area in which they're weakest.

definition: In a manner to produce an effect.
etymology: From operative + -ly.

definition: A short amusing opera.
etymology: Borrowed from Italian operetta.

definition: A narcotic drug that contains opium or an opium derivative.
etymology: From Medieval Latin opiātus.

definition: Express one's opinion openly and without fear or hesitation.
example: I opined that matters would soon become considerably worse.
etymology: Borrowed from Middle French opiner, from Latin opīnor (“to hold as an opinion”), from *opīnus (“thinking, expecting”), only in negative nec-opīnus (“not expecting”) and in-opīnus (“not expected”);

definition: An addictive narcotic extracted from seed capsules of the opium poppy.
etymology: Borrowed from Latin opium and Ancient Greek ὄπιον (ópion), from ὀπός (opós, “juice of a plant”), from Proto-Indo-European *sokʷós (“juice, resin”).

definition: Small furry Australian arboreal marsupials having long usually prehensile tails.
Terrestrial marsupials of southern South America that resemble shrews.
Shrimp-like crustaceans whose females carry eggs and young in a pouch between the legs.
etymology: So called due to members of this order having a marsupium or 'brood pouch,' similar to an opossum, which is a marsupial.

definition: Medium-sized tree of West Virginia to Florida and Texas.
One of two stereoisomers that are mirror images of each other that are non-superposable (not identical).
A worker who makes glasses for remedying defects of vision.
etymology: Borrowed from French opticien.

definition: With optimism; in an optimistic manner.
example: ‘We have a good chance of winning,’ he exclaimed optimistically.
etymology: From optimistic + -ally.

definition: (psychoanalysis) the first sexual and social stage of an infant's development; the mouth is the focus of the libido and satisfaction comes from suckling and chewing and biting.
Oral stimulation of the genitals.
(psychoanalysis) the first sexual and social stage of an infant's development; the mouth is the focus of the libido and satisfaction comes from suckling and chewing and biting.
Erect perennial of eastern and southern United States having showy orange flowers.
Man-made equipment that orbits around the earth or the moon.
etymology: From orbit + -er.

definition: The male is chestnut-and-black.
The moment of most intense pleasure in sexual intercourse.
example: Anally-induced orgasm.
etymology: From French orgasme or New Latin orgasmus, from Ancient Greek ὀργασμός (orgasmós, “excitement, swelling”), from ὀργάω (orgáō, “to swell with moisture”).

definition: A projecting bay window corbeled or cantilevered out from a wall.
etymology: From Middle English oriel, from Old French oriol (“gallery, corridor”), Late Latin oriolum (“portico, hall”), probably from Latin aureolus (“gilded”), applied to an apartment decorated with gilding. See oriole.

definition: A projecting bay window corbeled or cantilevered out from a wall.
A member of an Oriental race; the term is regarded as offensive by Asians (especially by Asian Americans).
The quality or customs or mannerisms characteristic of Asian civilizations.
example: Orientalisms can be found in Mozart's operas.
etymology: From French orientalisme, from oriental (“eastern, Oriental”). In the sense “patronizing Western attitude” popularized by Edward Said's 1978 book Orientalism. Equivalent to Oriental + -ism.

definition: A specialist in oriental subjects.
etymology: From oriental + -ist.

definition: Positioning with respect to a reference system or determining your bearings physically or intellectually.
example: Noticed the bee's momentary orienting pause before heading back to the hive.

definition: An aperture or hole that opens into a bodily cavity.
example: The orifice into the aorta from the lower left chamber of the heart.
etymology: From Middle French, from Old French, from Late Latin ōrificium (“an opening, literally the making of a mouth”), compound of ōs (“mouth”) + faciō (“to make”).

definition: Mostly tropical songbird; the male is usually bright orange and black.
etymology: A borrowing from Middle French oriol, from Old French oriol, from Latin aureolus, diminutive of aureus (“golden”). Doublet of aureole. First use appears c. 1776 in the writings of Thomas Pennant.

definition: Having a difficult and contrary disposition.
etymology: A contracted or dialectal pronunciation of ordinary. Sense 3 (“ordinary, commonplace”) was the earliest sense;

definition: Of or relating to ornithology.
example: Her ornithological interests.
etymology: From ornithology + -ical.

definition: A zoologist who studies birds.
etymology: From ornithology + -ist.

definition: Deprived of parents by death or desertion.
example: I found an orphaned project, half-completed before its author quit, and decided to finish it.

definition: Of or relating to or involving or practicing orthodontics.
example: Orthodontic braces.
etymology: From orthodontia + -ic, equivalent to ortho- + -odont + -ic.

definition: An appliance that corrects dental irregularities.
Dental treatment that corrects irregularities of the teeth or of the relation of the teeth to surrounding anatomy; treatment is usually by braces or mechanical aids.
example: Orthodontic treatment of facial abnormalities.

definition: The branch of dentistry dealing with the prevention or correction of irregularities of the teeth.
etymology: From orthodontic + -s, equivalent to ortho- (“correct, straight”) + -odont + -ics.

definition: Of or relating to or expressed in orthography.
etymology: From ortho- + -graph + -ic. Compare French orthographique, Latin orthographus, Ancient Greek ὀρθογράφος (orthográphos).

definition: The branch of medical science concerned with disorders or deformities of the spine and joints.
The branch of medical science concerned with disorders or deformities of the spine and joints.
etymology: From ortho- + Ancient Greek παιδεία (paideía, “upbringing, training”). Originally a branch of medicine correcting deformities in children.

definition: One of the three sections of the hipbone; together these two bones form the front of the pelvis.
Be undecided about something; waver between conflicting positions or courses of action.
example: He oscillates between accepting the new position and retirement.
etymology: First attested in 1726;

definition: Electronic equipment that provides visual images of varying electrical quantities.
etymology: From oscillo- + -scope.

definition: Of or relating to osmosis.
example: Osmotic pressure.

definition: (physical chemistry) the pressure exerted by a solution necessary to prevent osmosis into that solution when it is separated from the pure solvent by a semipermeable membrane.
The quality of being not alike; being distinct or different from that otherwise experienced or known.
etymology: From other + -ness.

definition: The medical specialty that deals with diseases of the ear, nose and throat.
etymology: From oto- (“ear”) + laryngo- (“throat”) + -logy.

definition: A motorboat with an outboard motor.
A building that is subordinate to and separate from a main building.
etymology: From out + building.

definition: Characteristic of or suitable to outdoor life.
example: A rugged outdoorsy life.
etymology: From outdoors + -y.

definition: The act of renovating and fitting out a ship.
Go around the flank of (an opposing army).
etymology: From out- + flank.

definition: Conspicuously or grossly unconventional or unusual.
example: The outlandish clothes of teenagers.
etymology: The adjective is derived from Middle English outlandisch, outlondish (“foreign”), from Old English ūtlendisċ (“foreign;

definition: Surpass in speed.
example: Malthus believed that population increase would outpace increases in the means of subsistence.
etymology: From out- + pace.

definition: Grossly offensive to decency or morality; causing horror.
example: Subjected to outrageous cruelty.
etymology: From Anglo-Norman outrageus, Middle French outrageus, from outrage; equivalent to outrage + -ous.

definition: In a very offensive manner.
example: He behaved outrageously.
etymology: From Middle English outrageously, equivalent to outrageous + -ly.

definition: A stabilizer for a canoe; spars attach to a shaped log or float parallel to the hull.
etymology: Modification of earlier outligger after rig (“to fit out”); equivalent to out- + ligger.

definition: A seagoing canoe (as in South Pacific) with an outrigger to prevent it from upsetting.
Larger than normal for its kind.
In an outstanding manner or to an outstanding degree.
example: She was outstandingly successful in her profession.
etymology: From outstanding + -ly.

definition: Be or do something to a greater degree.
example: We quickly outstripped the amateur runners.
etymology: From out- (prefix forming verbs with the sense of exceeding or surpassing) + strip (“(obsolete) to move or pass by quickly”).

definition: A scene that is filmed but is not used in the final editing of the film.
example: The DVD for that movie has ten minutes' worth of outtakes.
etymology: From Middle English outtaken (“to take out”), equivalent to out- + take.

definition: Beat through cleverness and wit.
etymology: From out- + wit.

definition: Cook under a broiler.
Too old to be useful.
etymology: From over- + age.

definition: The surface soil that must be moved away to get at coal seams and mineral deposits.
etymology: From over- + burden.

definition: Heavily burdened with work or cares.
example: Overburdened social workers.

definition: Rip off; ask an unreasonable price.
example: October 22, 1706, Alexander Pope, letter to Mr. Walsh Our language is naturally overcharged with consonants.
etymology: From Middle English overchargen, equivalent to over- + charge.

definition: Total certainty or greater certainty than circumstances warrant.
etymology: From over- + confidence.

definition: Marked by excessive confidence.
example: So overconfident and impudent as to speak to the queen.
etymology: From over- + confident.

definition: Overeat or eat immodestly; make a pig of oneself.
Unduly excited.
etymology: From over- + excited.

definition: Urinary incontinence that occurs when the bladder is so full that it continually leaks urine; often attributable to a blocked urethra (e.g., due to prostate enlargement) or weak bladder muscles or nerve damage.
Covered with growing plants.
example: He spends so much money on new technology: he's like an overgrown schoolboy buying toys.
etymology: From over- + grown.

definition: With hand brought forward and down from above shoulder level.
example: An overhand pitch.
etymology: From over- + hand.

definition: A simple small knot.
A baseball pitch in which the hand moves above the shoulder.
A stitch passing over an edge vertically.
The capability to obliterate a target with more weapons (especially nuclear weapons) than are required.
example: 24 hours of TV coverage of the US election verged on overkill.
etymology: From over- + kill.

definition: Pay too much.
example: Be careful not to overpay when buying second-hand items.
etymology: From over- + pay.

definition: A payment larger than needed or expected.
example: The employer sued to recover overpayment of wages.
etymology: From over- + payment.

definition: Too much production or more than expected.
etymology: From over- + production.

definition: Revealing excessive self-confidence; reaching for the heights.
etymology: From overreach + -ing.

definition: Being or passing over or across the sea.
example: Some overseas trade in grain arose.
etymology: From Middle English over-se, over see, ouer sea, from Old English ofer sǣ (literally “over/across (the) sea”); equivalent to over + sea. Compare West Frisian oerseesk, Dutch overzee, German Übersee, Danish oversøisk.

definition: Having an upper part projecting beyond the lower.
example: An overshot jaw.

definition: An act of excessive simplification; the act of making something seem simpler than it really is.
etymology: From over- + simplification.

definition: Making to seem more important than it really is.
example: The story he gave was something of an overstatement of the facts.

definition: Upholstered thickly and deeply.
example: An overstuffed sofa.
etymology: ] From over- + stuffed.

definition: A comfortable upholstered armchair.

definition: (usually plural) an ulterior implicit meaning or quality.
example: Overtones of despair.

definition: Write new data on top of existing data and thus erase the previously existing data.

definition: Deeply agitated especially from emotion.

definition: Rounded like an egg.

definition: The female reproductive cell; the female gamete.

definition: A salt or ester of oxalic acid.
etymology: From French oxalate, equivalent to oxalic acid + -ate (“salt or ester”).

definition: Domesticated bovine animals as a group regardless of sex or age.
example: A team of oxen.
etymology: From Middle English oxen, from Old English oxan, from Proto-West Germanic *ohsan, from Proto-Germanic *uhsniz, nominative and accusative plural of *uhsô (“ox”), equivalent to ox + -en (plural ending).

definition: A substance that oxidizes another substance.

definition: Enter into a combination with oxygen or become converted into an oxide.

definition: A substance that oxidizes another substance.
etymology: From oxidize + -er.

definition: The process of providing or combining or treating with oxygen.
example: The oxygenation of the blood.

Edible agaric with a soft greyish cap growing in shelving masses on dead wood.

A Japanese pinball game played on a vertical board.

definition: Someone who collects things that have been discarded by others.

definition: Pen where racehorses are saddled and paraded before a race.

definition: The system of numbering pages.

definition: Without pain.

definition: An air gun used in the game of paintball; designed to simulate a semiautomatic.
Freshwater turtles having bright yellow and red markings; common in the eastern United States.
Having qualities unique to the art of painting.

definition: A fractional monetary unit in Bangladesh and India and Nepal and Pakistan.
etymology: From Spanish paisa, a shortening of paisano.

definition: Of or relating to the second period of the Stone Age (following the eolithic).
The earth science that studies fossil organisms and related remains.
Relating to or lying near the palate.

definition: A territory under the jurisdiction of a count palatine.

definition: Of or relating to paleontology.
Abnormally deficient in color as suggesting physical or emotional distress.

definition: Drab yellowish big-eared bat that lives in caves.
(used colloquially) having the relationship of friends or pals.

definition: A horse of light tan or golden color with cream-colored or white mane and tail.
etymology: Borrowed from Spanish palomino, from paloma (“dove, pigeon”) + diminutive suffix -ino.

definition: Tall perennial grass of Pampas of South America having silvery plumes and growing in large dense clumps.

A complete and impressive array.

definition: A person who participates in (or is open to) sexual activities of many kinds.
etymology: From pan- + -sexual. First attested in 1926 (with pansexualism attested since 1917), as a descriptor of the psychological theory that all human activity is based on sexuality.

definition: Large-flowered garden plant derived chiefly from the wild pansy of Europe and having velvety petals of various colors.

definition: An abbreviation of pantomime.
A pair of pants and a matching jacket worn by women.

definition: Worthless or oversimplified ideas.

definition: The government of the Roman Catholic Church.

definition: Belief of the Roman Catholic Church that God protects the pope from error when the pope speaks about faith or morality.
(Roman Catholic Church) a diplomatic representative of the Pope having ambassadorial status.
A substance made from paper pulp that can be molded when wet and painted when dry.
A wire or plastic clip for holding sheets of paper together.

definition: A weight used to hold down a stack of papers.
example: John used his coffee mug as a paperweight.

definition: Calyx composed of scales or bristles or featherlike hairs in plants of the Compositae such as thistles and dandelions.

definition: A plane curve formed by the intersection of a right circular cone and a plane parallel to an element of the curve.
etymology: Borrowed from New Latin parabola, from Ancient Greek παραβολή (parabolḗ), from παραβάλλω (parabállō, “to set side by side”), from παρά (pará, “beside”) + βάλλω (bállō, “to throw”). Doublet of parable, parole, and palaver.

definition: Descent with a parachute.

etymology: From parachute + -ing.

definition: Gliding in a parasail.
etymology: From paraglider.

definition: Any of numerous small slender long-tailed parrots.

definition: The simultaneous execution of two or more operations.
Relating to or of the nature of paralysis.

etymology: Borrowed from French paralytique, from Latin paralyticus, from Ancient Greek παραλυτικός (paralutikós, “paralyzed”).

definition: A woman's lover.

definition: The relation between two different kinds of organisms in which one receives benefits from the other by causing damage to it (usually not fatal damage).

definition: Of or relating to the parasympathetic nervous system.

definition: Any one of four endocrine glands situated above or within the thyroid gland.

definition: Layers of ice cream and syrup and whipped cream.
etymology: Unadapted borrowing from French parfait (“perfect”). Doublet of parfit, perfect, perfecto, and perfectus.

Any of the convolutions of the outer surface of the parietal lobe of the cerebrum.
A member of a parish.

definition: A floor made of parquetry.
Seating at the rear of the main floor (beneath the balconies).
A floor made of parquetry.
The posterior lobe of the pituitary body; primarily glandular in nature.
The whitish root of cultivated parsnip.
A predisposition to like something.
The quality of being particular and pertaining to a specific case or instance.

definition: An ardent and enthusiastic supporter of some person or activity.
For less than the standard number of hours.
(ballet) a solo dance or dance figure.

A ballroom dance in fast duple time.

Having been subjected to pasteurization in order to halt fermentation.
Milk that has been exposed briefly to high temperatures to destroy microorganisms and prevent fermentation.
Highly seasoned cut of smoked beef.
etymology: Borrowed from Yiddish פּאַסטראַמע (pastrame), from Romanian pastramă, from Ottoman Turkish باصدرمه (modern Turkish pastırma), a variation of bastırma (“dried meat”), from root bas- (“to press”).

definition: Resembling paste in color; pallid.

A theory or argument made up of miscellaneous or incongruous ideas.

definition: A small flat triangular bone in front of the knee that protects the knee joint.

definition: The attitude (of a person or a government) that subordinates should be controlled in a fatherly way for their own good.

definition: Caused by or altered by or manifesting disease or pathology.

definition: A person who lends money at interest in exchange for personal property that is deposited as security.

definition: Aroused to impatience or anger.

definition: Disparaging terms for small people.

With undue hurry and confusion.

etymology: From French pêle-mêle, from Old French pesle-mesle, apparently a rhyme based on the stem of mesler (“to mix, meddle”). Compare meddle, melee.

definition: Anything happening rapidly or in quick successive.

definition: Brown tree shrew having a naked tail bilaterally fringed with long stiff hairs on the distal third; of Malaysia.
Drawn or written with a pencil.

Beautiful handwriting.

definition: Someone who is excessively careful with money (who pinches every penny before letting go of it).
example: Over the years, he developed a reputation as a penny pincher who wouldn't spend money for anything.
etymology: From pinchpenny.

definition: A fringe region of partial shadow around an umbra.

definition: Pungent seasoning from the berry of the common pepper plant of East India; use whole or ground.

definition: Very low or nominal rent.
Having the piquant burning taste of peppers.
example: Corn chips with peppery salsa.
etymology: From pepper + -y.

definition: (psychology) the tendency for perceived objects to give rise to very similar perceptual experiences in spite of wide variations in the conditions of observation.
A musician who plays percussion instruments.

definition: Through the unbroken skin; refers to medications applied directly to the skin (creams or ointments) or in time-release forms (skin patches).

definition: (Christianity) the abode of Satan and the forces of evil; where sinners suffer eternal punishment.
example: Hurl'd headlong … To bottomless perdition, there to dwell.

definition: In a perennial manner; repeatedly.

definition: An eardrum with a hole or tear in it; can interfere with normal hearing and cause other ear problems.
Perfumes in general.

definition: Hasty and without attention to detail; not thorough.

etymology: From Late Latin perfunctōrius (“careless, negligent”), from the past participial stem of perfungor, perfunct- (“perform, carry through”), from per- + fungor.

definition: A framework that supports climbing plants.

definition: Periapsis in Earth orbit; the point in its orbit where a satellite is nearest to the Earth.
etymology: From French périgée via Latin perigeum, perigaeum, ultimately from Ancient Greek περί (perí, “near”) + γῆ (gê, “Earth”).

definition: In a dangerous manner.

Liable to perish; subject to destruction or death or decay.

etymology: From Middle English *persishable, perysabyl, equivalent to perish + -able. Compare Old French perissable (and modern French périssable).

definition: The interior of the peritoneum; a potential space between layers of the peritoneum.
Inflammation of the peritoneum.

definition: Made or become more cheerful or lively.

Any of a group of enzymes (occurring especially in plant cells) that catalyze the oxidation of a compound by a peroxide.

definition: Perform an act, usually with a negative connotation.

Another word for person; a person not meriting identification.

definition: Military personnel lost by death or capture.

In a persuasive manner.

definition: Reading carefully with intent to remember.

definition: (used of sexual behavior) showing or appealing to bizarre or deviant tastes.

definition: Troubled persistently especially with petty annoyances.

A petty disparagement.
Any of numerous tropical herbs having fluted funnel-shaped flowers.
etymology: Borrowed from taxonomic name Petunia, from (now obsolete) French pétun (“tobacco”), from Old Tupi petyma (“tobacco”).

definition: (psychoanalysis) the third stage in a child's development when awareness of and manipulation of the genitals is supposed to be a primary source of pleasure.
(psychoanalysis) the third stage in a child's development when awareness of and manipulation of the genitals is supposed to be a primary source of pleasure.
The male sex organ.
etymology: Borrowed from Latin phallus (“membrum virile, phallus, or a figure thereof”), from Ancient Greek φαλλός (phallós).

definition: A ghostly appearing figure.
etymology: A learned variant of phantom; from Middle English fantosme, from Old French fantosme, fantasme, from Latin phantasma, from Ancient Greek φάντασμα (phántasma). Doublet of phantom.

definition: Something many people believe that is false.
An imaginary life lived in a fantasy world.
Something existing solely in the imagination (but often mistaken for reality).
A self-righteous or sanctimonious person.
The study of the action of drugs in the body: method and rate of excretion, duration of effect, etc.

definition: Of or relating to the throat.

A small recess in the wall of the pharynx.

A beneficial bacterium found in the intestinal tract of healthy mammals; often considered to be a plant.

definition: Characterized by profanity or cursing.

definition: Engaged in a profession or engaging in as a profession or means of livelihood.

definition: Relating to or characteristic of professors.

definition: Having cells that lack membrane-bound nuclei.

definition: An amino acid that is found in many proteins (especially collagen).
The act of prolonging something.

definition: Indulging in promiscuous (casual and indiscriminate) sexual relations.

definition: State or announce.

A branch of symbolic logic dealing with propositions as units and with their combinations and the connectives that relate them.
An unincorporated business owned by a single person who is responsible for its liabilities and entitled to its profits.

definition: Having the power to propel.

definition: Wood heaped for burning a dead body as a funeral rite.

Systematic killing of a racial or cultural group.
