definition: (numeration system) the positive integer that is equivalent to one in the next higher counting place.
example: 10 is the radix of the decimal system.
etymology: PIE word *wréh₂ds Etymology tree Proto-Indo-European *wréh₂ds Proto-Italic *wrādīks Latin rādīxlbor. English radix Learned borrowing from Latin rādīx (“a root”). Doublet of radish.

definition: Treat cruelly.
etymology: From Middle English ragge, from Old English ragg (suggested by derivative raggiġ (“shaggy; bristly; ragged”)), from Old Norse rǫgg (“tuft; shagginess”), from Proto-Germanic *rawwa-, probably related to *rūhaz.

definition: Disparaging terms for the common people.
etymology: From earlier tag-rag and tag and rag, from rag + tag.

definition: Complain bitterly.
example: They ought to rail off the playground.
etymology: From Middle English rail, rayl, *reȝel, *reȝol (found in reȝolsticke (“a ruler”)), partly from Old English regol (“a ruler, straight bar”) and partly from Old French reille;

definition: The activity of designing and constructing and operating railroads.
A drop of rain.
example: 1969, Hal David (lyricist), “Raindrops Keep Fallin' on My Head”.
etymology: From Middle English rein-drope, reyn-drope, reyn drope, from Old English reġndropa, from Proto-Germanic *regnadrupô. Equivalent to rain + drop.

definition: Executive who is very successful in bringing in business to their company or firm.
example: The law firm relied heavily on Charlotte as its main rainmaker to bring in new clients.
etymology: From rain + maker.

definition: Noisy and lacking in restraint or discipline.
example: A social gathering that became rambunctious and out of hand.
etymology: A variant of rumbustious (“boisterous and unruly”).

definition: Behave violently, as if in state of a great anger.
etymology: ]See ramson.

definition: In deplorable condition.
example: A ramshackle old pier.
etymology: First attested in 1830, a back-formation from ramshackled, from ransackled, past participle of ransackle (“to ransack”), frequentative of Middle English ransaken (“to pillage”).

definition: A deliberately haphazard arrangement of observations so as to simulate chance.
etymology: From random + -ization.

definition: Feeling great sexual desire.
example: If you're feeling randy, give me a call and I'll come round and give you some hot lovin'.
etymology: First use appears c. 1665 in a letter by the Earl of Argyll. From Scottish randy (“boisterous, aggressive”), of uncertain origin. Probably from rand (“to storm, rave”, verb), a variant of rant, see rant;

definition: A measuring instrument (acoustic or optical or electronic) for finding the distance of an object.
etymology: From range + finder.

definition: Having an offensive rancid odor.
Malicious software that makes a computer unusable unless a payment is made to the attacker.
etymology: From ransom + -ware.

definition: Living by preying on other animals especially by catching living prey.
example: The rapacious wolf.
etymology: Perhaps from rapacity + -ous, in any case ultimately from Latin rapāx (“grasping, greedy”) + -acious.

definition: Eurasian plant cultivated for its seed and as a forage crop.
example: The ear rape of that concert was so bad I can't even listen to their songs at work anymore.
etymology: From Middle English rapen, rappen (“to abduct; ravish; seduce; rape; seize; snatch; carry off;

definition: Conviction for rape.
Edible light yellow to brown oil from rapeseed used also as a lubricant or illuminant.
etymology: Inherited from Middle English rape oyle.

definition: Someone who is suspected of committing rape.
Someone who forces another to have sexual intercourse.
etymology: From rape + -er.

definition: Seed of rape plants; source of an edible oil.
etymology: From Middle English rape sede, rape seed, equivalent to rape (“rapeseed plant(s)”) + seed. As a meronym for the entire plant, from the need to distinguish the plant from the etymologically unrelated verb and act rape.

definition: Edible light yellow to brown oil from rapeseed used also as a lubricant or illuminant.
A rate that is rapid.
etymology: From rapid + -ity, from French rapidité, from Latin rapiditas.

definition: Someone who forces another to have sexual intercourse.
etymology: From rape + -ist.

definition: Any of numerous carnivorous birds that hunt and kill other animals.
etymology: From Middle English raptour, from Latin raptor (“kidnapper, thief”).

definition: Feeling great rapture or delight.
example: The rapturous applause.
etymology: From rapture + -ous.

definition: Having low density.
example: Lightheaded from the rarefied mountain air.

definition: (usually followed by ‘to’) full of eagerness.
example: Raring to go.
etymology: From rare (verb), a variant of rear (“to raise, rouse”). More at rear.

definition: In a hasty and foolhardy manner.
etymology: From rash + -ly.

definition: Uttering in an irritated tone.
example: The rasp of her perpetual cough.
etymology: The noun is from Middle French raspe (whence Modern French râpe), deverbal of rasper, from Old French rasper (see above).

definition: Any fern of the genus Doodia having pinnate fronds with sharply dentate pinnae.
Woody brambles bearing usually red but sometimes black or yellow fruits that separate from the receptacle when ripe and are rounder and smaller than blackberries.
etymology: From earlier raspis berry, possibly from raspise (a sweet rose-colored wine), from Anglo-Latin vinum raspeys, of uncertain origin. Possibly related to rasp (“coarse, rough”), of Germanic origin.

definition: Unpleasantly harsh or grating in sound.
example: He spoke in a rasping voice due to throat cancer.

definition: Desert one's party or group of friends, for example, for one's personal advantage.
example: He ratted on his coworker.
etymology: From Middle English ratten, further etymology unknown. Compare Middle Low German retten (“to tear, tear up”), Middle High German ratzen (“to scratch; rasp; tear”). Could be related to write. See also rit.

definition: A switch made from the stems of the rattan palms.
(psychiatry) a defense mechanism by which your true motivation is concealed by explaining your actions and feelings in a way that is not threatening.
etymology: Borrowed from French rationalisation, equivalent to rational + -isation or rationalise + -ation.

definition: Structure and run according to rational or scientific principles in order to achieve desired results.
example: We rationalized the factory's production and raised profits.
etymology: From French rationaliser. By surface analysis, rational + -ise.

definition: Substitute a natural for a supernatural explanation of.
example: You can rationalize away all the strange noises you hear — there is no poltergeist in the house!

definition: Distributed equitably in limited individual portions.
example: Got along as best we could on rationed meat and sugar.

definition: To furnish incriminating evidence to an officer of the law (usually in return for favors).
Pit viper with horny segments at the end of the tail that rattle when shaken.
etymology: From rattle + -er.

definition: Any of several small temperate and tropical orchids having mottled or striped leaves and spikes of small yellowish-white flowers in a twisted raceme.
Of or characteristic of rats.
etymology: From rat + -y (suffix meaning ‘having the quality of’ forming adjective).

definition: Earthy and sexually explicit.
example: A raunchy novel.
etymology: Of unknown etymology. Originally U.S. Army Air Corps slang; origins among cadets in Texas suggest a possible connection to Mexican Spanish rancho (see ranch), which had connotations of animal filth by 1864.

definition: Ruinously destructive and wasting.
example: A ravaging illness.

definition: Greenish brown pigment.
The event of a structure being completely demolished and leveled.
A mongrel hog with a thin body and long legs and a ridged back; a wild or semi-wild descendant of improved breeds; found chiefly in the southeastern United States.
etymology: From razor + back.

definition: A mongrel hog with a thin body and long legs and a ridged back; a wild or semi-wild descendant of improved breeds; found chiefly in the southeastern United States.
Any exciting and complex play intended to confuse (dazzle) the opponent.
Any exciting and complex play intended to confuse (dazzle) the opponent.
example: The razzmatazz of a razzle-dazzle of pairs figure skating.
etymology: Reduplication of dazzle.

definition: A chemical substance that is present at the start of a chemical reaction.
etymology: From react + -ant.

definition: The act of admitting someone again.
example: The surgery was performed on his readmission to the clinic.
etymology: From re- + admission.

definition: Align anew or better.
example: The surgeon realigned my jaw after the accident.
etymology: From re- + align.

definition: A share that has been allocated again.
etymology: From re- + allocation.

definition: Politics based on practical rather than moral or ideological considerations.
etymology: Borrowed from German Realpolitik (literally “practical, realistic, fact-based, realism-based politics”).

definition: Squeeze the juice out (of a fruit) with a reamer.
example: Ream oranges.
etymology: From Middle English rem, reme, from Old English rēam (“cream”), from Proto-West Germanic *raum, from Proto-Germanic *raumaz (“cream”), from Proto-Indo-European *réwgʰmn̥ (“to sour [milk]”).

definition: Given fresh life or vigor or spirit.
A new appraisal or evaluation.
etymology: From re- + appraisal.

definition: The back of a military formation or procession.
example: Infantrymen were in the rear.
etymology: From Middle English rere, from Anglo-Norman rere, ultimately from Latin retro. Compare arrear. Doublet of retro.

definition: The act of arming again.
example: He opposed the rearmament of Japan after World War II.
etymology: From re- + armament. Compare French réarmement.

definition: Located in or toward the back or rear.
example: On the rearward side.
etymology: From rear + -ward.

definition: Transfer somebody to a different position or location of work.
example: The offending employees were reassigned after the incident.
etymology: From re- + assign.

definition: In a reassuring manner.
example: The prime minister pointed reassuringly to the silence of the British press.
etymology: From reassuring + -ly.

definition: After death the soul begins a new cycle of existence in another human body.
etymology: From re- + birth.

definition: A broadcast that repeated at a later time.
etymology: From re- + broadcast.

definition: A deliberate discourteous act (usually as an expression of anger or disapproval).
example: He was surprised by her quick rebuff to his proposal.
etymology: From obsolete French rebuffer, from Middle French rebuffer (compare French rebiffer (“to rise up, revolt”)), from Italian ribuffare.

definition: Formally reject or disavow a formerly held belief, usually under pressure.
example: Convince me that I am wrong, and I will recant.
etymology: First attested in 1535, from Latin recantare (“to sing back, reecho, sing again, repeat in singing, recant, recall, revoke, charm back or away”), from re- (“back”) + canto (“to chant, to sing”), frequentative of cano.

definition: Changing a particular word or phrase.
Hybridization involving a pair of crosses that reverse the sexes associated with each genotype.
The act of making or doing something in return.
example: The reciprocation of kindness.
etymology: From reciprocate + -ion.

definition: Classifying something again (usually in a new category).
etymology: From re- + classification.

definition: (law) a security entered into before a court with a condition to perform some act required by law; on failure to perform that act a sum is forfeited.
example: The defendant was released on his own recognizance.
etymology: From Middle English reconisaunce, from Old French reconissance. Doublet of reconnaissance.

definition: Construct or form anew or provide with a new structure.
example: The governing board was reconstituted.
etymology: From re- + constitute.

definition: A narcotic drug that is used only occasionally and is claimed to be nonaddictive.
etymology: From recreational + drug.

definition: Of or involving the rectum.
example: Rectal cancer.
etymology: From rectum + -al.

definition: Normal response to the presence of feces in the rectum.
Any of several veins draining the walls of the anal canal and rectum.
A diode that can handle high electrical current flow (in only one direction), usually used to change alternating current into direct current.
A thermionic tube having two electrodes; used as a rectifier.
A thermionic tube having two electrodes; used as a rectifier.
The terminal section of the alimentary canal; from the sigmoid flexure to the anus.
etymology: Borrowed from New Latin rectum, clipping of Latin rectum intestinum (literally “the straight intestine”), rectum, neuter of rectus (“straight”). See right.

definition: Lying down; in a position of comfort or rest.
etymology: From Latin present participle recumbēns, from recumbō (“to recline”).

definition: Of a color at the end of the color spectrum (next to orange); resembling the color of blood or cherries or tomatoes or rubies.
etymology: See also West Frisian read, Low German root, rood, rot, rod, Dutch rood, German rot, Danish and Norwegian Bokmål rød, Norwegian Nynorsk raud, Swedish röd, Faroese reyður, Icelandic rauður;

definition: Tall showy tropical American annual having hairy stems and long spikes of usually red flowers above leaves deeply flushed with purple; seeds often used as cereal.
Bryony having fleshy roots pale green flowers and very small red berries; found in Europe, North Africa, western Asia.
Commonly cultivated Old World woody herb having large pinkish to red flowers.
Food fish of the Mediterranean and Atlantic coasts of Europe and America.
Trillium of northeastern United States with sessile leaves and red or purple flowers having a pungent odor.
(slang) offensive term for female Native Americans.
Having strong sexual appeal.
example: A red-hot mama.

definition: Putting something (as a literary work or a legislative bill) into acceptable form.
example: The government supplied only the redaction to the reporters; the original was kept secret.
etymology: From French rédaction or its etymon New Latin redactiō (“redaction”), from Latin redigō (“to lead back, collect, prepare, reduce to a certain state”), from red- (“back”) + agō (“to put in motion, to drive”).

definition: Turn red, as if in embarrassment or shame.
example: But I will make you blush; nay, I will make you redden all over.
etymology: From red + -en.

definition: Give an interpretation or explanation to.
etymology: From Middle English red, rede, from Old English rǣd, from Proto-West Germanic *rād, from Proto-Germanic *rēdaz. Cognate with Danish råd, Dutch raad, German Rat, Swedish råd, Norwegian Bokmål råd.

definition: Redo the decoration of an apartment or house.
etymology: From re- + decorate.

definition: The act of giving a new definition.
example: Words like ‘conservative’ require periodic redefinition.
etymology: From re- + definition.

definition: Deploy anew.
example: The U.S. must redeploy their troops in the Middle East.
etymology: From re- + deploy.

definition: The withdrawal and redistribution of forces in an attempt to use them more effectively.
etymology: From re- + deployment.

definition: A night flight from which the passengers emerge with eyes red from lack of sleep.
example: He took the redeye in order to get home the next morning.

definition: A night flight from which the passengers emerge with eyes red from lack of sleep.
example: He took the redeye in order to get home the next morning.

definition: Having red hair and usually fair skin.
etymology: From red + headed.

definition: Serving to bring to mind.
example: Cannot forbear to close on this redolent literary note.
etymology: From Middle English redolent (first attested in 1400), from Old French redolent, from Latin redolentem, present participle of redoleō (“to emit a scent”), from red- + oleō (“to smell”).

definition: Double in magnitude, extent, or intensity.
example: The enemy redoubled their screaming on the radio.
etymology: From Middle French redoubler. By surface analysis, re- + double.

definition: (military) a temporary or supplementary fortification; typically square or polygonal without flanking defenses.
etymology: From French redoute, from Italian ridotta, from Medieval Latin reductus (“refuge”), from Latin redūcō (“to withdraw”), with spelling influenced by doubt.

definition: A substance capable of bringing about the reduction of another substance as it itself is oxidized; used in photography to lessen the density of a negative or print by oxidizing some of the loose silver.
example: This reducer ring allows an E27 lampshade to be used on a B22 light fitting.
etymology: From reduce + -er.

definition: Capable of being reduced.
example: Reducible to a set of principles of human nature.
etymology: From reduce + -ible.

definition: (genetics) cell division that produces reproductive cells in sexually reproducing organisms; the nucleus divides into four nuclei each containing half the chromosome number (leading to gametes in animals and spores in plants).
Of or relating to the theory of reductionism.
example: Reductionist arguments.
etymology: From reduction + -ist.

definition: Marijuana leaves rolled into a cigarette for smoking.
etymology: From reef + -er.

definition: Wet with secreted or exuded moisture such as sweat or tears.
example: Wiped his reeking neck.

definition: Enact or perform again.
example: They reenacted the battle of Princeton.
etymology: From re- + enact.

definition: The evaluation of something a second time (or more).
etymology: From re- + evaluation.

definition: Look at again; examine again.
etymology: From re- + examine.

definition: A communal dining-hall (usually in a monastery).
etymology: Via Middle English refectori from Late Latin refectorium, from Latin reficere (“to remake, to rebuild”).

definition: A long narrow dining table supported by a stretcher between two trestles.
Something referred to; the object of a reference.
example: For quotations using this term, see Citations:referent.
etymology: From refer + -ent.

definition: One whose work is to refine a specific thing.
example: He was a sugar refiner.
etymology: From refine + -er.

definition: The fraction of radiant energy that is reflected from a surface.
etymology: From reflect + -ance.

definition: The fraction of radiant energy that is reflected from a surface.
etymology: From reflective + -ity.

definition: In a reflexive manner; by means of reflexes.
example: Such effects can be induced reflexly.
etymology: From reflexive + -ly.

definition: Tending to reform.
example: Reformative and rehabilitative agencies.

definition: Any of various anemic conditions that are not successfully treated by any means other than blood transfusions (and that are not associated with another primary disease).
An exile who flees for safety.
Provide with choice or abundant food or drink.
example: Please, regale us with your best tales!
etymology: From French régaler (“to entertain, feast”), from Old French regale, rigale, from gale (“merriment”), probably of Germanic origin (see Old French galer).

definition: Strictly controlled.
A feature (as a pronunciation or expression or custom) that is characteristic of a particular region.
etymology: From regional + -ism.

definition: Grow anew or continue growth after an injury or interruption.
example: Parts of the trunk of this tree can regrow.
etymology: From re- + grow.

definition: A tetrahedron with four equilateral triangular faces.
The condition of having been made regular (or more regular).
etymology: From regular + -ization.

definition: Pour or rush back.
example: The blood regurgitates into the heart ventricle.
etymology: From Late Latin regurgitātus, past participle of regurgitāre, combined form of re- (“back”) + gurgitāre (“to engulf, flood”), from gurges (“whirlpool, gulf, sea, abyss”).

definition: Backflow of blood through a defective heart valve.
Designed to accomplish rehabilitation.
example: From a penal to a rehabilitative philosophy.
etymology: From rehabilitate + -ive.

definition: Ignite anew, as of something burning.
example: The strong winds reignited the cooling embers.
etymology: From re- + ignite.

definition: Arctic deer with large antlers in both sexes; called ‘reindeer’ in Eurasia and ‘caribou’ in North America.
example: Santa Claus' sleigh is supposedly pulled by nine reindeer.
etymology: From Middle English reyndere, reynder, rayne-dere, from Old Norse hreindýri (“reindeer”), from hreinn (“reindeer”) + dýr (“animal”).

definition: Integrate again.
example: Russia must be reintegrated into Europe.
etymology: From re- + integrate.

definition: Interpret from a different viewpoint.
example: If you look at it that way, you can reinterpret all the old evidence so that it supports the new theory.
etymology: From re- + interpret.

definition: Impart vigor, strength, or vitality to.
etymology: From re- + invigorate.

definition: With restored energy.
Not accept something given or offered.
example: I reject the idea of starting a war.
etymology: From Late Middle English rejecten, from Latin reiectus, past participle of reicere (“to throw back”), from re- (“back”) + iacere (“to throw”). Displaced native Old English āweorpan (literally “to throw out”).

definition: A particular manner of connectedness.
example: The relatedness of all living things.
etymology: From related + -ness.

definition: Tending to relax or relieve muscular or nervous tension.
example: A relaxant drug.

definition: Learn something again, as after having forgotten or neglected it.
example: After the accident, he could not walk for months and had to relearn how to walk down stairs.
etymology: From re- + learn.

definition: Refer to another person for decision or judgment.
example: She likes to relegate difficult questions to her colleagues.
etymology: First attested in 1561, borrowed from Latin relēgātus, the past participle of relēgō (“to dispatch, banish”).

definition: Authorizing subordinates to make certain decisions.
Eliminate urine.
A container where religious relics are stored or displayed (especially relics of saints).
Without mercy or pity.
example: A monster of remorseless cruelty.
etymology: From remorse + -less.

definition: A structure shaped like a funnel in the outlet of the kidney into which urine is discharged before passing into the ureter.
Tear or be torn violently.
example: Powder rends a rock in blasting.
etymology: From Middle English renden, from Old English rendan (“to rend, tear, cut, lacerate, cut down”), from Proto-West Germanic *(h)randijan (“to tear”), of uncertain origin.

definition: Resembling a sound of violent tearing as of something ripped apart or lightning splitting a tree.
example: Heard a rending roar as the crowd surged forward.

definition: The mistake of not following suit when able to do so.
etymology: Borrowed from Latin renegō, from negō (“to deny”). Possibly influenced by renegotiate. Doublet of renay. See also renegade.

definition: Fail to fulfill a promise or obligation.
example: She reneged on her promise.

definition: Assign a new order to.
example: The books were sorted by title, but I'm going to reorder them by author's surname.
etymology: From re- + order.

definition: A rearrangement in a different order.
Organized again.
example: A reorganized business.

definition: Adroitness and cleverness in reply.
etymology: From French repartie, a deverbal of repartir (“to retort”).

definition: Send someone back to their homeland against their will, as of refugees.
example: Greece repatriated an Athenian frieze from France, arranging for it to be sent back to Athens.
etymology: Borrowed from Latin repatriare, from re- + patria (“homeland”). Cognate to repair (“to return”).

definition: A firearm that can fire several rounds without reloading.
Highly offensive; arousing aversion or disgust.
example: The idea of eating meat is repellent to me.

definition: Feeling or expressing remorse for misdeeds.
etymology: From Middle English repentant, from Old French repentant, present participle of repentir. By surface analysis, repent + -ant.

definition: A remote or indirect consequence of some action.
example: His declaration had unforeseen repercussions.
etymology: From Middle French répercussion, from Latin repercussio (“rebounding;

definition: Plant again or anew.
example: They replanted the land.
etymology: From re- + plant.

definition: (of income) required by law to be reported.
example: Reportable income.
etymology: From report + -able.

definition: The action of regaining possession (especially the seizure of collateral securing a loan that is in default).
etymology: From re- + possession.

definition: A publication (such as a book) that is reprinted without changes or editing and offered again for sale.
The quality of being reproducible.
etymology: From reproducible + -ity.

definition: Any organ involved in sexual reproduction.
Cast off.
example: The parents repudiated their son.
etymology: First attested in 1543; from Latin repudiātus, the perfect passive participle of repudiō (“to cast off, reject”) (see -ate (etymology 1, 2 and 3)), from repudium (“rejection, repudiation, divorce”).

definition: Offensive to the mind.
example: Morally repugnant customs.
etymology: From Middle English repugnaunt, from Old French repugnant, borrowed from Latin repugnans, present participle of repugnare (“to oppose, to fight against”), from re- (“back, against”) + pugnare (“to fight”); see pugnacious.

definition: Offensive to the mind.
example: Repulsive behavior.
etymology: Borrowed from Middle French repulsif, from Medieval Latin repulsivus, from Latin repulsus. By surface analysis, repuls(e) + -ive.

definition: One praying humbly for something.
etymology: From request + -er; compare requestor, requestress.

definition: A song or hymn of mourning composed or performed as a memorial to a dead person.
etymology: From French requin, altered by association with Etymology 1, above.

definition: A member of a military reserve.
etymology: From reserve + -ist.

definition: Settle in a new place.
example: The immigrants had to resettle.
etymology: From re- + settle.

definition: A material's opposition to the flow of electric current; measured in ohms.
etymology: From resistive + -ity.

definition: Change the size of; make the size more appropriate.
etymology: From re- + size.

definition: Ring or echo with sound.
example: The hall resounded with laughter.
etymology: From both of the following: * From Late Middle English resounen (“to return with an echo, resound; to make a sound, to sound;

definition: Acidosis resulting from reduced gas exchange in the lungs (as in emphysema or pneumonia); excess carbon dioxide combines with water to form carbonic acid which increases the acidity of the blood.
To say, state, or perform again.
etymology: From re- + state.

definition: A revised statement.
etymology: From re- + statement.

definition: Being in a tense state.
etymology: Modification of earlier restiff, from Middle English restyf, from Old French restif, from rester (“to stay, remain”), from Latin restō.

definition: A skilled worker who is employed to restore or refinish buildings or antique furniture.
etymology: From restore + -er.

definition: Submit (information) again to a program or automatic system.
etymology: From re- + submit.

definition: Restored to life or consciousness.
Cause to move more slowly or operate at a slower rate.
example: This drug will retard your heart rate.
etymology: From Middle English retarden, from Anglo-Norman retarder, from Latin retardō (“to retard”, from re- + tardus (“slow”)).

definition: A decrease in rate of change.
Relatively slow in mental or emotional or physical development.
example: Providing a secure and sometimes happy life for the retarded.
etymology: From retard + -ed.

definition: A type of firearms operating system which requires the bolt to overcome some initial resistance while not fully locked.
A network of fine lines, dots, cross hairs, or wires in the focal plane of the eyepiece of an optical instrument.
etymology: Borrowed from Late Latin rēticulum, diminutive of Latin rēte (“net”). Doublet of reticulum, Reticulum, and reticule.

definition: Of southeast Asia and East Indies; the largest snake in the world.
An unsaturated alcohol that occurs in marine fish-liver oils and is synthesized biologically from carotene.
etymology: From retina + -ol.

definition: A disease of the retina that can result in loss of vision.
etymology: From retino- + -pathy.

definition: Entrenchment consisting of an additional interior fortification to prolong the defense.
etymology: Probably partly from both of the following: * Middle French retrenchement, retranchement (“removal of a portion from a larger whole;

definition: Any of a group of viruses that contain two single-strand linear RNA molecules per virion and reverse transcriptase (RNA to DNA); the virus transcribes its RNA into a cDNA provirus that is then incorporated into the host cell.
etymology: From retro- + virus, from its reverse direction of replication.

definition: That may be returned.
example: Returnable bottles and cans.
etymology: From Middle French retournable.

definition: A process of using up or consuming again.
example: Psychopharmacologists discovered that amine reuptake is a process that inactivates monoamine neurotransmitters.
etymology: From re- + uptake.

definition: A program that can be loaded once and executed repeatedly.
A routine that can be loaded once and executed repeatedly.
A new appraisal or evaluation.
example: After the new party took power, the government declared a revaluation of the currency in an attempt to limit runaway inflation.
etymology: From re- + valuation.

definition: Account that records any surplus after the revaluation of assets.
(military) signal to wake up.
etymology: From French réveillez, imperative form of réveiller (“to wake”).

definition: (usually followed by ‘of’) pointing out or revealing clearly.
etymology: Borrowed from Latin revēlātōrius. By surface analysis, revelat(e) + -ory.

definition: Of or relating to or typical of a revenant.
example: Revenant shrieks and groans.
etymology: 19th century. From French revenant, the present participle of revenir (“to return”). Compare revenue.

definition: Ring or echo with sound.
example: Flame is reverberated in a furnace.
etymology: Borrowed from Latin reverberātus, perfect passive participle of reverberō (“to rebound; to reflect;

definition: Characterized by resonance.
The repetition of a sound resulting from reflection of the sound waves.
example: The discomfort caused by the bat's reverberation surprised Tommy.
etymology: From Old French reverberation, from Medieval Latin reverberātiō. Morphologically reverberate + -ion.

definition: Feeling or showing profound respect or veneration.
example: Maintained a reverent silence.
etymology: From Middle English reverent, from Middle French reverent (from Old French reverent) and its etymon Latin reverēns. By surface analysis, revere + -ent.

definition: (law) an interest in an estate that reverts to the grantor (or their heirs) at the end of some period (e.g., the death of the grantee).
etymology: Borrowed into late Middle English from Old French reversion (modern réversion), from Latin reversio, from revertō. By surface analysis, revert + -sion.

definition: Any dangerous departure from the teachings of Marx.
etymology: From revision + -ism.

definition: Capable of being revoked or annulled.
example: A revocable order.
etymology: Borrowed from Middle French révocable, from Old French revocable, from Latin revocabilis; equivalent to revoke + -able.

definition: Highly offensive; arousing aversion or disgust.
example: Revolting food.

definition: Fill with revolutionary ideas.
etymology: From revolution + -ise.

definition: Provide with new wiring.
example: The university rewired the dormitories when most students brought computers and television sets.
etymology: From re- + wire.

definition: A one-time fee usually charged by the county for a property rezoning request.
The branch of medicine dealing with the study and treatment of pathologies of the muscles or tendons or joints.
etymology: From Ancient Greek ῥεῦμα (rheûma) (whence also English rheum) + -ology.

definition: An inflammation of the mucous membrane lining the nose (usually associated with nasal discharge).
etymology: From rhin- + -itis.

definition: Cosmetic surgery to improve the appearance of your nose.
etymology: From rhino- + -plasty.

definition: A horizontal plant stem with shoots above and roots below serving as a reproductive structure.
etymology: Borrowed from Ancient Greek ῥίζωμα (rhízōma). As philosophical metaphor, used by Gilles Deleuze and Félix Guattari.

definition: The basic unit of money in Yemen; equal to 100 fils.
etymology: Borrowed from Persian ریال (riyâl) (in the case of Iran) and a variant transliteration of Arabic رِيَال (riyāl) (in the case of Oman and Yemen), from Spanish real. Doublet of real, royal, and regal.

definition: Western North American frog with a taillike copulatory organ.
A toxic protein extracted from castor beans; used as a chemical reagent; can be used as a bioweapon.
example: One milligram of ricin can kill an adult.
etymology: Borrowed from Latin ricinus.

definition: A toxic protein extracted from castor beans; used as a chemical reagent; can be used as a bioweapon.
example: One milligram of ricin can kill an adult.

definition: Childhood disease caused by deficiency of vitamin D and sunlight associated with impaired metabolism of calcium and phosphorus.
etymology: Unknown. Originally a local name for the disease in Dorset and Somerset, England.

definition: Sit and travel on the back of animal, usually while controlling its motions.
example: Did you ever ride a camel?

definition: Treat inconsiderately or harshly.
Having a ridge or shaped like a ridge or suggesting the keel of a ship.
etymology: From Middle English rigged, riggid, ryggyd, rugged, equivalent to ridge + -ed.

definition: A long narrow range of hills.
example: To either side there are beautiful views from the trail along the ridgeline.
etymology: From ridge + line.

definition: Of a firearm; having rifling or internal spiral grooves inside the barrel.
The cutting of spiral grooves on the inside of the barrel of a firearm.
Someone who rigs ships.
etymology: From rig + -er.

definition: A long slender pointed sable brush used by artists.
In a righteous manner.
example: Righteously indignant.
etymology: From Middle English rightwisly, from Old English rihtwīslīce; equivalent to righteous + -ly.

definition: Believing in or supporting tenets of the political right.
etymology: From right + -ist.

definition: According with conscience or morality.
etymology: From Middle English rightnesse, riȝtnesse, rihtnesse, from Old English rihtnes, rehtnis, from Proto-West Germanic *rehtanassī (“rightness, justice”), equivalent to right + -ness.

definition: Temporary stiffness of joints and muscular rigidity occurring after death.
etymology: Learned borrowing from New Latin rigor mortis (literally “stiffness of death”). First attested in 1842.

definition: Cause annoyance in; disturb, especially by minor irritations.
example: Money problems rile the underpaid worker every day.
etymology: From a dialectal pronunciation of roil.

definition: A narrow elongated opening or fissure between two symmetrical parts.
etymology: Borrowing from Latin rīma (“a cleft, crack, fissure, chink”).

definition: The person in charge of performances in a circus ring.
etymology: From ring + master.

definition: Infections of the skin or nails caused by fungi and appearing as itching circular patches.
etymology: From Middle English ringworm (“ringworm; intestinal worm”), from Old English rengwyrm (“maw-worm, intestinal worm”), equivalent to ring + worm.

definition: Tropical shrub (especially of Americas) having yellow flowers and large leaves whose juice is used as a cure for ringworm and poisonous bites; sometimes placed in genus Cassia.
A firearm designed to disperse rioters rather than to inflict serious injury or death.
Remove, usually with some force or effort; also used in an abstract sense.
Of wines, fruit, cheeses; having reached a desired or final condition; (‘aged’ pronounced as one syllable).
A quick reply to a question or remark (especially a witty or critical one).
etymology: From French riposte, taken from Italian risposta, a derivative of the verb rispondere (“to respond”).

definition: A murderer who slashes the victims with a knife.
example: Jack the Ripper was probably a madman.
etymology: From rip + -er; originated 1605–15.

definition: Uneven by virtue of having wrinkles or waves.
Suggestive of sexual impropriety.
example: A risque story.

definition: The act of killing (an animal or person) in order to propitiate a deity.
In a ceremonial manner.
etymology: From ritual + -ly.

definition: Tear or be torn violently.
etymology: Compare Latin ripa (“shore”).

definition: Large river turtle of the southern United States and northern Mexico.
Minute conical gastropod superficially resembling a limpet but living and feeding on freshwater plants.
A roll of hair brushed back from the forehead.
etymology: From Middle English roche, from Old French roche, from Middle Low German roche, ruche (“ray (fish)”), from Old Saxon *rūh, possibly from Proto-Germanic *rūhaz (“rough”). Cognate with Old English ruhha ("a ray";

definition: Metal tweezers used by marijuana smokers to hold a roach.
Metal tweezers used by marijuana smokers to hold a roach.
The dead body of an animal that has been killed on a road by a vehicle.
example: Vultures usually feed on carrion or roadkill.
etymology: From road + kill.

definition: Speedy largely terrestrial bird found from California and Mexico to Texas.
etymology: From road + runner, probably a calque of Spanish correcaminos (“roadrunner”), from correr (“to run”) + caminos (“roads”).

definition: A harsh or humorous critic (sometimes intended as a facetious compliment).
example: The honoree gave his roasters as good as he got.
etymology: From Middle English roster, roostare, equivalent to roast + -er (agent noun suffix) or + -er (patient suffix). Same formation as roster, although the words have very different meanings.

definition: Dressed or clothed especially in fine attire; often used in combination.
example: Professors robed in crimson.
etymology: From robe + -ed.

definition: Small Old World songbird with a reddish breast.
etymology: Short for robin redbreast. Also from Middle English robynet, robynett (“robin (bird)”), from the Middle English name Robynett, a diminutive of the Middle English name Robyn (“Robin”). ] ]

definition: In a robust manner.
example: He was robustly built.
etymology: From robust + -ly.

definition: Any of several rock-loving cresses of the genus Arabis.
Game and food fish of upper Mississippi and Great Lakes.
Noxious cress with yellow flowers; sometimes placed in genus Sisymbrium.
A long thin implement made of metal or wood.
example: The circus strong man proved his strength by bending an iron rod, and then straightening it.

definition: Relatively small placental mammals having a single pair of constantly growing incisor teeth specialized for gnawing.
etymology: From Latin rōdēns, rōdent- (“gnawer; one who gnaws”), present participle of rōdō (“to gnaw”).

definition: Given to merry frolicking.
A rotund individual.
etymology: The noun is apparently derived from roll (“to turn over and over”) + -y (suffix forming adjectives with the sense ‘having the quality of’), reduplicated with a change of the initial consonant.

definition: Interpret romantically.
example: Don't romanticize this uninteresting and hard work!
etymology: From romantic + -ize.

definition: A person who romps or frolics.
etymology: From romp + -er.

definition: A one-piece garment for children to wear at play; the lower part is shaped like bloomers.
A craftsman who lays or repairs roofs.
etymology: From roof + -er.

definition: The quantity a room will hold.
etymology: From room + -ful.

definition: An associate who shares a room with you.
etymology: From room + -ie.

definition: A skin disease of adults (more often women) in which blood vessels of the face enlarge resulting in a flushed appearance.
etymology: Clipping of acne rosacea, from New Latin acnē (“acne”) + rosācea, feminine of rosāceus (“rose-colored”).

definition: Showy shrub of salt marshes of the eastern United States having large rose-colored flowers.
etymology: From rose + mallow.

definition: Commonly cultivated Old World woody herb having large pinkish to red flowers.
Having the pinkish flush of health.
The bud of a rose.
etymology: From rose + bud.

definition: Having the pinkish flush of health.
The reovirus causing infant enteritis.
etymology: From Latin rota (“wheel”) + virus. The name was first proposed in July 1974 in an article in The Lancet.

definition: Spherical in shape.
etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin rotundus (“round”), from Latin rota (“wheel”), from Proto-Indo-European *Hreth₂- (“to run, to roll”). Doublet of round.

definition: (of a horse) having horseshoes with projecting nails to prevent slipping.
etymology: From rough + shod.

definition: A tournament in which every contestant plays every other contestant.
etymology: From round (adjective) + robin.

definition: A small boat of shallow draft with cross thwarts for seats and rowlocks for oars with which it is propelled.
etymology: From row + boat.

definition: Going about to look at places of interest.
A person who is not very intelligent or interested in culture.
etymology: Generic use of the name Rube. See hey rube for more.

definition: A spinel used as a gemstone (usually dark red).
Become wrinkled or drawn together.
A statement of fundamental facts or principles.
In a rueful manner.
example: ‘I made a big mistake,’ he said ruefully.
etymology: From rueful + -ly.

definition: A cruel and brutal fellow.
etymology: From Middle French rufian, from Italian ruffiano (“pimp”).

definition: Floor covering consisting of a piece of thick heavy fabric (usually with nap or pile).
etymology: Uncertain; probably of North Germanic origin;

definition: The first compartment of the stomach of a ruminant; here food is collected and returned to the mouth as cud for chewing.
etymology: Borrowed from Latin rūmen.

definition: A calm, lengthy, intent consideration.
etymology: From Latin rūminātio (“chewing the cud”); see ruminate.

definition: A chronic drinker.
etymology: Unknown, with much speculation. Perhaps related to rum via poker slang, or ultimately from German Ruhm (“fame, glory”).

definition: The part of an animal that corresponds to the human buttocks.
etymology: From Middle English rumpe, from Old Norse rumpr (“rump”), from Middle Low German rump (“the bulk or trunk of a body, trunk of a tree”), ultimately from Proto-Germanic *rumpō (“trunk of a tree, log”).

definition: The act of making a noisy disturbance.
etymology: Unknown. First use appears c. 1745. The OED indicates: "perhaps an arbitrary formation". Possibly an alteration of rumbustical or rumbustious (“boisterous, noisy”) + Latin -us (“nominative suffix”).

definition: A recreation room for noisy activities (parties or children's play etc.).
Injure or kill by knocking (someone or something) down and passing over the body, as with a vehicle.
example: The athletes must run over the bridge to reach the finish line.

definition: Treat inconsiderately or harshly.
An open automobile having a front seat and a rumble seat.
etymology: Deverbal from run about.

definition: One of the crosspieces that form the steps of a ladder.
etymology: From round. Compare rondle, roundel.

definition: Relating to or consisting of runes.
example: Runic inscription.
etymology: From rune + -ic.

definition: Any character from an ancient Germanic alphabet used in Scandinavia from the 3rd century to the Middle Ages.
Tropical American bean with red flowers and mottled black beans similar to Phaseolus vulgaris but perennial; a preferred food bean in Great Britain.
(football) a back on the offensive team (a fullback or halfback) who tries to advance the ball by carrying it on plays from the line of scrimmage.
Disparaging terms for small people.
example: The runt of the family.
etymology: The OED classifies this word as "of obscure origin". Some see a connection to Middle Dutch runt (“ox”), but the OED considers this to be unlikely. Possibly connected to Icelandic hrotti meaning "brute".

definition: The basic unit of money in Indonesia; equal to 100 sen.
etymology: Borrowed from Indonesian rupiah, in turn Borrowed from Pali rūpiya (“silver”), in turn borrowed from Sanskrit रूप्यक (rūpyaka, “a silver coin”), from रूप्य (rūpya, “wrought silver”). Doublet of rupee and rufiyaa.

definition: Of brown with a reddish tinge.
etymology: From Middle English russet, from Anglo-Norman russet, rossat, roset, and Middle French rosset, rousset (“reddish, reddish-brown; a rough wool cloth”), from Middle French rous, rus (“to rouse”) + -et (diminutive suffix);

definition: Rhizoctinia disease of potatoes.
Characteristic of rural life.
example: Rustic awkwardness.
etymology: Borrowed from Latin rūsticus. Doublet of roister.

definition: Someone who commits sabotage or deliberately causes wrecks.
Overly sweet.
etymology: From New Latin saccharum (“sugar”) + English -ine (suffix meaning ‘of or pertaining to’ forming adjectives).

definition: Make as a net profit.
A nerve plexus formed by the 4th and 5th lumbar and 1st, 2nd, 3rd sacral nerves; supplies the pelvic region and lower limbs.
One of 5 vertebrae in the human spine that fuse in the adult to form the sacrum.
Killing or injuring others while annihilating yourself; usually accomplished with a bomb.
Grossly irreverent toward what is held to be sacred.
example: It is sacrilegious to enter with shoes on.
etymology: Compare sacrilege, Latin sacrilegus. From Latin sacer + legō (“steal something sacred”).

definition: A room in a church where sacred vessels and vestments are kept or meetings are held.
etymology: From Anglo-Norman sacrestie, from Medieval Latin sacristia.

definition: Must be kept sacred.
etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin sacrōsānctus.

definition: Wedge-shaped bone consisting of five fused vertebrae forming the posterior part of the pelvis; its base connects with the lowest lumbar vertebra and its tip with the coccyx.
etymology: From Latin os sacrum (“holy bone”), a calque of Ancient Greek ἱερὸν ὀστέον (hieròn ostéon).

definition: A pass or ridge that slopes gently between two peaks (is shaped like a saddle).
etymology: From saddle + back.

definition: A double sloping roof with a ridge and gables at each end.
A maker and repairer and seller of equipment for horses.
etymology: From Middle English sadeler, sadelere, equivalent to saddle + -er. Cognate with Old Norse sǫðlari (“saddler”).

definition: Sexual pleasure obtained by inflicting harm (physical or psychological) on others.
etymology: From French sadisme and German Sadismus. Named after the Marquis de Sade, famed for his libertine writings depicting the pleasure of inflicting pain to others.

definition: Deriving pleasure or sexual gratification from inflicting pain on another.
etymology: From sadist + -ic.

definition: Sexual activity (especially sexual intercourse) with the use of measures (such as latex condoms) to avoid the transmission of disease (especially AIDS).
(American football) defensive players try to break through the offensive line.
Guard consisting of a locking device that prevents a weapon from being fired.
Guard consisting of a locking device that prevents a weapon from being fired.
Old World crocus having purple or white flowers with aromatic pungent orange stigmas used in flavoring food.
Small early-flowering buttercup with shiny yellow flowers of western North America.
Powdery starch from certain sago palms; used in Asia as a food thickener and textile stiffener.
etymology: From Malay sagu, via Portuguese sagu or Dutch sago.

definition: A showy tree fern of New Zealand and Australia having a crown of pinnated fronds with whitish undersides.
Any of various tropical Asian palm trees the trunks of which yield sago.
Saints collectively.
etymology: From saint + -hood.

definition: Characterized by lust.
example: Utterly salacious.
etymology: Derived from Latin salāx, salācis (“provocative, lustful”) + -ious, ultimately from saliō + -acious.

definition: Capable of being sold; fit for sale.
example: Saleable at a low price.
etymology: From sale + -able.

definition: A woman salesperson.
etymology: From sales + -woman.

definition: Loss of salt from the body without replacement (loss by vomiting or profuse perspiration or urination or diarrhea) thus upsetting the electrolyte balance.
A mine where salt is dug.
example: The fan forum was an absolute salt mine after the football team's loss to the last-place team in its division.

definition: The act of adding salt to food.
A cross resembling the letter x, with diagonal bars of equal length.
Tending to promote physical well-being; beneficial to health.
example: The salutary influence of pure air.
etymology: Borrowed from Middle French salutaire and its source, Latin salutaris (“healthful”), from salus (“health”).

definition: An act of honor or courteous recognition.
example: A musical salute to the composer on his birthday.
etymology: From Middle English salutacioun, from Old French salutacion, from Latin salutatio (“a greeting, a wishing health to”), from saluto (“wish one’s health, greet”), from salus (“well-being”).

definition: Capable of being saved from ruin.
example: Their marriage was not salvageable.
etymology: From salvage + -able.

definition: An outburst resembling the discharge of firearms or the release of bombs.
example: 1649, Charles I of England (attributed), Eikon Basilike They admit […] salvos, cautions, and reservations.
etymology: From Latin salvo, ablative of salvus, the past participle of salvāre (“to save, to reserve”), either from salvo jure (“the right being reserved”), or from salvo errore et omissone (“reserving error and omission”).

definition: The quality of being alike.
example: Sameness of purpose kept them together.
etymology: From same + -ness.

definition: (Hinduism and Buddhism) the endless cycle of birth and suffering and death and rebirth.
etymology: Borrowed from Sanskrit संसार (saṃsāra).

definition: Render holy by means of religious rites.
etymology: From Anglo-Norman seintefier, from Old French saintefier, from Late Latin sānctificō, from Latin sānctus (“holy”) + faciō (“do, make”). Form altered to conform with Latin.

definition: Low mat-forming herb of rocky places in United States.
Small nearly naked African mole rat of desert areas.
European maritime sedge naturalized along Atlantic coast of United States; rootstock has properties of sarsaparilla.
Small pallid fishes of shoal tropical waters of North America and South America having eyes on stalks atop head; they burrow in sand to await prey.
Any of various plants of the genus Abronia of western North America and Mexico having flowers resembling verbena.
Treat harshly or unfairly.
example: We sandbagged the basement windows against the floodwaters.
etymology: From sand + bag.

definition: A bar of sand.
etymology: From sand + bar.

definition: Widely distributed shallow-water shark with fins seemingly dipped in ink.
Any of numerous usually small wading birds having a slender bill and piping call; closely related to the plovers.
etymology: From sand + piper.

definition: Make sanitary by cleaning or sterilizing.
example: Remember to sanitize your query parameters to avoid SQL injection exploits.
etymology: From sanitary. By surface analysis, sanity + -ize.

definition: The frothy mixture of lube and fecal matter that is sometimes the byproduct of anal sex.
etymology: From the surname of former US Senator Rick Santorum (born 1958).

definition: Young tree.
etymology: From Middle English saplyng, seplyng, sapling, equivalent to sap + -ling.

definition: A military engineer who does sapping (digging trenches or undermining fortifications).
etymology: Borrowed from Middle French sappeur (French sapeur). By surface analysis, sap + -er.

definition: A chronic disease of unknown cause marked by the formation of nodules in the lungs and liver and lymph glands and salivary glands.
etymology: From sarcoid + -osis.

definition: A loose skirt consisting of brightly colored fabric wrapped around the body; worn by both women and men in the South Pacific.
etymology: Borrowed from Malay sarung.

definition: Of or relating to the sartorius muscle.
example: Suits are full of joy. They are the sartorial equivalent of a baby’s smile.
etymology: From New Latin sartorius (“pertaining to a tailor”), from Late Latin sartor (“tailor”), from Latin sarcire (“to patch, mend”) + -ial.

definition: A muscle in the thigh that helps to rotate the leg into the sitting position assumed by a tailor; the longest muscle in the human body.
etymology: From Latin sartor (“tailor, mender”) + -ius.

definition: A muscle in the thigh that helps to rotate the leg into the sitting position assumed by a tailor; the longest muscle in the human body.
Yellowwood tree with brittle wood and aromatic leaves and bark; source of sassafras oil; widely distributed in eastern North America.
etymology: From Spanish sasafrás, possibly from Latin saxifragus (“stone-breaking”) from the habit of certain plants growing in cracks in boulders. If this etymology is correct, it is a doublet of saxifrage.

definition: Pacific coast tree having aromatic foliage and small umbellate flowers followed by olivelike fruit; yields a hard tough wood.
Oil from root bark of sassafras trees; used in perfumery and as a disinfectant.
Yellowwood tree with brittle wood and aromatic leaves and bark; source of sassafras oil; widely distributed in eastern North America.
Fill to satisfaction.
example: Nothing seemed to satiate her desire for knowledge.
etymology: First attested in the 1440–1450s, in Middle English;

definition: Supplied (especially fed) to satisfaction.
Exposing human folly to ridicule.
example: A persistent campaign of mockery by the satirical fortnightly magazine.
etymology: From Middle French satirique, from Late Latin satiricus.

definition: A variety of mandarin orange, known commonly as cold hardy mandarin, Christmas orange, or tangerine.
etymology: After a Japanese place name in Kyūshū, 薩摩 (さつま, Satsuma), from where it was first exported to the west.

definition: A variety of mandarin orange, known commonly as cold hardy mandarin, Christmas orange, or tangerine.
Man with strong sexual desires.
etymology: From French satyre, from Latin satyrus, from Ancient Greek σάτυρος (sáturos).

definition: Orchid with broad ovate leaves and long-bracted green very irregular flowers.
An ancient Greek burlesque with a chorus of satyrs.
etymology: From satyr + play.

definition: Shredded cabbage fermented in brine.
etymology: Borrowed into English around 1600 from German Sauerkraut, from sauer (“sour, acidic, spoiled”) + Kraut (“herb; cabbage”). Doublet of choucroute.

definition: Fried quickly in a little fat.
Fried quickly in a little fat.
The ability to do or say what is appropriate for the occasion.
etymology: Borrowed from French savoir-faire (“know-how”), from savoir (“to know (how)”) + faire (“to do”).

definition: Taking a small amount into the mouth to test its quality.
example: Cooking was fine but it was the savoring that he enjoyed most.

definition: Fine particles of wood made by sawing wood.
etymology: From saw + dust.

definition: A serration on a saw blade.
etymology: From saw + tooth.

definition: Any of several beetles whose larvae bore holes in dead or dying trees especially conifers.
A farewell remark.
etymology: Borrowed from Japanese さようなら (sayōnara, “farewell”, literally “if that's the way it is”) or its shorter, less traditional form さよなら (sayonara).

definition: Someone who works (or provides workers) during a strike.
A sheath for a sword or dagger or bayonet.
A contagious skin infection caused by the itch mite; characterized by persistent itching and skin irritation.
etymology: From Middle English scabies, scabiez, from Latin scabiēs (“scurf; scab, mange, itch”), from scabō (“scratch, scrape”, verb).

definition: A platform from which criminals are executed (hanged or beheaded).
One who is playfully mischievous.
example: My nephew is a little scamp who likes to leave lighted firecrackers under the lawnchairs of his dozing elders.
etymology: From Middle Dutch schampen (“slip away”), from Old French escamper (“to run away, to make one's escape”), from Vulgar Latin *excampāre. Compare escape.

definition: Rushing about hastily in an undignified way.
etymology: First attested in 1687. Origin uncertain, but possibly from Dutch schamperen, from Old French escamper, from Vulgar Latin *excampāre.

definition: Lacking in magnitude or quantity.
example: A scanty harvest.
etymology: From scant + -y.

definition: Either of two flat triangular bones one on each side of the shoulder in human beings.
etymology: From Late Latin scapula (“shoulder”).

definition: An effigy in the shape of a man to frighten birds away from seeds.
etymology: The noun is derived from scare (“to frighten, startle, terrify”) + crow (“bird of the genus Corvus”).

definition: Masturbate while strangling oneself.
example: She scarfed her head.
etymology: Probably from Old Northern French escarpe (compare Old French escharpe (“pilgrim's purse suspended from the neck”), which see). The verb is derived from the noun. Doublet of scrip.

definition: In a terrifying manner.
etymology: From scary + -ly.

definition: Woody vine of Texas having showy solitary nodding scarlet flowers.
Tropical American bean with red flowers and mottled black beans similar to Phaseolus vulgaris but perennial; a preferred food bean in Great Britain.
etymology: In reference to its red flowers and climbing habit.

definition: Common nonpoisonous shrub of eastern North America with waxy compound leaves and green paniculate flowers followed by red berries.
A long steep slope or cliff at the edge of a plateau or ridge; usually formed by erosion.
etymology: Apheretic form of escarp. Doublet of escarp.

definition: Tropical American thorny shrub or small tree; fragrant yellow flowers used in making perfumery.
A planner who draws up a personal scheme of action.
etymology: From scheme + -er.

definition: Any metamorphic rock that can be split into thin layers.
etymology: From French schiste, from Latin schistos lapis (“the stone that is easy to split”), from Ancient Greek σχιστός (skhistós, “splittable”), from σχίζω (skhízō, “to split”).

definition: Of or relating to or characteristic of schizophrenia.
etymology: From schiz(ophrenia)- + -oid, from German, from Ancient Greek σχίζω (skhízō, “to split”) and εἶδος (eîdos, “form, likeness”).

definition: Old German breed of sturdy black or greyish wire-haired terriers having a blunt muzzle ranging in size from fairly small to very large; used as ratters and guard dogs or police dogs.
etymology: Borrowed from German Schnauzer.

definition: Deep-fried breaded veal cutlets.
etymology: Unadapted borrowing from German Schnitzel (“cutlet”).

definition: The educator who has executive authority for a school.
An acquaintance that you go to school with.
example: I've lost touch with all my old schoolmates: I only see them at class reunions.
etymology: From school + -mate.

definition: A room in a school where lessons take place.
etymology: From school + room.

definition: (Yiddish) a little; a piece.
etymology: Borrowed from Yiddish שטיק (shtik, “shtick, act, piece”).

A collection containing a variety of sorts of things.

definition: In a smug manner.

definition: Indicate contempt by breathing noisily and forcefully through the nose.
example: She snorted her disapproval of the proposed bridegroom.
etymology: From Middle English snorten, from earlier fnorten, from Old English *fnorettan, related to Middle English snoren, fnoren, from Old English fnora. See snore and sneeze for more on the change from fn- to sn-.

definition: A person regarded as arrogant and annoying.
Marked by casual disrespect.
A long projecting or anterior elongation of an animal's head; especially the nose.
example: The pig rooted around in the dirt with its snout.
etymology: From Middle English snowte, snout, snute, from Old English *snūt, *snūte or Middle Low German snûte, from Proto-West Germanic *snūt, from Proto-Germanic *snūtaz.

definition: A low perennial white-flowered trillium found in the southeastern United States.
Plant having heads of fragrant white trumpet-shaped flowers; grows in sandy arid regions.
example: It didn't take long to eat a packetful of snowballs — they are simply delicious.
etymology: From Middle English snoweball, snoweballe, snaweballe, snayballe, equivalent to snow + ball.

definition: A crystal of snow.

etymology: From snow + flake. Compare Saterland Frisian Sneeflokke (“snowflake”), Dutch sneeuwvlok, Luxembourgish Schnéiflack, German Schneeflocke.

Large large-footed North American hare; white in winter.
Small New World egret.

A crate for packing soap.

definition: A soft heavy compact variety of talc having a soapy feel; used to make hearths and tabletops and ornaments.
etymology: From soap + stone; so called because the archetypal varieties of the stone resemble soap in multiple ways: their feel, appearance, and carvability. First use appears c. 1681, in the writings of Nehemiah Grew.

definition: The relative tendency or disposition to be sociable or associate with one's fellows.
example: He was a true introvert, and his sociability lagged behind others of his age in the school.
etymology: From Middle French sociabilité, from Latin sociābilis.

definition: A communicable infection transmitted by sexual intercourse or genital contact.
Under group or government control.
example: Socialized ownership.

definition: A political theory advocating state ownership of industry.
etymology: Attested since 1832; either from French socialisme or from social + -ism.

definition: Advocating or following the socialist principles.
example: Socialistic government.
etymology: From socialist + -ic.

definition: Relating to both social and cultural matters.

definition: Fatty red flesh of salmon of Pacific coast and rivers.
Wet through and through; thoroughly wet.

etymology: From Middle English sodden, soden, from Old English soden, ġesoden, from Proto-Germanic *sudanaz, past participle of Proto-Germanic *seuþaną (“to seethe; boil”).

definition: Sexual activity between a person and an animal.
etymology: From Sodom, where the Bible, in Genesis chapters 18 and 19 and elsewhere, suggests sexual depravity.

definition: Of or relating to fish with soft fins.
A person who is weak and excessively sentimental.

etymology: From soft + -ie.

definition: Wood that is easy to saw (from conifers such as pine or fir).
example: SYP is a softwood, but it is harder than many hardwoods.

definition: The syllable naming the fifth (dominant) note of any musical scale in solmization.
The act of soiling something.
A party of people assembled in the evening (usually at a private house).

definition: A temporary resident.
etymology: From Middle English sogorner, sojorner, sugyner, equivalent to sojourn + -er.

definition: Skills that are required for the life of soldier.
Having a sole or soles especially as specified; used in combination.

definition: Leafless East Indian vine; its sour milky juice formerly used to make an intoxicating drink.
etymology: From New Latin, from Ancient Greek σῶμα (sôma, “body”).

definition: Any chromosome that is not a sex chromosome; appear in pairs in body cells but as single chromosomes in spermatozoa.
In some unspecified way or manner; or by some unspecified means.

definition: A waiter who manages wine service in a hotel or restaurant.

etymology: Borrowed from French sommelier (“originally, a person in charge of the beasts of burden carrying wine”), from somme (“pack”) + -ier (suffix forming the names of jobs).

definition: A male child (a familiar term of address to a boy).

definition: A device for making soundings.

definition: Impervious to, or not penetrable by, sound.

definition: Having the consistency and appearance of soup.

definition: Place (seeds) in or on the ground for future growth.

definition: Someone who seems unable to respond appropriately to reality (as if under the influence of some narcotic drug).

A male person trained to travel in a spacecraft.

Stupefied by (or as if by) some narcotic drug.

definition: Spaghetti served with a tomato sauce.

etymology: The noun is borrowed from Italian spaghetti, the plural of spaghetto (“strand of spaghetti”), from spago (“cord, string, twine; thread”) + -etto (diminutive suffix).

definition: Any of several breeds of small to medium-sized gun dogs with a long silky coat and long frilled ears.

definition: Remove the ovaries of.

etymology: From Middle English spayen, spaien, from the Anglo-Norman espeier, equivalent to the Old French espeer (“to cut with a sword”), from espee (“sword”), whence the Modern French épée.

definition: A telephone with a microphone and loudspeaker; can be used without picking up a handset; several people can participate in a call at the same time.

definition: Common garden herb having clusters of small purplish flowers and yielding an oil used as a flavoring.

Unique or specific to a person or thing or category.

etymology: From Middle English *special, especial, especiall, from Old French especial (whence also French spécial), from Latin speciālis (from speciēs). In this sense displaced native Old English synderlīċ. Doublet of especial.

definition: Become more focused on an area of activity or field of study.

etymology: From special + -ize.

definition: Coins collectively.
etymology: Originally in the phrase in specie; from Latin speciē, ablative singular of species. Compare in kind.

definition: An example regarded as typical of its class.

Plausible but false.

etymology: From spectro- + -graph.

definition: Someone who makes conjectures without knowing the facts.
etymology: From Latin speculātor (“spy, explorer, investigator”), from speculor (“to watch, to observe”) + -tor (“-er: forming agent nouns”), from specula (“watchtower”), from speciō (“to watch, to observe”), q.v.

definition: A mirror (especially one made of polished metal) for use in an optical instrument.
The intelligibility of speech (usually measured in the presence of noise or distortion).
A writer who composes speeches for others to deliver.
A driver who exceeds the safe speed limit.

definition: Attracting and holding interest as if by a spell.

definition: Any of various pale or ashy mosses of the genus Sphagnum whose decomposed remains form peat.

etymology: Borrowed from translingual Sphagnum, which is from Ancient Greek σφάγνος (sphágnos).

Marked by up-to-dateness in dress and manners.

etymology: From Middle English spigot (“wooden stopper”). Probably ultimately from Latin spīca via Old Occitan espiga and Middle French espigeot.

definition: Having or as if having especially high-pitched spots.
example: A spiky personality.
etymology: From spike (“kind of inflorescence in which sessile flowers are arranged on an unbranched elongated axis”) + -y (suffix forming adjectives with the sense “having the quality of”).

definition: The amount that has spilled.

Someone who spins (who twists fibers into threads).

Having spiny leaves.

Alleged form of communication with spirits of the dead.
Of or relating to or connected with spiritualism.

definition: A clear liquid secreted into the mouth by the salivary glands and mucous glands of the mouth; moistens the mouth and starts the digestion of starches.
etymology: Alteration of dialectal spattle (by association with spit (noun)), from Old English spātl, which is related to spǣtan (whence spit (verb)).

definition: Characterized by water flying about haphazardly.
example: His splashy car was supposed to show his wealth, but instead it showed his poor taste.
etymology: From splash + -y.

definition: Marijuana leaves rolled into a cigarette for smoking.
example: Smoke a spliff.
etymology: From Jamaican Creole, possibly a blend of split, referring to the ready-made wrap, + whiff, referring to the smell of the smoke.

definition: A flexible strip (wood or rubber) used in drawing curved lines.
etymology: Mid-1700s East Anglian dialect. Origin uncertain but perhaps from Old Danish splind or North Frisian splinj and ultimately related to the root of splinter.

(football) an offensive end who lines up at a distance from the other linemen.
example: I've got so many split ends – I think I must be working too hard.
etymology: From split + end.

definition: The amount that has spoiled.

A person (not necessarily a spouse) with whom you cohabit and share a long-term sexual relationship.

Paint applied with a spray gun.
A serial killer whose murders occur within a brief period of time.

Full of spirit and vitality.

definition: Reject with contempt.

definition: Expectorated matter; saliva mixed with discharges from the respiratory passages; in ancient and medieval physiology it was believed to cause sluggishness.
etymology: From New Latin, from Latin sputum (“that which is spit out, spittle”), from spuere (“to spit”).

definition: Any of several cytologic smears obtained from different parts of the lower respiratory tract; used for cytologic study of cancer and other diseases of the lungs.
A small refracting telescope.

definition: Spending resources lavishly and wastefully.
example: More wasteful than the squandering of time.

Small branching blueberry common in marshy areas of the eastern United States having greenish or yellowish unpalatable berries reputedly eaten by deer.
The noise of squawking.

definition: The loudspeaker on an intercom or public address system.
Any artifact that makes a squeaking sound when used.
