etymology: From Middle English swathe, swath, from Old English swaþu, swæþ (“bandage”), probably akin to Old English swaþul, sweþel (“a swathe, wrap, band, bandage”).

definition: Utter obscenities or profanities.
example: I swear I don't know what you're talking about.
etymology: From the above verb, or from Middle English sware, from Old English swaru, from Proto-Germanic *swarō.

definition: Profane or obscene expression usually of surprise or anger.
etymology: From Middle English swerynge; equivalent to swear + -ing.

definition: West Indian passionflower with edible apple-sized fruit.
European herb with soft ferny leaves and white flowers.
Mild vegetable oil when used as food; especially olive or edible rape oil.
A rate (usually rapid) at which something happens.
example: With remarkable swiftness.
etymology: From Middle English swiftnesse, swyftnesse, from Old English swiftnes (“swiftness”), equivalent to swift + -ness.

definition: Feed pigs.
etymology: From Middle English swilen (“to wash; swirl; wash away”), from Old English swillan, swilian (“to wash; wash down; swill;

definition: Drink large quantities of (liquid, especially alcoholic drink).
With no problems or difficulties.
example: Despite of some mishaps, everything went swimmingly.
etymology: From swimming (“(adj.) moving in water as an ordinary means of motion; without difficulty”) + -ly (suffix forming adverbs from adjectives).

definition: A person who swindles you by means of deception or fraud.
etymology: Borrowed from German Schwindler, 1774.

definition: Stout-bodied short-legged omnivorous animals.
example: The Zimmermann farm raises swine for their meat.
etymology: From Middle English swyn, swin; from Old English swīn; from Proto-West Germanic *swīn; from Proto-Germanic *swīną; from an adjectival form of Proto-Indo-European *suH- (“pig”).

definition: A pocketknife with a blade that springs open at the press of a button.
etymology: From switch + blade.

definition: A pocketknife with a blade that springs open at the press of a button.
Extremely muscled.
example: I ain't swole enough, brah. I gotta work out in the gym more.

definition: Weak and likely to lose consciousness.
example: A swooning fit.

definition: The noise produced by the sudden rush of a fluid (a gas or liquid).
etymology: From imitation of the sound.

definition: A cutting or thrusting weapon that has a long metal blade and a hilt with a hand guard.
Of or relating to syllables.
example: Syllabic accent.
etymology: From Medieval Latin syllabicus, from Ancient Greek συλλαβικός (sullabikós), from συλλαβή (sullabḗ, “syllable”).

definition: A writing system whose characters represent syllables.
Represent or identify by using a symbol; use symbols.
example: The poet symbolizes love in this poem.

definition: In a symmetrical manner.
example: They were symmetrically arranged.
etymology: From symmetrical + -ly.

definition: The relation that exists when things occur at the same time.
example: The drug produces an increased synchrony of the brain waves.

definition: The relation that exists when things occur at the same time.
example: The drug produces an increased synchrony of the brain waves.
etymology: From synchronise + -ation.

definition: The relation that exists when things occur at the same time.
example: The drug produces an increased synchrony of the brain waves.

definition: The relation that exists when things occur at the same time.
example: The drug produces an increased synchrony of the brain waves.
etymology: By surface analysis, syn- + chron- + -y; historically, see synchronous § Etymology.

definition: Stressing a normally weak beat.
A spontaneous loss of consciousness caused by insufficient blood to the brain.
etymology: Usage in the form syncope, with the phonological meaning "contraction of a word by omission of middle sounds or letters" attested from the 1520s.

definition: A radical political movement that advocates bringing industry and government under the control of labor unions.
etymology: From French syndicalisme.

definition: A sensation that normally occurs in one sense modality occurs when another modality is stimulated.
etymology: From syn- + -esthesia.

definition: The semantic relation that holds between two words that can (in a given context) express the same meaning.
example: Sink into synonymy.
etymology: From French synonymie and its etymon Late Latin synōnymia, from Ancient Greek συνωνυμία (sunōnumía), from συνώνυμος (sunṓnumos, “of like name”) + -ία (-ía, abstract noun suffix).

definition: Presenting a summary or general view of a whole.
example: A synoptic presentation of a physical theory.
etymology: From New Latin synopticus, from Ancient Greek συνοπτικός (sunoptikós, “seeing the whole together or at a glance”), from σύνοψις (súnopsis, “a general view, synopsis”), from συν- (sun-, “with”) + ὄψις (ópsis, “view”).

definition: Relating to or secreting synovia.
etymology: From synovia + -al, related to New Latin synoviālis.

definition: Viscid lubricating fluid secreted by the membrane lining joints and tendon sheaths etc.
A joint so articulated as to move freely.
A thin membrane in synovial (freely moving) joints that lines the joint capsule and secretes synovial fluid.
The late phase of cubism.
Synthetic narcotic drug similar to morphine but less habit-forming; used in narcotic detoxification and maintenance of heroin addiction.
Overly sweet.
etymology: From syrup + -y.

definition: An instruction that interrupts the program being executed and passes control to the supervisor.
example: The OS provides a system call to open a file, returning file descriptor that can be used to access it.

definition: A computer user's instruction (not part of a program) that calls for action by the computer's executive program.
A sock with a separation for the big toe; worn with thong sandals by the Japanese.
etymology: From Japanese 足袋 (tabi, “foot pouch”).

definition: Alleged form of communication with spirits of the dead.
Alleged form of communication with spirits of the dead.
Forbidden to profane use especially in South Pacific islands.
Of or pertaining to or arranged in table form.
example: Mesas got their name from being tabular.
etymology: From Late Latin tabulāris. By surface analysis, tabula + -ar, or, by surface analysis, table + -ar. Compare fabular.

definition: A set of data arranged in rows and columns.
Information set out in tabular form.
Information set out in tabular form.
example: Here is a tabulation of baseless claims made in the last month.
etymology: From tabulate + -ion.

definition: Habitually reserved and uncommunicative.
example: The two sisters could hardly have been more different, one so boisterous and expressive, the other so taciturn and calm.
etymology: Back-formation from taciturnity, from Middle English taciturnite, from Latin taciturnitās; or alternatively from French taciturne, likely reinforced by Latin taciturnus, from tacitus (“secret, tacit”).

definition: The person who plays offensive or defensive tackle on a football team.
example: The right tackle is a straight A student.
etymology: From Middle English takel (“gear, apparatus”), from Middle Dutch or Middle Low German takel (“ship's rigging”), perhaps related to Middle Dutch taken (“to grasp, seize”).

definition: A football player who tackles the ball carrier.
etymology: From tackle + -er.

definition: Showing tact or tactfulness; in a tactful manner.
example: He stepped tactfully in to prevent trouble.
etymology: From tactful + -ly.

definition: Lacking or showing a lack of what is fitting and considerate in dealing with others.
example: In the circumstances it was tactless to ask her age.
etymology: From tact + -less.

definition: A larval frog or toad.
example: Salamander tadpole.
etymology: From Middle English tadpolle, taddepol, equivalent to toad + poll (“head”).

definition: A kind of branchiopod crustacean.
A crisp smooth lustrous fabric.
etymology: From Late Middle English, from Old French taffetas, from Medieval Latin taffata, from Classical Persian تافته (tāfta), from تافتن (tāftan).

definition: A basic style of weave in which the weft and warp threads intertwine alternately to produce a checkerboard effect.
Chewy candy of sugar or syrup boiled until thick and pulled until glossy.
etymology: Probably related to tafia (“a type of rum”).

definition: A thick Middle Eastern paste made from ground sesame seeds.
etymology: From Arabic طَحِينَة (ṭaḥīna), from the root ط ح ن (ṭ-ḥ-n) related to grinding. Final -i most probably from North Levantine dialects or from Greek ταχίνι (tachíni).

definition: A Chinese system of slow meditative physical exercise designed for relaxation and balance and health.
(American football) the person who plays tailback.
etymology: From tail + back.

definition: Western North American frog with a taillike copulatory organ.
Western North American frog with a taillike copulatory organ.
Lamp (usually red) mounted at the rear of a motor vehicle.
etymology: From tail + light.

definition: A pipe carrying fumes from the muffler to the rear of a car.
example: This car doesn't have a tailpipe because it has sidepipes instead.
etymology: From tail + pipe.

definition: Loss of emotional control often resulting in emotional collapse.
example: The loss of the third engine threw the plane into a tailspin.
etymology: From tail + spin.

definition: Wind blowing in the same direction as the path of a ship or aircraft.
etymology: From tail + wind.

definition: Point or cause to go (blows, weapons, or objects such as photographic equipment) towards.
example: Take a swipe at one's opponent.

definition: The basic unit of money in Western Samoa.
etymology: Borrowed from Samoan tālā, in turn from English dollar.

definition: A fine grained mineral having a soft soapy feel and consisting of hydrated magnesium silicate; used in a variety of products including talcum powder.
etymology: From talc + -um, from Medieval Latin talcum, from Arabic طَلْق (ṭalq).

definition: A toilet powder made of purified talc and usually scented; absorbs excess moisture.
Devoid of talent; not gifted.
etymology: By surface analysis, talent + -less.

definition: Erect or decumbent Old World perennial with axillary clusters of rosy-purple flowers; introduced in United States.
Obtained from suet and used in making soap, candles and lubricants.
An animal oil obtained by pressing tallow; used as a lubricant.
A sloping mass of loose rocks at the base of a cliff.
etymology: Borrowed from French talus.

definition: Dough stuffed with a meat mixture and sometimes wrapped in corn husks and steamed.
etymology: Back-formation from the plural tamales, derived from Latin American Spanish tamales, plural of tamal, derived from Nahuatl tamalli (“wrapped”), derived from Proto-Uto-Aztecan *tïmaL-.

definition: A meat mixture covered with cornbread topping that resembles a Mexican dish.
An antagonist for estrogen that is used in the treatment of breast cancer.
etymology: From t(rans)- + am(ine) + oxy- + phen(yl).

definition: A tool for tamping (e.g., for tamping tobacco into a pipe bowl or a charge into a drill hole etc.).
etymology: Probably a back-formation from tampin (misinterpreted as tamping), a variant of tampion.

definition: Press down tightly.
example: Tamp the coffee grinds in the container to make espresso.

definition: 100 tanga equal 1 Tajikistani ruble.
etymology: From Portuguese tanga, from Kimbundu tanga or ntanga (“coarse cloth; loincloth”).

definition: Peripherally.
example: Touched on it tangentially.
etymology: From tangential + -ly.

definition: An armored vehicle equipped with an antitank gun and capable of high speeds.
Large drinking vessel with one handle.
Workplace where skins and hides are tanned.
etymology: From tan + -ery; compare Old French tannerie.

definition: Any of various complex phenolic substances of plant origin; used in tanning and in medicine.
etymology: From French tannin, from Latin tannum (“oak bark”), from Gaulish *tannos (“oak”). Related to tan. By surface analysis, tann- + -in.

definition: Arousing desire or expectation for something unattainable or mockingly out of reach.
example: A tantalizing taste of success.

definition: A hard grey lustrous metallic element that is highly resistant to corrosion; occurs in niobite and fergusonite and tantalite.
etymology: A New Latin word derived by Swedish chemist Anders Gustaf Ekeberg in 1802, from Latin Tantalus, named after Tantalus, alluding to the element's incapacity to absorb acid. See -ium.

definition: The prime minister of the Irish Republic.
etymology: See Taoiseach.

definition: Cassava with long tuberous edible roots and soft brittle stems; used especially to make cassiri (an intoxicating drink) and tapioca.
Large inoffensive chiefly nocturnal ungulate of tropical America and southeast Asia having a heavy body and fleshy snout.
etymology: Borrowed from French tapir, from Old Tupi tapi'ira.

definition: The quality or habit of not adhering to a correct or usual or expected time.
etymology: From tardy + -ness.

definition: An adjustment made for the weight of the packaging in order to determine the net weight of the goods.
example: But while men slept, his enemy came and sowed tares among the wheat, and went his way.
etymology: From Middle English tare (“vetch”), from Old English *taru, from Proto-West Germanic *taru.

definition: Any of a set of (usually 78) cards that include 22 cards representing virtues and vices and death and fortune etc.; used for playing card games and for divination by fortunetellers.
etymology: Borrowed from French tarot, from Italian tarocco. Compare tarok, German Tarock.

definition: Any of a set of (usually 78) cards that include 22 cards representing virtues and vices and death and fortune etc.; used for playing card games and for divination by fortunetellers.
Waterproofed canvas.
example: Throw a tarpaulin over that woodpile before it gets wet.
etymology: From tar + pall (“heavy canvas”) + -ing. The sailor sense reflects that sailors of centuries past often wore garments made of tarred cloth (for weatherproofing).

definition: Large silvery game fish of warm Atlantic coastal waters especially off Florida.
etymology: Compare Dutch tarpoen. Suggestions that the term derives from a Native American term are unlikely.

definition: Aromatic perennial of southeastern Russia.
etymology: Borrowed from Middle French targon (cf.

definition: Be about a place without any apparent purpose.
etymology: From Middle English terrie, equivalent to tar + -y.

definition: A woman who engages in sexual intercourse for money.
etymology: From Middle English tart, tarte, from Old French tarte, tartre (“flat pastry”) (compare Medieval Latin tarta), of unknown origin.

definition: Mayonnaise with chopped pickles and sometimes capers and shallots and parsley and hard-cooked egg; sauce for seafood especially fried fish.
etymology: From French sauce tartare.

definition: Someone who imposes hard or continuous work.
etymology: From task + master.

definition: Large beautiful Mediterranean species having sterile bluish-violet flowers with fringed corollas forming a tuft above the fertile flowers.
Tastelessness by virtue of being cheap and vulgar.
etymology: From Hindi टाट (ṭāṭ, “thick canvas”).

definition: Speak (about unimportant matters) rapidly and incessantly.
etymology: From Middle Dutch tatelen, tateren (“to babble, chatter”) (modern Dutch tatelen, tateren (“to talk, chatter”)), originally imitative.

definition: Abusing vocally; expressing contempt or ridicule.
example: Taunting shouts of ‘coward’ and ‘sissy’.
etymology: From taunt + -ing.

definition: Of or relating to or resembling a bull.
etymology: From Latin taurīnus, from taurus (“bull”).

definition: The 23rd letter of the Hebrew alphabet.
example: Walk around your corner; see-saw around your taw.
etymology: Unknown. Attested in English from the 18th century. Compare Old English tāw (“instrument”). Also compare Irish togh (“choose, elect”).

definition: Tastelessly showy.
example: Tawdry ornaments.
etymology: Shortened from tawdry lace; originally a corruption and rebracketing of Saint Audrey lace (from Old English Æðelþrȳð).

definition: A paved surface in the form of a strip; used by planes taxiing to or from the runway at an airport.
etymology: From taxi + way.

definition: A restaurant where tea and light meals are available.
etymology: From tea + house.

definition: Tear into shreds.
example: I finally persuaded the landlord to tear up the lease and move to a month-by-month rental.
etymology: See: tear (“to rip, shred”).

definition: With tears; in a tearful manner.
example: The man confessed tearfully to having beaten his wife.
etymology: From tearful + -ly.

definition: A gas that makes the eyes fill with tears but does not damage them; used in dispersing crowds.
A light midafternoon meal of tea and sandwiches or cakes.
etymology: From tea + time.

definition: (used informally) little or tiny.
example: There's only a teensy chance that I'll be able to make your party, as I'm up to my eyeballs in work.
etymology: Baby-talk alteration of teeny, from tiny, probably modelled after itsy, itsy-bitsy, etc.; see -sy.

definition: A Native American tent; usually of conical shape.
A plaything consisting of a board balanced on a fulcrum; the board is ridden up and down by children at either end.
etymology: Alteration of titter.

definition: The kind and number and arrangement of teeth (collectively) in a person or animal.
example: She gives straight teeth.

definition: A television broadcaster.
etymology: From telecast + -er.

definition: A conference of people who are in different locations that is made possible by the use of such telecommunications equipment as closed-circuit television.
example: The four of us should have a teleconference next week.
etymology: A contraction of telephone conference. By surface analysis, tele- + conference.

definition: Of or relating to or transmitted by telegraph.
example: A telegraphic machine.
etymology: From telegraph + -ic.

definition: A signal transmitted by telegraphy.
Communicating at a distance by electric transmission over wire.
etymology: From telegraph + -y (suffix forming abstract nouns), q.v., equivalent to tele- (“far, distant, telegraph”) + -graphy (“writings on a subject, area of study, etc.”).

definition: The power to move something by thinking about it without the application of physical force.
etymology: From tele- + -kinesis.

definition: The use of the telephone as an interactive medium for promotion and sales.
example: The newspaper started a telemarketing campaign to boost its subscriptions by calling non-subscribers.
etymology: Blend of telephone + marketing.

definition: Gunsight consisting of a telescope on a firearm for use as a sight.
Gunsight consisting of a telescope on a firearm for use as a sight.
A character printer connected to a telegraph that operates like a typewriter.
etymology: From genericization of Telex Printergram and Telex, derived as a blend of tele- (“telegraph, teletype, teleprinter, etc.”) + exchange.

definition: A character printer connected to a telegraph that operates like a typewriter.
One of the conveyances (or cars) in a telpherage.
Either (free) end of a eukaryotic chromosome.
example: Telomeres act as caps to keep the sticky ends of chromosomes from randomly clumping together.
etymology: From telo- (“end”) + -mere (“part”).

definition: Fearless daring.
etymology: From Middle English temerite, temeryte, from Old French temerité, from Latin temeritās (“chance, accident, rashness”), from temere (“by chance, casually, rashly”). By surface analysis, temer(arious) + -ity.

definition: Pigment mixed with water-soluble glutinous materials such as size and egg yolk.
etymology: Borrowed from Italian tempera.

definition: Characterized by violent emotions or behavior.
example: After their tempestuous argument, they did not speak to each other for weeks.

definition: With regard to temporal order.
example: Temporally processed.
etymology: From Middle English temperally, temperaly, temporally; equivalent to temporal + -ly.

definition: A woman who is considered to be dangerously seductive.
example: Marilyn Monroe, the iconic temptress of the 20th century.
etymology: From tempter + -ess.

definition: Vegetables and seafood dipped in batter and deep-fried.
etymology: Borrowed from Japanese 天(てん)麩(ぷ)羅(ら) (tenpura), from Portuguese, ultimately from Latin. Different dictionaries link two different original terms: * Portuguese tempero (“seasoning”) or tempera (“he/she/it seasons;

definition: Of a chemical compound having a ring with ten members.
Based on sound reasoning or evidence.
example: Back in the 1800s, many did not consider Darwin's theory of evolution to be tenable at all.
etymology: From the French tenable, from tenir (“to hold”); compare tenible.

definition: Inflammation of a tendon.
etymology: From New Latin tendin-, stem of Medieval Latin tendō, from Ancient Greek τένων (ténōn, “tendon, sinew”). By surface analysis, tendon + -itis and tendo- + -itis but not actually formed in this way;

definition: A clef that puts middle C on the fourth line of the staff; used for writing music for bassoons or cellos or tenor horns.

A cock ring is a ring that can be placed around a penis, usually at the base, primarily to slow the flow of blood from the erect penile tissue, thus maintaining an erection for a much longer period of time.
The solid part of the earth's surface.
example: It's nice to be back on terra firma after a long session of analyzing the philosopher's abstruse theories.
etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin terra firma (“solid land”).

definition: Any of various edible North American web-footed turtles living in fresh or brackish water.
A vivarium in which selected living plants are kept and observed.
etymology: From Latin terra (“earth”) + -arium, by analogy with aquarium.

definition: A radical who employs terror as a political weapon; usually organizes with other terrorists in small cells; often uses religion as a cover for terrorist activities.
etymology: From terror + -ist. In the historical sense, after French terroriste. First used in 1794 in the Courier and Evening Gazette.

definition: A political movement that uses terror as a weapon to achieve its goals.
A political movement that uses terror as a weapon to achieve its goals.
The four-dimensional analogue of a cube.
etymology: Word created by Charles Howard Hinton, in his book A New Era of Thought published in 1888, from Ancient Greek tessara- (“four-”) + Ancient Greek ἀκτίς (aktís, “ray”).

definition: A ban on the testing of nuclear weapons that is mutually agreed to by countries that possess nuclear weapons.
A branch of the aorta supplying the testicles.
A vein from the testicles.
One of the two male reproductive glands that produce spermatozoa and secrete androgens.
etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin testis.

definition: A potent androgenic hormone produced chiefly by the testes; responsible for the development of male secondary sex characteristics.
example: Mother encouraged James to rely more on intelligence and less on testosterone to deal with the neighbor's son.
etymology: From test(is) + -o- + -sterone (“steroid hormone”).

definition: Sterile solution of globulins derived from the blood plasma of a person who has been immunized for tetanus; provides short-term immunization against tetanus in cases of possible exposure to the tetanus bacillus.
An antibiotic (trade name Achromycin) derived from microorganisms of the genus Streptomyces and used broadly to treat infections.
etymology: From tetracyclic + -ine.

definition: Any polyhedron having four plane faces.
etymology: From Ancient Greek τετράεδρον (tetráedron, “triangle-based pyramid”), from τετράεδρος (tetráedros), from τετράς (tetrás, “four”) + ἕδρα (hédra, “seat”). By surface analysis, tetra- + -hedron.

definition: Large egg-shaped structures of grey matter that form the dorsal subdivision of the diencephalon.
etymology: Borrowed from Latin thalamus, from Ancient Greek θάλαμος (thálamos, “an inner chamber, a bedroom, a bed”).

definition: A sedative and hypnotic drug; withdrawn from sale after discovered to cause severe birth defects because it inhibits angiogenesis.
etymology: From (ph)thal(ic acid) + (im)ido + (i)mide. The chemical was synthesized and marketed in the 1950s.

definition: A soft grey malleable metallic element that resembles tin but discolors on exposure to air; it is highly toxic and is used in rodent and insect poisons; occurs in zinc blende and some iron ores.
etymology: Coined based on Ancient Greek θαλλός (thallós, “green branch”) (after the color of the radiation spectra), + -ium.

definition: Warm friendly feelings of gratitude.
etymology: From thankful + -ness.

definition: A person who shows no gratitude.
An instrument of torture that is used to heat or crush the foot and leg.
Intense sexual desire.
Obscene terms for diarrhea.
An artificial and mannered quality.
etymology: From theatrical + -ity.

definition: In a stagy and theatrical manner.
example: ‘I cannot show my face at her house,’ he declared theatrically.
etymology: From theatrical + -ly.

definition: Of or relating to or being a theocracy.
example: A theocratic state.
etymology: From theocrat + -ic or theo- + -cratic.

definition: Of or relating to theosophy.
example: Theosophical writings.
etymology: From theosophy + -ical.

definition: A system of belief based on mystical insight into the nature of God and the soul.
etymology: From Medieval Latin theosophia, from Ancient Greek θεοσοφῐ́ᾱ (theosophĭ́ā, “knowledge of things divine”, from θεός (theós, “god”) + σοφῐ́ᾱ (sophĭ́ā, “wisdom”)); By surface analysis, theo- + -sophy.

definition: A legally induced abortion for medical reasons (as when the mother's life is threatened).
For therapeutic purposes.
example: This drug cannot be used therapeutically except as a placebo.
etymology: From therapeutic + -ally.

definition: From that circumstance or source.
example: Public interest and a policy deriving therefrom.
etymology: From Middle English therfrom, þærfrom, þarvram (also as ther-fro, þer-fro, þarfra), equivalent to there + from.

definition: Involving or resulting from thermoelectricity.
etymology: From thermo- + electric.

definition: Using nuclear weapons based on fusion as distinguished from fission.
etymology: From thermo- + nuclear.

definition: A nuclear weapon that releases atomic energy by union of light (hydrogen) nuclei at high temperatures to form helium.
Of or relating to drama.
example: The movie director had thespian cooperation.
etymology: From Latin Thespis, from the name of the Ancient Greek actor Thespis (fl. 6th century BCE), from Θέσπις (Théspis) + -ian.

definition: A B vitamin that prevents beriberi; maintains appetite and growth.
etymology: From thio- + amine.

definition: A joke that seems extremely funny.
Relatively small dimension through an object as opposed to its length or width.
example: The thinness of a rope.
etymology: From Middle English thynnesse, from Old English þynnes (“thinness, slightness of density, lack of density, tenuity, fluidity, poverty, feebleness of sight, weakness”), equivalent to thin + -ness.

definition: Interrogation often accompanied by torture to extort information or a confession.
example: When I came home at 4 a.m., my dad really gave me the third degree.
etymology: Attested from 1900. The phrase, meaning "intense interrogation by police," likely refers to the Third Degree of Master Mason in Freemasonry, the ceremony for which included an interrogation.

definition: A collection of lymphatic tissue in the throat behind the uvula (on the posterior wall and roof of the nasopharynx).
The property of having three dimensions.
One who is third-rate or distinctly inferior.
Coming next after the twenty-ninth in position.
etymology: From earlier thirteth, from Middle English thrittithe, threttiþe, thrittyde, from Old English þrītigoþa; equivalent to thirty + -eth. For the modern form, see the etymological notes at twentieth.

definition: Erect annual of tropical central Asia and Africa having a pair of divergent spines at most leaf nodes.
Conscientiousness in performing all aspects of a task.
etymology: From thorough + -ness.

definition: Fish having greatly elongated front rays on dorsal and anal fins.
Repeated too often; overfamiliar through overuse.
example: Repeating threadbare jokes.
etymology: PIE word *bʰosós From Middle English thred-bar, thred-bare (“of cloth, clothing, etc.: worn to such an extent that the warp and weft threads show, shabby, worn-out;

definition: A base hit at which the batter stops safely at third base.
The property of having three dimensions.
Having or as if having three legs.
example: A three-legged stool.

definition: Of a chemical compound having a ring with three members.
A colorless crystalline amino acid found in protein; occurs in the hydrolysates of certain proteins; an essential component of human nutrition.
etymology: From threose.

definition: A farm machine for separating seeds or grain from the husks and straw.
etymology: From Middle English threschere; equivalent to thresh + -er. The shark's tail is thought to resemble the implement.

definition: Large pelagic shark of warm seas with a whiplike tail used to round up small fish on which to feed.
The separation of grain or seeds from the husks and straw.
example: They used to do the threshing by hand but now there are machines to do it.
etymology: From Middle English thresshyng; equivalent to thresh + -ing.

definition: A floor or ground area for threshing or treading out grain.
A farm machine for separating seeds or grain from the husks and straw.
Any of various small to minute sucking insects with narrow feathery wings if any; they feed on plant sap and many are destructive.
etymology: Borrowed from Ancient Greek θρίψ (thríps, “wood-worm”).

definition: Filled with great numbers crowded together.
example: I try to avoid the thronged streets and stores just before Christmas.

definition: (sometimes offensive) a homeless boy who has been abandoned and roams the streets.
etymology: Deverbal from throw away.

etymology: Borrowed from New Latin vāgīnālis, from vāgīna (“a covering, sheath; the vagina”) + -ālis (“-al”, adjectival suffix); equivalent to vagina + -al.

definition: A branch of the internal iliac that provides blood for the vagina and the base of the bladder and the rectum.
Discharge of secretions from the cervical glands of the vagina; normally clear or white.
Smear taken from the vaginal mucosa for cytological analysis.
A mixed nerve that supplies the pharynx and larynx and lungs and heart and esophagus and stomach and most of the abdominal viscera.
etymology: Borrowing from Latin vagus (“wandering, rambling, strolling”).

definition: A mixed nerve that supplies the pharynx and larynx and lungs and heart and esophagus and stomach and most of the abdominal viscera.
etymology: Partial calque of New Latin nervus vagus (literally “wandering nerve”).

definition: To no avail.
example: The city fathers tried vainly to find a solution.
etymology: Inherited from Middle English vaynly, veynly, vaynely, veynely, equivalent to vain + -ly.

definition: A decorative framework to conceal curtain fixtures at the top of a window casing.
etymology: From Middle English valance, valans, valaunce, valence, valons. Origin uncertain. Probably from Anglo-Norman valaunce, valence, from valer (“go down, let down”), aphetic form of Old French avaler (“to descend, go down”).

definition: A decorative framework to conceal curtain fixtures at the top of a window casing.
A girl who grew up in the tract housing in the San Fernando Valley.
etymology: From Valley, short for San Fernando Valley. Popularized by the Frank/Moon Zappa song Valley Girl (1982).

definition: (folklore) a corpse that rises at night to drink the blood of the living.
An antibiotic (trade name Vancocin) effective against some bacterial infections.
etymology: From vanquish + -o- + -mycin (“antibiotic produced by a Streptomyces strain”).

definition: Any of numerous showy orchids of the genus Vanda having many large flowers in loose racemes.
etymology: From the genus name.

definition: Any of numerous climbing plants of the genus Vanilla having fleshy leaves and clusters of large waxy highly fragrant white or green or topaz flowers.
etymology: Borrowed from Spanish vainilla, a diminutive form of vaina (“pod”). "Plain" senses derive from the perceived plainness of vanilla ice cream.

definition: Annihilation by vaporizing something.
etymology: From vapor + -ization.

definition: Kill with or as if with a burst of gunfire or electric current or as if by shooting.
example: In this computer game, space travellers are vaporized by aliens.
etymology: From vapor + -ize.

definition: With variation; in a variable manner or to a variable degree.

definition: A wine made principally from one grape and carrying the name of that grape.
etymology: From variety + -al.

definition: A wine made principally from one grape and carrying the name of that grape.

definition: Having a coating of stain or varnish.
A deformity in which part of a limb is turned inward to an abnormal degree.

definition: A form of hemophilia discovered by Erik von Willebrand; a genetic disorder that is inherited as an autosomal recessive trait; characterized by a deficiency of the coagulation factor and by mucosal bleeding.
Inflammation of a blood vessel.
etymology: From vasculo- + -itis.

definition: Meat from a calf.
etymology: From Middle English veel, from Anglo-Norman veel, from Latin vitellus, diminutive of vitulus (“calf”). Doublet of vitellus.

definition: Edible seeds or roots or stems or leaves or bulbs or tubers or nonsweet fruits of any of numerous herbaceous plant.
etymology: Related to vigil, vigour, vajra, and waker.

definition: A waxy fat obtained from certain plants (e.g. bayberry) and used as tallow.
Composed of vegetation or plants.
example: Regions rich in vegetal products.
etymology: Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin vegetālis, from Latin vegetō.

definition: Having or showing markings that resemble veins.
example: Veined cheese, veined marble.

definition: Of or relating to the velum.
etymology: Borrowed from Latin vēlāris, from vēlum (“sail; veil, awning”). By surface analysis, vel(um) + -ar.

definition: Elevated open grassland in southern Africa.
etymology: Borrowed from Afrikaans veld, or from its etymon Dutch veld (“field; open country”) (formerly spelled veldt), ultimately from Proto-Germanic *felþuz (“field, plain”), possibly from Proto-Indo-European *pleh₂- (“flat”).

definition: Small active carnivore that probably fed on protoceratops; possibly related more closely to birds than to other dinosaurs.
etymology: From taxonomic name Velociraptor genus name, from vēlōx (“swift”) + raptor (“thief”). The application to Deinonychus came about because Gregory S.

definition: Heavy fabric that resembles velvet.
etymology: Borrowed from French velours (“velvet”).

definition: Deciduous shrubby tree or eastern North America with compound leaves that turn brilliant red in fall and dense panicles of greenish yellow flowers followed by crimson acidic berries.
A blood vessel that carries blood from the capillaries toward the heart.
etymology: From Latin vēna. Doublet of vein.

definition: A vein that drains the back of the hand and forearm and empties into the axillary vein.
Either of two large veins that return oxygen-depleted blood to the right atrium of the heart.
etymology: Literally "hollow vein."

definition: The veins draining the cerebellum.
Veins that drain blood from structures around the knee; empty into the popliteal vein.
Capable of being corrupted.
example: A venal police officer.
etymology: From Latin vēna (“vein”) + -al.

definition: A feud in which members of the opposing parties murder each other.
example: The families had been locked in a bitter vendetta for generations.
etymology: Borrowed from Italian vendetta (“revenge”), from Latin vindicta. See vindicate, avenge.

definition: Regard with feelings of respect and reverence; consider hallowed or exalted or be in awe of.
example: We venerate genius.
etymology: First attested in 1623; borrowed from Latin venerātus, perfect active participle of veneror (“to worship, venerate”), see -ate (verb-forming suffix).

definition: Of or relating to the external sex organs.
example: Venereal disease.

definition: A communicable infection transmitted by sexual intercourse or genital contact.
A communicable infection transmitted by sexual intercourse or genital contact.
A small benign wart on or around the genitals and anus.
Expose to cool or cold air so as to cool or freshen.
etymology: From Middle English, borrowed from Latin ventilātus, past participle of ventilō.

definition: A mechanical system in a building that provides fresh air.
example: She was continually adjusting the ventilation.

definition: A performer who projects the voice into a wooden dummy.
etymology: From ventriloquy + -ist.

definition: Any of numerous tropical or subtropical American plants of the genus Verbena grown for their showy spikes of variously colored flowers.
example: Linda pulled a piece of verbena and crumpled it, and held her hands to her mother. -.
etymology: Borrowed from translingual Verbena, from Latin verbēna (“leaves or twigs of olive, myrtle, laurel, or other sacred plants employed in religious ceremonies”), from Proto-Indo-European *werbʰ-.

definition: Overabundance of words.
example: Bureaucratic verbiage.
etymology: From French verbiage. Compare verb meaning "word" in verbal and verbose.

definition: Using or containing too many words.
example: Verbose and ineffective instructional methods.
etymology: From Latin verbōsus (“prolix, wordy, verbose”).

definition: March 21.
Unrhymed verse without a consistent metrical pattern.
A small anatomically normal sac or bladderlike structure (especially one containing fluid).
etymology: From Middle French vesicule, from Latin vēsīcula. By surface analysis, vesic- + -le. Doublet of vesicule.

definition: A late afternoon or evening worship service.
example: Almost all vespers are insect catchers.
etymology: From Old French vespre, from Latin vesper (“evening star”).

definition: American woodland mouse with white feet and underparts.
Common North American finch noted for its evening song.
The sixth of the seven canonical hours of the divine office; early evening; now often made a public service on Sundays.
etymology: From Middle English vespers, from Old French vespres (French vêpres), from Ecclesiastical Latin vesperae (“vespers”), substantivisation of relational Late Latin vesperus (“evening”), from vesper (“evening”) + -us.

definition: Of or relating to Vesta.
example: Vestal virgin.
etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin Vestālis.

definition: (Roman mythology) one of the virgin priestesses consecrated to the Roman goddess Vesta and to maintaining the sacred fire in her temple.
etymology: From Latin; virgines Vestales referred to the priestesses in charge of the sacred fire in the temple of Vesta in Rome.

definition: A gland that opens into the vestibule of the vagina; secretions lubricate the vagina during coitus.
Not fully developed in mature animals.
etymology: From Latin vestīgium + -al. By surface analysis, vestige + -ial.

definition: Causing irritation or annoyance.
example: A vexatious child.
etymology: a 1650 vexation + -ous

definition: Litigation shown to have been instituted maliciously and without probable cause.
example: He got an injunction against vexatious litigation by his enemies.

definition: Moving very rapidly to and fro or up and down.
example: The vibrating piano strings.

definition: A pile hammer that uses vibrations.
An executive officer ranking immediately below a president; may serve in the president's place under certain circumstances.
etymology: From vice- + president.

definition: A police group to enforce laws against gambling and prostitution.
The trait of extreme cruelty.

An act that is legally a crime but that seem to have no victims.
example: He considers prostitution to be a victimless crime.

definition: The process of capturing and converting and storing video images for use by a computer.
The actions of a vigilance committee in trying to enforce the laws.
etymology: From vigilante + -ism.

definition: Slanderous defamation.
Spread negative information about.
example: The Nazi propaganda vilified the Jews.
etymology: From Late Latin vīlificāre (“vilify”). Equivalent to vile + -ify. Compare vilipend.

definition: Desert shrub of southwestern United States and Mexico having slender naked spiny branches that after the rainy season put forth foliage and clusters of red flowers.
Any of a family of bowed stringed instruments that preceded the violin family.
example: Near-synonym: viola d'amore.
etymology: Borrowed from Middle French viole, from Old French viol, from Old Occitan viola (modern Occitan viula), from Medieval Latin vitula (“stringed instrument”). Doublet of viola.

definition: A clef that puts middle C on the third line of a staff.
etymology: Derived from its usage primarily in viola music.

definition: Someone who violates the law.
etymology: From Middle English violator, from Latin violātor. By surface analysis, violate + -or.

definition: An event that causes someone to die.
Characteristic of a virgin or virginity.
example: Virginal white dresses.
etymology: From Middle English virginal, from Middle French virginal, from Latin virginālis. The musical instrument is probably so called from being played by young girls.

definition: A fold of tissue that partly covers the entrance to the vagina of a virgin.
etymology: So called because the membrane is usually damaged by sexual intercourse.

definition: The masculine property of being capable of copulation and procreation.
etymology: From virile + -ity, from Middle French virilité, from Latin virīlitās.

definition: Drug to treat impotence attributable to erectile dysfunction.
Internal organs collectively (especially those in the abdominal cavity).

etymology: Borrowed from Latin viscera (“internal organs; bowels”).

definition: A cellulose ester obtained by treating cellulose with caustic soda.
etymology: From Latin viscōsus, from viscum (“birdlime”); by surface analysis, visco- + -ose. Doublet of viscous.

definition: The cultivation of grapes and grape vines; grape growing.
example: The old French farmer practiced viticulture and raised some of the best grapes in the world. He is knowledgeable in viticulture.
etymology: From viti- + culture, from Latin vītis + cultūra (“cultivation of the vine, vine-growing”). Compare agriculture.

definition: An acquired skin disease characterized by patches of unpigmented skin (often surrounded by a heavily pigmented border).
etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin vitilīgō.

definition: Of or relating to or constituting the vitreous humor of the eye.

definition: The clear colorless transparent jelly that fills the posterior chamber of the eyeball.
The clear colorless transparent jelly that fills the posterior chamber of the eyeball.
The clear colorless transparent jelly that fills the posterior chamber of the eyeball.
Colorless glass made of almost pure silica.
An examination conducted by spoken communication.

definition: Expressed orally.
example: A viva-voce report.

definition: Characterized by high spirits and animation.
etymology: From Latin vīvācitās (whence -acity).

definition: The act of operating on living animals (especially in scientific research).
etymology: From Latin vīvus (“alive”) + sectiō (“cutting”). Compare French vivisection. See also vivid and section.

definition: A video blogger.

definition: The sound made by the vibration of vocal folds modified by the resonance of the vocal tract.

definition: Conspicuously and offensively loud; given to vehement outcry.

etymology: From Latin vōcifer + -ous.

example: He complained vociferously.

definition: A major change in attitude or principle or point of view.
example: Shakespeare often used volte-faces in the rhyming couplets at the end of his sonnets.
etymology: Borrowed from French volte-face.

definition: Having strong sexual appeal.

etymology: From Middle French voluptueux, from Latin voluptuōsus (“delightful”), from voluptās (“pleasure, delight”), from volup (“with pleasure”).

definition: A charm superstitiously believed to embody magical powers.
example: I want a real explanation, not this statistical voodoo.
etymology: From Louisiana Creole voudou, from Haitian Creole Vodou, from a West African language, such as Ewe vódũ (“deity, idol”), Fon vòdún (“fetish”) or the Kwa languages vodũ.

definition: A viewer who enjoys seeing the sex acts or sex organs of others.
etymology: Borrowed from French voyeur, from voir (“to see”).

definition: A perversion in which a person receives sexual gratification from seeing the genitalia of others or witnessing others' sexual behavior.
etymology: From voyeur + -ism.

definition: Any of various large diurnal birds of prey having naked heads and weak claws and feeding chiefly on carrion.
example: Within ten minutes of the accident, the vultures appeared and were organizing lawsuits.
etymology: Borrowed into Middle English from Anglo-Norman vultur, from Old French voutoir, voutre, from Latin vultur, voltur. Displaced native Old English ūf.

definition: External parts of the female genitalia.
etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin vulva, earlier volva (“womb, female sexual organ”), probably from volvō (“to turn, wrap around”).

definition: A small mass of soft material.
example: He used a wad of cotton to wipe the counter.
etymology: Probably short for Middle English wadmal (“woolen cloth”), from Old Norse váðmál (“woolen stuff”), from váð (“cloth”) + mál (“measure”). See wadmal.

definition: Waterproof hip boots (sometimes extending to the chest) worn by anglers.
A large number or amount.
Be driven or carried along, as by the air.

definition: The driver of a wagon.
etymology: From waggon + -er.

definition: Any of various kinds of wheeled vehicles drawn by an animal or a tractor.
etymology: Borrowed from Middle Dutch wagen, from Old Dutch *wagan, from Proto-West Germanic *wagn, from Proto-Germanic *wagnaz (“wagon”), from Proto-Indo-European *weǵʰ- (“to transport”).

definition: The driver of a wagon.
etymology: From wagon + -er.

definition: A homeless child especially one forsaken or orphaned.

definition: Large open farm wagon.

definition: A periodic state during which you are conscious and aware of the world.
example: Consciousness during wakefulness in a sane person is pretty well ordered and familiar.
etymology: From wakeful + -ness.

definition: Cause to become awake or conscious.
etymology: From Middle English waknen, from Old English wæcnan, from Proto-Germanic *waknaną.

definition: In a wanton manner.

definition: An extraordinary power exercised (usually by the executive branch) in the prosecution of a war and involving an extension of the powers that the government normally has in peacetime.
A person who works in a prison and is in charge of prisoners.
etymology: From Middle English warder, wardere, perhaps in part continuing Old English weardere (“one who holds a country;

definition: In a wary manner.
example: The sailor watched the sky warily.
etymology: From wary + -ly.

definition: A policy of advocating war.
Hostile or belligerent mood.
example: The chief is on the warpath today.
etymology: From war + path.

definition: Any small rounded protuberance (as on certain plants or animals).
example: A wart has appeared on my toe.
etymology: From Middle English warte, werte, from Old English wearte, from Proto-West Germanic *wartā, from Proto-Germanic *wartǭ. Cognate with Dutch wrat, German Warze, Hunsrik Waarz, Swedish vårta and Danish vorte.

definition: African wild swine with warty protuberances on the face and large protruding tusks.
etymology: From wart + hog.

definition: Device consisting of a corrugated surface to scrub clothes on.
example: Washboard road.
etymology: From wash + board.

definition: Bath linen consisting of a piece of cloth used to wash the face and body.
etymology: From wash + cloth.

definition: A machine mainly used for the compaction of waste, cardboard, plastic and other recyclable materials.
Someone who dissipates resources self-indulgently.
etymology: From Middle English wastere, waister, wastar, wastour, equivalent to waste + -er. Compare Anglo-Norman wastur, Old French gastëor.

definition: Plant of wetlands and bogs of temperate regions having small greenish flowers partly enclosed in a white spathe and red berries.

Venomous semiaquatic snake of swamps in southern United States.
Stout white-flowered perennial found wild in shallow fresh water; northern United States and Asia.
Any substance that tends to increase the flow of urine, which causes the body to get rid of excess water.
Torture where water is poured over the face of a captive simulating drowning.

definition: Transported by water.

definition: The 6th letter of the Hebrew alphabet.

definition: Any of various plants of the genus Malvaviscus having brilliant bell-shaped drooping flowers like incompletely opened hibiscus flowers.
A pedestrian who walks from place to place.
etymology: From Middle English weyfarere, weifarere; equivalent to way + farer.

definition: Lacking will power or resolution.
example: The role of the dissenter is not for the weak-kneed.

definition: A person who is physically weak and ineffectual.
etymology: From weak + -ling.

definition: An area of open or forested country.
Any instrument or instrumentality used in fighting or hunting.
example: He was licensed to carry a weapon.
etymology: From Middle English wepen, from Old English wǣpn, from Proto-West Germanic *wāpn, from Proto-Germanic *wēpną (“weapon”), of unknown origin, possibly from Proto-Indo-European *wēbnom.

definition: Weapons considered collectively.
example: The army has a wide array of weaponry.
etymology: From weapon + -ry.

definition: An emplacement for a gun.
Any military structure or vehicle bearing weapons.
Plutonium 239 that is recovered when nuclear weapons are disassembled; it is stored in plutonium pits.
Weapons considered collectively.
Of a quality adequate for use in weapons (especially in weapons of mass destruction).
example: Weapons-grade plutonium.

definition: In a weary manner.
etymology: From Middle English werily, werelye, equivalent to weary + -ly.

definition: A person who is regarded as treacherous or sneaky.
etymology: The verb is from c. 1900, from the supposed cunningness of the weasel.

definition: Someone who predicts the weather.
Having open interstices or resembling a web.
etymology: From web + -y.

definition: A technician who designs or maintains a website.
etymology: From Web + master.

definition: A shoe with a wedge heel.
etymology: From wedge + -ie.

definition: Eliminate urine.
etymology: Reduplication of wee; onomatopoeic for the sound of urination.

definition: Abounding with or resembling weeds.
example: A weedy path.
etymology: From weed + -y.

definition: Someone who vacations on a weekend.
example: We have a nice little weekender up in the mountains.
etymology: From weekend + -er.

definition: Lasting through a week.
example: Her weeklong vacation.
etymology: From week + -long.

definition: A smooth-textured sausage of minced beef or pork usually smoked; often served on a bread roll.
Liable to weep easily.
etymology: From weep + -y.

definition: Any of several families of mostly small beetles that feed on plants and plant products; especially snout beetles and seed beetles.
The yarn woven across the warp yarn in weaving.
etymology: From Middle English wefte, from Old English wefan (“to weave”), from Proto-West Germanic *weban, from Proto-Germanic *webaną. Equivalent to weave + -t (abstract nominal suffix).

definition: The property of being comparatively small in weight.
etymology: From weightless + -ness.

definition: An athlete who lifts barbells.
etymology: From weight + lifter.

definition: The source of water for a well.
etymology: From Middle English wellespring, from Old English wiellspring, wiellġespring (“spring, fount, fountain”), corresponding to well + spring. More at well, spring.

definition: Toss, roll, or rise and fall in an uncontrolled way.
example: The shipwrecked survivors weltered in the sea for hours.
etymology: From Middle English welteren, equivalent to welt + -er (frequentative suffix). Cognates include German Low German weltern (“to wallow; roll”), Old Norse velta (Danish vælte), German wälzen, Gothic 𐍅𐌰𐌻𐍄𐌾𐌰𐌽 (waltjan).

definition: Wind that blows from west to east.
etymology: From west + -er.

definition: Valuable forage grass of western United States.
Farthest to the west.
example: Zeeland is the westernmost province of the Netherlands.
etymology: From western + -most.

definition: Timber tree of New Zealand having shiny white wood.
An erotic dream (usually at night) accompanied by the (nocturnal) emission of semen.
example: His mother is having an affair with the man next door, is reading Germain Greer's The Female Eunuch—which spawns Adrian's first wet dream.

definition: A seaman who works on a ship that hunts whales.
etymology: From whale + -er. In sense 1, displaced Old English hwælhunta (literally “whale hunter”).

definition: A gun (or device resembling a gun) for discharging a projectile (especially a harpoon) at a whale.
A grass of the genus Agropyron.
etymology: From wheat + grass.

definition: Someone who makes and repairs wooden wheels.
etymology: From Middle English whelwryghte; equivalent to wheel + wright.

definition: Breathing with a husky or whistling sound.
example: The new comedy is a wheeze.
etymology: From Middle English whesen, perhaps from Old Norse hvæsa (“to hiss”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *ḱwes- (“to pant”).

definition: Young of any of various canines such as a dog or wolf.
etymology: From Middle English whelpen, from Old English hwelpian, derived from hwelp.

definition: A flat stone for sharpening edged tools or knives.
etymology: From Middle English whetston, wheston, from Old English hwetstān, from Proto-West Germanic *hwattjastain (“whetstone”). Equivalent to whet (“to sharpen”) + stone.

definition: Small slender dog of greyhound type developed in England.
etymology: Probably from whip (“to move quickly”) + -et.

definition: Like the sound of rapidly vibrating wings.
The organized dissemination of derogatory rumors designed to discredit a candidate.
A card game for four players who form two partnerships; a pack of 52 cards is dealt and each side scores one point for each trick it takes in excess of six.
etymology: Alteration of whisk, perhaps so called from the notion of “whisking” up cards after each trick. Altered perhaps on assumption that the word was an interjection invoking silence, by influence of whist (“silent”).

definition: A progressive whist party.
Large North American mountain marmot.
A white powdered poisonous trioxide of arsenic; used in manufacturing glass and as a pesticide (rat poison) and weed killer.
Backlash by white racists against black civil rights advances.
A variant of sour rye soup made with wheat flour instead of soured rye flour.
White-flowered vine having thick roots and bearing small black berries; Europe to Iran.
Bluish-green herb having sticky stems and clusters of large evening-opening white flowers with much-inflated calyx; sometimes placed in genus Lychnis.
A crappie that is white.
A widely distributed feldspar that forms rocks.
A wave that is blown by the wind so its crest is broken and appears white.
Small New Zealand tree having red pulpy one-seeded fruit.
European perennial plant naturalized in United States having triangular ovate leaves and lilac-pink flowers.
Meat carved from the breast of a fowl.

definition: Tall herb with leafless white waxy stems and whitish starlike flowers; southwestern United States.
A woman sold into prostitution.
A person who forces women to become prostitutes.
etymology: From white slave + -er.

definition: Shrub or small tree of southeastern United States to West Indies and Brazil; grown for the slender racemes of white flowers and orange and crimson foliage.
(slang) an offensive term for White people who are impoverished.
Turn white.

etymology: From Middle English whitenen, whitnen, from Old Norse hvítna (“to whiten”), from Proto-Germanic *hwītnōną (“to whiten, become white”), from Proto-Indo-European *kwind-, *kwint- (“bright”), equivalent to white + -en.

definition: Cover up with a liquid correction fluid.
example: White-out the typo.
etymology: Deverbal from white out.

definition: A defeat in which the losing person or team fails to score.
etymology: The noun is derived from white (adjective) + wash (noun). Noun sense 5.1 (“medicinal preparation for treating skin diseases”) is a calque of New Latin lōtiō alba (literally “white wash”).

definition: Someone who is dazzlingly skilled in any field.
example: He's a whiz with the computers.
